Thousands march in Spain over eviction of 87-year-old woman Maricarmen Abascal
Images of her being carried from her lifelong home after police broke down her door have put a spotlight on the country’s housing crisis
Thousands of people marched through Madrid on Saturday to protest the eviction earlier this week of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong home, calling for greater protection for tenants.
Images of Maricarmen Abascal being carried from her Madrid flat on a stretcher on Wednesday after police broke down her door have thrust Spain’s housing crisis back into the spotlight ahead of a general election due in 2027.
Protesters rattled keys, blew whistles, chanted slogans and held banners calling for measures to curb rising housing costs and make evictions more difficult as they marched through central Madrid.
“You could be the next Maricarmen,” read one banner.

Pope Leo arrives in Lourdes for Second Leg of France visit after historic Paris crowds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
20:15:56 UTC
05:15:56 KST

Leo opened his pilgrimage in Lourdes with a prayer at the Grotto of the Apparitions, the site where Catholics believe the Virgin Mary appeared to Bernadette Soubirous in 1858 and one of the faith's most-visited shrines.
Pope Leo XIV arrived in Lourdes on Saturday evening, landing at Tarbes-Lourdes-Pyrénées International Airport to begin the next stage of his four-day France visit, hours after drawing hundreds of thousands of worshippers to an outdoor Mass at Paris' Place de la Concorde.
Leo opened his pilgrimage in Lourdes with a prayer at the Grotto of the Apparitions, the site where Catholics believe the Virgin Mary appeared to Bernadette Soubirous in 1858 and one of the faith's most-visited shrines.
On Sunday, the pope will meet with French bishops before celebrating an outdoor Mass in the sanctuary's Prairie, followed by the Angelus prayer. In the afternoon, he is due to meet staff and sick people at the Accueil Notre-Dame and hold a private meeting with contemplative religious sisters.
Leo will also meet privately with seven survivors of sexual abuse by priests and other Catholic personnel — a moment likely to be closely watched by critics who argue the church has not done enough to address the issue. Some survivors' groups have criticised the Vatican's choice to meet with individuals rather than representatives of established advocacy organisations. The visit to Lourdes will close Sunday evening with one of the sanctuary's signature rites, a Rosary recitation and torchlight procession.
A record-breaking mass in Paris
Leo's arrival in Lourdes capped a whirlwind of roughly 32 hours in the French capital, where he paraded through central Paris in his popemobile, addressed UNESCO's headquarters, and celebrated an open-air Mass that drew far more people than organisers had anticipated.
Around 600,000 people had registered in advance for Saturday's Mass at Place de la Concorde, but the Vatican estimated actual turnout at roughly 800,000 — about 200,000 more than expected. Some 2,400 priests and deacons and about 100 bishops took part in the service.
As the pope travelled down the Champs-Élysées toward the Concorde, crowds lined a security perimeter stretching nearly two miles from the square past the Arc de Triomphe. Metro stations along the route were closed as part of the security operation, and chants of "Leo! Leo!" rang out as he passed. Parents lifted babies and young children toward the popemobile throughout the ride, and the pope reached out to touch dozens of them.
In his homily, Leo urged the faithful not to keep their beliefs private but to let their faith be visible enough to bring comfort to others.
French President Emmanuel Macron did not attend Saturday's Mass and is not expected to attend any of the pope's Masses during the visit. His wife, Brigitte Macron, was present, alongside Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.
A test of faith in a secularising country
The visit has doubled as a message to French Catholics to hold onto their faith even as church attendance declines nationally. Leo began the trip on Friday with a visit to the newly restored Notre-Dame Cathedral, the first papal visit there since the fire that devastated the building in 2019.
Speaking earlier Saturday at the Catholic Institute of Paris, the pope said he had been struck by the growing number of adults converting to Catholicism in France, describing it as a small but resilient flame worth protecting. Adult baptisms in the country have nearly tripled since 2016, reaching about 13,000 this year — though the increase, also seen recently in Spain, hasn't reversed the broader decline. France recorded 513,000 baptisms in 1980, compared with 186,000 in 2024.
Observers noted that Saturday's crowds and their enthusiasm echoed other moments of mass celebration on the Champs-Élysées in recent decades, including France's World Cup victories in 1998 and 2018.
Many of those who turned out, organisers said, were not just practising Catholics but those who came simply to witness the event.

In the southwestern pilgrimage town the US pontiff prayed at the Grotto of Massabielle, where Catholic tradition holds that the Virgin Mary appeared in 1858 to a peasant girl, later Saint Bernadette.

The first US pontiff was visiting France seven months before voters choose a successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron.

Negative feelings about life are more common among teens on Instagram and TikTok
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
20:00:24 UTC
05:00:24 KST

A recent survey of teenagers suggests that a large portion of young people encounter negative experiences on the internet, and the types of harm they face tend to vary depending on which apps they use. The research indicates that while some issues like bullying occur at similar rates in person and online, teenagers are much more likely to be exposed to violent imagery or unwanted sexual content through digital platforms. The findings were published in JAMA Pediatrics.
The term “online harms” refers to a wide range of negative experiences on digital platforms, such as cyberbullying, unwanted sexual advances, or exposure to content that encourages self-injury. Prior studies have demonstrated that digital platforms host a variety of risks for adolescents.
For example, a 2022 survey study found that different types of online sexual abuse, such as nonconsensual sexting or grooming by adults, occur at varying rates among youth. Additionally, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 indicated that nearly half of adolescents who send sexually explicit images experience nonconsensual sharing or extortion.
Most existing research tends to examine one specific type of negative experience at a time, such as harassment, rather than capturing the full spectrum of issues adolescents face. When studies do measure these risks, they rarely break the numbers down by specific platforms to see how experiences might differ on an app like TikTok compared to an app like YouTube. To explore this, research covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that short-form video apps are associated with more severe body image concerns, suggesting that specific app designs might play a role in user well-being.
The research, led by Angela Y. Lee, an assistant professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s School of Journalism and Mass Communication who was a postdoctoral fellow at Stanford Medicine’s Center for Digital Health when the study was conducted, aimed to estimate how often adolescents report various negative experiences both online and offline. “This study was the product of a great collaboration of researchers from Stanford, USC, NYU, and UW-Madison, working across psychology, communication, medicine, technology policy, and consumer science,” Lee told PsyPost.
“There are widespread concerns about youth online safety and recent steps, like social media bans and age-gating policies, have been recently implemented around the world,” Lee noted. “At the same time, there are ongoing debates about how people interpret the research on social media’s effects on youth psychological well-being, and what kinds of interventions should be implemented.”
By tracking how these experiences differ across twenty popular communication platforms, the researchers hoped to demonstrate a method for gathering platform-specific data that could inform targeted prevention efforts.
“This study was motivated by something that I feel is a common goal across researchers across the aisle and policymakers, which is a need for clear, consistent, and granular measurement of youth’s online experiences,” Lee explained. “Our team’s hope is that knowing how often teens report having negative experiences on specific platforms can help add specificity to conversations about social media and well-being effects, and inform efforts to track if interventions that are implemented are meaningfully reducing reported harms.”
To conduct the study, the researchers used a nationally representative, probability-based sample of 472 adolescents in the United States between the ages of 13 and 17. The survey was administered between February and December 2025. Participants answered questions about their use of 20 online communication platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube, over the previous four weeks.
The survey asked the teenagers to report whether they had encountered specific negative experiences either offline or across the various platforms they used. These experiences included direct harassment, witnessing harassment, receiving unwanted sexual images, encountering violent content, seeing content that encouraged self-harm, and experiencing sleep disruption due to technology use. The research team then applied statistical weights to the data to ensure the results accurately reflected the broader population of adolescents in the United States.
The results indicated that exposure to negative experiences is common among teenagers. Across both online and offline contexts, 44.7% of the adolescents had witnessed someone else being harassed, and 29.8% reported experiencing direct harassment themselves within the four-week window. Interestingly, direct harassment was reported at similar rates offline (18.5%) and online (16.4%), suggesting that this type of conflict happens across all areas of a teenager’s life.
For other types of harm, the internet proved to be a much more common source of exposure than the offline world. The teenagers reported seeing violent imagery online at a rate of 10.7%, compared to just 1.6% offline. Similarly, 13.4% of respondents encountered unwanted sexual images online, while only 2.0% experienced this offline. Content encouraging self-harm was seen by 9.7% of adolescents online, compared to 5.2% offline. Additionally, over half of the participants (51.5%) reported that their technology use disrupted their sleep.
The study also found substantial variations depending on the specific platforms the adolescents were using. For instance, 9.1% of Instagram users reported seeing violent imagery, compared to just 1.9% of YouTube users. The feeling that one’s life is worse because of other people’s posts was most common on Instagram (16.6%) and TikTok (13.4%), while it was much lower on YouTube (4.1%) and text messaging (5.6%).
Sleep disruption also seemed to be concentrated on certain apps. A total of 42.2% of TikTok users and 27.8% of Instagram users attributed their disrupted sleep to those platforms. In comparison, only 10.2% of teenagers blamed text messaging for their sleep issues.
The researchers noted that factors like parental education, household income, and the presence of parental controls on smartphones were not statistically associated with a higher or lower likelihood of experiencing online harm.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. First, the study relies on a relatively modest sample size of 472 adolescents. When looking at less popular platforms or rare experiences, the small number of users limits how precise the estimates can be.
“Although this is a nationally representative sample of American teens, it’s a relatively small sample and this was a pilot study,” Lee said. “The results should not be taken to say definitively that X platform has Y amount of harms, but rather can be thought of as illustrating how reported harms vary from platform to platform and from harm to harm. We do hope to be quite clear that this is a pilot!”
Second, the findings are based on self-reported memories over a four-week period. This approach is subject to recall bias, meaning teenagers might be more likely to remember highly emotional events while forgetting milder, everyday interactions. Stigmatized events, such as receiving or sending explicit images, might also be underreported due to social desirability or embarrassment.
Another detail to consider is that adolescents might simply attribute their negative experiences to the apps they spend the most time on, rather than the exact place the harm occurred. Because teenagers often use multiple apps at once, it can be difficult for them to pinpoint exactly where they saw a distressing video or received a hurtful message.
Finally, the differences in reported harms across platforms might reflect the types of people who choose to use those apps, rather than just the design of the apps themselves. For instance, if a specific platform is highly popular among teenage girls, who generally report higher susceptibility to social comparison, that app might show elevated rates of body image concerns regardless of its layout or content moderation policies.
“This is cross-sectional survey data, so it cannot be used to draw causal claims,” Lee added. “We can’t say that ‘using platform X causes American teens to see unwanted content Y’ but we can say that adolescents using platform X were more likely to report seeing content Y. We also do not know what the effects of such reported harms are on youth well-being, though that is something we hope to address in future research.”
Future research using larger samples could help clarify how specific platform features directly influence user experiences.
“In the near future, we’re in the process of preparing to field a new, larger study with American adolescents and their parents that will allow us to examine how youth report experiencing online harms across a broader set of platforms – including AI chatbots and AI companion apps,” she said. “We think this next step is important because the digital landscape of youth media use is changing rapidly, and measurement efforts need to keep up to understand where, when, and how youth are being negatively impacted.”
“Long-term, I am hopeful that studies like ours – and those conducted by nonprofit and academic entities – can show that investment in monitoring youth online experiences can provide valuable insights that can help inform efforts to implement and evaluate interventions,” Lee concluded.
The study, “Adolescents’ Experiences of Online Harms by Platform,” was authored by Angela Y. Lee, Carmen H. J. Lim, Sunny Xun Liu, R. Kang Xing Jin, Anneke Buffone, Ravi Iyer, Zachary Rausch, Jonathan Haidt, Nathanael J. Fast, Jeffrey T. Hancock, and Eleni Linos.

Facebook deceived users over data privacy – US jury
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:51:00 UTC
04:51:00 KST

Facebook deceived users over data privacy – US jury
A New Mexico jury has found Meta Platforms liable for willfully deceiving Facebook users over privacy and platform policies, handing the social media giant yet another major legal defeat this year.
The case stems from the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which erupted in 2018 after a whistleblower report claiming that the British political consultancy obtained data from tens of millions of Facebook users without their consent through a third-party app.
The data was used for voter profiling and political targeting, including during Donald Trump’s successful 2016 presidential campaign. Cambridge Analytica collapsed within months, while Facebook was hit with billions in fines and settlements over its handling of user data.
New Mexico filed its case in 2021, joining a wave of legal action over the scandal. The state accused Meta of misleading users about third-party access to their data and Facebook’s investigations into data brokers after the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
After a two-week trial, jurors ruled on Friday that Meta had willfully deceived consumers, amounting to more than 43 million violations affecting New Mexico’s entire population of over 2 million. A judge will now determine the penalty, with the state seeking up to $5,000 per violation – putting the theoretical maximum at a staggering $219 billion.
Meta denied wrongdoing and insisted it had been transparent about the shortcomings in its handling of privacy and misinformation. A spokesperson said the company disagreed with the verdict and will continue defending itself “against efforts to distort our record.”
New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez argued that the trial exposed “in stark detail the way in which this company plays fast and loose with the rules,” calling the outcome a “historic verdict” in efforts to hold Big Tech accountable.
The ruling is Meta’s latest major defeat in New Mexico. In March, another Santa Fe jury found it liable for 75,000 violations over child safety and imposed $375 million in penalties. A local judge later branded Meta’s platforms a “public nuisance” and ordered another $567 million in remedies. Meta has said it will appeal.
Meta’s legal exposure extends beyond New Mexico. Last month, the company agreed to pay roughly $17 billion to settle claims by dozens of US states and territories that it deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to addict children and misled the public about the risks. That deal included a settlement of claims tied to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, but New Mexico did not join it, allowing its case to proceed to trial.
Meta is not alone in facing mounting scrutiny over Big Tech’s data practices. Last month, TikTok and parent ByteDance agreed to pay $400 million to settle US allegations that the platform illegally collected children’s personal data without required parental consent. Google, Apple, Netflix and other tech giants have likewise faced privacy-related litigation.

Fremantle's recovery from inexplicable collapse begins by sitting in grief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:49:51 UTC
04:49:51 KST

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
analysis
Fremantle's recovery from AFL grand final devastation begins by sitting in its grief
Fremantle's devastated players had not even left the field of play at the Melbourne Cricket Ground and the recovery from what is one of the most heartbreaking grand final losses ever had already begun.
The bowels of the MCG acted as a safety bunker for Freo's players, a sanctuary away from prying eyes in the aftermath of a crushing loss.
Fremantle's team bus was parked and ready to depart as family members, club employees and reporters filed in and out of the rooms.
Amid the cloud of devastation, the rays of hope already began to shine through.
Before the players retreated to the rooms, their crestfallen loved ones looked to console them, even though it seemed an impossible task, before trying to impart whatever positive vibes they'd managed to summon.
Eventually the players started filtering through. Some in tears, some clutching their jerseys in disbelief, others simply looking into any space possible that meant they could avoid eye contact.
One middle-aged man, presumably a father of one of the players, embraced each of them, telling them to keep their heads up.
It is this positivity that will help Fremantle get back up off the canvas after an unspeakably traumatic defeat.
Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir, a man who has overseen this team's rise to be a bona fide contender over the past seven seasons, admitted there was no way to soften the blow for his "devastated" charges.
Brisbane's incredible heist left Longmuir in tears before the final siren, and when he gathered his players on the ground in the immediate aftermath, the message was clear: "Have each other's back."
"We play an imperfect game that is full of mistakes, and every game that they have played across their journey they would have made mistakes, it just feels a bit bigger right now," he said.
"If we had've won, we would've won together. We lost, we lose together, so have each other's back."
Brisbane's three-peat may have made winning premierships look easy, but it is anything but.
It is easy to forget that before their crowning moments of the last three years, the Lions too experienced significant heartbreak.
For some reason in sport, you often need to experience ultimate grief before you get the opportunity to experience ultimate joy.
The sporting Gods are cruel like that.
As difficult and gut-wrenching as it may be right now, Longmuir wants his players to sit in the grief.
"We're devastated, but we need to make sure that we've got each other's back and support each other and make sure we're not too hard on ourselves through this moment," he said.
"The time to move on is not now, and we've got to sit in this and help each other through it and then the time to move on and worrying about next year is down the track."
And what is to come of the now-infamous and probably haunted Wharfie Time? Do we ever see it again?
Longmuir continued the theme of positivity by saying he would like to see Wharfie Time return, downplaying the impact it had on Fremantle's collapse, but when your opponent openly speaks about using it as motivation, it is time to bury the gimmick.
The bells tolling after Patrick Voss's goal with just over four minutes left certainly allowed Fremantle's fans to dare to dream, and in the aftermath, the players revealed they did as well.
Norm Smith Medal winner Shai Bolton and teammate Judd McVee both admitted they thought they were home, before the Lions avalanche, which the Norm Smith Medal winner described as a "blur".
"Finals football is all about moments and in the last four minutes we didn't take our moments and Brisbane probably did," Bolton said.
"They've got the experience and in the last four minutes they played their way and came home with the chocolates."
Fremantle is a family club and will need to summon all that positivity to get over this.
"We'll stick together after this, we're like brothers," McVee told ABC Sport.
"Everyone plays a part in it. It is a very tight group here, and we just love each other."
Fremantle, like Brisbane three years ago, will be back. They are too young and too talented not to.
The Dockers ranked 13th in the league in experience in terms of games played and have the 11th-youngest list in the AFL.
Like Brisbane under Chris Fagan, the Dockers also have the power of continuity behind them, something many of their rivals are chasing in a league that is increasingly obsessed with instant results over the ups and downs of a long journey.
One of the best-known adages in the AFL world is legendary former Brisbane coach Leigh Matthews's minutes and goals equation. Watch any close game and you are likely to hear commentators refer to it.
During his time as a coach, Matthews had always believed that you could still win a game if you had more minutes left than goals behind.
Brisbane needed three goals with four minutes remaining and wound up kicking four. Their legendary coach's equation came through again.
Never again will Fremantle's supporters or its players feel like a victory is truly in the bag.
Not when Matthews's equation is on their side, not when they get on a run midway through the third quarter, and certainly not when the Wharfie Time bell tolls, if it ever tolls again.

At UN, Singapore warns AI safeguards must keep pace as capabilities race ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:48:55 UTC
04:48:55 KST

Faisal Mahmud
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
Singapore’s Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan warned Saturday that artificial intelligence is advancing faster than the world’s understanding of its risks, calling for stronger safeguards and international rules while insisting that humans must remain ultimately in control.
Addressing the 81st UN General Assembly in New York, Balakrishnan described AI as “arguably the most urgent frontier,” saying the technology offered extraordinary potential but also posed risks ranging from autonomous systems escaping human control to its use by rogue actors to develop biological or other weapons of mass destruction.
“The genie is already out of the bottle,” he said, arguing that halting AI development was unrealistic amid superpower competition and strong commercial incentives.
Comparing AI development to driving a high-performance car, Balakrishnan said innovation provided the “powerful engine,” but safe deployment also required “good brakes” — including rigorous testing, clear limits on autonomous systems and mechanisms for human intervention.
“Most importantly, human beings must ultimately remain in control and accountable,” he said, asking whether anyone would want “the nuclear button” in the hands of an AI.
Balakrishnan also warned that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the Persian Gulf war was putting the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) through a “severe stress test.”
He said transit passage through international straits was a right, not a privilege subject to fees or tolls, and warned that allowing any country to veto navigational freedoms could have global consequences.
The strait normally carries around a fifth of global oil supplies, he said, with its disruption driving up energy prices, damaging supply chains and stranding seafarers.

He later held a press conference, answering questions from journalists. TASS has compiled his key statements.
Unpredictability and adventures of the West
- As Lavrov said, "the West increasingly resorts to brute force as it acts unpredictably and recklessly, jeopardizing the life and wellbeing of millions if not billions of people on our planet."
- According to the minister, the West dreams of inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia, while Europe is preparing for war with Russia. "They confirm every day that Europeans should be ready for war by 2030 at the latest," he said.
- According to Lavrov, "pursuing the utopian goal of containing Russia, the West destroyed the European security system with its own hands and fostered the Russophobic regime in Kiev."
- Moreover, "judging by statements from their representatives, the ruling elites of many European Union countries are clearly infected with the virus of racial superiority -- they are harboring extremist, Russophobic ideas and indulging the leaders of the Ukrainian regime when they honor in Kiev notorious war criminals and Nazi collaborators whose hands are stained with the blood of Russians, Jews, Belarusians, Ukrainians and people of other nationalities."
- Lavrov recalled that almost the entire West votes annually against Russia’s resolution condemning the glorification of Nazism: "Metastases of this inhumane ideology can now be seen in other countries on our continent, primarily among EU and NATO members, in the Baltic countries and in Germany as well"
- Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said he learned nothing new from German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul’s remarks at a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, as he fully repeated Berlin’s longstanding position: "I asked him to set out what he had come in with. He took out his notes and read a text that fully reproduced what Germany, through its leaders, officially and publicly says every day. I learned nothing new from it."
Ukraine
-Lavrov stressed that Moscow does not suffer from a lack of trust in the context of the Ukraine negotiation track, but continues to insist that "one must prove that one is capable of reaching agreements and prove that one can be trusted," while Kiev has failed to do so, encouraged by Western representatives.
- According to the Russian foreign minister, "Europe is making every effort to hamper a peace settlement and disrupt potential negotiations being sought by the [US President Donald] Trump administration, among other players. The West is pumping the Ukrainian regime with weapons as it also helps Kiev to target drones and missiles at civilians and civilian infrastructure."
- Ukraine is solely responsible for damage to shipping in the Black Sea, including damage to Western commercial companies: "Name at least one case when commercial vessels operating in your (Western -- TASS) interests have been targeted by Russian strikes. That is where the conversation ends. There are no such cases."
Middle East crisis
- Lavrov said that "the UN and all of us, the member states, need to take urgent unconventional steps to reverse negative trends in the Middle East and neighboring areas. This concerns not only Palestine, but also Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iraq, Sudan, Somalia, South Sudan and other African countries where conflicts are raging."
- Speaking about the situation around the Strait of Hormuz, Lavrov said that Russia views "establishing trust in relations between the coastal [Persian] Gulf states -- Arab nations and Iran -- as a precondition for resolving the [Hormuz] crisis."
- Lavrov said Russia’s concept for collective security in the Persian Gulf aims "to build a sustainable regional architecture." Russia, together with other "responsible countries," is ready to make a "constructive contribution" to stabilizing the strategically important Middle East.
- The minister recalled that almost a year ago, the UN Security Council approved a Washington-backed peace plan for the Gaza Strip, but peace has still not been achieved and the humanitarian situation remains critical.
- According to him, Russia believes that "the time has come to address the main issue in the Middle East, namely ensuring Palestinian statehood based on numerous UN decisions."
Adapting the UN to new realities
- Western countries are "overrepresented" on the UN Security Council, which should be expanded to include more representatives from Asia, Africa, and Latin America, while Moscow cannot allow any new "Western seats": "We cannot provide for or allow any new 'Western seats, ' because the West is already overrepresented," Lavrov stressed, adding that reform must not include additional seats for Western countries, "especially Germany and Japan, which have embarked on a path of militarization and revanchism."
- He reiterated support for permanent seats for Brazil and India while meeting Africa’s interests in line with the Ezulwini Consensus and Sirte Declaration.
- Russia expects "that the new Secretary-General whom we should elect between the end of this year will <…> represent the entire international community, rather than serve the interests of separate countries, and refrain from undermining the intergovernmental nature of the UN system or the prerogatives of the [UN] Security Council and its permanent members." Lavrov said several candidates for the post have the necessary qualities.
- Speaking about the current UN Secretariat headed by Antonio Guterres, Lavrov said it "is unable to implement the key requirements of this document, which underpins the entire UN. It promotes biased approaches and double standards, essentially serving a group of Western countries," Lavrov said, noting that seven or eight of the most important positions in the UN Secretariat are held by citizens or nationals of NATO countries.
- Moscow, Lavrov stressed, wants "the United Nations to truly become a center for coordinating the interests of all states, as required by its Charter.".

Azerbaijan marks its Remembrance Day looking forward to a future of peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:48:15 UTC
04:48:15 KST

Azerbaijan observes its annual Remembrance Day by honouring its soldiers fallen in 2020, but also building on six years of peace for post-war recovery, new opportunities and regional normalisation.
Azerbaijan marks the annual Remembrance Day with a nationwide tribute to the soldiers who lost their lives during the 44-day war in 2020, but also with a renewed hope brought by the historic peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia, after decades of bitter conflict.
The events of that autumn in 2020 changed the 30-year status quo generated by the dissolution of the Soviet Union which had brought decades of deep-rooted conflict and regional stagnation between Azerbaijan and Armenia.
The cessation of hostilities in November 2020 reshaped the strategic landscape of the region establishing a new political framework which culminated with the two former rivals reaching a peace agreement which includes borders delimitation, the start of a reconciliation process, but also kickstarting an economic expansion and launching new regional transport corridors for global opportunities.
Six years after the end of the war, this legacy has transitioned from post-war recovery into active regional integration and development. The true dividends of this hard-won peace are now materialising not just in diplomatic halls, but on the ground, fundamentally altering the economic landscape of the South Caucasus.
Opening the railways
The most visible sign of this evolving relationship is the movement of rail freight, and following the lifting of transit restrictions by Azerbaijan in late 2025, a steady flow of cargo has travelled towards Armenia.
Routed primarily via Azerbaijan Railways from Bilajari station towards the Boyuk Kasik junction at the Georgian border, shipments move into Armenia.
This transport artery facilitates both direct bilateral sales and international transit and has established a new economic dynamic.
According to state customs data, direct exports from Azerbaijan to Armenia between January and August 2026 reached over $17 million (over €15 million). While this accounts for just 0.08% of Azerbaijan's total global exports, the physical volume is substantial.
Direct shipments have included approximately 17,000 tonnes of diesel fuel and roughly 5,000 tonnes of AI-92 and AI-95 petrol.
The trade even saw a brief reciprocal exchange, with Azerbaijan recording a symbolic $960 in imports from Armenia in March.
The route also serves as a vital corridor for third-country transit.
Recent freight shifted around Azerbaijani territory includes nearly 60,000 tonnes of agricultural products, such as wheat, barley, and buckwheat, alongside more than 9,000 tonnes of fertiliser and over 1,400 tonnes of propane gas.
Industrial materials are also moving steadily through the corridor, comprising 1,114 tonnes of coal, 608 tonnes of timber, and 133 tonnes of aluminium.
A new era of digital transit
Beyond physical rail freight, bilateral cooperation has achieved significant progress in the digital domain. The two countries have implemented a digital transit agreement between national operators AzerTelecom and Telecom Armenia.
Under this arrangement, a portion of Armenia’s international internet traffic is routed across Azerbaijan. Both companies noted that such agreements aim at "diversifying connection routes in the region" and "increasing the reliability of telecommunication networks".
This cooperation also aligns with broader regional infrastructure goals, including the Digital Silk Way project. In return, the arrangement allows Azerbaijan to transmit data traffic to its Nakhchivan exclave directly through the Armenian telecommunications network.
Restoring infrastructure
Both countries are laying the groundwork for expanding multi-directional transit. While physical exports from Armenia across Azerbaijani territory are not yet active, official frameworks anticipate future integration.
The Armenian government’s state programme for 2026 to 2031 outlines plans to build full-scale commercial ties with Azerbaijan and unblock regional transport links following a final peace treaty.
Meanwhile, regional transport infrastructure is being restored rapidly, including ongoing railway construction in the Ordubad direction.
Once a comprehensive peace agreement is finalised, the full opening of transport corridors is expected to enable Armenia to utilise Azerbaijan's transit network for broader international trade, establishing a fully interconnected economic corridor across the South Caucasus.
A historic summit in Washington
This deepening economic integration is underpinned by key high-level diplomatic milestones.
The strategic framework for the current bilateral political process was formalised on 8 August 2025 during a historic trilateral summit in Washington.
Hosted at the White House by US President Donald Trump, the meeting brought together Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan who signed the joint declaration for the comprehensive peace agreement.
Building trust towards reconciliation
Meanwhile, the normalisation process is also extending beyond state-level diplomacy and taking root at the community and institutional levels.
Armenia supported Azerbaijan’s successful bid to host the UN Climate Change Conference (COP29) in Baku, while Azerbaijan supported Armenia’s candidacy for membership in the Eastern European Group COP Bureau.
In April 2026, the "Peace Bridge" format facilitated a fourth round of dialogue between Armenian and Azerbaijani civil society representatives in the town of Gabala.
Participants from both nations emphasised the importance of crossing borders and maintaining consistent dialogue to prepare their respective societies for the eventual outcomes of a final peace treaty.
Furthermore, civil engagement is progressing alongside the joint development of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a transit corridor through Armenia's Syunik region that connects Azerbaijan directly to its Nakhchivan exclave.
On 18 September 2026, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan was awarded the Hessian Peace Prize during a formal ceremony at the Hesse State Parliament in Wiesbaden, Germany.
The award recognises efforts to establish peace in the South Caucasus and has provided a platform for a notable diplomatic gesture.
During the ceremony, Pashinyan publicly expressed his gratitude for the peace process with Azerbaijan. Acknowledging the leaders' joint efforts, the Armenian prime minister stated that the Azerbaijani president was "equally deserving of this award" for his contribution to regional peace.

Five 'change bloc' leaders hold coordinating meeting ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:46:26 UTC
04:46:26 KST

Opposition party leaders in the bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Saturday evening and signed a document agreeing on shared principles and pledging to work together ahead of the October elections.
The meeting took place between the four main party leaders in the bloc: Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar), Naftali Bennett (B’Yachad), Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beytenu), and Yair Golan (The Democrats).
The joint document signed by the party leaders included a commitment to work together to increase voter turnout and a pledge not to launch attacks against each other, along with a plan to formulate principles for the next government.
The document did not address how the leader of the opposition bloc should be determined. Eisenkot has called for the leader of the largest party to be a candidate for prime minister.
The meeting was held at opposition leader Yair Lapid’s house. Lapid holds the second slot on the B’Yachad slate. Arab party leaders were not invited to the meeting.
Bennett said after the meeting that he was confident in the bloc’s “ability to win 63 seats and, together, fix Israel.”
“Everyone understood the magnitude of the moment and put aside all personal considerations.”
“We agreed on full cooperation until the election, on Election Day and after the election, in order to establish a government of correction for Israel,” he added.
Change bloc leaders hold meeting to coordinate ahead of October elections
The meeting comes as the bloc’s leaders seek to tighten coordination while grappling with disagreements over election strategy, the identity of the candidate who will lead the camp, and possible paths toward forming a government after the elections. Some of those disagreements have already spilled into the public arena in recent weeks.
Eisenkot and Liberman met at Yashar’s offices on Wednesday, their second meeting in about two weeks.
Eisenkot addressed coordination within the camp on Wednesday, telling 103FM, “There are weekly meetings to coordinate between the parties, and there are also substantive disagreements. We have a common goal, and I am certain it will be expressed by the elections and will lead to us defeating this failed government.”
The meeting at Lapid’s home took place against the backdrop of efforts to coordinate among parties that differ in their positions and voter bases.
Alongside their shared objective of replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, the camp’s leaders have yet to reach full agreement on who should be their candidate for prime minister or on some of the coalition issues that would arise after the elections.
Relations among the key players have also been tense. Over the past week, Eisenkot and figures in Yisrael Beytenu have exchanged remarks after Liberman’s party criticized the strategy led by the Yashar chairman.
MK Oded Forer, one of Yisrael Beytenu’s senior figures, said last week that Eisenkot was “fueling Bibi’s campaign” and that winning would require drawing votes from other political camps as well.
According to a Maariv poll published on Friday, the coalition bloc fell by one seat to just 49 as both haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties lost one seat each.
The poll also found that Otzma Yehudit gained one seat, rising to nine, while Likud remained at 18 seats, the Religious Zionist Party-Zehut joint list at six, and People of Israel at four.
In the opposition bloc, Eisenkot’s Yashar continued its downward trend, losing another seat this week to stand at 22.
Elsewhere in the bloc, The Democrats gained two seats to reach 11, while B’Yachad remained at 13 and Yisrael Beytenu at nine. The joint Reservists-Economic Party remained at four seats, while the Arab parties also remained unchanged with a combined 12 seats. Overall, the Zionist opposition bloc gained one seat, rising to 55.
Meanwhile, Blue and White, led by Benny Gantz, received 1.3% of the vote; the Haredi Public party, led by Moti Leitner, received 0.9%; and Noam for Israel, led by Avi Maoz, received 0.7%. None crossed the electoral threshold.
Asked which party they would vote for if Knesset elections were held now, respondents gave Yashar 22 seats, Likud 18, B’Yachad 13, The Democrats 11, Yisrael Beytenu nine, Otzma Yehudit nine, the Joint Arab List seven, United Torah Judaism six, Shas six, Religious Zionist Party-Zehut six, Ra’am five, People of Israel four, and the Reservists-Economic Party four.•

Fatih Erel, Aysu Biçer
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands in recognition of the lives lost in the Gaza conflict during Sunday’s Nations League match against Israel in Hungary, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) said Saturday.
FAI Chief Executive David Courell also confirmed that one player had withdrawn from the squad ahead of the match.
Courell said the squad had held a vote on whether to play the fixture, with a “significant majority” voting in favor of proceeding with the game.
The match has been the subject of controversy since Ireland and Israel were drawn together in Group B3.
The players had faced calls from the Stop The Game campaign, organized by the group Irish Sport for Palestine, to withdraw from the fixtures.
“They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the (Gaza) conflict,” Courell said at a delayed news conference.
Ireland-Israel game to go ahead despite ‘different views’
The Republic of Ireland confirmed the UEFA Nations League game against Israel to be played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday will go ahead despite having "different views."
"The 2026-27 UEFA Nations League fixtures against Israel will be fulfilled," The Football Association of Ireland confirmed in a statement on Saturday.
"The Association made this decision following consultation with the Republic of Ireland players who shared different views and a majority expressed that the fixtures should be played. The Association respects the views of all players involved and appreciates the level of sensitivity concerning these fixtures," it said.
A pre-match press conference with the Irish team's manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player was postponed for 15 minutes before it was due to begin on Saturday morning amid speculation over whether the match would take place on Sunday.
According to Irish media reports, several players, including goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, requested to withdraw from the match against Israel.
Playing ‘against genocide’
Republic of Ireland midfielder Jason Knight had become the first national team player to publicly say that the country should not play its upcoming UEFA Nations League match against Israel.
"I don’t think the game should be going ahead, but it is going ahead," he said.
The 25-year-old Bristol City midfielder said the squad would hold more detailed discussions before deciding how to approach Sunday’s match in Hungary.
More than 160 Irish athletes have signed an open letter urging the national team not to play, while the Stop The Game campaign has organized demonstrations demanding Israel’s suspension from international football.
Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson previously said some players felt “really uncomfortable” about the matches and described the team as playing “against genocide,” prompting a sharp response from the Israeli Football Association.
The first match will take place at the Nagyerdei Stadium in Debrecen on Sunday. The return fixture, officially Ireland’s home game, has been moved from Dublin to Backa Topola, Serbia, and will be played behind closed doors on Oct. 4.

AI generated
MADRID - Thousands of people marched through Madrid on Sept 26 to protest the eviction earlier this week of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong home, calling for greater protection for tenants.
Images of Maricarmen Abascal being carried from her Madrid flat on a stretcher on Sept 23 after police broke down her door have thrust Spain’s housing crisis back into the spotlight ahead of a general election due in 2027.
Protesters chanted slogans and held banners calling for measures to curb rising housing costs and make evictions more difficult as they marched through central Madrid.
“You could be the next Maricarmen,” read one banner.
Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain’s housing crisis, urged Spaniards to join the fight in a video message posted online just hours before the protest.
“I want what has happened to me to serve so that it does not happen to other people,” she said from hospital, where she has been treated for exhaustion since her eviction.
“I want it to encourage people to fight and to help change the laws that have allowed me to be evicted,” she added in the video, posted by Spain’s main tenants’ union.
Abascal was forced to leave the apartment where she had lived for 70 years after a real estate firm acquired the property and raised the rent by 275 per cent to €2,650 (S$3,850), according to the union.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who in 2025 pledged to make housing a government priority, is under growing pressure to act. There have been regular protests across Spain since Abascal’s eviction.
His government is expected to approve a package of measures dubbed the “Maricarmen decree” at its next Cabinet meeting, including the automatic renewal of rental contracts and further restrictions on evictions.
But it is unclear whether the package will be approved by parliament, where Sanchez’s government lacks a majority.
While a similar Bill was defeated earlier this year, Abascal’s case has increased pressure on political parties to act. AFP

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Saturday said Moscow is committed to holding peace talks with Ukraine, rejecting claims that Moscow is avoiding negotiations.
Speaking to reporters after his address to the UN General Assembly in New York, Lavrov said previous rounds of talks were not halted by Moscow, "but rather by those who today claim that the Russians are avoiding contact and have nothing to say."
On US-Russia relations, Lavrov said the two countries maintain regular dialogue through various channels.
“We are ready; we will always engage in dialogue – especially with countries like the United States," he said. "We will always listen, and we will always speak honestly about what we disagree with."
He said Moscow considers the understandings reached during last year’s summit in the US state of Alaska to remain valid and is ready to return to them.
On ties with Berlin, Lavrov said his meeting with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, requested by Berlin "at the very last minute" – the first meeting between the countries’ foreign ministers since 2022, the year the Ukraine war began – produced no new proposals.
"When asked to outline the purpose of his visit, the German minister took out his notes and read a text that merely reiterated what Germany’s leaders officially and publicly declare on a daily basis. I gleaned nothing new from it—a point I made to Mr. Wadephul," he said.
Lavrov said there was an implication that Germany’s foreign minister had “come down” to establish contact with Russia and that Moscow was now expected to make concessions on the Ukraine war in return for the gesture.
Asked about US President Donald Trump’s public rejection of a plan proposed by Iran to address their conflict, Lavrov said the parties could consider returning to the June framework deal reached through Pakistani mediation, called the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.
“We believe the Islamabad Memorandum was a fair deal. As the saying goes – and given that it was signed at the highest level, presumably with full awareness of what was being done – why not revisit it?” he said.
On the election of the next UN secretary-general, Lavrov said he expects the new chief to represent the interests of the international community as a whole, adding that several candidates for the post have the qualities required under the UN Charter.
The term of Antonio Guterres, the current secretary-general, is ending at the close of this year.

Germany urges ‘profound’ reforms to United Nations
Unknown

04:37:44 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
Germany on Saturday called for “profound” United Nations reforms to make the world body more effective.
A new secretary-general is needed “to lead a profound process of reform. Above all, we must close the gap between what we expect from the United Nations and the capabilities we give to the organization,” Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said in his speech to the UN General Assembly in New York. Antonio Guterres, the current secretary-general, is due to step down at the end of this year.
“First we need a functioning UN that plays an active role in resolving conflicts rather than merely managing them. In times when the Security Council as the central decision-making body is paralyzed, this is more difficult than ever. We need to keep its reform high on our agenda,” he added, while also warning of “the erosion of international law.”
The UN Security Council is made up of 15 of the 193 UN member states. Five nuclear powers and victors of World War II are permanent members and have veto rights: the US, China, Russia, Great Britain, and France.
Some of the other 188 member states take turns in the remaining 10 seats every two years.
Türkiye has long spoken out in favor of reforming the Security Council, as did Germany, Brazil, India, and Japan collectively during UN General Assembly week.
Such reforms are more important than ever “given the increasingly challenging geopolitical environment,” the foreign ministers of the so-called G4 group said in a joint statement on Tuesday.
The UN Security Council, in its current form, is unable to fulfill its central mission, said Wadephul and his counterparts from Brazil, India, and Japan.
The “representativeness, legitimacy, and capacity to act” of the UN’s highest body are currently in question. One reason for this is “an anachronistic, eight-decade-old architecture.”
The Security Council’s current composition is “an obstacle to adequately addressing present and future challenges,” the four countries said.

The Philippines called for an immediate and sustained ceasefire in Gaza and said disputes in the South China Sea must be resolved through international law rather than force, Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa P. Lazaro told the 81st UN General Assembly.
Lazaro called for the protection of civilians, the release of all hostages and full compliance with international law, including international humanitarian law.
She reaffirmed Manila’s support for the Palestinian people’s “inalienable right” to self-determination.
“We firmly believe that the two-state solution remains the only viable path to lasting and durable peace, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace and security,” she said.
Turning to maritime security, Lazaro said open and secure seas, “free from interference and coercion,” were vital to the Philippines’ security and economy as well as global commerce.
She described the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) as the “Constitution of the Oceans” and highlighted that a decade had passed since the 2016 South China Sea arbitral award, which she called “final and legally binding.”
“The Philippines stands firm in its conviction that disputes must be resolved through diplomacy and law, not violence and might,” Lazaro said.
The Philippines and China have overlapping claims in the disputed South China Sea, while Beijing has rejected the 2016 arbitral ruling.
Lazaro also called for stronger global governance of artificial intelligence, warning that without “robust governance, enforceable ethical standards, and strong legal guardrails,” AI could deepen inequality and pose systemic risks.
On climate change, Lazaro said storms and monsoons had affected more than 2.7 million Filipino families since August, urging implementation of the Paris Agreement and the full operationalization of the fund for responding to loss and damage.
She also highlighted threats facing seafarers, saying Filipinos comprise more than 25% of the nearly 2 million seafarers supporting global commerce.
Lazaro called for UN Security Council reform to make it more representative, transparent and accountable, with greater representation for developing regions.
She also voiced what she described as a “historic aspiration” for the UN to appoint a woman secretary-general.

UN warns actions undermining Libya's oil infrastructure could trigger Security Council measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:31:41 UTC
04:31:41 KST

Mohammad Sio
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
The UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) warned Saturday that attacks against or actions undermining Libya’s oil and energy infrastructure could constitute grounds for measures under relevant UN Security Council resolutions.
In a statement on US social media company X, UNSMIL said the continued disruption of the Sharara-Zawiya oil pipeline “is adversely affecting Libya's principal source of national income, causing significant losses in oil production and public revenues.”
The mission said prolonged disruption also risks affecting fuel supplies, electricity generation and other essential services relied upon by Libyans across the country.
“Prolonged disruption would increase the need for fuel imports and place additional pressure on public finances,” it added.
While acknowledging workers’ right to peacefully raise legitimate socio-economic demands, UNSMIL called on all actors to protect oil and energy facilities and ensure that technical and operational personnel can safely access and maintain them.
It said oil and energy infrastructure and public resources “must remain protected from political and security disputes, which should be addressed through peaceful means, and preserved in the interests of all Libyans.”
UNSMIL specifically recalled that attacks against, or actions that undermine, Libya’s oil and energy infrastructure “may constitute grounds for the imposition of measures” under relevant Security Council resolutions, including Resolution 2213 (2015).
Resolution 2213 (2015), adopted by the UN Security Council in March 2015, allows sanctions including travel bans and asset freezes against individuals or entities whose actions threaten Libya’s peace and stability, including attacks on state institutions and oil facilities.
The mission urged the relevant authorities and security actors to engage urgently and take necessary measures to resolve disputes peacefully, restore the flow of crude oil and safeguard operations at the Zawiya refinery and related facilities.
The warning comes after Libya’s National Oil Corporation said on Monday that an armed group had shut Valve No. 7 on the crude pipeline linking the Sharara field to Zawiya Port, sharply reducing production at the country’s largest oil field.
Sharara, located in the Murzuq Desert around 800 kilometers (500 miles) south of Tripoli, has a production capacity of about 340,000 barrels per day.
The NOC warned that a prolonged closure could halt production at Sharara as well as oil transport and exports, damage state revenues, disrupt operations at the Zawiya refinery and increase Libya’s fuel import costs. It also said it could declare force majeure if the disruption continued.
On Sept. 15, members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard had also shut the main Hamada-Zawiya pipeline, forcing the suspension of production and operations at three oil sites. The NOC warned that extended closures will harm the national economy and threaten the state’s ability to meet its financial obligations.
The Hamada field is located in the Hamada al-Hamra area of the Ghadames Basin in western Libya, about 400 kilometers (250 miles) south of Tripoli. It is considered one of the key oil and natural gas fields in western Libya and produces around 700 barrels per day.
The disruptions have come amid protests by members of Libya’s Petroleum Facilities Guard over financial and employment demands. Guards had carried out a series of closures to pressure authorities to meet their demands.

Trump and Xi to set up AI safety channel as military, trade talks continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:26:53 UTC
04:26:53 KST

Trump and Xi agree to set up AI safety channel as military and trade talks continue
China and the United States agreed to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents and accelerate work on military crisis communications following a three-day summit between President Xi Jinping and President Trump in Washington, the two governments said Saturday.
They also agreed to continue cooperating through a Board of Trade focused on selected bilateral issues. The White House said the board began operating this week.
The summit produced no major breakthroughs, but analysts said the steps toward greater cooperation were important because they established working groups that could help prevent disputes from escalating.
Xi returned to Beijing on Saturday, according to the state-run Xinhua News Agency. During the visit, Mr. Trump displayed unusual warmth toward Xi, despite having escalated a trade war with China the previous year that had global repercussions.
The two sides agreed to sign a memorandum of understanding on strengthening crisis communications and preventing crises between the two militaries, China's Foreign Ministry said Saturday in its readout. The one-page statement from the Chinese side was light on details.
Both sides will set up a communication mechanism for artificial intelligence-related incidents, to discuss related risks and benefits, with an AI-specific dialogue scheduled for November.
The White House said the two leaders agreed on using the term "super intelligence" rather than "artificial intelligence" to describe the technology. Mr. Trump has been outspoken about his preference for the alternate term.
"I call it SI because it's a much better name," he told reporters Saturday on the White House's south lawn. "It's a much more accurate name because when you say the other, it means it's fake. Artificial means it's fake, and it's not fake."
Mr. Trump also indicated that there would be limits on what the U.S. would share with China and said that Washington would not slow its AI efforts.
The "United States of America is not going to be putting on brakes," Mr. Trump told reporters outside the White House. "They want to stop our progress because we're leading China by a lot and we're going to keep it that way."
He added: "I would rather not integrate because we're leading by a lot. When you're leading, you don't open it up to each other. We're leading by at least a year, maybe a year and a half. Some people say two years. I'm not looking to open it up."
The statement from China said both sides will continue to work together on the pledge to reduce reciprocal tariffs on roughly $30 billion worth of goods. During the summit, the two leaders agreed to extend a trade truce by two months. The White House statement said China agreed to import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the U.S. in 2027 and 2028.
Most of the reduction in tariffs is aimed at non-sensitive goods, such as agricultural products or holiday decorations.
The two countries also established the Board of Investment to "discuss potential investment opportunities and investment-related impediments and to provide a structured channel for the two sides to address commercially meaningful investment-related issues," the White House said.
The statement from the White House also said the two sides continued to work on American concerns about rare earths supply, "with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels." China put export controls on rare earths last year in response to the U.S. tariffs, cutting the supply sent to the U.S. and other countries.
Both sides agreed to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, and then later at the G20 at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.
Both governments said Iran should honor its stated commitment not to develop nuclear weapons. They also said no country should charge tolls on international waterways, an apparent reference to the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic has fallen significantly since the U.S. war with Iran began.
The U.S. statement welcomed China's decision to impose export controls on two additional precursor chemicals used to produce fentanyl. Both sides also noted recent arrests in fentanyl-related cases.
Although the summit did not resolve the countries' fundamental differences, analysts said the incremental progress was noteworthy.
"Personal diplomacy between the two leaders is important, but the emphasis on working-level engagement, military-to-military dialogue and crisis-management mechanisms suggests an effort to make that stability more durable and institutionalized," said Wang Zichen, deputy secretary-general of the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization.

====================================================================================================

The next war will be fought here. America and Europe will be enemies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:26:46 UTC
04:26:46 KST

The next war will be fought here. America and Europe will be enemies
This September, the Arctic quietly widened the rift between presumed transatlantic allies. Brussels’ attempts to mitigate growing US influence in the region have so far been unsystematic but intense. The Arctic Summit held in Finnish Lapland and the subsequent EU-Canada talks, where European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed granting Ottawa associate member status, should be viewed in the context of the new agreement between the US and Greenland.
The EU is using its usual competitive methods in the polar race, plunging into a de facto confrontation with the US. An alternative to this could have been attempts to find its own legitimate place among the major players; however, the window of opportunity for such initiatives has closed, which leaves the space no alternatives other than the prospects of a hybrid war in which Brussels and Washington are rivals.
The EU’s familiar patterns beyond the Arctic Circle
Twelve EU countries and the bloc’s leadership attended the Arctic Summit in Lapland this month, where they agreed upon a radical securitization of polar policy, officially recognizing the region as a “geopolitical hotspot.”
To understand the specifics of the bloc’s Arctic ambitions, it’s important to note that the union’s members lack any significant infrastructure of their own on the polar map. In the wake of Brexit, the EU no longer has its own sovereign Arctic borders directly connected to the Arctic Ocean. Norway and Iceland remain outside the union, Greenland remains an autonomous Danish overseas territory, and Finland and Sweden are geographically cut off from the ocean. Moreover, the EU as a single bloc completely lacks its own Arctic icebreaker fleet – the few national vessels of the Scandinavian countries are incapable of ensuring true strategic dominance.
Lacking either geographical rights or military hardware, Brussels has reduced its Arctic strategy solely to environmental concerns, climate monitoring, and the protection of indigenous peoples. In 2008, the EU formally designated the Arctic as a zone of its strategic interests, and in 2016 and 2021, key EU Arctic strategies were adopted.
This approach began to change in 2022–2025, when, against the backdrop of a rapidly shifting geopolitical situation in the world, US claims to Greenland triggered the performative landing of European troops on the island. The Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi this month, which was informal in nature, confirmed the shift in the focus of the EU’s interests.
The final agreement formalized the shift from an environmental agenda to a “hard power” strategy: the parties pledged to sharply increase investment in military mobility, satellite surveillance, and cross-border infrastructure in the north, as well as coordinate the blocking of Russia’s “shadow fleet” under the pretext of environmental protection. These decisions, reinforced by the leaders’ demonstrative visit to the Finnish Lapland Air Wing military airbase, formed the basis of the new EU Arctic Strategy, which Foreign Minister Kaja Kallas promised to present in October 2026.
After the summit, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen went on to invite Canada to become an associate member of the EU in the context of trade and tariff disagreements between Ottawa and Washington. The mere suggestion of such an alliance has maximized the politicization of the Arctic agenda, making the outcome highly unpredictable.
It’s worth noting that Brussels’ aspirations for leadership are always specific. It’s enough to recall Francois Duchene’s concepts of “civic” power and Jan Manners’ idea of “normative” power, which explain that Brussels projects its influence on the international stage through its economic model, diplomacy, and the export of legal and ethical standards. This approach has been further developed by Mark Leonard, who called the EU an expanding “invisible empire” and argued that the EU’s influence is based on the mechanism of attracting and integrating its neighbors, and Ana Bradford, who described the phenomenon of the “Brussels effect” – a mechanism by which the EU’s vast internal market allows it to unilaterally dictate regulatory rules to transnational corporations and governments around the world.
It is precisely in this vein that we should understand what is happening. Brussels is employing its standard, decades-old methods of supranational control. Unable to compete in the realm of real icebreaker technology and innovative logistics, the EU is attempting to redirect the race to its familiar channel of bureaucratic regulations, climate quotas, and virtual budget allocations, all while cloaking it in the most anti-Russian, defensive rhetoric possible.
Its urgent proposal to pursue a “unique” alliance with Canada is a classic attempt at normatively co-opting another country’s sovereignty. Brussels seeks to act as an “environmental and technological sponsor” and thus gain access to Canadian resources, thereby legitimizing its presence in the high north through the use of foreign geography.
It is for this reason that seemingly unrelated countries, including some of Moscow’s most committed foes, were invited to the summit in Lapland: a crowd had to be assembled to give the story a larger scope. It included Mediterranean Greece and Black Sea Romania, as well as the Baltic states, which were simply counting on participating in the new EU “polar” grants.
Why doesn’t this work?
Until recently, European activity has served as a mere backdrop for US policy in the Arctic. Washington has spent decades building an Arctic empire of steel, radar arrays, and military bases, relying on a strategy of strict deterrence. In Alaska, the US has deployed a powerful air force hub of fifth-generation F-35 and F-22 fighter jets, and American nuclear submarines have learned to maneuver under the ice. In September 2026, the White House and Ottawa began the practical phase of deploying Arctic Over-the-Horizon Radars (A-OTHR) as part of the modernization of NORAD, which will allow US command to monitor airspace all the way to the Arctic Circle in real time.
At the same time, Washington is accelerating the elimination of its main vulnerability – its backlog of icebreakers: the Bollinger shipyards are assembling the first heavy polar ship in half a century, the USCGC Polar Sentinel. Washington’s plans by 2030 include the launch of two more heavy icebreakers and the construction of the deep-water military port of Nome near the Bering Strait. Furthermore, active lobbying is underway to promote the concept of “freedom of navigation” to allow unimpeded passage through the Northwest Passage, significantly shortening the sea route from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean.
The US’s greatest geopolitical victory, however, was the signing of a trilateral agreement with Denmark and Greenland in September. Under the agreement, the Pentagon takes permanent military control of Greenland’s security, urgently reopening the bases in Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig and expanding and modernizing the Pituffik air force base in the north. This document imposed a direct veto on major investments by non-NATO and non-European countries, turning the island into a closed American bastion and blocking European businesses from accessing local rare earth metals.
In the European press, attitudes toward the trilateral defense agreement range from irony to muted relief, but the key leitmotif is the thesis of Donald Trump’s “defeat” and concessions. However, an analysis of the benefits to both sides reveals something else. The United States, having expanded its defense rights on the island and gained complete control over its economic resources, skillfully left any social obligations outside the agreement.
American strategists magnanimously left the obligation to provide benefits, subsidies, and social guarantees for the local Greenlandic population of fewer than 60,000 people out of the state budget, as it was the “sovereign right” of Copenhagen. Washington pocketed all the geostrategic and raw material dividends while shifting the maintenance of the depressed territory to weakening European taxpayers. It turns out that Trump’s European allies were willing to sign what he wanted, while publicly declaring that they had won.
This episode aptly characterizes the nature of the escalating standoff between the allies, in which the US, with its aggressiveness, puts the Europeans on the defensive, leaving them unable to maintain their positions. What makes this standoff unique is that there is no direct military clash between the US and the EU in the Arctic – they ostensibly remain NATO allies facing Russia and China. However, the region has de facto become a zone of intense geoeconomic espionage, trade wars, competition for ports, and the monopolization of polar resources, with the US securing military control of Greenland and the EU attempting to maintain its economic position through Canada and the Scandinavian countries. Interesting developments in the struggle for the Northwest Passage are likely to emerge.
The EU is extremely vulnerable in this standoff. This is due to its geographic isolation, a complete lack of hard power instruments, and a critical defense dependence on its main competitor. The attempt by European “hawks” to turn Article 42.7 of the Lisbon Treaty into a political shield and send symbolic contingents to Greenland in January turned out to be a bluff, which Donald Trump simply ignored, blackmailing countries with the threat of 25% tariffs. In the context of harsh American neo-mercantilism, under pressure from competition with China, Anu Bradford’s vaunted “Brussels effect” has collapsed: by establishing strict “green” standards at the Lapland summit, Europe had hoped to regulate the polar market. But the US, acting on the principle of “like it or not,” is hijacking the agenda, proving that in this polar race, Brussels’ old models simply will not work.
Prospects and Alternatives: Effects for Russia and China
As political scientist and Valdai Club program director Timofey Bordachev rightly notes, historical experience shows that conflicts among the Western elites have typically led to the large-scale restructuring of the international order, helping to keep the global system under the control of a narrow group of states. However, today, in the changed historical context, the results of the polar confrontation between Washington and Brussels are completely unpredictable. On the world stage, the number of sovereign players has radically expanded, and the West’s influence over them is either completely absent or negligible.
The growing transatlantic rift is opening up crucial strategic advantages for the Arctic’s major players – Moscow and Beijing. Russia is systematically developing the Northern Sea Route (NSR) as a key, protected, year-round global artery. While Washington is still attempting to complete its first heavy icebreaker in half a century, Russia possesses the world’s only and absolutely unparalleled nuclear icebreaker fleet.
For China, Brussels’ polar impasse serves as a direct call to action. Under American pressure, Beijing is pushing forward with its “Ice Silk Road” doctrine. Chinese businesses are freely redirecting investments into Russia’s Arctic LNG megaprojects, bypassing vulnerable southern routes. The EU states, having maneuvered but failed to escape American traps, are leaving the region with nothing, cementing the absolute geopolitical dominance of Moscow and Beijing in the ice.

Russia plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones, loitering munitions next year, Zelensky says
Russia plans to spend $12 billion next year on the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 26, citing Ukrainian military intelligence.
Zelensky said Ukrainian intelligence had obtained Russian internal documents showing the volumes of weapons Russia is preparing to produce next year and the funding allocated for them.
In recent months, Russia has increasingly relied on jet-powered drones in attacks on Ukrainian cities. In some attacks on Kyiv, jet-powered drones have accounted for around two-thirds of all drones launched.
"Next year, just for the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, Russia plans to spend $12 billion on this one category of weapons," Zelensky said.
Zelensky said Ukraine is scaling up production of interceptor drones to counter Russia's increasingly widespread use of jet-powered drones. Several interceptor prototypes are already being tested in combat, he said, with some identified as potential primary means of defense against the weapons.
"We are scaling up production and components. There will be a response," Zelensky said.
The remarks come as Russia has intensified its attacks against Ukraine in recent days, despite renewed international efforts to secure a ceasefire. U.S. President Donald Trump called for an end to the war during his address to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, while Zelensky said following their meeting that Ukraine was ready to accept a ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure if Russia agreed to the same terms.
Zelensky said Russia's planned spending on attack drones shows that Moscow is not preparing to halt the war "at least for now."
He also said Ukraine's partners need to increase pressure on Russia through sanctions and strengthen joint efforts to defend against drones.
Ukraine currently intercepts about 55% of Russia's jet-powered Shahed-type drones, according to Zelensky. More than 2,730 jet-powered Shaheds were launched against Ukraine in September, he said.
Zelensky said Ukraine aims to raise the interception rate to the level achieved against conventional Shahed drones, which he said is above 90%.
Ukraine has already signed 11 drone deals, according to Zelensky. The 11th, with Finland, was signed this week in New York on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
He said Ukraine is preparing a 12th agreement, which it expects to sign with another country in the coming weeks.
"For Ukraine, this means more production capacity, more funding, and more technological advantages," Zelensky said.
Zelensky also said Russia is conducting a campaign targeting Ukrainian data centers, infrastructure, and communications. He said the goal is to leave Ukrainians without internet access, communications, and digital services.
Earlier, Russia's attacks on Kyiv on Sept. 26 caused internet outages across the capital and disrupted access to some online services.
