Israel's Elor Azaria syndrome has come full circle - and 'NAZA' is the consequence - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
18:37:13 UTC
03:37:13 KST

In a single week, Israel was confronted with two stories about the moral character of its army.
The first was NAZA, a documentary built around anonymous testimony from soldiers and intelligence personnel alleging grave misconduct in Gaza.
The government and the IDF responded with categorical denials, attacks on the witnesses’ credibility, threats, and accusations that the film was defamatory.
The second was President Isaac Herzog’s decision to erase the criminal record of Elor Azaria, the soldier convicted of killing a wounded and incapacitated Palestinian terrorist in Hebron in 2016.
These events are not separate. One helps explain the other.
Azaria served his sentence and is entitled to rebuild his life. Mercy after punishment is a legitimate principle. But the public presentation of Herzog’s decision was not primarily about rehabilitation.
Politicians and headlines treated it as vindication: the symbolic correction of an injustice committed against a soldier who had supposedly been persecuted for protecting Israelis.
It was no such thing. The conviction has not been overturned. A military court examined the evidence and concluded that Azaria shot Abdel Fattah al-Sharif after he had been wounded, disarmed, and no longer posed an immediate threat.
The ability to distinguish between killing an active threat and killing someone after that threat has passed is not weakness. It is the difference between a disciplined military and an armed mob.
At the time, the affair rapidly transformed into a political loyalty test. Azaria became “everyone’s child,” while the commanders, investigators, and military judges who fulfilled their duties were accused of abandoning a soldier.
The shameful call against the then-IDF chief of staff, Gadi Eisenkot, was the realization and birth of the “Azaria syndrome”: “Gadi Gadi beware, Rabin seeks a friend.”
In a private letter to Herzog from IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir, which was later leaked, he objected to the motion. Azaria still has not voiced any remorse over his unlawful action.
A dictionary definition might define this syndrome as a political condition in which a soldier who violates military orders is recast as the victim, while the commanders and legal officers who enforce those orders are treated as traitors.
Its principal symptom is the transformation of accountability into betrayal, discipline into abandonment, and misconduct into heroism.
Its damage extends far beyond one soldier.
The political campaign surrounding Azaria delivered an unmistakable warning to every IDF commander: when you choose to investigate suspected wrongdoing, you may be accused of betraying the troops. When you defend the rules of engagement, you yourself may become a political target.
If you have the audacity to state publicly that even in war there are limits, politicians, activists, and commentators will most likely come after your career, your reputation, and your family.
The military institution learned the lesson, and since then caution has become the starting point. Ambiguity, slow action, and silence when controversy strikes have become safer than voicing moral clarity and publicly admitting any failure.
That is where NAZA enters the story.
The film presents 24 anonymous soldiers and intelligence officers making allegations about the conduct of the Gaza war.
Validity of the witnesses
The IDF argues that the identities and service histories of the witnesses cannot be verified, that some make claims beyond what people in their positions could have known, that the film misuses legal terminology, and that there are factual errors.
Those objections deserve serious consideration. Anonymous testimony is not beyond scrutiny. Nor should allegations of war crimes or systematic policy be accepted simply because they appear in a documentary.
War crimes have indeed been a part of warfare since the dawn of war. But a categorical denial is not enough.
When an army is politically punished for acknowledging moral failure, it gradually loses the ability to persuade the public that it can investigate itself. When commanders have learned that saying “this conduct violated our values” carries a personal price, even a truthful official denial may sound automatic.
That credibility vacuum is where films such as NAZA acquire their power.
The choice is not between accepting every anonymous allegation as fact and dismissing every allegation as anti-Israel or antisemitic propaganda.
A military confident in its values should be capable of distinguishing among false accusations, operational mistakes, unlawful orders, and individual crimes, and of speaking honestly about each.
For that to happen, commanders must know that the country will protect them when they enforce the law, including when their findings embarrass the government.
As someone who served in uniform and returned to reserve duty during war, I reject the claim that accountability means abandoning our soldiers.
Supporting soldiers means giving them clear, lawful orders; protecting them when they follow those orders; and investigating them fairly when evidence shows they did not.
Accountability is not betrayal. It is command.
It also protects Israel. The credibility of the IDF’s investigative mechanisms is one of the country’s most important moral and legal defenses. Israel has celebrated its legal institutions.
But every time politicians attack those mechanisms for political currency or for reaching an inconvenient conclusion, they strengthen the argument that Israel is incapable of investigating itself.
One cannot demand that the world trust the IDF’s investigations while politically persecuting the commanders who conduct them. One cannot dismiss NAZA by insisting that wrongdoing must be reported through official channels while teaching soldiers that those who report or acknowledge wrongdoing will be branded traitors.
The Azaria affair once demonstrated that the IDF could draw a line even amid terrorism and public anger. Since then, the political system, under Netanyahu, has spent the last decade trying to blur that line.
Herzog’s decision does not legally erase the conviction, but the celebration surrounding it rewrites its meaning.
Elor Azaria deserves to move forward with his life. Israel, however, cannot pardon itself from the lesson of his case.
The stain that should concern us is not the one removed from Azaria’s record. It is the fear left inside the IDF: that publicly defending the army’s values may be more dangerous than violating them.
The writer is director-general of International Relations at the Histadrut. He served in the IDF for 25 years, including as a spokesperson, and is an adjunct professor at Reichman University. Follow him on X: @LTCPeterLerner

Reading fiction has unique benefits for language and empathy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

For author Melanie Saward, stories are so much more than words.
"I think it's a safe way of confronting the parts of ourselves that we don't often like and that we need to sit with in order to grow," she says.
Dr Saward is a Bigambul and Wakka Wakka woman, academic and publishing all-rounder, who writes across multiple genres including Aboriginal romance novels.
She recognises the power of fiction to unpack biases.
"We all have these biases — I have things that I have to unpack that make me really, really uncomfortable — it's just because of society and how you're raised, your standpoint, and all those things that make you, you.
"Fiction is such a powerful way of privately confronting you with those things."
Studies show reading can increase empathy as we experience new perspectives and is linked with better brain health, cognition and mental wellbeing.
It is associated with a lower risk of dementia and slower cognitive decline in adults, and better attention, memory, executive function, academic achievement and mental health in children and adolescents.
So how does reading work in the brain?
Reading is an invented skill, according to Lili Yu, senior lecturer of psychological sciences at Macquarie University who studies how people read.
Dr Yu says reading uses parts of the brain, such as our attention and memory systems, we used for other purposes prior to the invention of the skill.
"Because reading is kind of a recent invention, that essentially means the processes involved in reading rely on lots of the cognitive systems we have already," she says.
Loading...
Put simply, when we encounter written text, the first thing our brain observes is the shape, or the "orthographic information", of the word.
We attach that visual information to what the word sounds like, known as the "phonological information".
Then we take those two different forms of information and mentally attach it to the meaning of the word. This is called lexical processing, Dr Yu explains.
Although this is the most common way to read, some people do this process slightly differently.
"Sometimes people see the form and go straight to the meaning, a tendency more commonly seen in logographic scripts like Chinese," she says.
Reading sentences is more complicated, requiring multiple cognitive systems to work together, including our memory, language and visual processing systems.
Dr Lili Yu says reading can strengthen our memory. It also increases our vocabulary and allows us to better understand nuances between words, she tells All In The Mind.
"The way we organise the words in our head becomes more sophisticated, and we know more of the nuances between different words."
Reading narrative fiction comes with its own unique benefits, Raymond Mar, a professor of psychology at York University in Toronto, adds.
"Fiction is a much stronger predictor of verbal abilities than non-fiction," he says.
"We know that language abilities are a great predictor of things like educational achievement and then later on, career achievement and success.
"So, given that we all recognise how important our verbal abilities are, I think it's really interesting that fiction is the one that seems to have the stronger influence."
Despite the benefits of reading for developing language, Australians are reading less than ever before and literacy levels in many OECD countries are declining or stagnating.
Beyond developing literacy, reading introduces us to different perspectives.
The relationship between reading and empathy
Professor Mar says there are two ways stories help us become better at navigating the world we live in.
"We know that reading fiction can help to hone the same sort of mental processes that we use to understand other people, including empathy and perspective-taking."
This effect has been observed in brain studies.
"What we find is parts of the brain that become active while we're reading narrative fiction are the same parts of the brain that are activated when we're trying to understand other people."
As reading improves empathy, increasing empathy may improve our reading skills.
"The better our empathy, the better our perspective-taking, the easier it is for us to understand stories," Professor Mar says.
Stories also may contain social knowledge about the world we can learn from.
For example, in one study, adolescents talk about how books helped them reflect on their emotions and gain greater insight into some of the challenging parts of their life.
And for older adults, reading can foster social connection, such as through book clubs.
"Getting together to discuss different perspectives on a novel that everyone's read is a great way to spend time and a great way to bond with others."
The benefits of reading aren't limited to physical books, Professor Mar says.
Listening to audiobooks can also boost empathy.
"The content matters so much more than the modality so I don't think people should feel guilty at all for listening to audiobooks.
"As long as what we have is a representation of other people, their experiences, their interior life, we would see kind of similar results, similar benefits."
Reading to expand your world view
Dr Saward remembers a book that was particularly impactful for her: Claire G Coleman's Terra Nullius.
"It just was a moment where you go, 'Wow, even me, with my brain, I've still got things to unlearn and learn,' and that's kind of exciting.
"I love that every book you pick up could have something like that in there," she says.
Her advice to readers is to diversity your bookshelf.
"Find the thing that you like and then try and find it from a perspective outside your own," she says.
"If it's a hockey romance and you're a straight woman, maybe read one of the queer hockey romances.
"Try and read a little bit outside of your comfort zone, you never know what you might find."
Listen to All In The Mind to hear the episode and subscribe to the podcast for more stories about mental health and wellbeing.

In Germany, the routes of around 300 trains were disrupted due to the theft of railway cables
Kyiv • UNN
Railway cables were stolen in the Gelsenkirchen area, causing disruptions to the movement of around 300 trains. Police are investigating the theft.
On Saturday, September 26, major disruptions to train services occurred in Germany in the area of the city of Gelsenkirchen due to railway cables being cut and stolen. About 300 regional and intercity trains were affected by the incident. This was reported by dpa, writes UNN.
Details
At around 4:15 a.m., several malfunctions in the signaling systems were recorded near Gelsenkirchen. According to Deutsche Bahn, unknown individuals cut several cables, some of which were subsequently stolen.
The damage disrupted, among other services, intercity connections from Dortmund to Munich, from Hamburg to Basel, and from northern Germany to Cologne. Trains were forced to take diversionary routes or skip certain stops.
Repair work was completed around noon. After that, the first trains began running through the Gelsenkirchen area, but Deutsche Bahn warned that delays and other disruptions could continue throughout the second half of the day.
State and federal police inspected the scene and collected evidence. Law enforcement officials believe that the incident was caused by cable theft rather than deliberate sabotage.

Netanyahu backed Hamas civilian understandings one day after ‘major attack’ warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26

The New York Times reported overnight that during a security assessment on Oct. 1, 2023, six days before the massacre, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu disregarded warnings he had received and did not mention them. Now, documents revealed Saturday evening by Israel’s Channel 13 News explicitly show that one of the decisions made at that meeting was to “advance a civilian understandings with Hamas.”
That security assessment followed a telephone situation review on Sept. 27. According to a report published Saturday night by The Atlantic, Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel had arrived in Israel a day earlier and warned of a “major attack” by Hamas. According to The New York Times and other reports, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed also warned Netanyahu, apparently during the same week.
Participants in that situation review included then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, then-IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Herzi Halevi and the heads of the Mossad and Shin Bet at the time, David Barnea and Ronen Bar.
At the start of the discussion, Netanyahu said: “There are changing trends in all the arenas that we are required to address — in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, as a central driver of terrorism. We are working to contain and reduce the escalation through the judicious and controlled use of force (rather than completely refraining from it).”
Regarding Gaza, the document said officials should “continue preparations and activity along the fence in response to disturbances; sharpen and intensify the messages and actions regarding incendiary balloons; and begin and expand the use of measures involving humanitarian benefits, with an emphasis on workers (adding or reducing them depending on the conduct of the opposing side), as an additional tool alongside offensive measures.”
The document said Netanyahu stressed that “although we do not want to reach an escalation, preparations are required for flare-ups in both arenas.”
He therefore instructed officials to hold, under his leadership, “an in-depth security assessment as soon as possible, as well as a limited security consultation that will address ‘Ma’aseh Bereshit.’”
That security assessment was held several days later, on Oct. 1. According to the transcript, Netanyahu said at the outset: “From a broad national perspective, Israel currently has an opportunity to advance a historic peace agreement with Saudi Arabia. There are countries, actors and organizations that seek and are trying to derail the normalization process with Saudi Arabia, and we are required to fight and thwart those attempts.”
He said there was a need to “maintain an effective and measured level of security activity in response to the actions of our enemies (rather than ignoring and yielding to provocations).”
The document went on to say that, in light of this, the prime minister approved and clarified the operational policy, directives and priorities for the various arenas. Regarding Gaza, the decisions were:
- “Expand the use of measures involving humanitarian benefits, both granting and withdrawing them (‘accordion’), to influence Hamas’ conduct and policy. In the future, this should also be linked to terrorist intentions.”
- “Advance the civilian understandings with Hamas.”
- “Advance operational readiness for the recommended targeted operations — Hamas leaders (with an emphasis on emergencies), West Bank headquarters (in routine and emergency situations, from the air and covertly).”

Bangladeshi woman says Bengaluru hospital withheld husband’s body for 8 days over Rs 35L bill; High Commission intervenes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
18:19:21 UTC
03:19:21 KST

Tangila Islam Asha with her husband, Mohd Abdul Hakim Shabuj, when he was alive. (PC: Tangila Islam Asha)
A 26-year-old Bangladeshi woman has alleged that a leading private hospital in Bengaluru withheld her husband’s body for eight days over unpaid dues of Rs 35.79 lakh and retained her passport after he died during treatment. She received the body on Saturday after seeking help from Bangladesh High Commission. The hospital confirmed releasing the body but did not respond to her allegations. The hospital later said the patient had undergone critical care and surgical treatment after arriving with severe breathing difficulty and died despite the efforts of its medical teams.Tangila Islam Asha, 26, of Naugaon, told TOI that she and her husband, Mohammed Abdul Hakim Shabuj, 32, a contractual govt teacher in Bangladesh, arrived in Bengaluru on Sept 5 for treatment of his kidney ailment. Shabuj was admitted to ICU at Manipal Hospital on Old Airport Road the next day after developing severe chest pain and breathing difficulty.Asha said Shabuj underwent multiple procedures over the following days and his right leg was amputated on Sept 14 after it developed an infection. His condition subsequently deteriorated and he died around 1.30pm on Sept 18.“During his treatment, I paid a total of Rs 7.5 lakh in several instalments whenever they asked.
After his death, I was trying to understand how I would take his body back to Bangladesh when the hospital asked me to pay Rs 35.79 lakh and said the body would not be released without payment,” Asha told TOI.She alleged that the hospital neither provided receipts for the Rs 7.5 lakh nor gave her a prior cost estimate or explanation for the outstanding amount. “I was completely helpless. After they withheld the body for eight days and retained my passport, I wrote to hospital management and also contacted Bangladesh High Commission for help. Finally, they handed over the body on Saturday after making the dues nil,” she said.Mohammed Moqtadir Hossain, Shabuj’s friend from West Bengal, who travelled to Bengaluru after learning of her situation, said local activists helped Asha recover her passport on Friday and complete formalities for taking the body home. “Apart from the Rs 7.5 lakh she had already paid, she paid nothing more,” he told TOI.
When contacted, a Manipal Hospital office-bearer confirmed that the body was handed over on Saturday but declined to respond to Asha’s allegations. In a statement issued later, the hospital said Shabuj arrived with severe breathing difficulty, was found hypoxic and shifted to ICU, where he suffered a cardiac arrest and was resuscitated twice before being put on ECMO and ventilator support.The hospital said surgeons performed a pulmonary thromboendarterectomy on Sept 9 after tests showed clot formation and blockages in several regions. “Despite best efforts from the critical care as well as the surgical team, the patient succumbed to his illnesses on 18th September 2026,” it said.’

"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," he said.
"The kingdom stresses the importance of guaranteeing the protection of freedom of navigation in all international waterways, foremost among them the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al Mandab Strait, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Aden," he added.

On Palestine, Farhan said obstructing humanitarian aid to Gaza and attempts to displace Palestinians constitute violations of international law.
He also said the continued expansion of illegal Israeli settlements represents a serious violation of international law and international humanitarian law.
On Syria, he reiterated Riyadh’s rejection of any violations that threaten the country’s security and stability.
He also welcomed the US decision to remove Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
Turning to Iraq, the top Saudi diplomat affirmed Saudi support for Iraq’s sovereignty, security, and stability.
He stressed that Iraqi territory should not be used as a launching point for attacks against neighbouring countries.

South African police discover body of 10th woman near Johannesburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
18:08:12 UTC
03:08:12 KST

South African police discover body of 10th woman near Johannesburg
Police are investigating the killings in a country with one of the highest femicide rates in the world.
South African police have discovered the body of another woman east of the country’s commercial capital, Johannesburg, bringing the total number of female bodies found near the city since mid-July to 10.
Police confirmed the discovery in Thembisa, Ekurhuleni, on Saturday but have not provided any further information. The body was found in the morning, according to the daily newspaper, The Sowetan.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3South Africa gender commissioner: women ‘hunted’ amid femicide crisis
- list 2 of 3‘This is a war’: South Africa battles femicide as women’s bodies pile up
- list 3 of 3Fear and anger in South Africa as bodies of nine women found: What we know
The discovery adds to growing concern over violence against women in a country long plagued by violent crime. While police work to establish whether the killings are connected, there have been community concerns that the murders are being carried out by the same killer or killers.
Provincial police chief Tommy Mthombeni said the latest victim appeared to have been stoned to death, and a post-mortem examination would be conducted to determine the cause of death.
“We have put highly capable investigators on this case,” he told reporters at the scene, pledging to find those responsible for the killings.
President Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged the latest discovery while on the campaign trail for upcoming local elections, broadcaster eNCA reported.
“I’ve sadly heard about 10th body of a woman found in Thembisa,” Ramaphosa said. “This continues to make us very sad, and in many ways, it’s a shame on the men of South Africa that we continue to kill the women of our beautiful country.”
South Africa has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, with an average of 15 women killed per day.
Two women have been charged with the murder of the woman whose body was the ninth discovered, last week. Police have said that the killing may have stemmed from a relationship-related matter.
Mthombeni told state broadcaster SABC that investigators believe the ninth killing was an isolated case. However, he said it is possible some of the other killings are connected.
He added that some of the murders shared similarities, but cautioned that there is no conclusive evidence to suggest the same person or group is responsible.
Police discovered three bodies in July and August within six kilometres (four miles) of one another in Ekurhuleni. Earlier this month, six bodies were found in 10 days, also in Ekurhuleni.
Prior to Saturday’s discovery, all of the deceased women were in their 20s or 30s. Several of them were found completely or partially nude. Police have not yet confirmed the age of the 10th woman or whether she was clothed.
The first body, discovered in mid-July, was found naked. The deceased had been restrained with cable ties. Her boyfriend was subsequently arrested, but no charges were filed.

Europe's data centers may drive digital sovereignty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
18:08:00 UTC
03:08:00 KST

Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
September 26, 2026
Like coal-fired power plants and wind turbines, few people actually want a data center in their backyard. But they do want to use their services. As a global debate rages about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence, there are also many local discussions about where exactly the data centers needed to train and run AI should be built.
This is currently a major issue in Europe, where many governments and companies have decided that they would prefer to store data in Europe rather than in the United States, which is the global leader in computing. But more digital sovereignty in Europe will mean more consumption of the continent's resources.
According to the German Ministry for Economic Affairs, for every kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed, an average of between 0.4 and 4.4 liters (0.8 and 9.3 pints) of water is used to cool data centers, with the water either evaporating or being diverted back to tanks in a warmed state.
Massive water consumption
The summer that just ended was the hottest on record in Europe — in some areas, water use was restricted for residents, agriculture and even nuclear power plants. The summers are expected to get warmer, so many are wondering about the potential water consumption of data centers in the future.
They are also worried about the high electricity consumption of the centers. Fingrid, Finland's national grid operator, recently forecast that electricity consumption would rise by almost 40% if all projects with signed connection agreements were implemented in full.
This week, the European Commission announced a new scheme for data centers to increase transparency on their energy and water use. Those with a capacity of more than 500 kW will receive an efficiency grade that will also take into account their contribution to the grid, such as the reuse of waste heat. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills," said Teresa Ribera, the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.
Data centers in urban hubs and rural areas
Europe's most powerful data centers have primarily been built near the major cities of Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin (FLAP-D) because of high connectivity, proximity to users and businesses, and well-established ecosystems with specialized engineers and secure supply chains.
However, according to a report by the investment group CBRE, the situation is changing as these markets face power and grid infrastructure constraints. New data centers are being built in the Dutch city of Groningen, Barcelona in Spain or the Belgian capital Brussels, as well as in more rural areas.
And as this happens, there are more and more protests taking place, both on and offline. Earlier this month, hundreds turned up for a protest in front of tech giant Google's offices in the Austrian city of Linz, demonstrating against its already advanced plans to build a data center in the small town of Kronstorf.
Earlier this month, bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney successfully led a campaign to overturn planning permission for a proposed data center in the village of Killala, arguing that it would breach national climate policy.
In central France, meanwhile, several elected officials in the village of Etrechet have resigned over Google's plans to build a massive data center, which, at full capacity, would require between 880 megawatts and 1.1 gigawatts of electricity or the equivalent of the total output of a nuclear power plant. Etrechet mayor Florence Laurent told the French daily Le Monde that she was resigning out of a "sense of powerlessness, since the village has no decision-making power" regarding the project.
Some operators of data centers argue that the facilities can be built in such a way that they save energy. A large data center currently being built in Marseille will reportedly use a cooling system that requires 30% less power and consumes no water.
Other data centers, in Scandinavia, for example, use waste heat from the servers and route it into district heating networks via heat exchangers and pumps.
This spring, the German energy company E.ON published the results of a survey that found nearly three-quarters of people would be more likely to welcome data centers near residential areas if they fed their waste heat into the heating network.
Data center operators also argue that the facilities can serve the public by connecting the batteries that usually provide backup power to local grids so that there is uninterrupted service in the event of power outages or at times of peak demand.
For proponents of building more data centers in Europe, the facilities not only contribute to the continent's digital sovereignty but also help to strengthen energy independence.
Monir Ghaedi contributed to this article, which was translated from German.

Indoor gardening improves mental health and quality of life for cancer patients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
18:00:22 UTC
03:00:22 KST

Growing vegetables indoors without soil might help cancer patients feel better emotionally and physically. A recent study found that patients who tended to countertop hydroponic gardens experienced improved mental health and an enhanced overall quality of life. The research was published in Frontiers in Public Health.
A cancer diagnosis often brings severe physical and emotional challenges that extend far beyond the immediate medical treatment. Estimates suggest that one in four cancer patients in the United States experiences depression. Poor mental health can negatively affect a patient’s recovery, sometimes leading to unplanned treatment interruptions. Patients battling depression also face a higher risk of cancer recurrence and reduced survival rates. Pain is another distressing symptom, and the perception of that pain is often influenced by emotional and cognitive factors.
To address these overlapping challenges, medical professionals sometimes recommend non-clinical activities to support patient wellbeing, an approach known as social prescribing. Traditional outdoor gardening often provides psychological relief, lowers stress, and encourages healthier eating. It offers moderate physical activity and a connection to nature, which can improve mood and reduce fatigue. Studies indicate that time spent around plants can even shorten hospital stays and boost overall patient satisfaction.
However, outdoor gardening requires a yard, physical stamina, and favorable weather. These requirements exclude many people, especially those living in dense urban areas, apartment buildings, or those undergoing exhausting medical treatments. Recognizing this limitation, researchers sought an alternative that could be easily managed inside the home.
Lead author Taehyun Roh, a public health researcher at Texas A&M University, alongside colleagues from Houston Methodist Hospital and Texas A&M, initiated this research to test an indoor solution. They focused on hydroponics, a method of growing plants in water rather than soil. By adding liquid nutrients directly to a water reservoir and using artificial light, people can cultivate vegetables indoors year-round. This approach eliminates exposure to soil-borne diseases, weeds, and toxic chemicals like herbicides.
The team recruited adult cancer patients receiving outpatient infusion therapy at a specialized cancer center in Houston. The small study ultimately included thirty-six participants with an average age of fifty-seven. These individuals had various types of cancer and had completed at least one cycle of chemotherapy. Instead of using a separate control group, the researchers used a case-crossover design where each patient served as their own baseline for comparison over time.
Each participant received a countertop hydroponic system called an AeroGarden. The kits included everything needed to grow heirloom salad greens. They featured a growing container, an automated light-emitting diode (LED) grow light, liquid plant food, and twelve seed pods. The systems were designed to be highly accessible, ensuring that even people with no previous gardening experience could participate.
For eight weeks, the patients managed the kits in their own homes. They independently planted the seeds, monitored the water levels, and eventually harvested the greens. The researchers provided instructional materials and manufacturer manuals to help the patients optimize plant growth. These materials included troubleshooting advice to resolve common issues associated with indoor plant cultivation.
To track the intervention, the researchers surveyed the participants at the beginning of the study, at the four-week mark, and at the end of the eight weeks. They used standardized questionnaires to measure changes in mental wellbeing, psychological distress, and overall quality of life. The surveys evaluated multiple functional domains, including how well patients could perform physical activities and manage their emotions. They also asked the patients to rate their pain levels and frequency of fruit and vegetable consumption.
Over the course of the eight weeks, the participants reported steady improvements in their mental health. Their overall mental wellbeing scores rose steadily during the intervention. At the same time, their self-reported symptoms of depression declined steadily from the baseline to the end of the study.
The patients also experienced enhancements in their daily quality of life. They reported better emotional and social functioning, meaning they felt more capable of managing their feelings and interacting with friends and family. At the same time, their struggles with a lack of appetite diminished over the study period.
Growing food at home also appeared to influence the participants’ eating habits. By the end of the study, the patients were eating more fruits and dark green leafy vegetables than they had at the start. Experiencing a direct connection between their own efforts and tangible, edible rewards might help sustain long-term dietary changes.
Not all metrics changed during the intervention. While overall pain management scores trended downward slightly, those changes were not statistically significant. Changes in anxiety and stress levels were also not statistically significant during the eight-week period.
The researchers noted several psychological mechanisms that could explain the benefits of therapeutic horticulture. Nurturing plants fosters a sense of responsibility and achievement. This feeling of control can be especially helpful for patients who might feel a sudden loss of autonomy during rigorous medical treatments. The multisensory engagement of interacting with plants also supports cognitive restoration and natural stress relief.
This single-arm design means there was no separate control group to compare against the participants. Because all participants received the gardening kits, the setup introduces a risk of self-selection bias. The people who agreed to participate might have already had a positive attitude toward gardening, which could influence how much they benefited from the activity.
The eight-week timeframe is relatively short, preventing the researchers from observing any long-term effects on the patients’ mental or physical health. Kit usage was reported entirely by the patients themselves without independent verification. Future investigations with larger groups of people, longer observation periods, and more objective tracking methods are necessary to determine if these benefits endure over time.
The study, “Indoor hydroponic vegetable gardening to improve mental health and quality of life in cancer patients: a pilot study,” was authored by Taehyun Roh, Laura Ashley Verzwyvelt, Anisha Aggarwal, Raj Satkunasivam, Nishat Tasnim Hasan, Nusrat Fahmida Trisha, and Charles Hall.

Congress leader Jairam Ramesh said the Commission had issued the statement only after the media reports and nationwide protests seeking Kumar's removal.
NEW DELHI: The Congress on Saturday demanded the immediate suspension of the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and called for chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation or prosecution. Their demand comes after the Election Commission issued a fresh statement defending its decisions amid reported differences within the poll body.Congress leaders Pawan Khera and Jairam Ramesh accused the EC of going into "damage control" mode following an Indian Express report and subsequent media coverage on differences between the three election commissioners. The party alleged that the SIR exercise had led to the "disenfranchisement" of crores of voters and questioned the Commission's explanation on changes to Form 6, used to add names to electoral rolls.
"The ECI's press note today is too lame, too little, too late," Congress' head of media and publicity department Pawan Khera said.Ramesh said the Commission had issued the statement only after the media reports and nationwide protests seeking Kumar's removal."It has just issued a wishy-washy Press Note that raises further questions on its intent, integrity, impartiality and credibility," he said on X."The ongoing SIR, which has turned out to be a method of massive disenfranchisement of several crores of Indians, must be suspended immediately without delay.
"In the meantime, nothing short of the CEC's resignation or prosecution will suffice," he said in a two-page statement.
Congress questions EC's explanation
The Election Commission said all SIR orders were issued after approval from all three Election Commissioners. It also said changes to Form 6 had been upheld by the Supreme Court.The Commission further said letters written by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi to the Cabinet Secretary were not related to any policy decision of the Commission or its IT division. According to the EC, the letters concerned the functioning of an officer deputed to the poll body.Ramesh said the EC statement did not directly deny the findings reported by the Indian Express."First, the Press note does not directly deny the story or its findings. It makes a defensive attempt to downplay the same in paragraph 3(i) and 3(ii) but does not say that the allegations are baseless," he said.On Goa, he said the EC's response showed that 81 of the 97 deleted voters had already filled Form 6 to be included again in the electoral rolls."To put this another way, you disenfranchise voters through a broken and corrupt system, and when caught say that they are being added back," Ramesh said.Khera also alleged that the EC had not addressed objections raised by the other two Election Commissioners over changes to Form 6."That objection was not resolved then. It was not resolved since. And this 'mother of all objections' has still not been addressed - even after today's so-called unanimous meeting," Khera said on X."So until the ECI answers this specific legal objection, no length of press notes, no claim of unanimity or any other clownery can save Gyanesh Kumar Gupta's face," he said."It is still not too late for him. He should resign and turn approver, or prepare for jail," Khera added.
Congress raises questions over voter deletions
Ramesh also questioned the EC's reliance on a Supreme Court order of May 27 saying the order had preceded the recent media revelations."The order which was pronounced well before the recent revelations will not save the CEC for the malicious deletion of targeted voters, for the incompetence that has resulted in citizens being wiped off the roles, for the crores lost in both expenses and man-hours due to the confusion and harassment caused to entire families," he said.He also questioned the extension of voter registration deadlines in Delhi and Maharashtra and asked what would happen to voters in Karnataka, Telangana, Bihar and West Bengal."What happens to the voters disenfranchised in Bihar and West Bengal? The ECI has no answer for its targeted disenfranchisement, beginning mid-July through wholly illegal changes made to Form 6 (unseen and unapproved by Parliament) which placed an unfair burden on them to find and disclose their parents and/or grandparents' details," he said.He listed several allegations that he said required answers, including the "unilateral nature of decision making by the CEC", alleged bias against the Opposition, alleged participation in "vote chori", the enrolment of Gen Z voters and alleged negligence in the deletion and updating of electoral rolls.Ramesh said the CEC could not avoid scrutiny through bureaucratic procedures."He stands exposed and is now petrified as an entire country seeks to hold him accountable," Ramesh said.

Belfast court injuncts decision to allow Orange Order march down Garvaghy Road
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
17:48:38 UTC
02:48:38 KST

A controversial loyalist parade down a nationalist street in Portadown has been temporarily injuncted after a high court judge urged all sides to “step back from the abyss” and take responsible decisions for “the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland”.
The ruling was made amid rising fears that a parade could unleash fresh sectarian violence, 28 years after the parade route was banned due to disorder.
After a five-hour hearing at a special sitting of the high court, Justice Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade, which was due to take place at 8am on Sunday, until a judicial review application can be fully heard.
She has also suspended the determination by the Parades Commission on Friday that the event could take place, albeit with restrictions on numbers.
However tensions remain with an appeal against her decision by loyalists to be heard at a second special hearing on Saturday night.
Smyth arrived at her conclusions after several attempts to coax the parties, the Loyalist Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, to reach a voluntary agreement.
After it was clear that was not possible, she said: “The level of mistrust between residents and Portadown Loyalist Lodge cannot be overstated. Neither side accepts any of the reassurances of the other.”
The march down Garvaghy Road has been banned for 28 years due to widespread sectarian violence in 1998 outside Drumcree church.
“It is also clear to me that this particular long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland,” Smyth said.
The court was sitting on Saturday after a last-minute legal challenge by the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition.
Smyth urged the parties to reach a voluntary agreement to delay the march, given few had time to digest the reasoning behind the commission’s decision.
It was important “to reach an agreement for the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland, not just for your sake” to have the issues “properly aired” so that “everybody knows they’ve had a fair hearing”.
“Be big enough to step back from the abyss,” she told the parties in court.
This followed a high court ruling quashing the restrictions on the annual parade route.
The Portadown loyalist Orange Lodge was not represented at the hearing. But after a request from the judge for its view through the individual who had sought permission for the parade, the lodge made it clear it would not agree to suspending the procession.
The SDLP leader, Claire Hanna, said the parade plan was “provocative”. She told residents she was “so sorry” that some “bad faith actors” were “intent on reopening the hurt and the traumas of the past”.
Fears of clashes increased on Saturday after a request to the commission for permission for a countermarch, a protest that, it was estimated, could be attended by up to 5,000 people, the court heard. That was later revised to 300.
On Friday night, the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, appealed to leaders to “work calmly” through the weekend while the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, called for “cool heads”, saying Northern Ireland had “withstood many moments of sharp disagreement over the years” and must do so again.
Before her ruling, Smyth asked the parties in court, including the Police Service of Northern Ireland and the Parades Commission, to “consider carefully the very important issues to our society” raised in this case, and the importance that they were dealt with properly given the “importance of this case to community relations”.
She also noted that the issues of judicial review were of “such fundamental importance” that it could be unwise to hold a full hearing without all the facts.
Delivering her ruling, Smyth said: “The level of mistrust between the residents and the Portadown Orange lodge cannot be overstated.
“Neither side accepts any reassurance provided by the other or that there’s any genuine reason for the stance adopted by the other.”
She added: “It’s also clear to me that this particular long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland.
“Against that background I am thoroughly of the view that the issues of all three parties must be properly ventilated so that whenever an ultimate decision is made by this court the parties know they were heard.”
Democratic Unionist MP Carla Lockhart insisted nationalist residents on the road had “nothing to fear” from the march on Sunday, but Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald described the decision as “utterly reckless”.
The Parades Commission has placed a number of restrictions on the procession, including an 8am start and limiting the number of participants to 35 people, but not placing any restrictions on the route.

WASHINGTON/UNITED NATIONS/CAIRO - US President Donald Trump said on Sept 26 he had rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the Middle East.
Iran raised the initiative at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators and that it could reopen the strategic waterway and put an end to hostilities in the region within seven days.
But in comments to reporters at the White House, Trump said: “I reject their proposal... I rejected their deal.”
“They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” he said, before leaving for Tennessee.
“We’re winning tremendously. They want to make a deal and I think that’s fine, I like making a deal too. What they want to do is immediately open the Hormuz Strait... because they have no money coming in, because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait,” Trump said.
The US has imposed an economic blockade on Iran to put pressure on Tehran to lift its blockade of Hormuz, which has drastically reduced shipping through the strait, even though Trump again asserted that the US had control of the waterway.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed US officials.
It said Trump was privately sceptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm elections to Congress.
A US official had said earlier that discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive”.
Conflict has disrupted oil flows, hramed global economy
The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through a critical shipping lane and taken a toll on the global economy.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters at the United Nations on Sept 25 the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.
“If there is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared,” Araqchi said. If the US were to agree, the warring parties could start wider talks “on mutually agreed subjects.”
That could potentially include discussions of Iran’s nuclear programme. Trump has said Tehran must never acquire a nuclear bomb, while a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear programme even if the US accepted its peace deal.
Iran would grant no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, the official said.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face The Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons.”
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed to end the war, which began on Feb 28 with US and Israeli attacks.
Since then the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging Iran’s already ailing economy.
Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. REUTERS

Nearly one million people attend Pope Leo's open-air mass in Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
17:41:38 UTC
02:41:38 KST

Crowds stretched the length of the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in Paris on Saturday, as Pope Leo XIV urged Catholics to find happiness in faith, not material things, at the biggest event of his visit to France, an outdoor Mass with an estimated 800,000 people.
Chants of "Leo, Leo" and "Long live the Pope" echoed down the roughly 2 km (1.2 miles) tree-lined boulevard, from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe, as people pressed against security barriers for a glimpse of Leo as he arrived in an open-top popemobile.
The vehicle paused frequently as people waved white and yellow Vatican flags and Leo blessed people with disabilities, children and babies passed forward by volunteers.
Attendees included Brigitte Macron, the French president's wife, far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls ahead of next year's presidential election, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and Bernard Arnault, the billionaire chairman of French luxury group LVMH.
Cheers rang out in the crowd as Leo thanked God in his sermon for the chance to visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour, during which he is seeking to repair the Church's standing after abuse scandals caused nationwide shock.
The pope told Catholics that only their faith would provide true happiness.
"Only God can fill the emptiness within us," said the pope.
Benoit Dedieu-Anglade, 67, said after the Mass that he had been impressed by the speech.
"We must not give in to the easy path or distractions — and I was moved by how he expressed this in such clear, lucid French," he said.
Praise for Pope Leo's message of peace
Attendees began assembling before sunrise to hear the pontiff speak at the mid-afternoon Mass.
The pope, who has forcefully decried the direction of global leadership in recent months, warned in a speech on Friday at the Paris headquarters of the UN culture and education body, UNESCO, that the UN and other multilateral groups were in crisis.
He also repeated his frequent appeal for the world to reconsider the development of artificial intelligence, telling French leaders that AI could create a future where "a paradise of machines" takes control of the Earth.
He has also frequently spoken out for peace, including in remarks with French leaders at the Elysee on Friday, with his comments criticizing the Iran war earlier this year drawing a rebuke from US President Donald Trump.
Pierre-Marie Estienne, 36, was in the crowd for Leo's Mass in central Paris with his wife and their four young children.
"We live in an era of great materialism," he said before Leo arrived. "There is a lot of evil around us, so we need a message of hope and love."
Pope visits newly baptized Catholics
France, a secular nation where the separation of church and state is enshrined in a 1905 law, has witnessed a steady decline in affiliation to the Catholic Church since World War Two, mirroring a trend in other traditionally Catholic countries.
Although the French Bishops' Conference points to an increase in baptisms of adults, including a record 21,000 last Easter, a report published by the official statistics agency, INSEE, showed that only 25% of French 18-to-49-year-olds identified as Catholic, compared with 43% a decade earlier.
In a visit on Saturday with newly baptized Catholics at the Catholic University of Paris before the Mass, Leo urged the French church not to be "naively optimistic" about the recent increase in adherents.
"We must recognize, welcome and protect the small flame that the Holy Spirit has kindled in the darkness of the night, the tiny seed that strives to grow even amid the thorns," he said.
Leo heads later on Saturday to Lourdes, home to a Catholic shrine. He will meet seven French victims of abuse by clergy there on Sunday.

Iran responsible for antisemitic terror attacks in Liège, Antwerp earlier this year - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
17:41:37 UTC
02:41:37 KST

The Islamic regime is directly responsible for two separate terrorist attacks in the Belgian cities of Liège and Antwerp earlier this year, KAN News reported on Saturday.
The report cited the Belgian Coordination Unit for Threat Analysis (CUTA) Director Gert Vercauteren, who told French broadcaster RTBF on Thursday that the terrorists in both attacks "certainly" acted on instructions from Tehran to attack Jewish targets around the world.
The attacks referred to by Vercauteren include an arson attack against a vehicle outside a Jewish-owned business in Antwerp and an explosion at a synagogue in Liège, with both attacks occurring in March.
The Ashab al-Yamin Islamist group claimed responsibility for the Antwerp attack, publishing a video that appeared to show three masked individuals setting a vehicle on fire. Two minors were arrested in connection with the attack, while Ynet News reported at the time that the targeted vehicle's owner was not Jewish despite the attackers believing him to be haredi (ultra-Orthodox).
According to KAN, Vercauteren said both attacks were part of a coordinated campaign, including an additional attempted attack targeting a Dutch synagogue, which was foiled by Belgian intelligence agencies.
Vercauteren: Belgium threat level 'very serious' primarily due to Iran war
CUTA currently lists the threat level in Belgium as "very serious," according to the agency's website. Vercauteren attributed the high threat level to the "geopolitical context, particularly the war in Iran."
"In 2025, the main threat continued to come from the Islamist jihadist movement, even though this share decreased," he told RTBF. "These are primarily newly radicalized individuals, because those who have returned from Syria or Iraq in the meantime generally do not pose a threat."
"There has been significant disillusionment," he added. "Generally speaking."
US extremism a 'dystopian vision,' Vercauteren says
Vercauteren further attributed the threat level to rising extremism in the United States, describing the situation to RTBF as a "dystopian vision."
"They want to sow chaos and violence," he emphasized. "They are fascinated by extreme violence. And the images they circulate among themselves come from various scenes, from the neo-Nazi world, for example, even Satanist ones."
He stressed that such extremists seek out "vulnerable victims," noting that this often includes minors.
"We learned our lessons, I must say," he said. "They were hard lessons, but the government and the services understood that we had to do things differently and better."
He concluded that the issues of extremism are a "societal problem that security services alone cannot solve. Therefore, security, prevention, and reintegration must be linked."
Mathilda Heller and Reuters contributed to this report.

Is LBank Safe? Five Checks Before You Deposit in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
17:31:30 UTC
02:31:30 KST

Is LBank Safe? Five Checks Before You Deposit in 2026
LBank has been in business since 2015 and has spent the past year on the shirts of Argentina's national football team, so the name now reaches far beyond crypto circles. Whether it is safe for you depends on five things you can check yourself in about twenty minutes: whether you are allowed to open an account, whether the exchange proves its reserves, what its licences really cover, how well you lock your own account, and what the bonus terms ask of you.
Read this first. LBank's own User Service Agreement lists Iran, the United States, Canada and mainland China among the regions it does not serve. If you live in one of them, the rest of this checklist does not change that clause. This article explains a verification method; it is not a recommendation to open an account or to invest.
LBank at a glance: what can actually be verified
A handful of facts about LBank are easy to confirm from public sources. The company dates its founding to 2015. In late September 2025 it signed a multi-year deal with the Argentine Football Association to become a regional sponsor of the national team, running through the 2026 FIFA World Cup, and it has kept the partnership visible with fan campaigns since the tournament.
Other figures belong in a different column. LBank's press releases speak of more than 15 million registered users, a presence in over 210 countries and regions, daily volume above 4 billion dollars and a record of zero security incidents. These numbers come from the platform itself. They may be accurate, but nobody outside the company audits them, so a careful reader notes them without leaning on them.
Keep two columns: what public sources confirm, and what only the platform says.
Check 1: Are you allowed to open an account?
This is the question most reviews skip, and it matters most. The version of LBank's User Service Agreement published on its support centre (checked September 2026) names the countries and regions the exchange does not serve. The list includes Afghanistan, Belarus, mainland China, Hong Kong, Cuba, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, North Korea, Syria, Venezuela, the United States and Canada, among others.
The practical consequence is simple. An account opened from a restricted region can be frozen when the platform's compliance checks catch up with it, and the agreement leaves the user with little recourse. Using a VPN to hide your location does not change your residency; it only changes when the problem surfaces. LBank also has no local currency gateway for these markets, so any route that starts with a domestic exchange and ends with a crypto transfer still runs into the same residency clause.
Check 2: Does the exchange prove its reserves?
Since the collapse of FTX in 2022, the minimum sign of good faith from a centralised exchange has been a proof of reserves report: a published snapshot showing that customer balances are backed one to one, usually with a Merkle tree that lets each user confirm their own balance is included.
LBank does not publish such a report. That does not prove anything is wrong, but it removes the one tool an ordinary user has to check solvency from the outside. The reasonable response is to treat the exchange as a place to trade, not a place to store: keep only the balance you are actively using and withdraw the rest to a wallet you control.
Check 3: What do the licences and claims really cover?
Exchange marketing often lists registrations in several jurisdictions next to phrases such as "safe operations". Read each one for what it is. A money services registration is an anti money laundering filing, not a prudential licence that requires capital reserves or protects client funds. A claim of zero security incidents is a statement about the past made by the company. Neither replaces the verifiable evidence in Check 2.
Check 4: How well is your own account locked?
Most losses on large exchanges come from compromised accounts, not from the exchange failing. Three settings do most of the work: an authenticator app rather than SMS codes for two step verification, an anti phishing code if the platform offers one, so genuine emails can be told apart from fakes, and a withdrawal address whitelist, so a stolen session cannot send funds to a new address.
For readers more comfortable in Persian, there is a Persian-language walkthrough of LBank's Google Authenticator setup that also covers what to do when the recovery key is lost. Whatever the language, store that recovery key offline before you enable the app, not after.
Check 5: What do the bonus terms ask of you?
The Argentina partnership came with a promotional campaign that, as reported at launch, offered new users a 100 dollar welcome bonus after basic verification and a 100 percent bonus on deposits moved into the futures account. Both are designed to be used in leveraged contract trading, which is where the risk sits.
Leverage shortens the distance between entry and liquidation. In a simplified hypothetical example that ignores fees, funding and maintenance margin, a position at 10x loses its margin after a move of roughly 10 percent against it, and at 20x after roughly 5 percent. A deposit bonus that doubles your trading power doubles the size of what that small move can erase.
Hypothetical, simplified: the higher the leverage, the smaller the move that wipes out the margin.
Before accepting any bonus, read the exact campaign terms on the exchange, including volume requirements and whether the bonus can ever be withdrawn. l-learn.com, a Persian-language tutorial site, keeps a summary of LBank's futures trading rules that is useful for comparing against the official pages.
Frequently asked questions
Can residents of Iran open an LBank account?
LBank's User Service Agreement lists Iran among the regions it does not serve. Beyond the risk of a frozen account, identity verification documents from a restricted country are typically rejected, which blocks access to higher withdrawal limits even if registration goes through.
If LBank has no proof of reserves, how do I limit my exposure?
Decide on a maximum balance you are willing to leave on any single exchange and withdraw above it on a schedule, for example after each trading week. Test every new withdrawal address with a small amount first, because a transfer on the wrong network is usually unrecoverable.
Is the welcome bonus withdrawable cash?
As reported, the campaign bonuses are credited for contract trading rather than paid out as cash, and conditions can change between campaigns. Treat a bonus as extra risk budget, not as money you own, and check whether losses are deducted from the bonus or from your own deposit first.
This article is for information only and is not investment advice. Crypto assets and leveraged trading can lose their entire value.

Gharibabadi: Territorial integrity cannot be violated or bargained away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
17:20:57 UTC
02:20:57 KST

Gharibabadi: Territorial integrity cannot be violated or bargained away
TEHRAN — Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi has warned that the credibility of international law depends on the equal treatment of all states, stressing that national sovereignty and territorial integrity cannot be violated or made the subject of political bargaining.
Addressing a high-level meeting on the defense of international law at the United Nations on Friday, Gharibabadi said international law could fulfill its role in protecting peace, justice and human dignity only if its principles were applied universally and without discrimination.
 
 “The sovereignty and territorial integrity of states are not subject to violation or bargaining,” he said, arguing that no state has the right to disregard the prohibition on the use of force based on political assertions or its unilateral interpretation of a perceived threat.
Iran warns against selective application of international law
Gharibabadi said the credibility of the international legal order ultimately rests on the principle that all states are equal before the law.
He criticized 'the selective application of international law,' saying that legal principles are sometimes invoked rigorously against certain countries while being set aside in other cases because of political considerations and geopolitical interests.
He pointed specifically to Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits states from using force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state.
“No country can preserve its security and sovereignty if the fundamental principle of Article 2(4) is undermined,” the Iranian diplomat said.
He argued that allowing political considerations to override the prohibition on the use of force would weaken a central pillar of the international legal system and create a precedent in which powerful states could interpret international rules in their own interests.
Right to self-defense must be upheld
Gharibabadi also stressed the right of countries subjected to aggression to defend themselves, saying such a right must be exercised within the framework of the UN Charter and international law.
He further called for the consistent application of international humanitarian law, particularly the protection of civilians and the distinction between military and civilian targets.
These principles, he said, must apply universally, whether in Palestine, Iran, Lebanon, Yemen or any other part of the world.
The Iranian diplomat's remarks placed civilian protection and the rules governing armed conflict within the broader question of the credibility of international law, arguing that humanitarian principles cannot be selectively applied according to the identity of the parties involved.
Double standards undermine confidence in multilateralism
Gharibabadi identified 'double standards' in the application of international law as one of the major challenges facing the international system.
He said the UN Charter is invoked in some circumstances, while geopolitical interests are allowed to prevail in others. Similarly, he said, strict compliance with UN Security Council resolutions is demanded in some cases, while violations of the same resolutions may go unanswered elsewhere.
The Iranian deputy foreign minister also pointed to differing approaches to accountability.
“In one case, investigations and accountability are called for, while in another, political backing obstructs accountability,” he said.
Such inconsistency, Gharibabadi argued, does more than weaken the principle of justice. It also erodes the confidence of nations in multilateralism and international institutions.
“If international law is not applied equally to all states, its credibility will inevitably be undermined,” he warned.
Iran stresses role of International Court of Justice
Gharibabadi also highlighted the importance of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, in maintaining the authority of international law.
He said the Court must be able to adjudicate disputes between states independently of political pressure and clarify the legal obligations of the parties involved.
“As the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, the Court must be able to adjudicate disputes between states independently of political pressure and clarify their legal obligations,” he said.
Tehran calls for stronger multilateral system
Gharibabadi said Iran was prepared to cooperate with countries that support the sovereign equality of states, multilateralism, the peaceful settlement of disputes and the non-discriminatory application of international law.
He said such cooperation could contribute to strengthening the multilateral system, with the United Nations at its center.

Farhadi’s “Parallel Tales” wins best screenplay award at Silk Road International Film Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
17:16:38 UTC
02:16:38 KST

Farhadi’s “Parallel Tales” wins best screenplay award at Silk Road International Film Festival
TEHRAN – Asghar Farhadi’s latest film “Parallel Tales” won an award at the 13th Silk Road International Film Festival in China.
At the closing ceremony of the festival, held in Xi’an on September 23, the film won the Best Screenplay award, ISNA reported.
Co-written by Asghar Farhadi and his brother Saeed Farhadi, “Parallel Tales” had its world premiere at the 79th Cannes Film Festival and received a warm welcome from the enthusiastic audience, who gave it a seven-minute ovation.
The new film by the two-time Oscar-winning filmmaker was shot in Paris during fall 2025. It was released in French theaters concurrently with its Cannes unveiling.
The film’s stellar cast includes Isabelle Huppert, Virginie Efira, Catherine Deneuve, Vincent Cassel, Pierre Niney, and Adam Bessa.
Taking its cue from an episode in Krzysztof Kieslowski’s television series “Dekalog,” the Paris-set drama stars Huppert as a reclusive writer who spies incessantly on her neighbors (Cassel, Efira, and Niney) across the street and weaves imaginary stories around its occupants. Fact and fiction collide when a young homeless man (Bessa) hired as home help unleashes these stories into the real world.
“Parallel Tales” marks Farhadi’s second French-language film after “The Past” with Berenice Bejo, who won the Best Actress award for her performance at Cannes in 2013.
A French-Italian-Belgian coproduction, the film is produced by long-time collaborator Alexandre Mallet-Guy alongside Farhadi and David Levine.
It is the fifth collaboration between Farhadi and Memento Production after “The Past,” Oscar-winner “The Salesman,” “Everybody Knows,” and “A Hero”.
One of Iran's most prominent cinematic voices, Farhadi, 54, is known for his thought-provoking films that explore social issues.
He won the Best Foreign Film Oscar in 2012 for “A Separation” (which was also nominated for Best Screenplay) and once again in 2017 for “The Salesman”.
He has been selected four times in competition at Cannes with “The Past,” “The Salesman,” “Everybody Knows,” and “A Hero”.
“The Salesman” won Best Screenplay and Best Actor awards at Cannes in 2016, and “A Hero” scooped the Grand Prize at the 2021 festival.
“Everybody Knows,” Farhadi’s Spanish-language debut starring Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem, opened and competed at Cannes in 2018.
Farhadi was also selected twice in Berlin. He was awarded the Silver Bear for Best Director in 2009 for “About Elly” and the 2011 Golden Bear for “A Separation”.
On September 19, the 13th Silk Road International Film Festival opened in Xi’an under the theme “Silk Road Connects the World, Light and Shadow Shine over Chang’an”.
It received 2,130 entries from 139 countries and regions, with 23 works shortlisted for the final evaluation of the Golden Silk Road Awards.
The festival hosted a series of events focusing on international co-production, industrial cooperation, micro-dramas and virtual reality films.
The Silk Road International Film Festival (SRIFF) was founded by the State Administration of Press, Publication, Radio, Film, and Television in 2014 to comprehensively implement China’s national strategy of The Belt and Road Initiative. It aims to promote cultural exchanges and cooperation among countries along The Belt and Road routes and to further develop the Chinese audiovisual industry.
SRIFF is held annually (alternating every year between the cities of Xi’an and Fuzhou) and is co-sponsored by the Shaanxi Provincial People’s Government and Fujian Provincial People’s Government.
It is divided into the following sections and a mutable number of special presentations: Competition, Film Panorama, Film Forum, Film Market, Interactive Activities.

“Memories of My Father” offers intimate portrait of Martyr Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah
TEHRAN- “Memories of My Father,” written by Sayyed Mohammad Mahdi Nasrallah and translated into Persian by Bushra Sahebi, offers a firsthand account of the personal, family and ethical dimensions of Martyr Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah, the late secretary-general of Lebanon’s Hezbollah.
The Persian edition of the book has recently been published by Amirkabir Publications in Tehran, with the translation seeking to preserve the original tone and personal character of the author while presenting the work in accessible Persian.
Published on the occasion of the second anniversary of Nasrallah’s martyrdom, the book is described as the first official and intimate written work published by his family, providing an account of the resistance figure through the perspective of his son.
Originally written in Arabic under the title “Dhikrayati ma‘a Abi”, the book presents a personal portrait of Nasrallah’s life away from the public and political spotlight, focusing on his conduct and relationships within the family.
The work is divided into two main sections: “What I Heard from My Father,” based on accounts and recollections, and “What I Saw While Accompanying Him,” which draws on the author’s direct observations.
Across 82 narratives, the book recounts various aspects of Nasrallah’s life, including his affection toward family members, his attention to the upbringing of his children, and his role as a caring father and grandfather. It also touches on his simple lifestyle, his approach to reading and his close relationship with books.
A significant part of the memoir addresses how Nasrallah confronted hardship and lived under difficult security conditions, offering readers a perspective on his daily life that has received comparatively little attention.
“Memories of My Father” is aimed at readers interested in literature of resistance, the history of the region and contemporary history, providing a family-centered account of a prominent figure associated with Lebanon’s Hezbollah and the broader regional resistance movement.
Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah became secretary-general of Hezbollah in 1992, following the assassination of his predecessor, Sayyed Abbas al-Musawi. He led the movement for more than three decades, during a period that included the Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000 and the 2006 war between Hezbollah and Israel. Under his leadership, Hezbollah developed into a major political and military force in Lebanon and assumed a broader role in regional affairs.
Nasrallah was also widely known for his televised speeches, through which he addressed supporters and commented on major developments in Lebanon and the wider region. Born and raised in Beirut, he came from a family with roots in Bazouriyeh in southern Lebanon. While his public life was closely followed across the region, his personal and family life largely remained outside the spotlight.
He was tragically killed at the age of 64 during a series of intense Israeli airstrikes in southern Beirut on September 27, 2024.
The attack that claimed Nasrallah’s life was carried out by Israeli fighter jets targeting Hezbollah’s main headquarters, resulting in the martyrdom of several senior Hezbollah commanders and prominent Iranian Revolutionary Guards Lieutenant General Abbas Nilforoushan, who was present at the scene.
Under Nasrallah's leadership, whose name means "victory through God," Hezbollah evolved from a grassroots armed movement into the largest political party in Lebanon's recent history. Renowned for his captivating speeches, Nasrallah garnered attention throughout the West Asia and beyond, establishing himself as a significant figure within the Axis of Resistance, which includes Hezbollah, the Palestinian groups Hamas and Islamic Jihad, the Houthi movement in Yemen, and various Iraqi paramilitary factions.
