D. The Halo Effect
According to the manager’s observation, Alisha performed exceptionally well at work and produced excellent reports. Based on this strong impression, he thought she must also be a capable leader and promoted her to team leader. After some time, the team started to fall apart and worked without clear direction, showing that Alisha’s leadership skills were actually weak. In hindsight, the manager realized that his judgment had been influenced too much by a single positive trait.
E. The Bandwagon Effect
Hailey passed by a drink shop she had never heard of before and noticed a long queue stretching outside the store. Seeing so many people waiting in line, she became convinced that the drink must be worth trying and joined the crowd. In the end, she waited for an hour. Her decision was influenced more by other people’s behavior than by her own evaluation.
F. The Anchoring Effect
Jeremy went shopping for a jacket and first saw one priced at NT$2,000. This price quickly became a standard in his mind. Later, he came across a similar jacket on sale for NT$1,500 and immediately bought it. He ended up spending more than he had planned. The initial price acted as an anchor and guided his judgment, making the discount seem more attractive than it actually was.
D. 月暈效應
根據經理的觀察，艾莉莎的工作表現極佳，且撰寫的報告也很優秀。根據這個強烈的印象，他認為她一定也是個有能力的領導者，並將她升遷為組長。過了一陣子，該團隊開始分崩離析、工作缺乏明確方向，顯示艾莉莎的領導能力其實很薄弱。事後來看，經理意識到自己的判斷過度受到單一優點的影響。
E. 從眾效應
海莉經過一間她從沒聽過的飲料店，注意到延伸至店外的長長排隊人龍。看到這麼多人在排隊等待，她深信那間店的飲料一定值得一試，於是她加入人群。最後，她等了一小時。她的決定更多是受到他人行為的影響，而非基於自己的評估。
F. 定錨效應
傑洛米去逛街買外套，一開始看上一件定價新臺幣兩千元的外套。這個價格很快成為他心目中的標準。後來，他發現一件類似的外套特價新臺幣一千五百元，馬上就買了下來。他最後花的錢比原本預計的金額還多。最初的價格是個錨點，引導了他的判斷，讓後來那件外套的折扣看起來比實際上更具吸引力。

1. exceptionally adv. 特別，格外地

Andrew proved himself a capable engineer during the project.

Our manager’s leadership style focuses on collaboration rather than strict control.

in hindsight 事後看來
I changed my major in college. In hindsight, it turned out to be a very good decision.

那場演唱會的門票依座位不同而有不同定價。

We came across a small village hidden deep in the mountains while we were hiking.

I chatted happily with my friend at the cafe and ended up missing the last bus.

Rescued alive 10 days after catastrophic floods trapped him in a tunnel, Nepalese hydropower worker Kabir Maharjan is determined to help rebuild his country despite his own harrowing ordeal.
Traditional music and tearful relatives welcomed the 45-year-old when he returned home on Friday after spending weeks recovering at a hospital in Kathmandu.
“Life is precious. Hundreds of people have died but I survived,” the father of two said in an interview, his voice choked with emotion. “Perhaps I still have work to do for my society, for the country, and my home and family.”
Photo: AFP
The Aug. 26 flood, triggered by a glacial mountain collapse near the China-Nepal border, killed at least 1,400 people, the majority in Nepal.
More than 5,000 people remain missing in Nepal after the tsunami-like waves swept away roads, bridges and settlements in the mountainous northern regions, and battered crucial hydropower projects.
Maharjan, who was among hundreds of workers employed at projects hit by the floods, was eventually airlifted from the worst-hit Rasuwa region.
His miraculous rescue on Sept. 4, alongside fellow worker Sanjay Sah, offered a rare moment of hope during the disaster.
As Nepal shifts from emergency response to reconstruction, he said he hopes to return to his profession.
“There is risk in everything, but still we have to win over it,” he said.
In Nepal, more than 800 hydropower project workers remain unaccounted for, the energy minister told parliament last week.
Rescue teams continue to comb through the ruins, and 47 bodies have been recovered from flood-hit project sites.
Maharjan said he survived by reaching an upper floor of the tunnel site and drinking water while waiting for help.
“Whenever I was awake, I would try to find a way out,” he said. Days later, he saw what appeared to be a light and heard voices. “I thought I imagined it. But I called out, and they answered.”
For Maharjan, the country’s long road to recovery mirrors his own — he is still recovering from wounds on his hand and leg.
He said the rebuilding efforts could provide spiritual sustenance.
“While we are alive we must be patient and do our work,” he said. “Work is our karma.”
The flooding dealt a major blow to Nepal’s hydropower generation system, which is central to the country’s development ambitions and export earnings.
The government estimates overall reconstruction could cost US$4.8 billion, with thousands of people displaced and key infrastructure damaged.
The disaster has renewed scrutiny of how roads, hydropower plants and trade corridors are built in Nepal’s challenging mountain terrain.
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the UN on Thursday that the flooding was “a warning to the world” about the growing dangers posed by climate change, urging greater international support to help Nepal adapt and rebuild.
Aid groups have warned that the humanitarian crisis is far from over.
“The floodwaters may have receded, but for thousands of people, the crisis is far from over,” David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Nepal, said on Friday. “It is urgent to take the next steps in the recovery process to keep people healthy and avoid a spiral into poverty.”

Austria ‘ghetto’ language classes leave children behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:53 UTC
01:37:53 KST

For two years after he first arrived in Austria, Iraqi pupil Abdlrahman Aljanabi did not follow maths, science and other subjects like the rest of his peers.
Instead, he was pulled out of his class every day for several hours to learn German under a flagship program meant to bring newcomers like him up to par with the national language.
However, an assessment has shown the program — long decried by critics as “ghetto” classes — leaves a number of pupils to repeat at least one school year, contributing to a relatively high number of over-age pupils in the Alpine EU member.
Photo: AFP
“I was a bit lost, a bit upset ... because I didn’t understand why I was the only one who had to leave to go to another class,” said the 19-year-old refugee, who has yet to take his end-of-school exam.
The language classes differ from many other European countries where newly arrived pupils are fully immersed in the regular school system right away.
Introduced eight years ago under a conservative-far-right government, it was mandatory for schools to provide the program.
However, given the assessment that one-quarter of students who took the classes lose at least one year, the government has relaxed the rule from this school year onwards.
Schools can now decide for themselves how they want to support non-native German speakers, leading to half of them to abolish the separate classes.
However, their legacy is bound to stay for some years to come.
Austria has a comparatively large number of over-age pupils — those who are at least two years older than the intended age for their grade level — according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD): figures.
From 2015 to 2023, the proportion of such pupils rose from 4.1 percent to 5.8 percent in primary schools and from 6.5 percent to 9.1 percent in secondary school, the OECD said.
In the last school year, there were almost 60,000 so-called “non-regular students” who had to take the special classes. In Vienna, this was one-fifth of children in elementary school.
Among them, 35 percent are from Syria and 27 percent from Ukraine, Austrian Integration Fund figures showed.
“When you arrive at a school, you just want to blend in,” said a 16-year-old Ukrainian student, who only gave his first name Makarii and who fled Kyiv in 2022 at the start of Russia’s invasion.
“You spend time in a group that is then dissolved, you lose your friends, and you don’t know the teachers in the regular class,” he said.
A recent assessment by the Austrian Ministry of Education found that 22 percent of 22,800 students deemed “non-regular” in the school year 2022-2023 had to repeat the year once and 3 percent twice.
Austrian Minister of Education Christoph Wiederkehr told the Austria Press Agency this was a “far too high” number.
The program leads to an “automatic repetition” of pupils who stay in it for a long time, because they are not graded in core subjects such as maths, and so cannot move up to the next level, University of Vienna expert Susanne Schwab said.
“As a consequence, it becomes apparent that students who attend German support classes are highly likely to suffer a significant learning delay, and repeating a grade is a real part of their educational trajectory,” said Schwab, who has studied the program’s effects.
The program, adopted against the “scientific consensus,” does not “create solutions, but generates additional problems,” she added.
A 2022 report by experts evoked “racist mechanisms” and “institutional discrimination... under the guise of language support.”
The country of 9 million inhabitants has long drawn people from poorer nearby nations, as well as asylum seekers, although numbers have slumped due to anti-migration policies.
The anti-immigration far-right Freedom Party (FPO) has already slammed the change of relaxing the rules for schools.
The FPOe won the last parliamentary elections, in 2024, for the first time, but it failed to find partners to govern.

Unknown Publisher

Oktoberfest reaches its halfway point as Italian weekend looms. Could the festival grounds be closed again, as they were in 2025?
The traditionally particularly busy "Italian weekend" is just around the corner and on 26 and 27 September will mark the halfway point of this year's Oktoberfest. After the extreme overcrowding last year, organisers are looking with particular attention at visitor flows in 2026.
On the middle Wiesn Saturday in 2025, the festival grounds reached their capacity limits, so that access to the Theresienwiese had to be temporarily closed due to overcrowding.
In parts of Wirtsbudenstraße there was such a crush at the time that nobody could move forwards or backwards – visitors spoke in videos of "nightmare" scenes on the verge of a mass panic.
The upcoming weekend is traditionally referred to as the "Italian weekend", as tens of thousands of guests from the neighbouring country flock to Munich at this time. According to the Oktoberfest press office, the term has developed historically over decades, without a specific historical trigger or an exact start year.
The mass influx is fuelled above all by the short journey from northern Italy over the Brenner Pass by car, coach or motorhome. Regional public holidays and long weekends in the Italian September calendar also offer the ideal opportunity for a short break. The Italian flair on the festival grounds is unmistakable: Munich daily newspapers often print their front pages in two languages on these days, and Italian Carabinieri as well as fire crews from Bolzano support Munich police directly on site with patrols and communication.
To prevent critical overcrowding like last year in good time, the city is increasingly relying on a network of surveillance cameras and AI-based crowd-tracking software.
Incidentally, those who made it to the Wiesn stayed longer. An analysis of mobile phone data showed that visitors remained on the festival grounds an average of 15 minutes longer than in 2025. The absolute peak period in the first week was between 17:00 and 18:00 each day.

Before lacing up her running shoes, Nancy Masha checked the knife and pepper spray she carried to protect herself on her daily jog, a ritual born of fear after the murder of a fellow runner sent shock waves across South Africa.
Masha is among those taking extra precautions after nine women, including avid runner Elizabeth Moselakgomo, were found murdered in Johannesburg’s East Rand in two months — some of them partially naked and battered.
“Our runner was brutally killed. I needed a way to protect myself, because I am a woman and also a runner,” said Masha, 39, who usually runs alone.
Photo: AFP
Moselakgomo, 38, left home on Sept. 9 for a run and never returned, leaving behind her eight-year-old daughter. Her body was found three days later in the same area around Kempton Park where eight others were discovered since mid-July, prompting police to investigate whether a serial killer or killers were responsible, and fueling anxiety and anger across the country.
Two days after Moselakgomo’s body was found, Masha started carrying pepper spray and a knife on her daily runs.
“Her murder really traumatized me,” the mother-of-two said. “We run in awkward spaces and at awkward times, but I won’t stop running.”
Masha said she had once taken part in a marathon with Moselakgomo, whom she described as “bubbly.”
The discovery of the bodies has triggered vigils, protests and solidarity runs across South Africa, drawing hundreds of people from Kempton Park to Cape Town to honor the victims and demand action to protect women.
Gender-based violence remains endemic in South Africa, despite years of government pledges to tackle the problem and its declaration last year as a national disaster.
The government said its 24-hour Gender-Based Violence Command Centre received 6,782 distress calls between Sept. 1 and 16, averaging 424 a day, a 21 percent increase from the same period last month.
The killings have heightened concerns among women already accustomed to taking precautions in their daily lives.
Chulumanco Mahamba, 31, said since Moselakgomo’s death she has cut back her daily walks to twice a week. The discovery on Sunday last week in Johannesburg’s Soweto area of another woman — whose body was wrapped in a duvet — made her question her routine.
Mahamba already carried pepper spray as a precaution. Now she avoids secluded routes and shares her live location with loved ones before leaving home. She also sends photographs of what she is wearing.
“It feels unfair that we have to change our routines, but I do feel safer when I’m carrying pepper spray,” she said.
However, not all women feel comfortable carrying a weapon.
“We are not trained to use those things,” said Hlompho Matji, 47, a data analyst and runner. “It’s also a risk to carry pepper spray, because someone could overpower you and use it against you. The same goes for a knife. We don’t know how to use them.”
Babalwa Melitafa, 46, said she did not consider carrying weapons, but preferred running only within a gated community’s sports oval.
“I would not run outside the oval alone because of what has happened. I am scared,” she said.
Even in Cape Town, about 1,400km away, women said the killings had altered their routines. Filmmaker Andiswa Siwela, 43, a runner and mountain hiker, said the killings had left her more suspicious of strangers.
Siwela said she had always carried her car keys to use as a weapon, but now also takes pepper spray, which she previously left in her car.
“We want to be free. We want to do things without fear; we want to live,” she said.
Nkululeko Molosi, 47, captain of the Sunrise Athletics Club, said runners should not have to “choose between our passion for the sport and our personal safety.”
South African police have so far arrested three people in connection with the Kempton Park killings, which they have not said are linked. A man is in custody for one of the murders and two women have been charged over another.
However, the arrests have done little to ease concerns. Speaking at a public holiday gathering on Thursday, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the “pain and suffering that the women of South Africa have been put through stands out as a national shame.”
“The women of South Africa have the right to walk the streets of their country at any hour without fear,” he added.

Photo: AFP
The US had originally planned for Xi to visit the National Archives to view the Declaration of Independence, the US constitution and the Bill of Rights, all documents associated with US democracy and freedom, the sources said.
The itinerary also included the Treaty of Wangxia and the Treaty of Tianjin, which are regarded as unequal treaties, followed by a viewing of the Treaty of San Francisco, to which neither the People’s Republic of China or the Republic of China was a signatory, they said.
The seemingly pointed diplomatic arrangements are believed to have sparked strong objections from Xi’s delegation, the sources said, adding that as a result, after briefly accompanying Trump to view the Declaration of Independence and the constitution, Xi’s delegation called off the rest of the planned itinerary at the last minute.
Trump and Xi ultimately spent only about 10 minutes at the National Archives, far shorter than originally scheduled, the sources said.
The 1951 Treaty of San Francisco was a formal agreement signed between Japan and 48 Allied nations after World War II.
Article 2 of the treaty stipulates that “Japan renounces all right, title and claim to Formosa and the Pescadores,” without explicitly specifying which country sovereignty over Taiwan should belong to.
That provision later became a central basis for the “undetermined status of Taiwan” argument in international legal and political debates, a position China has never recognized.
Documents the Chinese side wanted to see, including the Three Joint Communiques, were never considered for inclusion by the US side, the sources said.

====================================================================================================

Bilingual 2030 and the elephant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:46 UTC
01:37:46 KST

In a recent exchange over Bilingual 2030, Gerhard Erasmus (“Bilingual 2030,” Sept. 5, page 8) declared that “time’s up for opinions.”
However, the time is hardly up for ideas about how to confront the elephant in the room — the core problem barely mentioned in the discussion.
The elephant does not speak.
Contributors Paul Garrelfs and Daniel Eyrich pointed upstream to junior-high school and earlier, with Eyrich noting that what we assess influences what teachers and students prioritize.
Exactly: Taiwan wants university students to learn academic subjects through English as the medium of instruction (EMI), yet its school system gives them remarkably little incentive to develop spontaneous spoken English. How does it make sense to expect students to learn academic subjects in English when they struggle to formulate spoken questions?
The General Scholastic Ability Test English section assesses reading and writing, but not speaking. Yet the Ministry of Education’s statements and curriculum guidelines have repeatedly stressed using English for interpersonal communication — that developing students’ spoken English matters.
Taiwan’s principal university entrance exam, through its design, tells students, teachers and parents otherwise.
It is as if the system assumes that because high-school students can develop substantial reading competence despite having little speaking practice, this particular receptive competence will somehow carry them through university EMI lectures. Reading a difficult English text at one’s own pace — pausing, rereading and reconsidering — and processing a chain of academic ideas in real time are fundamentally different tasks. Listening proficiency requires extensive comprehensible listening input, while speaking and interaction add productive practice and opportunities for deeper processing of spoken language. Students need both; Taiwan’s school English system cannot reasonably expect strong EMI readiness while giving either one short shrift.
In his influential, research-based Four Strands framework, Paul Nation, one of the world’s leading authorities on second-language vocabulary, recommends roughly equal attention to meaning-focused input, meaning-focused output, deliberate language study and fluency development. Deliberate study is necessary, but focusing on it almost exclusively is like building a diet around just one food group.
Education First’s 2025 English Proficiency Index reports substantially higher speaking scores in Malaysia and the Philippines — where historical circumstances have left English with strong social and educational functions. Taiwan lacks that environment. For Bilingual 2030 to achieve its goals, the ministry must create in junior-high schools the productive speaking practice society does not naturally provide — and make speaking count.
An obvious objection: How can schools possibly test speaking? Individual schools might lack the resources, but national testing at intervals need not be left to individual schools; the technology already exists to administer speaking tests nationally at scale.
An extensive international research literature documents the linguistic difficulties students can face when they undertake EMI without sufficient English proficiency. As Jye Smallwood (“Basic misunderstanding of EMI,” Aug. 9, page 8) wrote, EMI is not a substitute for the English proficiency needed to participate in it successfully.
That does not mean the proper choice is no EMI. The proper choice is bridges.
A few Taiwanese educators are already experimenting with such bridges. At National Chiayi University, Lin Keng-ta (林庚達) teaches the core concepts of difficult engineering material in Mandarin, after which Chen Chien-chung (陳建中) of Marian University in the US explains the same material in English. Students can approach already-familiar professional content through a second language.
Meanwhile, National Taiwan University offers one-credit “Mini-EMI” courses — condensed or introductory versions of regular academic courses designed to ease students into learning and discussing subject matter in English.
Why not extend these types of approaches to junior-high school education? Suppose students complete a history course in Mandarin and, during the summer, those choosing a more ambitious English pathway take a shorter English extension built on material they already understand. Students could examine another source, compare interpretations, discuss causes and complete a project in English. Such an approach could also be tried in other subjects.
Also, why not handle Taiwan’s approximately 6,000-word junior-high-school reference vocabulary more dynamically? The ministry could designate a core portion as productive vocabulary, supplement it with common chunks and collocations and regularly have students build “language islands” — short, prepared passages about their own lives and interests. That would serve as a flexible foundation for real interactions.
Erasmus is right that we need evidence. So run pilot programs and gather it: measure speaking development, subject retention and subsequent readiness for EMI. Student choice should be part of such experiments, too: productive language learning requires sustained participation, so the effects of motivation and student buy-in should themselves be measured.
Taiwan’s education system can produce outstanding results, as demonstrated by its consistently top-tier math, science and reading performances in international assessments like the Programme for International Student Assessment. These achievements hardly suggest, though, that the same system can deliver an outcome it neither cultivates nor directly assesses.
The broad evidence is already clear about what Bilingual 2030 most needs to achieve its goals: much more speaking practice and consequential testing of speaking ability at the junior-high school level, along with appropriate scaffolding for EMI at university whenever students are not yet linguistically ready.
What is needed now are more ideas about how best to accomplish these things, not an end to such opinions. Then put the most promising ideas to the test — and get the elephant to speak.
Kevin Fitzpatrick has taught English in Taiwan for 35 years.
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from
When Panama severed diplomatic relations with Taiwan and recognized China in 2017, Beijing achieved one of its most important diplomatic victories in Central America. However, nearly a decade later, Panama is demonstrating that diplomatic recognition does not necessarily eliminate Taiwan from a country’s political system. Panama and Taiwan had diplomatic relations for more than 100 years and the goodwill between the countries was displayed last week when Panama’s National Assembly established an interparliamentary exchange group with the Legislative Yuan. Forty-five of the assembly’s 71 lawmakers joined the group, representing more than 60 percent of the legislature. Its members include National Assembly President Shirley

“China undoubtedly tried to score on the Taiwan issue, but would a concession on Taiwan be in the US’ interests?” Wu said on the sidelines of a forum in Taipei on the implications of a meeting between Trump and Xi at the White House on Thursday.
The two leaders reportedly discussed trade, artificial intelligence, Iran and Taiwan.
Photo: Screen grab from Lockheed Martin’s YouTube channel
It would be in the US’ “vital interests” to move the arms sales forward, allowing Taiwan to defend itself, and its free and democratic political system, so that “its 23 million people would not live under the same system as [people in] China,” Wu said.
Backing Taiwan’s self-defense and freedom is necessary for it to continue making contributions to the world in the field of semiconductors, he said.
Some media had reported that Xi likely pressed Trump to formally halt the planned arms sale package to Taiwan and publicly state his opposition to Taiwan independence during the meeting, Wu said.
However, “as far as I know, the US has not responded to these issues,” he added.
Wu referenced a joint statement by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Japanese Minister of Foreign Affairs Toshimitsu Motegi and South Korean Minister of Foreign Affairs Cho Hyun on Sept. 21 during the UN General Assembly in New York. The statement emphasized the importance of peace across the Taiwan Strait.
Wu also mentioned another joint statement issued during the UN General Assembly on Sept. 22 by the foreign ministers and high-level representatives of eight governments: Australia, France, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Poland, South Korea and the UK.

The joint statements showed that US interests in Taiwan are “aligned with interests of mainstream countries,” Wu said.

“China has been aggressively pursuing narrative diplomacy and through information manipulation tries to replace our role in World War II,” Wu said, adding that his ministry will not stop countering China’s narratives in the international arena.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency reported that Xi told Trump at their meeting that “during the Second World War, Chinese and Americans fought shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression. Chinese people have never forgotten that part of history, nor have the American people.”
Meanwhile, Trump invoked the First American Volunteer Group of the Republic of China Air Force, also known as the Flying Tigers, and praised the “bravery during their joint combat with Chinese soldiers and civilians against the Japanese invasion,” Xinhua reported.
Wu did not comment on Trump’s remarks.
Republic of China (ROC) and US forces fought against the Japanese invasion of China during World War II, with the Flying Tigers operating as part of the ROC Air Force. The PRC was not formed until after the war ended.
After the war, the ROC, led by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), retreated to Taiwan in 1949 following its defeat in the Chinese Civil War by the CCP.

Institute touts its new umami seasoning powder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:39 UTC
01:37:39 KST

The Ministry of Agriculture’s Taiwan Agricultural Research Institute on Wednesday said it has developed soybean-based umami seasoning powder that is low in sodium and sugar, and high in protein.
The institute said that it fermented and aged domestically produced soybeans, converting their soy protein into free, umami amino acids.
The amino acids were further processed into additive-free umami seasoning powder, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Agriculture’s Taiwan Agricultural Research Institute
Typical salt consumption in Taiwan tends to be high and most umami seasoning products on the market, such as mushroom seasoning powder, have relatively high sodium content, the institute said.
A key concern for Taiwan’s food industry is to balance keeping the umami flavor while reducing sodium content in seasonings, it said.
Its technique helps microorganisms decompose the proteins in soybeans, which releases a lot of umami amino acids and flavor compounds, the institute said.
The substances can be processed into seasoning products via drying, milling and sieving before being mixed with other raw materials, it said.
Soybean-based umami seasoning alone can provide rich flavors without any additives, it added.
The technique shortens the fermentation and aging process compared with other processes to produce fermented soybean seasonings such as soy sauce and miso, it said.
It also produces seasoning with lower sodium content, given that it does not rely on salt preservation, the institute said.
Most seasoning products on the market either have low sodium and high sugar, or low sugar and high sodium, it said.
However, the newly developed soybean seasoning has low sodium and sugar, it said.
It contains about 2.9g of sodium and 2g of sugar per 100g of powder, much lower than its counterparts’ sodium levels ranging from 15.5g to 20.2g and sugar content at up to 71g per 100g of powder, the institute said.
Its powder also boasts higher protein content at 30.3g per 100g than all of the seasoning products it was compared against, it said.
The seasoning has broad applications, such as becoming an ingredient in the food processing industry that intensifies the flavors of instant foods, soups and snacks, it said.
Aside from the business-to-business market, it can also penetrate the business-to-consumer market to fulfill consumers’ demand for healthy and low-salt foods, it said, adding that its technique was transferred to industry players in May.

Taiwan in Time: Carrying Taiwan’s stage  to Singapore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:39 UTC
01:37:39 KST

Sept. 28 to Oct. 4
Opening in 1971, Singapore’s Wisma Theatre (海燕歌劇院) was entirely modeled after Taiwanese live variety shows, combining singing, dancing and drama. Even its performers were recruited from Taiwan. The formula was an instant hit, selling out on the third night with the crowd fighting outside for tickets.
Among its key figures was 31-year-old Chi Li-nan (紀利男), an acclaimed saxophonist and band leader who had entered Taiwan’s live entertainment scene at age 19 with zero musical training.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan Music Institute
Chi wasn’t even supposed to be there. He had accompanied his girlfriend, pop singer Shang Kuan Ping (上官萍), to negotiations with Wisma’s agent. He casually remarked, “You’re recruiting so many singers, why don’t you recruit musicians too?” The agent, who had recognized Chi from his live performances, surprisingly agreed, and the couple ended up heading to Singapore together.
Upon arriving, Chi noticed that the stage was poorly designed and persuaded the owners to rebuild it, delaying opening for a month. He then saved the first show from disaster with quick thinking and held a meeting that night to establish protocol for future performances. Three months later, he was promoted to the theater’s musical director and programmer.
A year later, Chi tried his hand at composing. His first song, Regret Loving You (後悔愛上你), was a huge success, with Teresa Teng (鄧麗君) among the singers who recorded it. Chi would go on to become better known as a songwriter and producer, creating more than 1,000 songs and numerous hits.
JOINING THE GOLDEN CATS
Chi was born in 1940 in Shuinan Village (水南) Yunlin County, where his grandfather started out poor but became the area’s largest sugarcane grower. By the time Chi was in elementary school, however, the family had lost their fortune to land reform and bad deals.
Chi was expelled from high school in Chiayi after a physical altercation with a teacher, he recalls in his memoir, Life in Music (音樂人生). Afraid to go home, he wandered the streets for a while before heading to Taipei to find his father, who worked as a firetruck driver.
Chi was interested in the music industry, as he had been an avid listener since childhood, particularly enamored with the songs of Japanese crooner Hibari Misora. His father connected him with pop singer Chi Lu-hsia (紀露霞, no relation), who introduced him to acclaimed composer Yang San-lang (楊三郎).
Yang had just sold his popular Black Cat Song and Dance Troupe (黑貓歌舞團) and was preparing to form the Golden Cat troupe with younger, trendier performers. He immediately took Chi in as a disciple.
Learning vocal techniques from Yang while helping out with the troupe, Chi took the stage a month later. The 30-plus-member troupe traveled around Taiwan, staying about 10 days in each town. The show consisted of an hour of singing and dancing, and an hour of musical drama.
FALL AND RISE
After about eight months, Chi expressed an interest in musical arranging. Yang wanted him to focus on singing first, but after being impressed by the work Chi did in his free time, he began teaching him music theory. Chi could not afford an instrument, but Yang happened to have a saxophone that one of his students had sold to a pawn shop without his knowledge. Chi Lu-hsia gave Chi the money to buy it back, and it became his main instrument.
Yang taught Chi every night after performances, and Chi recalls asking exhaustive questions because he needed to understand everything thoroughly. The two often argued, but Yang remained patient and recognized his talent.
Two years later, the troupe had fallen on hard times. Audiences preferred the more experienced Black Cats and their bigger-name performers, and eventually all the musicians quit, leaving only Yang and Chi. The Golden Cats eventually disbanded.
The two worked at a Taichung nightclub before joining the Black Cats for a short period. They eventually found themselves playing in bars and sharing a small borrowed room. Chi recalls seeing Yang cry for the first time, saddened that despite his fame and talent, he had been reduced to such a life.
Yang later moved to Taipei and became one of the scene’s most in-demand saxophone players, known for his improvisational ability. He met Shang Kuan through work, and the two began dating.
SONGWRITING
In 1970, Singaporean entrepreneur Wang Te-nan (王德南) visited Taiwan and was impressed by its live entertainment scene. He established Wisma Theatre in a building leased for 10 years from the Indonesian Embassy, and began recruiting performers from Taiwan.
Chi brought his own nine-person band, and helped guide the theater to quick success.
He and Shang Kuan married in 1972. That year, Chi tried his hand at songwriting for a Wisma compilation album. Regret Loving You was originally written for singer Hung Yen-ping (洪燕萍), but Life Records (麗風唱片) artist Yang Hsiao-ping (楊小萍) heard someone humming it backstage and decided to record it as well. During production in Hong Kong, a 19-year-old Teresa Teng heard the song and recorded it too.
Chi initially struggled with his next compositions, which Life Records considered “too artistic.” But he soon grasped the nuances of pop-writing with Shang Kuan’s help. His next major hit was the 1976 Sunset Again for Yu Tien (余天).
Other notable works included A Boat in the Vast Ocean (汪洋中的一條船), based on the story of Cheng Feng-hsi (鄭豐喜), who overcame physical disability to earn a law degree, and a rearrangement of Plum Blossom (梅花) into a military march commissioned by general Chiang Wei-kuo (蔣緯國).
PROLIFIC PRODUCER
In 1978, Chi decided to test the Japanese market. Through Yang’s connections, he became the first foreigner to join the Japan Composer’s Association. A year later, he won a silver medal at the Koga Awards with First Love (初戀).
Wisma closed in 1981, and Chi returned to Taiwan while visiting Taiwan monthly in an attempt to break into the industry. He also continued working with Taiwanese and Hong Kong artists, notably penning 11 songs for Liza Wang (汪明荃), including Hot Coffee (熱咖啡).
But the Japanese market proved difficult and he abandoned the effort after seven years. Chi recalled struggling to get major stars to sing his songs — though he was too stubborn to give them to lesser-known singers. He recalled that the sign to give up was when a friend of Misora, his childhood idol, promised to introduce his songs to the singer but died before it could happen.
After seeing CD technology in Japan, Chi recorded an album with Shang Kuan on vocals in 1984 — at a time when no producer in Taiwan was familiar with the technology and the couple didn’t even have the means to play it at home.
Back in Taiwan, record companies considered Chi’s music “too progressive,” prompting him to move his family to Singapore and start his own production company. He found renewed success there. In 1992, he staged a Wisma reunion concert and even ran the New Wisma Theatre for a year.
He had wanted to produce a greatest-hits album for Yang, but Yang died in 1989 before the project could begin. Chi eventually enlisted singer Chen Fen-lan (陳芬蘭) and a Chinese orchestra to record 10 of Yang’s Taiwanese songs. The album won Best Record at the Golden Tripod Awards.
During the 2000s, Chi focused on producing audiophile recordings with well-known singers and Buddhist pop music. He continued recording until about 10 months before his death from a liver tumor on Oct. 4, 2016.

AI is not capable of keeping city hall accountable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:39 UTC
01:37:39 KST

If artificial intelligence (AI) has not finished off your local newspaper yet, just wait. It will. OpenAI, the company that built ChatGPT, has called itself an “existential threat” to news publishers.
Americans do not fully appreciate what that means. We are overdue for a serious conversation — and a tech reckoning.
Just more than a week ago, McClatchy, which owns the Miami Herald — my former employer — announced it was laying off more than 90 journalists across 17 of its publications, including one-third of the Herald’s staff.
The cuts followed similar mass reductions this year at the Washington Post, Lee Enterprises and the Associated Press. Other local news organizations have closed altogether.
McClatchy blamed subscriber economics and a 41 percent decline in consumer revenue over the past five years, but there is more to the story. McClatchy is owned by Chatham Asset Management, a hedge fund. In June, as McClatchy was bleeding revenue, executives announced a massive investment in AI-generated content. AI agents would repackage the work of its reporters and affix their bylines to work they had not written — all in an effort to drive traffic.
What they did not say is that for the past three years, AI has been capsizing the industry’s business model. News organizations had shifted their focus to generating Web traffic following a 92 percent decline of print ad revenues between 2000 and 2023. With the emergence of AI, tech companies decided they could stop directing traffic to news sites and supplant them altogether by stealing and regurgitating their journalism.
It might be “the largest theft of labor in human history,” Microsoft’s director of applied science Brent Hecht said in company communications unsealed in a copyright infringement lawsuit against Microsoft and OpenAI by the New York Times and other news organizations.
The newspapers alleged that tech firms have been bypassing news site paywalls and scraping content to train their large language models since 2022, when OpenAI launched ChatGPT, and creating products that replace the news sites. Microsoft and OpenAI said that their use of copyright material constitutes “fair use” and that they alter the content enough to shield them from liability for infringement.
What is especially troubling — but perhaps not surprising — is that according to the unsealed documents, the tech industry executives understood there would be a cost to creating a product that substituted for the original work of journalists, but they proceeded anyway.
“Almost no one intended for content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use,” Hecht said.
One Microsoft policy document acknowledged the risk succinctly: Generative AI “destroys its supply chain.”
Now, consider what that “supply chain” produces and what we lose when it is gone.
On the same day McClatchy gave the Charlotte Observer’s two investigative reporters the pink slip, the paper published a deeply disturbing investigation by one of them into a local log cabin company accused of defrauding customers. The chain slashed the Idaho reporter who exposed a hospital for covering up the injury record of a surgeon. The Miami Herald dismissed a city hall reporter who broke story after story of conflict and corruption. The Lexington Herald-Leader jettisoned the entire team covering city and Kentucky state government.
McClatchy eliminated dozens of jobs of veteran reporters who covered school boards, county commissions and the environment. It laid off editorial writers, gutted positions dedicated to Spanish-language readers and axed some of the chain’s hardest-working sports reporters.
None of these journalists did their job for the pay. Many barely made enough to cover their mortgages. However, despite the growing distrust of national media — fueled by a dysfunctional social media environment and polarized politics — local reporting can be one of the most gratifying jobs in journalism. Good reporters can explain confusing issues, elevate the voices of the powerless, hold the powerful to account and bring simple joy by posting Little League box scores and write-ups of homegrown businesses. When a community loses those reporters, it loses its connective tissue.
Losing that connective tissue also hurts democracy. Studies showed that when people rely less on local news sources and more on social media for information, they become more vulnerable to misinformation and manipulation — and more isolated. As political information becomes more nationalized, voter polarization increases, election turnout plummets and civic engagement falls. When there are no reporters covering government officials, they are more likely to engage in wasteful spending.
Local nonprofit news sites are filling some of those gaps, and organizations such as Rebuild Local News are working to sustain community journalism. One of its most promising ideas is a statewide tax credit awarded to eligible news organizations to fund the salaries of local reporters. Six states have adopted the policy. California lawmakers are the latest to pass it, and the proposal is awaiting the approval of California Governor Gavin Newsom. He should sign it.
However, tech companies should not get off the hook, either. They should be required to pay for every bit of intellectual property they have stolen from publishers without compensation, because without reporters, how are their AI agents going to get new intelligence? Make it up?
Local newspapers as we know them are dying, but local journalism is not. Our communities — and even our democracy — depend on keeping it alive.
Mary Ellen Klas is a politics and policy columnist for Bloomberg Opinion. A former capital bureau chief for the Miami Herald, she has covered politics and government for more than three decades. All-night stores disappearing: association
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:37 UTC
01:37:37 KST

Nearly 10 percent of convenience stores nationwide were not operating around the clock in 2022 and the figure is projected to rise this year, the Association of Chain and Franchise Promotion, Taiwan said yesterday.
Convenience stores run by the four major operators — 7-Eleven, FamilyMart, Hi-Life and OK Mart — totaled 12,630 in 2022, of which 1,203 stores, or 9.5 percent, did not operate at all hours, association data showed.
The percentage would increase this year due to a shortage of labor and the low birthrate over the past four years, the association said.
Photo: CNA
“No one wants to work graveyard shifts,” a former convenience store franchisee said on condition of anonymity.
Stores running short of graveyard shift workers must have a store manager cover the shifts, they said.
The Ministry of Labor has increased the minimum wage for 10 consecutive years, from NT$120 per hour in 2016 to NT$196 per hour this year, or up 63.3 percent over the decade.
Personnel expenses make up more than 70 percent of a convenience store’s total operating costs, the former franchisee said.
Wages for graveyard shifts are 20 percent higher than day or swing shifts, but that is still insufficient to maintain sufficient workforce, they said.
Huang Yen-tsung (黃延聰), a professor of business administration at Tunghai University, said that graveyard shifts at convenience stores might run at a loss — if the store is not in an area with sufficient foot traffic at night — requiring managers to offset the deficit with daytime income.
An eight-hour graveyard shift still generates operational costs from utility and personnel expenses, Huang said.
Moreover, the low birthrate has created a new mindset among young people, he said.
They are not as motivated to take on night shifts to earn more money as people were 20 years ago, he said, adding that freelance work offers greater freedom.
Most college students are not keen about trainee positions at convenience stores either, he said.
Moreover, a store clerk’s job is not no longer limited to handling a cash register, they also have to make coffee, serve ice cream, cook tea eggs and sausages, handle bill payments and operate multifunction printers, while those on night shifts must clean coffee and oden machines, as well as take inventory and restock shelves, he said.
A franchisee speaking on condition of anonymity said that their store received no applications for clerk positions over the past half year, requiring the store manager to cover shifts.
Feng Chia University assistant marketing professor Yeh Jun-heng (葉俊亨) said that most convenience stores in residential-based shopping areas have few customers late at night.
Maintaining around-the-clock operations is not cost-effective for such stores, given the operating and personnel costs, Yeh said.
Convenience stores that never close would not disappear, but would become more tailored to the needs of local shopping areas, he said, adding that all-hours operations would depend on economic benefits.
Association deputy secretary-general Ku Shang-chun (顧上鈞) said that many convenience stores are trialing personnel-less operations for graveyard-shift hours or refraining from opening all night.
President Chain Store Corp (PCSC) runs more than 7,340 7-Eleven stores nationwide.
Adding 7-Eleven smart vending machines and other operations, PCSC has 8,398 service locations in Taiwan.
It has canceled around-the-clock operations at some stores since 2015, but it did not provide specific data.
Some 7-Eleven stores in closed commercial areas, such as industrial office buildings, department stores or hospitals, have adjusted their hours as required by the property owners, the firm said.
Its smart vending machines have been introduced near those places to meet consumers’ needs around the clock, it said.
The out-of-store operations help boost operating efficiency as well as improve the operation of its stores, it added.
Regarding the shortage of workers willing to work overnight, PCSC said it is continuing to develop its middle-aged and elderly workforce, adding that its employees aged 45 or older account for up to 32 percent of its total workforce.
PCSC not only took the lead in launching an onboarding training program for middle-aged and elderly employees, but was also the first to set up a training program for international students in Taiwan, it said.
As of this year, the company has set up 24 demonstration stores hiring international students nationwide, PCSC said.
Taiwan FamilyMart Co said FamilyMart stores focus on around-the-clock operations.
However, some stores’ hours have been adjusted according to actual consumer demand and shopping area characteristics, especially those in industrial zones or office buildings, where demand is low late at night, it said.

Good luck to Canada and the EU, they will need it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:35 UTC
01:37:35 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has raised a seemingly incongruous possibility: Perhaps Canada, 3,500 miles from Brussels, might become an “associate member” of the EU. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seems open to the idea.
Exactly what this might mean is far from clear. Whether Canada or the EU’s member governments would actually want such an arrangement once they have sorted out the details is even more uncertain. Still, the effort to build a closer relationship is to be commended. With luck, it could also be a useful model for the EU to adopt with the UK and other partners.
Washington’s turn to tariffs and peremptory demands as weapons of economic warfare has hit Canada with particular force. The US and its northern neighbor have built a tightly integrated system of commerce. Dismantling it is hurting both countries — but the shock to Canada’s much smaller and more specialized economy is especially severe.
In response, Carney has rightly emphasized the need to form closer ties with other countries. A deal with the EU offers mutual gains and new opportunities. As a tactic for negotiations, it also tells Washington that Canada has alternatives — and assures its furious citizens that their government is not about to roll over.
Unfortunately, though, the EU has no template for “associate membership.” By now, to be sure, it should have one, to replace the numerous complex pacts with neighbors that it is reluctant to admit to full membership or that reject the deep political integration the union expects. In different ways, Norway, Iceland (whose voters recently halted talks toward full membership), Liechtenstein, Switzerland, Ukraine, Turkey, the UK and others all fall into this category.
In one sense, you could say that Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are already associate members, because, as part of the European Economic Area, they are in the EU’s single market. Yet, they are required to be “rule-takers” — with no say on the rules in question or in EU decisionmaking more broadly. It is hard to imagine Canada’s government, much less its citizens, accepting any such dispensation.
On the other hand, if Canada’s associate membership allowed real input into the union’s rules, Norway and the others would surely demand no less.
A deal that balances rights and obligations more fairly in this way would indeed be a good outcome — and one that might very well appeal to the UK and others. However, for the EU this would be a radical departure, likely requiring a new overarching treaty and unanimous agreement among current members. Also, more than a few of those members might prefer this model of associate membership to the deal they already have. That prospect would call Brexit to mind and alarm the EU’s champions of “ever-closer union.” The chances of any such deal, desirable as it might be, are therefore slim.
Instead, something along the lines of the bloc’s arrangements with Switzerland is more likely: a vastly complicated, ever-shifting tangle of separate agreements, which EU officials often say should not be replicated. In that case, Canada had better moderate its ambitions and settle in for years (or decades) of talks.
Speaking of years, Ottawa ought to bear one more thing in mind: The White House’s devotion to tariffs and disdain for allies is, one hopes, temporary, while the logic of close economic integration between the two countries would remain compelling over the long term. A new trade deal with the EU might serve Canada’s interests — so long as it does not complicate or, worst of all, foreclose restoring partnership with the US when Washington finally comes to its senses.

====================================================================================================

European fisheries struggling to cope with rising sea temperatures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:32 UTC
01:37:32 KST

As drought spread and wildfires raged across Europe this summer, the extraordinary heat did not stop at the shoreline.
European waters had their hottest summer months since satellite sensors began providing reliable data in 1982, according to analysis of sea surface temperatures.
Records were broken from the English Channel to the Mediterranean Sea. An offshore buoy near Mallorca recorded a temperature of 33.02°C on Aug. 5, the highest ever registered in the Spanish port authority’s buoy network.
Photo: EPA
Scientists say that events such as marine heatwaves are becoming more frequent, more intense and more widespread as greenhouse gas emissions drive up atmospheric temperatures around the globe. Oceans absorb the majority of the excess heat and retain it longer than the land or atmosphere.
That is transforming marine ecosystems, with catastrophic consequences for European fisheries and the people who rely on them. Species that have sustained coastal communities in Spain and southern England for generations are disappearing, as unfamiliar arrivals surge into warming waters.
“What is surprising is the speed at which this occurs,” Jean-Pierre Gattuso, senior research scientist at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research, said of the warming seas. “Records are broken almost every day in many places.”
Taken together, European seas averaged 21.6°C between June and last month, the highest in 45 years of available data.
Few areas strayed further from the norm than the Bay of Biscay, off the Atlantic-facing coast of France and Spain.
Stretching from Cape Ortegal in Galicia to the Pointe de Penmarch in southern Brittany, the bay’s traditionally cool waters averaged 21.4°C between June and last month, more than 2.4°C above the 1991-2020 average. Readings from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration peaked on Aug. 13 at 23.2°C, the highest of the satellite era.
Scientists define a marine heatwave as five or more days of water temperatures well above an area’s historic norm. In the 1980s, the Bay of Biscay averaged a handful of heatwave days per year. By the end of last month, it had logged 186 this year, more than three out of every four days, Reuters found.
DISAPPEARING SEA LIFE
The Bay of Biscay’s cool waters, long prized by those seeking relief from the heat of the Mediterranean coast, were enshrined in Ernest Hemingway’s famous novel “The Sun Also Rises.” The book’s protagonist recovers after weeks of dissolution on the beaches of San Sebastian.
“Now if you want to swim in cold water, you have to go to the westernmost portion of Galicia,” in the far northwestern corner of Spain, said Jose Manuel Rico Ordas, a marine ecology professor at the University of Oviedo..
Galicia benefits from strong winds that push warm surface water away from the coast during the summer months, allowing cold, deep-sea water to take its place in a process known as upwelling.
Ordas has spent summers on the bay since he was a child and studies its transformation.
Back then, there were extensive underwater forests of kelp, which provide vital food, shelter and nurseries for dozens of species that sustain the region’s small-scale fisheries. He estimates about 95 percent of the large, brown seaweed stands have disappeared, based on sampling along the Asturias coast since 2010. He attributes the decline primarily to climate change.
Kelp needs cold water — typically below 20 C (68 F) — to survive. Higher temperatures were once rare in the bay, Ordas said.
“Now, it’s the opposite,” he said.
Fish overgrazing — in particular by dreamfish, which thrive in warmer temperatures — has added to the kelp’s decline, he said.
The impacts are stark.
“We are finding no more lobster, no more crayfish, no more sea urchins and many other species that are associated with the good status of kelp forests,” Ordas said.
Concerned fishing crews are working with scientists and environmental activists to try to restore kelp forests by planting seedlings grown in laboratories.
Manuel Angel Reiriz Gonzalez, president of a local fishing guild in Galicia, ferried members of one such project in a boat he uses for sport fishing charters out of the port of Ribeira. The group brought a box full of small stones seeded with kelp, which they tossed into the choppy waters.
Climate change threatens a way of life that has sustained Gonzalez’s community for generations, he said. His family has been diving for sea urchins and harvesting clams for more than a century. Recurring heatwaves are hurting shellfish stocks, he said.
The area has also seen an influx of Portuguese man o’ war and triggerfish from warmer climes to the south — species that prey on local fish and crustaceans.
“We had some very bad years for clam production, but we worked on seeding them and the species gradually adapted,” Gonzalez said.
He hopes the seabed restoration efforts can do the same for kelp forests.
The disappearance of kelp could lead to the decline of sea urchins and other species fishing crews depend on, he said.
“At that point, as a fishing guild, we would cease to exist,” he added
OCTOPUS APOCALYPSE
In other European waters, new, invasive species from the Red Sea and beyond are entering the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal, displacing native populations, reshaping food chains and threatening fisheries, researchers say. In all, there are more than 1,000 nonindigenous species in the Mediterranean, according to a report by the Cyprus Academy of Sciences, Letters and Arts, based on surveys by scientists in 11 countries.
Some native species are coping with the warmer temperatures better than others.
A massive swarm of jellyfish shut down reactors at France’s Gravelines nuclear power plant last month when they clogged its cooling system — for the second time in as many years. The plant in northern France is cooled from a canal connected to the North Sea.
Fishing crews on the south coast of England are reporting a surge in landings of common octopus. About 2,600 tonnes were caught last year and upwards of 3,000 tonnes so far this year, according to figures compiled by the UK Marine Management Organisation. Before last year, annual landings were less than 30 tonnes.
Octopus larvae are carried into British waters on currents from breeding grounds near the Channel Islands, Brittany and places further south, said Bryce Stewart, senior research fellow at the Plymouth-based Marine Biological Association (MBA).
Many would not survive the frigid temperatures. However, since 2022, the English Channel has been under heatwave conditions for around six months out of the year on average, logging more than 900 days in all, the Reuters analysis found.
“Now they’re actually breeding in UK water quite prolifically,” Stewart said.
For Ian Perkes, owner of the eponymous fish merchants in the south Devon seaside town of Brixham, the octopus bloom has proved a boon.
There is a ready market in southern Europe for the once-rare species and no fishing quotas, he said. “There was one week where we had 200,000 kilos.”
Not everyone profits from the shellfish-loving octopuses, which feed on local lobsters, brown crabs and scallops.
For members of the South Devon and Channel Shellfishermen’s cooperative, this year has been an “octopus apocalypse,” according to its executive officer, Beshlie Pool. One fishing trip yielded a single crab all day, she said.
The MBA estimates the octopus bloom could account for about ￡10 million (US$13.25 million) in lost shellfish catches against about ￡12 million in octopus landings between January and September of last year.
The benefits are not evenly distributed. Some shellfishers have switched to catching octopuses, but many do not have the necessary equipment, Pool said. Four of the co-op’s 90-some vessels have gone out of business in the past 12 months.
The unpredictability of the changes makes it hard to adapt, Stewart added.
“Will the octopus still be here next year?” he asked. “If they’ve eaten all the crabs and lobsters, and the octopus die off, then what do we do?”

16:37:31 UTC
01:37:31 KST

TikTok on Friday agreed to pay Alabama at least US$100 million, and enact time limits and other restrictions for teen users, avoiding trial with a settlement modeled on Instagram owner Meta’s agreement with US states.
A trial had been set to begin tomorrow in the southern US state over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content.
Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall hailed the settlement as “a great day for Alabama parents.”
Photo: Getty Images via AFP
“Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction,” he said.
Under the settlement, TikTok would send US$100 million to Alabama and could possibly pay up to US$300 million in total if other states accept similar agreements.
Alabama’s suit was the latest in a wave of litigation targeting social media companies across the US over the harm their apps allegedly cause young users.
Last month, Meta agreed to pay US$18 billion to settle a sweeping lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook to get children addicted.
TikTok’s settlement with Alabama mirrors safety provisions agreed by Meta, including a two-hour daily time limit for teens, restricted access from midnight to 6am, and suspending notifications during school hours.
It would also strengthen age verification, ban beauty filters for teenagers and offer young users a non-personalized content feed.
In addition, it includes a conditional restriction that Meta also agreed to: expanding the nighttime shutdown period to 10pm to 7am, if other platforms also commit to do the same.
“TikTok’s priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community,” a company spokesperson said.
“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” the spokesperson added.
More than a dozen other states, including California and New York, still have active lawsuits against TikTok.
The company has previously settled cases against it that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
Meta has taken its chances in court — with bruising results.
In March, a jury in New Mexico ordered the Facebook and Instagram owner to pay US$375 million after finding it had misled the public about the safety of its platforms for children.
That same month, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent in the case of a 20-year-old woman who said she became hooked on social media as a child, awarding her US$6 million.
Going to trial would have exposed TikTok to unprecedented public scrutiny of how it handles safety internally, with company documents and executive testimony potentially aired in open court.
Alabama originally sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company, ByteDance, in April last year, saying that the app was engineered to hook young users “just like a sophisticated gambling machine.”
The state later narrowed its case to claims under Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, focusing on whether TikTok misrepresented the effectiveness of features such as “Restricted Mode” and “Kids Mode.”
Despite TikTok’s assurances that users in that mode should not see mature themes, the accounts were quickly served videos about suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, alcohol and sex, the filing said.

Taiwan in global education studies top 5
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:31 UTC
01:37:31 KST

Taiwanese students have over the past few years ranked among the top five in the world in four major international assessments, taking first place in civic knowledge and computational thinking.
The evaluations spanned mathematics, science, reading, civic knowledge, computer and information literacy, computational thinking and computational problem-solving.
In the 2022 International Civic and Citizenship Education Study (ICCS), Taiwan rose from second place in the previous survey to first in civic knowledge.
Photo: Rachel Lin, Taipei Times
In 2023, Taiwan ranked first in computational thinking and fourth in computer and information literacy in the International Computer and Information Literacy Study. In the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study, Taiwanese fourth-grade students ranked second worldwide in mathematics and third in science, while eighth-grade students placed second in both subjects.
In last year’s Programme for International Student Assessment, Taiwan placed fourth in science, third in reading, fourth in mathematics and fifth in computational problem-solving, a new category.
Minister of Education Cheng Ying-yao (鄭英耀) said the nation is proud of the students’ outstanding performances in reading, science, mathematics, civic literacy and technological literacy.
Cheng thanked elementary and secondary-school teachers for their professionalism and dedication, as well as parents for their support.
Society should have greater confidence in Taiwan’s education system, Cheng said.
Teachers the unsung heroes behind the talent pipeline that supports the nation’s technology industry and development, he added.
Taiwan has maintained a leading global position in three key areas — academic achievement, digital literacy and civic literacy — demonstrating a comprehensive advantage in talent cultivation rather than excellence in a single subject, said Tseng Feng-lan (曾芬蘭), deputy director of Research Center for Psychological and Education Testing at National Taiwan Normal University .
Taiwan’s success stems from a stable basic education system, a solid foundation in mathematics and science, literacy-oriented curriculum reforms, and long-term investment in reading, information technology and civic education, she said.
The 12-Year Basic Education Curriculum has enabled most students to receive relatively balanced educational opportunities, while the “108 Curriculum Guidelines” implemented in 2019 further bolstered inquiry-based learning, interdisciplinary studies and problem-solving skills, she said.
Taiwan’s mathematics and science education emphasizes logical reasoning, problem analysis and mastery learning, while reading remains the foundation for understanding information, evaluating evidence and developing critical thinking, she added.
As international assessments increasingly emphasize the application of knowledge in real-world contexts, civic judgement and digital problem-solving, Taiwan’s high rankings reflect the success of the nation’s literacy-oriented reforms, she said.
Deputy Minister of Education Chang Liao Wan-chien (張廖萬堅) attributed the results to the long-term efforts of teachers and the outcomes of curriculum reforms promoting literacy orientation, hands-on inquiry and cross-disciplinary learning.
International evaluations are critical references for curriculum and policies, as they help identify students’ strengths and areas that need improvement, he said.
National Chinan University honorary chair professor Wu Ching-shan (吳清山) said Taiwan’s strong performance showed that its elementary and secondary education system has a more solid foundation than the US and Europe.
However, there remains room for improvement, particularly in fostering student interest in learning, and addressing systemic and structural disparities within the education system that affect students from low-income families and rural areas, he said.
He suggested improving teacher training, including helping educators integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into instruction and using technology to develop more innovative teaching.
He also called for cross-ministerial cooperation to address factors affecting student learning, including population decline in rural areas, weakened family support systems, and limited social and cultural stimulation.
He proposed a comprehensive program to boost learning motivation and interest among elementary and secondary-school students, helping lower-achieving students build confidence through positive learning experiences while encouraging schools to improve curricula, teaching methods and assessments.
National Chung Cheng University vice president Chan Sheng-ju (詹盛如) suggested the establishment of stronger support mechanisms to channel resources to disadvantaged groups, and adopting more targeted educational strategies at different stages of schooling — focusing on language and numeracy foundations in elementary school, and expanding to problem-solving and civic participation skills in junior-high school, for example.
National Taiwan Normal University professor Liu Mei-hui (劉美慧) said next year’s ICCS would include more questions related to evaluating AI-generated information, so Taiwan should continue to enhance students’ analytical and critical thinking skills.

Trump, Xi, Takaichi and tale of headlines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:37:29 UTC
01:37:29 KST

The main front-page headline of the Nikkei on Thursday said that Japan and the US closely coordinated on their response to China. Just one day later, the headline read that China urged the US to make concessions on Taiwan.
Placed side by side, the headlines neatly capture the two competing voices on the Taiwan Strait issue that now stand before US President Donald Trump.
The first voice is from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Two days before Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), Takaichi spoke with Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
The two leaders reportedly exchanged views on China, economic security and other issues, and affirmed the close cooperation of their countries. Takaichi emphasized that holding the meeting at that time was itself a way of demonstrating to the world the strength of the US-Japan alliance, highlighting the increasingly close connection between the alliance and peace in the Taiwan Strait.
The latter voice is from Xi.
Two days later, Xi met with Trump, calling on the US to “oppose Taiwan independence” and handle the Taiwan issue cautiously. What Beijing is seeking is no longer merely Washington’s existing position of “not supporting” Taiwan independence, but a further step toward explicitly opposing it.
First Takaichi, then Xi. The diplomatic sequence is noteworthy.
It was no coincidence that Takaichi met with Trump before Xi. After her meeting, she said that the timing was due to the upcoming US-China summit. In other words, before Trump and Xi sat down at the negotiating table, Japan had already taken its security concerns to Washington.
The reason behind this is not difficult to understand. If conflict were to erupt in the Taiwan Strait, those immediately affected would not only include Taiwan, but also Japan’s Okinawa and the Ryukyu Islands, US forces stationed in Japan, maritime shipping routes and semiconductor supply chains.
For Japan, peace in the Taiwan Strait is not a matter to be watched from the sidelines — it is directly tied to its own national security.
The significance of the Nikkei report on Thursday about US-Japan coordination only truly came into focus when the following day’s headline was published. The concerns Japan had raised the previous day had, as it turned out, become real issues on the US-China negotiating table.
Xi’s demand that the US “oppose Taiwan independence” underscores exactly why Takaichi had to take proactive measures. Trump’s response has not yet been clarified by Washington, but at least before Beijing made its demands, Tokyo had already communicated its position — Japan’s voice had been heard loud and clear.
The US and China can negotiate, and Trump and Xi can strike deals, but if peace in the Taiwan Strait becomes a bargaining chip between great powers, Taiwan would not be the only one to bear the costs — Japan and the wider Asia-Pacific region would be affected as well.
The two contrasting headlines in the Nikkei made clear that the two meetings — first Takaichi, then Xi — were not simply items on the US’ diplomatic calendar, but part of a larger diplomatic power struggle that has profound implications for security in the Taiwan Strait and Japan.
Wang Hui-sheng is a founding member of the East Asian Research Institute.

A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Fears of possible serial killer rise in South Africa after body of 10th woman found
South African police said Saturday that another woman's body had been found near Johannesburg, bringing the number of victims to 10 in a series of killings under investigation.
Police began investigating after the bodies of three women were found in July and August within about 4.3 miles of one another in the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg.
The discovery of six bodies in Ekurhuleni over 10 days earlier this month raised fears that a serial killer or killers were responsible.
Two women were arrested and charged last week with murder in relation to the ninth body, discovered on Sept. 17. The victim had been stabbed and had her throat cut, police said. Police did not link the two women charged to any of the other killings.
Provincial police commissioner Lt. Gen. Tommy Mthombeni told state broadcaster SABC on Saturday that investigators believed the ninth killing was an isolated case but could not rule out the possibility that some of the other cases were linked.
Police had issued a warning for women to use caution while in the area.
Police have identified similarities in some of the killings but said they had not found conclusive evidence that the same person or people were responsible.
All nine of the bodies discovered before Saturday were those of women in their 20s or 30s, according to police. Several were naked or partially clothed and left in open areas near main roads. Officers from the Investigative Psychology Unit, which specializes in complex or serial violent crimes, are part of the investigation.
Police released limited details about the 10th body, which was found early Saturday, and did not immediately identify the victim.
"We can only confirm the discovery of the body," the South African Police Service said in a statement. "Crime scene management and all the necessary role players are currently on the scene."
South Africa has high rates of violent crime and violence against women. Three women were killed every day by an intimate partner from 2020-2021, a recent study found.
The country has one of the highest global murder rates, with more than 60 a day on average.
The killings in Ekurhuleni have sparked a national outcry over women's safety.
