====================================================================================================

New study of Brazilian twins sheds light on the heritability of our creative confidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
16:00:21 UTC
01:00:21 KST

A recent study of Brazilian twins suggests that people’s beliefs about their own artistic and practical creativity are modestly influenced by their genetics. The research, published in Personality and Individual Differences, indicates that while inherited factors play a role, unique life experiences account for the vast majority of differences in how creative individuals think they are. The findings provide behavioral genetics data from a South American population, expanding a field that traditionally relies on North American and European samples.
Creativity is generally understood as the ability to generate original and useful ideas in response to environmental demands or social challenges. The concept is often broken down into specific domains. Artistic creativity involves expressive and aesthetic pursuits like visual arts, music, and performance. Practical or everyday creativity involves finding functional solutions to daily problems, such as improvising a fix for a broken household item or navigating a complex social situation.
Instead of measuring objective creative performance, the current research focuses on creative self-beliefs. This term refers to how people perceive their own creative capacities. A person’s belief in their own creativity is a psychological trait that influences whether they seek out creative opportunities or persist when faced with complicated challenges.
To understand how much of a trait is inherited, scientists often rely on twin studies. By comparing identical twins, who share all of their DNA, with fraternal twins, who share about half of their DNA, researchers can estimate the relative contributions of genetics and the environment. Environmental influences are further divided into shared environments, like growing up in the same household, and non-shared environments, which include unique personal experiences such as individual friendships, specific mentors, or personal hobbies.
Most of what scientists know about the genetics of creativity comes from populations in industrialized Western nations. However, a 2024 review pointed out a regional blind spot, noting that Brazilian twins have been largely missing from global genetic research. The research team, led by João Vitor Rodrigues Costa and Marco Antonio Corrêa Varella at the University of São Paulo, set out to provide initial estimates of genetic and environmental influences on creative self-beliefs in a South American context.
Varella, a biologist and research fellow at the Institute for Research on Sociocultural Variations who also authored an open access book about the ecological and evolutionary bases of human behavior, was drawn to the topic through his interest in evolutionary psychology. “From the evolutionary perspective, the only way to empirically be confident that something morphological or psychological evolved is to reunite a converging line of evidence stemming from different areas and fields,” Varella told PsyPost. “One of these sources of evidence is indeed twin studies, which tell us how much genetic variation lies underneath individual variation in psychological and bodily traits.”
To conduct the new study, the researchers recruited 196 participants, making up 98 twin pairs. The sample included 79 pairs of identical twins and 19 pairs of fraternal twins. The participants were predominantly female, mostly young adults, and primarily from middle-class backgrounds in Brazil. Data collection occurred in two phases, with 74 twin pairs visiting a laboratory for an extensive session of psychological and physical assessments prior to the pandemic, and an additional 24 twin pairs completing the study through an online survey at a later date.
The participants answered a brief questionnaire designed to measure their self-perceived creativity and curiosity. They rated their own artistic creativity and practical creativity on an 11-point scale ranging from zero to ten. They also answered a single question about their general curiosity using the same scale. The researchers then used statistical models to compare the scores of identical and fraternal twins, allowing them to calculate the percentage of variance explained by genetics, shared family environments, and unique individual experiences.
The researchers found that genetic factors accounted for about 22 percent of the variation in artistic creative self-beliefs. For practical creativity, genetic factors accounted for a nearly identical 21 percent of the variation. This means that roughly one-fifth of the differences in how creative these individuals believed themselves to be can be traced back to their genetic makeup. When the researchers combined both measures into a single general factor of creative self-belief, the genetic influence was estimated at 24 percent.
The remaining variation in creative self-beliefs was almost entirely explained by non-shared environmental factors. Unique life experiences accounted for about 78 percent of the variance in artistic creativity and 79 percent in practical creativity. Shared environmental factors, such as being raised in the same household or having the same parents, had no statistically significant effect on the twins’ creative self-beliefs. The statistical models for the curiosity question did not fit the data well, so the researchers did not interpret those specific results.
“How one considers oneself as creative varies among people, and we found that in a small and unrepresentative sample of Brazil, about a quarter and a fifth of this interpersonal variation is due to genetic factors,” Varella explained. “The majority of this individual variation is due to each one’s unique individual environment (the one not shared with our siblings or no one else).”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a relatively small number of participants, particularly in the group of fraternal twins. This small sample size means that the exact statistical estimates have wide margins of error and should be viewed as preliminary approximations. A larger sample of fraternal twins would help to provide more precise calculations of genetic and environmental influences in this population.
Varella noted the difficulty in recruiting a sample of twins, “particularly because they are less than two percent of the population and because the USP Twin Panel is still in its initial phase, so the size of the twin register and the proportion of twins who want to be part of research is still small, unfortunately.” He added that identical twins generally participate at higher rates because they “are more intrigued by their similarity.”
The study also used single-item questions to measure creativity and curiosity. “Because we had little access to twins and little time with them, we had to compromise and use only a single item question about creativity self-belief,” Varella said. While these brief measures are useful for keeping surveys short, they do not capture the full complexity of human creativity.
The results reflect how participants view their own abilities, which is not necessarily the same as how they would perform on objective tests of creative thinking or problem solving. People’s self-ratings can be influenced by cultural norms regarding modesty, self-esteem, and what a specific society considers creative.
“Heritability is not about how much of my or your creativity is due to my genes, but instead it is a measure of the genetic contribution to the individual differences in traits in a given population,” Varella explained. “The more one knows about modern genetics and behavioral genetics, the less one is afraid of genes as being the destiny or immutable fatality. Heritability or genes can never really be used as excuses because the most important factor that affects individual differences across traits and population is the unique environment; what we do with our life and all the random factors that we face.”
Future research could build on these findings by combining self-reported beliefs with actual performance tasks, such as generating alternative uses for everyday objects or having independent judges evaluate creative products. Exploring these traits in larger and more diverse groups of twins across Latin America could also help clarify how cultural and educational opportunities interact with genetic predispositions to shape the creative mind.
“We hope our humble study serves a bigger purpose of inspiring more researchers in Latin America to study behavioral genetics and other biological perspectives to psychology and behavior, so that we get to a more integrated and richer notion of humans,” Varella concluded.
The study, “Heritability of self-reported artistic and practical/everyday creative self-beliefs in Brazilian twins,” was authored by João Vitor Rodrigues Costa, Yago Lukševičius de Moraes, and Marco Antonio Corrêa Varella.

BAE wins four-year deal to support UK artillery
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
17:00:20 BST
01:00:20 KST

BAE Systems has been awarded a four-year framework agreement to supply artillery and armoured vehicle weapon system components for the UK Armed Forces, including support for the British Army’s 105mm Light Gun, according to the company.
The agreement was awarded by Babcock Land Defence on behalf of the Ministry of Defence and will cover the continued supply of components across the Light Gun and BAE Systems’ wider artillery portfolio. The work is intended to support availability of the systems already in service, with replacement parts and other components supplied over the duration of the framework.
The 105mm Light Gun remains in British Army service as a lightweight artillery system designed to be moved rapidly between positions and deployed by a range of transport aircraft and helicopters. Under the new arrangement, BAE Systems will continue supporting the weapon alongside components for other artillery and armoured vehicle weapon systems used by the Armed Forces.
Laurie Ellis, Managing Director at BAE Systems, said: “This agreement reflects the confidence placed in us as artillery experts and our commitment to supporting the British Army with world-class capability. We are incredibly proud of our heritage in artillery design, manufacture and support, and of the skilled people across our business who ensure these critical capabilities remain available where they are needed most.
“The Light Gun continues to demonstrate value through its mobility, reliability and battlefield effectiveness. We are committed to continuing our support for this important capability and the service members who rely on it.”
The framework follows further BAE Systems investment in artillery manufacturing in the UK, including work to restore domestic production capacity for British-designed 105mm and 155mm gun barrels at Sheffield. That programme is intended to rebuild production capability for artillery barrels in Britain while supporting current and future land systems.

Poland detains 17-year-old over alleged mosque and school terror plot
Poland's Internal Security Agency (ABW) has detained a 17-year-old boy plotting a large-scale terrorist attack on a mosque and a school, while a court has ordered the teenager to remain in pre-trial detention for three months, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said on Tuesday.
"Weapons, explosives, and Nazi symbols were seized from his home," Zurek wrote on X. "The court, at the prosecutor's request, ordered his temporary arrest."
Jacek Dobrzynski, spokesperson for the minister-coordinator of special services, also commented on the case in a post on X.
"Fascinated by Nazi ideology, he was preparing a terrorist attack in which many people were to die," Dobrzynski wrote, adding that the teenager allegedly planned to purchase weapons and military equipment.
The National Prosecutor's Office (PK) said Tuesday that Pawel G., whose surname is withheld under Polish law, was detained on Sept. 18 and charged with three offences allegedly committed between May 28 and Sept. 20.
The first charge concerns participation in a terrorist criminal organisation that incited hatred and promoted fascist and Nazi ideologies. He was also accused of publicly disseminating hate speech online and possessing illegal Nazi and fascist materials intended for digital distribution. A further charge relates to allegedly planning a mass-casualty terrorist attack, including conspiring with an accomplice, acquiring weapons and gathering information related to extremist activities.
Pawel G. pleaded not guilty and refused to testify, the PK said. If convicted, he faces up to 15 years in prison.
Dobrzynski also recalled in a post last week that the ABW had detained two 16-year-old teenagers in southern Poland's Silesian province. Authorities reportedly seized electronic devices containing neo-Nazi and anti-Semitic material, as well as content concerning terrorist attacks, mass killings and so-called lone-wolf attackers.
"Youth radicalisation does not start with an attack. It starts much earlier - with content, contacts, and environments that can lead to real threats," he wrote. (PAP)

Ukraine’s biggest steelmaker halts production
Ukraine’s largest steel producer, ArcelorMittal Krivoy Rog, has halted production after repeated Russian missile strikes caused extensive damage to the plant, the company announced on Friday.
The Russian Defense Ministry has said that Moscow is targeting Ukrainian military and defense-related facilities and supporting infrastructure in response to Kiev’s escalating long-range attacks on Russian energy and industrial sites.
The steelworks, located in the central Ukrainian city of Krivoy Rog, also includes iron ore mining operations. Before the escalation of the conflict in 2022, it produced 4.9 million tons of steel annually.
ArcelorMittal said the facility had been hit four times over the past five weeks, most recently on September 21. The strikes caused extensive damage to production facilities, leaving the company unable to restart operations “in a safe and sustainable manner.”
CEO Mauro Longobardo said the company would focus on preserving the plant’s infrastructure so production could eventually resume. ArcelorMittal expects to take a charge of around $1 billion due to the reduced value of the facility and its equipment.
The shutdown follows stoppages at Zaporozhstal and Kamet Steel, both owned by Ukrainian metals giant Metinvest. Together with ArcelorMittal Krivoy Rog, the three plants accounted for about 90% of Ukraine’s steel output before Russian strikes brought production to a halt, according to the Financial Times. 
“As of today, [Ukraine] doesn’t have a steel industry anymore,” Aleksandr Vodoviz, head of the CEO’s office at Metinvest, told the FT, adding that repairs could take “days, weeks, months, or years.”
The Russian Defense Ministry said this week that it had struck the Krivoy Rog steelworks and other industrial facilities involved in Ukrainian military production. Other recent targets cited by the ministry include drone production and storage sites, power infrastructure, bridges, ports, warehouses, and logistics hubs.
A day before the latest strike on the steelworks, Ukraine launched its largest drone attack on Moscow, killing several people and hitting a major oil refinery.
Russia has condemned strikes on civilians as acts of terrorism, while maintaining that its forces only target military and defense-related facilities.

‘You can’t win’: Ireland’s football team to play Israel despite player protest
“Nobody is comfortable playing this game,” Ireland’s coach declares after a tense locker-room vote to proceed with Sunday’s Nations League match against Israel.
DUBLIN — Ireland’s football players voted behind closed doors Saturday to proceed with their match against Israel — but their coach conceded that his squad was close to “breaking” over the matter.
Ireland’s Icelandic coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, faced a locker-room revolt as one of his players, substitute goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, told him he wouldn’t suit up. Training and press conferences were postponed as rumors swirled as to whether others would join Bazunu, potentially leaving Hallgrímsson with too small of a squad to compete.
But after several hours of closed-doors discussions, Ireland’s 26-player squad voted on whether to play Israel — and, according to the Football Association of Ireland (FAI), most said yes.
Advertisement
The Nations League clash will be played Sunday at a neutral Hungarian venue and without Irish fans, amid demands of pro-Palestinian protesters in Ireland for the match to be cancelled.
During a press conference in Debrecen, Hungary, FAI chief executive David Courell said the match had been approved by “a significant majority,” but he declined to break down the precise vote.
Beside him, a downcast Hallgrímsson said they were legally and professionally obligated to play Israel even though his squad was “almost to a breaking limit now.”
“Nobody is comfortable playing this game,” Hallgrímsson said, describing the situation as a Catch-22. “It’s two choices and both are tough and bad. It’s a situation where you can’t win.”
When asked to confirm whether other players would join Bazunu in boycotting the match, Hallgrímsson demurred. “We haven’t come to a conclusion on this, but the game is going ahead,” he said. “We are trying to limit the damage.”
He said the Irish players planned to avoid any pre-game ceremonies with Israeli players, including the traditional handshakes, and would wear black armbands during the match “in recognition of all lives lost in the conflict.”
Advertisement
The FAI has been resisting protesters’ calls to boycott Israel ever since Ireland was drawn in February to play the Israelis twice. Sunday’s match in Debrecen is Israel’s “home” game, while the Dublin fixture set for October 4 has been moved to Serbia. Both matches are being televised in Ireland but with minimal commentary.
Relations between the two countries have steadily deteriorated since Israel launched its offensive on Gaza following Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel in 2023.
Ireland, who has long sympathized with the Palestinian cause, infuriated Israel in 2024 by becoming one of the first European countries to recognize Palestinian statehood. Israel shut its Dublin embassy after Irish government leaders started to describe the mounting Gaza death toll and destruction as “genocidal”.
Israel’s coach, Ran Ben-Shimon, said he hoped Ireland’s staff and players would accept handshakes.
“We will put out our hands. If they don’t want to shake it, fine,” he told reporters Saturday night.
Earlier this week, in response to Hallgrímsson’s comment that Ireland’s team would be “playing against genocide,” the Israel Football Association condemned him as a figure of “ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity.”

Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:50:27 UTC
00:50:27 KST

Hundreds of thousands of people lined the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in Paris on Saturday to attend an open-air mass with Pope Leo, on the second day of his visit to France.
The Vatican estimated 700,000 people turned out for the outdoor mass with the 71-year-old American pope – about 100,000 more than the number of people who had registered to attend.
It took place at the Place de la Concorde, the site of bloody executions by guillotine during the French Revolution – when Louis XVI’s staunchly Catholic rule was overthrown – and now the centre of the secular republic.
The choice of the site, a symbol of the French republic to many, was criticised by supporters of France’s strict legislation separating church and state in public life.
But cheers rang out in the crowd as the pope thanked God in his homily for the chance to visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour to promote Catholicism and its teachings.
It is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.
Pope Leo asked those in the crowd not to keep their faith to themselves. “Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied,” he said. “From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.”
He told Catholics that only their faith, and not material things, can provide true happiness.
“Only God can fill the emptiness within us,” he said.
The security zone for the event – the biggest of the papal tour – stretched about 1.4 miles (2.2km), shutting down road traffic in central Paris from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.
Chanting “Leo, Leo” and “Long live the pope”, crowds of people waved French and Vatican flags as the pontiff rode slowly down the grand boulevard of the Champs-Élysées aboard a popemobile – a specially designed, partly open vehicle used during public appearances.
He stopped frequently along the way as babies were lifted out of the crowd and brought to him to receive a papal caress on their heads. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops.
About 14,500 police officers, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters were deployed to the event, which was attended by 2,400 priests and deacons, and about 100 bishops.
Marie-Élisabeth, a 44-year-old nun from Burgundy, told a reporter for France 24: “This event is a way for us to say loud and proud that Christians are here.”
Speaking to reporters from Agence France-Presse, Sylvie Leclerc, a 51-year-old teacher, also said she and her fellow Christians want to share their fervour for their faith. “You don’t hear much from us Catholics, but now we’re going to make some noise!” she said. “But to proclaim love, peace, joy.”

Combat shows speed alone can’t catch Russia’s jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers’ assurances. So why can’t they stop them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:48:44 UTC
00:48:44 KST

Last winter, eight Ukrainian companies told the defense minister that their interceptors were ready to knock Russia's jet-powered drones out of the sky. They were not. A fast-flying drone is the easy part of the design, while combat testing exposed what the interceptors lacked in key features to chase an evading jet-powered Geran, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, said in an interview with NV.
Ukraine's answer to Russia's fast, hard-to-stop jet drones was supposed to be cheap interceptors, and last winter, their makers said they had them. But a jet Geran flies 450 to 500 kilometers an hour, up from the Geran-3's 320, varies its speed to slip past defenses, and will dodge harder once interceptors appear.
Catching one takes maneuverability, machine-vision target-lock, and fuel to loiter and search, not just speed, Flash said. Ukraine's cheap interceptors have already downed about half of Russia's slower drones, but the jet-powered systems have stayed a step ahead.
Eight makers said "ready"
At a meeting last winter called by Mykhailo Fedorov, then-defense minister, all eight interceptor makers reported the same thing: "everything's ready, the solution exists, it flies, we tested it, speed is sufficient," Flash recalled.
The mistake, he said, was that no one checked on them week to week. There were also too few jet Gerans in the skies then to test against.
"On the range, they showed: it flies. That was the problem," explained Flash.
Speed is the easy part
The engines are not the obstacle, Flash continues, since they can be bought abroad, and neither is a plane that flies fast in a straight line. The hard part is a machine agile enough to chase a jet-powered Geran, which is far more maneuverable than the propeller kind and will start changing altitude and throwing evasive maneuvers once interceptors appear.
Because an operator's aim frays at such speeds, he said, the decisive pieces are automatic target capture by machine vision and automatic terminal guidance.
"Building a construction that just flies fast is the easiest part," he added.
Mass orders must wait
That is why Ukraine cannot simply order thousands to blanket the country, Flash said: it first needs a proven design that works for any crew, from Security Service specialists to territorial defense soldiers, and is simple to launch, operate, and maintain.
Once such a sample exists, he said, scaling up is only a question of money. Meanwhile, the work is moving: a Ukrainian interceptor recently notched its first kills against jet Gerans and is heading toward mass production.

Netanyahu faces his nightmare at UN: The Soleimani portrait in Iran’s empty seat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:48:00 UTC

Netanyahu faces his nightmare at UN: The Soleimani portrait in Iran’s empty seat
TEHRAN — Benjamin Netanyahu arrived at the United Nations determined to turn the General Assembly into a stage for Israel’s military narrative.
But behind the speeches and threats was a more striking image: the portrait of Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani sitting on the desk of the absent Iranian delegation.
Netanyahu, the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, was permitted to enter the United States and address the world’s foremost international body without arrest. The war criminal spoke as if international accountability were a concept reserved for others.
As he began speaking, dozens of delegations rose from their seats and walked out. Israeli officials counted 77 delegations as absent or having walked out — nearly 40 percent of the UN’s 193 member states.
Netanyahu brought a pager to the UN podium—a device now associated with Israel’s September 2024 operation, when thousands of pagers exploded in Lebanon, killing many and wounding more than 3,000, including civilians.
And the symbolism did not stop there. Netanyahu had also presented Donald Trump with a pager, turning a device associated with the deadly operation into a political prop shared with the U.S. president. Then, standing before the world, Netanyahu raised one at the UN and issued threats. The message was stark: a device associated with bloodshed had been transformed into a symbol of defiance on the world’s diplomatic stage.
At the institution created in the name of international peace, the Israeli leader chose to display technology associated with a mass-casualty operation as a symbol of military achievement.
He insulted delegations that had walked out, calling them “moral cowards.” He celebrated Israel’s military actions, repeated lies about the war in Gaza, defended the occupation of Palestinian and Syrian territories, and labeled human rights defenders as “antisemites.”
He also claimed the bombardment of Iran’s nuclear facilities was one of the easiest decisions he had made as prime minister.
But there was another object in the room.
On the Iranian delegation’s desk, where diplomats should have been seated, a portrait sat quietly: the face of Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani — Iran’s commander assassinated in a U.S. drone attack in Baghdad in January 2020 — watching over the empty chairs.
That photograph carried a message of its own.
Netanyahu displayed the weaponized technology associated with Israel’s war of atrocities. Iran left behind the face of a commander whose death was supposed to demonstrate the reach of American power.
Washington and Tel Aviv believed that assassinating Soleimani would eliminate a major figure of the resistance. They believed that removing a man from the battlefield would weaken the cause he represented. Years later, his portrait remains capable of transforming an empty diplomatic desk into a political statement.
For Iran, Soleimani remains an embodiment of the resistance strategy that challenged American and Israeli influence across West Asia. For Israel and the United States, he represented a major adversary. His assassination did not eliminate an individual; it became another chapter in the confrontation between Iran and the American-Israeli security order in the region.
The legal dimension of Netanyahu’s appearance was equally difficult to ignore.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former war minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024. The ICC said there were reasonable grounds to believe they bore criminal responsibility for acts including starvation as a method of warfare, murder, persecution, other inhumane acts and intentionally directing attacks against civilians.
The United States, which presents itself as a guardian of a rules-based international order, has meanwhile challenged the authority of the very institution that issued the warrants.
Trump called on ICC member states to withdraw from the court during his UN address, while his administration has pursued measures against the ICC. Washington’s campaign has targeted an institution that has acted against Israeli officials and investigated U.S. conduct in Afghanistan.
This is the contradiction at the heart of the so-called rules-based order: when an international court takes action against a close American ally, Washington moves against the court itself. When Israel faces allegations of war crimes, the United States provides diplomatic and political protection. When Iran defends its sovereignty, it is portrayed as the aggressor.
Iran’s representative, Nasser Asadi, delivered a forceful response at the UN, criticizing the decision to give Netanyahu a platform while Palestinians are denied one. He condemned Israel’s actions, criticized U.S. support for Israel and rejected the narrative presented by Netanyahu.
He closed with a direct warning: “Any further act of aggression against our sovereignty, territorial integrity, or national interests will be met with a decisive and devastating response.”
This is where the Soleimani portrait acquires its deeper meaning.
Washington and Tel Aviv repeatedly kill commanders, destroy infrastructure and launch attacks beyond their own borders. But military superiority does not automatically produce political surrender. The continued resonance of Soleimani’s image illustrates the limits of that assumption.
Netanyahu can stand at the UN podium and declare victory. He can display a pager and recount battlefield achievements. But he cannot decide what the region remembers.
Washington can pressure international institutions, deliver advanced weapons to Israel and blindly provide political and diplomatic protection for it. But Iran continues to deliver its own message. General Soleimani remains a powerful symbol of resistance to Israel and the U.S. His portrait remained while Netanyahu spoke to empty seats.
That is perhaps the most striking image of Netanyahu’s UN appearance: while the war criminal spoke, General Soleimani — the immortalized and unforgettable figure— was still sitting in the room.
Israel cannot kill an idea. America cannot bomb a memory. The resistance runs in our blood, and no pager, drone or speech at the United Nations can extinguish it.
The Zionists have weapons. The Americans have their veto. But Iran has its martyrs — and martyrs never die.

Xi's state visit leads to new progress in constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability: Chinese FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
23:46:52 CST
00:46:52 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States has led to new progress in a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said after Xi wrapped up his U.S. visit on Friday.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks while briefing reporters on Xi's state visit to the United States from Sept. 23 to 25.
President Xi and President Donald Trump had a candid and in-depth exchange of views in a friendly atmosphere of mutual respect on strategic and overarching issues concerning China-U.S. relations and the broader global landscape, Wang said.
Since President Trump began his second term, the two heads of state have maintained close exchanges, including three in-person meetings and five phone talks, and fostered a pattern of interaction marked by mutual respect and sincerity, said Wang, noting this has become the most valuable strategic asset in China-U.S. relations.
An important political outcome of the visit is that President Xi and President Trump further enriched the substance of the new positioning of China-U.S. relations and have agreed to build a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, Wang said.
Respect means respecting each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity, respecting each country's choice of social system and development path, and respecting the other side's core interests and major concerns, Wang said.
Fairness, Wang continued, means pursuing mutually beneficial cooperation and handling differences through consultation, rejecting a zero-sum game in which one side's gain comes at the expense of the other's, and not seeking unilateral absolute advantage.
Reciprocity means that the two countries are equal in sovereignty, that neither side stands above the other, that neither engages in hegemonic nor bullying behavior, that each side's concerns are addressed on an equal basis, and that cooperation across various fields develops in a balanced manner, Wang said.
Noting that President Xi has pointed out that a stable China-U.S. economic and trade relationship requires both expanding the list of cooperation and shortening the list of problems, Wang said that the U.S. side should treat Chinese companies fairly, resolve problems through dialogue and negotiations, and promote the sustained, stable and positive development of China-U.S. economic and trade relations.
The fentanyl abuse problem in the United States is not caused by China, but China has always acted with the utmost goodwill and made every effort to assist the U.S. side in addressing the fentanyl crisis, Wang noted, adding that the two heads of state tasked the law enforcement agencies of the two countries with continuing to strengthen cooperation and jointly combat transnational crime.
To promote people-to-people exchanges between China and the United States, President Xi has announced a series of new measures, including inviting 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchange and study programs over the next five years, Wang said.
One piece of good news that has been particularly welcomed by the American public is that two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will soon arrive at Zoo Atlanta, Wang added.
During the visit, Wang said, the two heads of state had an in-depth exchange of views on major international and regional issues of common concern and agreed to strengthen coordination to make due contributions to world peace and development.
President Xi also encouraged relevant parties to stay committed to peace, supported the United States and Iran in returning to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, resuming dialogue and negotiations at an early date, and ultimately reaching a comprehensive agreement covering the nuclear issue, Wang said.
During the visit, President Xi and President Trump also had an in-depth exchange of views on artificial intelligence (AI), pointing out that the two countries should leverage respective strengths rather than guard against each other, Wang said.
The two heads of state agreed to make good use of AI dialogue mechanisms between the two countries and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI, Wang added.
Noting that this year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, Wang said that China and the United States are both permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, and it is their shared responsibility to uphold the postwar international order and prevent the resurgence of militarism.
China and the United States will respectively host the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and the G20 Leaders' Summit in the fourth quarter of this year, Wang said, adding that the two heads of state confirmed their mutual support, which will continue to inject momentum into cooperation in the Asia-Pacific and global governance. ■

Bahrain's Salwa Eid Naser reclaimed the women's 400m title in 49.20 seconds, breaking the Games record of 50.09 she set on her way to gold in 2018. Iran's Zahra Zarei Manoujan was a distant second in 52.38, with India's Prachi third in 53.21.
On the roads, Japan's Ichitaka Yamashita broke away after 38 kilometers to win the men's marathon in 2:10:49. India's Sawan Barwal took silver in 2:11:37, while China's Feng Peiyou passed a rival late on to secure bronze in 2:12:13.
Bahrain's Shitaye Habte made her move around the 37km mark in the women's race, pulling clear to win in 2:27:31. China's Cirencuomu finished 12 seconds behind for silver, with Japan's Mikuni Yada third in 2:27:56 after setting the pace for much of the race.
Thailand's Joshua Atkinson won the men's 400m in a personal-best 44.90 seconds. Bahrain's Nelly Korir took the women's 1,500m in 4:04.50, ahead of China's Li Chunhui, who ran a personal best of 4:05.50, and Japan's Nozomi Tanaka.
The lineup for Sunday's finals also began to take shape. China's 17-year-old Chen Yujie, crowned women's 100m champion on Friday, won her 200m heat in 23.29 seconds to keep her sprint double hopes alive.
"My legs felt heavy throughout," Chen said after the race. "I'll definitely give it everything in the final and try to win a medal."
Chinese hurdlers Wu Yanni and defending champion Lin Yuwei reached Sunday's women's 100m hurdles final, while Chen Yuanjiang and Liu Junxi advanced in the men's 110m hurdles. Japan's Mako Fukube and Hitomi Nakajima shared the fastest women's qualifying time of 12.85 seconds, while their compatriot Rachid Muratake led the men's heats in 13.27.
Thailand's Puripol Boonson, who won the men's 100m on Friday, was fastest in the 200m semifinals in 20.10 seconds. ■

Several hundred thousand people have gathered in the French capital to attend Pope Leo XIV’s outdoor mass.
The Vatican estimated that 700,000 people came out in Paris on Saturday, more than the 600,000 who had registered in advance.

The American pope greeted flag-waving, cheering throngs from his popemobile as he rode along France’s 1.9 kilometres (1.2 miles) famous avenue, the Champs-Elysees.
Upon arriving at Place de la Concorde, Paris’s largest public square, Leo held an outdoor mass and led hundreds of thousands of people in prayer.
The pontiff began his four-day tour of France on Friday, marking the first official papal visit to the country in 18 years.
The pope is seeking to improve the Roman Catholic Church’s standing in France, five years after an inquiry found that 330,000 children were abused by its clergy and lay members over the span of seven decades. The religious leader has also been challenging France’s recently approved law allowing assisted dying.
French President Emmanuel Macron was not present for the mass and was represented by his wife, Brigitte. Far-right presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen was also among the attendees. Le Pen currently leads the polls in advance of next year’s election, which is due to take place in mid-April.

On Friday, an estimated 300,000 people turned out to see the pontiff as he waved from the popemobile on the way to the Notre Dame Cathedral.
“There is a sense of fervour reminiscent of that experienced over 40 years ago with John Paul II,” Francois Mabille, director of the Geopolitical Observatory on Religion, told broadcaster RMC.
The pontiff met Macron on Friday and gave a rare speech at his official residence, the Elysee Palace.
He praised French society, describing it as the result of “a people whose diverse origins have enlivened and enriched the nation and its democracy”.
He also spoke out against AI, warning that “a paradise of machines” could cause people to lose their humanity.
The Catholic Church has gradually seen its influence in secular France dwindle in recent decades.

Both Moscow and Kyiv have stepped up attacks after the deadliest summer since 2022 – the year Russia launched its full-scale invasion, starting Europe's worst war since World War II.
US-led talks to end fighting have not led to a breakthrough and the Kremlin has repeatedly said it intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.

Ukrainian air defences are currently intercepting 55 percent of jet-powered drones launched by Russia, the Ukrainian president said in his evening address Saturday.
In Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, residents of a typical Soviet-era apartment block hit by a Russian drone were cleaning up their building – already worried about what might come next.

Early Saturday morning however, he was woken up by a video call from his elderly parents – who are both deaf – and rushed back to help.
"I watched as my mother is standing there in her nightgown, my father in his underwear, outside the building in tears ... and there are flames, everything is burning," he said.
"The apartment is completely smashed up."
His mother, he said, is a seamstress.
"Her sewing machine was there. She was in tears because it's broken now. So, well, it's a tragedy. But in my family everyone is alive and for that I thank God," he said.
With mounting Russian attacks on the capital, his family is in "constant stress" and he tries to distract himself by planting tomatoes.
"They don't have enough land," he said, mocking Russia – the world's largest country. "They want to simply wipe out our nation."

Despite Russia making life in Kyiv increasingly tough, Gorlachov said he "wasn't going anywhere".
But fellow resident Anastasiia Grygorovych – woken up when her window "fell on me" – had already fled her hometown of Gorlivka, now occupied by Russia.
Now she was considering leaving Ukraine altogether.
"In general, I’m already thinking that I need to leave," she said.
Russia's invasion has forced millions to flee their homes.

====================================================================================================

Northern Israel’s children need protected classrooms, not more promises - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:40:01 UTC
00:40:01 KST

Some 250 kindergartens across the North opened the school year without full protection. The need has been recognized, the plans approved, the budgets promised. What is missing now is a single address that can move quickly from decision to execution on the ground.
On September 1, as the school year began, a mother from Kfar Vradim, about 15 km. east of Nahariya, said that all she wants for her children is one uninterrupted year of school. Not exceptional achievements, not ambitious programs. Just one year in the same classroom, with the same friends and teachers, without sirens, without evacuations, and without moving from one temporary arrangement to the next.
After what the children of the North have lived through, that is not a wish anyone can take for granted. The continuity they need begins with one basic condition: the ability to learn in safety. Yet according to a report by KAN News, Israel’s public broadcaster, roughly 250 kindergartens in the North, from communities along the Lebanese border down to the Krayot just outside Haifa, opened this year without full protection. That means no standard safe room inside the building, or within a few seconds’ walk of it, as the region’s short warning time requires.
Many children in the area have already been through long months of remote learning, classes in temporary structures, and separation from their communities. Even now that they are home, the return to normal life cannot be complete as long as parents do not know whether, when the siren sounds, their children have a protected space they can reach in time.
Amit Sofer, head of the Merom Hagalil Regional Council, has warned about the same gap. More than six months ago, he says, the Defense Ministry informed the council that its protection requests had been approved. The promised funding has still not been transferred, and the school year is already underway.
Approving those requests matters. It shows that the need is recognized and that there is a willingness to meet it. And protective construction is not the work of a single day: it requires engineering plans, budget authorization, and tenders. That is precisely why it has to begin months before the school year opens, rather than be measured against it. In border communities, protecting a school is not one more infrastructure project. It is what allows a family to stay.
This reality calls for a different way of working. Israel’s government machinery was built mostly for ordinary times, when budgets pass between ministries, authorizations are signed, and plans advance one stage at a time. Rebuilding a border region after a war requires faster and more creative channels, ones that connect decisions to what actually happens on the ground.
After October 7, the Tekuma Directorate was established to concentrate authority, funding, and execution capacity for the damaged communities of the western Negev, along the Gaza border. In the North, the Tenufa Directorate now operates, having been folded into Tekuma and upgraded from a coordinating staff body into a directorate with its own positions and a multi-year budget.
Time between approval, execution
The gap, then, is not the absence of a coordinating body. It is the absence of the authority to shorten the distance between approval and execution. Protecting a single kindergarten is specified by the Home Front Command, budgeted by the Finance Ministry, carried out through the Defense Ministry, and dependent on the local council. Not one of them answers for the result. An urgent national mission needs a single address, clear authority, available funding, and short timelines.
For the mother in Kfar Vradim, the picture is far simpler: either there is a protected space in her children’s kindergarten or there isn’t. A dedicated track of this kind would allow government ministries, local authorities, and contractors to work together. It is needed for protecting schools, and after that for the rest of the tasks that will determine whether the North merely resumes functioning or genuinely recovers.
The Galilee sends a respectable delegation to the Knesset, across several parties. This is not a political or partisan issue. The safety of children on the border and the continuity of their education are a shared national responsibility. The students are already in their classrooms, the need has already been approved, and the people on the ground are ready to act. What they need now is a track that lets them carry it out.
Because for a mother in Kfar Vradim, one uninterrupted year of school is a wish. For the State of Israel, making it real should be a mission.
The writer is the president and founder of the Kedma pioneering social-Zionist organization.

A voyage through northern Greek Macedonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:39:59 UTC
00:39:59 KST

September is a symbolic month to travel to northern Greece and discover what Macedonia is all about. Thirty-five years ago this month, Greece’s northern neighbor declared its independence from Yugoslavia as the Republic of Macedonia. A name that triggered one of Europe’s most unusual and persistent diplomatic disputes.
For Greece, “Macedonia” is not simply a name; it is the name of its own northern region and an inseparable part of its historical heritage, associated with Alexander the Great. For nearly three decades, the two neighbors wrestled over identity, history, and terminology.
In 1992, as Greece’s dispute with its newly independent northern neighbor over the name Macedonia intensified, Thessaloniki’s Mikra Airport was renamed “Makedonia.” The new name referred to the Greek region of Macedonia and carried powerful symbolism at a time when Greece was asserting its own historical and geographical connection to the name.
The 2018 Prespa Agreement eventually produced a compromise: the neighboring country became North Macedonia, explicitly distinguishing it from Macedonia in Greece.
I was curious to explore Greek Macedonia and, along the way, to investigate this question of identity. It is a vast and surprisingly diverse corner of northern Greece, where history is only the beginning of the story.
Turquoise coves, forested hills, seaside villages
At its heart is Thessaloniki, facing the Thermaic Gulf with its celebrated waterfront, Byzantine heritage, multicultural past, and increasingly exciting food scene. Along the waterfront, the imposing statue of Alexander the Great stands as a proud symbol of the city and its Macedonian heritage.
Eight shields and long Macedonian sarissas (spears) surround the monument, evoking the soldiers who accompanied Alexander on his campaigns. Over the years, the site in Thessaloniki (how many of you know that Thessalonike was Alexander the Great’s half-sister?) has also served as a ceremonial gathering point, with wreath-laying commemorative events held at the statue, including an annual tribute by schoolchildren ahead of Greece’s Independence Day.
My destination was pine-covered Sithonia, the middle of the three-pronged Halkidiki peninsula. Here, barely an hour or two from the urban energy of Thessaloniki, Macedonia exchanges monuments and boulevards for turquoise coves, forested hills, seaside villages, and some of northern Greece’s most compelling resorts.
The journey heads east and south into the peninsula stretching into the Aegean. A fascinating story made me curious. Yiannis Carras, a shipping magnate from Chios who sailed into Greek Macedonia, fell in love with this stretch of coastline in the 1960s and went on to create one of the region’s most iconic tourism landmarks. He was the man behind the Porto Carras Grand Resort complex on Sithonia and had a very specific vision when he acquired this vast stretch of land.
Carras envisioned a hotel designed like a cruise ship sailing out to sea, embraced by the coastline and its marina. That vision shaped the Porto Carras Meliton, and more than half a century later, that is still very much the feeling here.
Carras acquired a vast 1,763-hectare estate and set about transforming what was then a largely untouched corner of Sithonia into an extraordinary resort. Today, the Meliton feels almost like a destination in itself: a family resort with four swimming pools, remarkably clear and calm waters along Porto Carras’s nine-kilometer coastline, a wide choice of restaurants, a spacious fitness center, and an impressive variety of activities.
Guests can taste wines at the renowned Domaine Porto Carras winery within the estate, play golf, go horse riding, or choose from sailing excursions departing directly from the adjacent marina.
The scale of the Meliton becomes particularly apparent at breakfast. During our stay, more than a thousand guests were staying at the resort. Yet despite that almost unimaginable number, everyone seemed to find their place with surprising ease. Families gathered in the Athos restaurant facing lavish buffets, their plates piled high with vegetables, cheeses, and freshly prepared omelets, while the morning unfolded at an unexpectedly relaxed pace.
Everyone finds their own rhythm
Anyone who has been on a cruise will know exactly what I mean. There may be a thousand people around you, yet somehow everyone finds their own table, their own corner, their own rhythm.
Perhaps that is the most striking confirmation that Carras’s original vision ultimately succeeded: the Meliton was conceived with the spirit of a cruise ship, and decades later, in more ways than one, it still feels like one.
The resort has changed hands since Carras’s time. In 2020, Porto Carras was acquired by Belterra Investments, associated with the family of Greek-Russian businessman Ivan Savvidis, which subsequently embarked on a major redevelopment of the historic resort. Ownership may have changed, but Carras’s vision remains firmly anchored here.
“What can Macedonia, and Halkidiki in particular, offer Israeli travelers that the Greek islands cannot?” I asked Konstantinos Arvanitis, the general manager.
He answered without hesitation. “The growing number of flights from Israel to Thessaloniki compared with previous years has made the region far more accessible. It allows Israeli travelers to create a much more diverse holiday, combining Thessaloniki, Greece’s second-largest city, with nature, beautiful beaches, and a full resort experience, all within the same trip.
“That variety is one of Macedonia’s great advantages. You don’t have to choose between a city break, a beach holiday, and exploring nature. You can combine all three.
“And then there are the beaches,” he continued. “While many Mediterranean islands are known for smaller or rockier beaches, Halkidiki offers long, wide stretches of sandy coastline and exceptionally clear water.
“As Greece increasingly looks to develop tourism beyond its most saturated island destinations, Macedonia and Halkidiki are becoming a much more important part of the country’s tourism map,” Arvanitis said.
Yet on this journey, I was determined to better understand this Greek Macedonian identity by speaking with guests and hotel staff along the way. Among them was Katerina Athanasiadou, a senior executive at the hotel, whose deep connection to her Macedonian heritage struck me as she spoke passionately about what it means to her to be a Greek Macedonian.
“I still remember an incident from the very beginning of my hospitality career, about 25 years ago, when I was working as a waitress at a hotel in Thessaloniki,” she recalled. “I was serving a couple from overseas who asked me how they could get to Macedonia. I didn’t understand the question. I told them, ‘But you are already in Macedonia.’ They insisted that they were in Greece, not Macedonia.
“It took quite some time to explain that there was no contradiction. Thessaloniki is in Greece, but it is also the capital of the Greek region of Macedonia. Eventually, those guests were referring to what is today North Macedonia.”
For Athanasiadou, the encounter was revealing. “That was when I realized how many people from other countries simply don’t understand how important our Macedonian identity is to us here in northern Greece. Macedonia has been alive here for thousands of years, long before Yugoslavia was created, long before it broke apart, and long before the neighboring country became today’s North Macedonia.”
Yet she is keen to separate that strong sense of identity from tension toward Greece’s northern neighbor. “We are proud Greek Macedonians, but that doesn’t mean we cannot feel close to the people across the border. Today, we have friendly relations, and many guests from North Macedonia stay at the resort and love it. For us, being Macedonian is simply part of who we are as Greeks.”
Back in Thessaloniki before departing home, I spent four fascinating hours on a walking tour of the city, guided by the knowledgeable Alana Ditsolas of Saloniki IL. Partly Israeli, she has lived in Thessaloniki for the past 14 years and leads Israeli groups on walking tours of the city. She is married to George, a Greek Macedonian.
During one of our breaks, I ask her how her husband feels about the neighboring country of North Macedonia; she smiles and says its name is best not mentioned around him. “His blue eyes turn red: ‘They are stealing our Greek history,’” she said. “He protests, raising his voice and blaming the Greek government for compromising by giving up Greece’s exclusive claim to the name Macedonia.”
Yet beyond the sensitivities of history and identity, everyday life tells a more relaxed story. People cross the border, travel, shop, and holiday in each other’s countries, while visitors from North Macedonia are a familiar presence in northern Greece and Halkidiki. History may still stir emotions, but on the ground, the two neighbors increasingly share a very normal relationship.
The writer is the publisher of Travel Flash Tips.

The tribal members then “succeeded in recovering a ship owned by a businessman from the tribe.” The ship, which was apparently transporting oil from the UAE to Europe, had been in the hands of pirates for a month, who were demanding ransom for its release.
Tribal members went out to the sea off Somalia, apparently in coordination with the Somali government, and then fought a gun battle with the pirates. Video posted online showed two men, apparently from the tribe, with belt-fed machine guns shooting at the pirates.
The alleged battle at sea lasted around five hours, and several of the pirates were killed or wounded and then captured. Video and photos show several vessels involved in the clash. It was not clear how it developed. Basra Today released a statement attributed to the Al-Shaghanba “clan,” or asirat, saying it is part of the Obadah tribe, or qabilat. This usually indicates that the Al-Shaghanba is part of a larger tribal group.
Al-Shaghanba quotes Islamic text, calls actions of pirates 'sinful aggression'
The statement quoted an Islamic text that says, “But if anyone transgresses against you, then transgress against him in the same way as he transgressed against you. And fear Allah; and know that Allah is with those who fear Him."
“Following the sinful aggression carried out by Somali pirates against one of our ships, and after communication, coordination, and obtaining authorization from the fraternal government of the Republic of Somalia, we were able to recover the ship in Somali waters, arrest the aggressors, and take measures against them,” the statement continued.
Kurdistan24 noted that “forty members of a Basra tribe helped free an oil tanker seized by pirates in the Gulf of Aden, capturing seven alleged attackers and securing the release of the crew, according to a local media report citing a tribal sheikh.” It added that Sheikh Ali al-Shaghanba described the incident.
Sheikh says tribal group captured seven pirates during battle
The tribal members are from Abu al-Khasib, south of Basra, on the Shatt al Arab waterway. The men come from the village of Jaykur, close to the Iranian border. The sheikh said, “Seven alleged pirates were captured during the operation, while others escaped.”
In another incident off Somalia in August, the Turkish Navy said it had also battled pirates. In a 10-day operation, the Turkish Navy eliminated four boats used by pirates, killing 14 of them.

Why Joseph Hotel TLV offers comfort, community, great value - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:39:49 UTC
00:39:49 KST

If you’re looking for a nice hotel in Tel Aviv that won’t break the bank, consider the Joseph Hotel TLV, just steps from the Bloomfield Stadium light rail station.
Cross the street, take the elevator up one floor, and you’ll find 19 clean, comfortable rooms. The floor is black marble, and the walls are painted green, giving an interesting color contrast. There is coffee and fruit available all day and a nice breakfast that even includes lox (my standard for a good hotel breakfast).
The hotel is just on the edge of Jaffa, with easy access to an “unofficial” beach across the street that had very few people on a weekday morning. It is very close to “shuk hapishpeshim” (the flea market) and the Jaffa clock tower.
The hotel opened just before the pandemic and was forced to close soon afterward. Then October 7 happened, and for two and a half years, they housed evacuees from Kiryat Shmona.
“We went through all the life-cycle events here – everything from a newborn baby’s first smile to engagements and, sadly, even deaths. We became like family. We’re still in touch today, and we’ve even gone up to Kiryat Shmona to visit them,” Tzvi Dahan, one of the owners of the hotel, told The Jerusalem Post.
That family feeling
Living in a hotel while their home was being attacked wasn’t easy, he said. While the government was giving them compensation for not being able to work, many of them wanted to work and feel productive.
“One became our night clerk,” Dahan said. “Another liked to cook, so he would make the breakfasts, and another became the security guard. It really became like a family.”
Dahan saw that on Friday nights, the hotel provided catered meals. But he saw that guests were just picking up the meals and eating in their rooms. So he started bringing his family to the hotel for Shabbat, helping to create a suitable atmosphere. In fact, the hotel won a special award for its work with evacuees.
Even after the evacuees returned home, several decided to move permanently to Tel Aviv and continued working at the hotel. In the past, about half of the clientele were tourists and the other half Israelis, who still come on weekends. But tourist numbers are down, and the hotel is often almost empty during the week.
Dahan said that, as the hotel is small, they try to keep that family feeling.
“These days, even though we’re back to operating purely as a hotel, we wanted to keep some of that same warmth and closeness with our guests,” he said. “We hear it quite a lot – people tell us they feel at home here, that they feel genuinely welcome.”
Best of all is the price. Rooms start at under NIS 600 a night during the week, and kids are free.
The writer was a guest of the hotel.

On Michigan doorsteps, Republicans sell Democrats-as-extremists message with mixed success
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:39:10 UTC
00:39:10 KST

The pitch was simple: Republican US Senate candidate Mike Rogers is a common-sense conservative, while Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed is a big-government socialist aligned with the party's left wing.
But when a canvasser backing Rogers delivered that message to Nick Delise, a three-time Donald Trump voter in suburban Detroit, he encountered some skepticism. Though Delise said he would probably vote for Rogers, he rejected the notion that Democrats were controlled by the far left, saying the party was focused on practical solutions to voters' problems.
The exchange offered a first-hand look at a strategy Republicans are deploying in Michigan and other battleground states: to portray Democrats as ideological extremists who have moved too far to the left, while turning out less-engaged supporters needed to keep their congressional majorities in November.
Reuters accompanied door-knockers with Americans for Prosperity Action, the super PAC arm of the conservative network backed by billionaire Charles Koch, in the city of Livonia last week as they sought to mobilize voters for Rogers in the tightly contested race.
The conversations highlighted both the appeal and limits of Republican messaging. With many Americans unhappy with President Donald Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, Republicans have been struggling to find messages that will get voters grappling with the high cost of living to the polls on Election Day.
Thwarting a 'socialist' turn by Democrats
Delise, 32, seemed like an ideal audience for the pitch. An American flag hung from the porch of his modest, single-story home, two pickup trucks sat in the driveway, and a pro-police "Thin Blue Line" banner was displayed in the garage.
He acknowledged he knew little about the candidates and typically skips midterm elections, while attributing his conservative leanings to the influence of relatives in law enforcement. He complained about the cost of fueling his trucks.
"I'm not hardcore like I have to vote Republican," Delise told Reuters in a follow-up interview, adding that he had not ruled out backing a Democrat if he decides to vote. "I'd be open. I'm not saying there's not a chance."
Many people canvassers encountered were already in Rogers' camp, making the conversations less about persuasion than turnout. One Trump supporter in her 50s said she and two family members had already committed to Rogers, while a middle-aged man chatting in a neighbor's yard said he would back Rogers to thwart what he described as Democrats' socialist turn.
Trump and his allies have sought to capitalize on recent primary victories by some left-leaning Democrats like El-Sayed to argue that the party is veering toward socialism and poses a threat to the country, a claim Democratic leaders dismiss as false and fearmongering. At the same time, Trump has called on his party to put him at the center of their election efforts to excite his base, despite his growing unpopularity.
A Republican couple in their 80s illustrated a potential weakness in the Trump-centric turnout strategy. While the wife said she would vote for Rogers, her husband said dissatisfaction with the president had left him unsure whether he could back the Republican Senate nominee. A canvasser sought to redirect the conversation to policy differences and away from Trump.
"People aren't super happy with the situation in the world right now," Tim Golding, senior adviser to AFP Action in Michigan, said in an interview. "But we try to pivot off that conversation and go back to the policies and the agenda that our candidates have, and not have a conversation about Trump as best we can."
El-Sayed has pushed back against the characterization that he is a radical socialist, calling himself a capitalist. Campaign spokesperson Cole Wozniak said the campaign had built a motivated grassroots base of more than 21,000 volunteers.
The Rogers campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Enthusiasm gap
With Trump posting weak approval ratings and not on the ballot, Republicans must mobilize supporters who might otherwise skip the midterms, when turnout typically falls by more than 10 percentage points from presidential-election levels. That historic trend is raising the stakes for the Republicans' national door-knocking and other get-out-the-vote efforts this election.
Democrats appear more energized, with 42% of self-described Democrats saying they are "very enthusiastic" about voting, compared with 28% of Republican voters, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.
In Michigan, concerns about an enthusiasm gap recently spilled into public view when a Republican working with the Rogers campaign complained about a lack of energy among volunteers for door-knocking and other activities.
"The vibes on the ground are the worst I've seen in my life," Jackson Karki, a college student who had been helping the campaign organize several northern counties, posted to X last week. "No one wants to promote candidates, no one wants to knock doors, no one wants to do shit."
Other Republicans dispute that characterization. In Oakland County, one of Michigan's most important battlegrounds and home to more than 1 million registered voters, Republican Party Chair Vance Patrick said volunteer enthusiasm remains strong.
In an interview, he said Trump was set to visit the state twice before the election on November 3, which he predicted would further encourage volunteers and boost turnout. County party organizations like Patrick's have grown more important in Michigan as the state Republican Party's operations have weakened in recent years.
Patrick said the county's top targets include roughly 20,000 Jewish voters, a key constituency for Rogers given El-Sayed's opposition to military aid for Israel and his characterization of Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide. It is also chasing 38,000 so-called sleeping giants - infrequent voters who they believe would back Rogers if persuaded to cast a ballot.
Case study of national effort
Including AFP and other outside groups, Rogers' campaign plans to knock on six million to eight million doors by Election Day, according to a person familiar with the matter, roughly double the 2024 total, when he lost the Senate race by 19,000 votes.
The effort reflects the scale of the Republican turnout strategy nationally, as campaigns and allied groups invest heavily in door-knocking and other voter-targeting operations amid concerns about voter enthusiasm.
Republicans hold a $637 million cash lead nationally over Democrats across super PACs and party committees, dwarfing Democrats' edge in candidate fundraising and potentially helping fund a more expansive turnout operation, said Brendan Glavin, OpenSecrets' director of insights.
Yet Democrats say money alone will not decide the race. The Michigan Democratic Party says its active volunteer ranks have grown by 267% since the primary as the party has rallied behind El-Sayed.
Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said Democrats will knock on 1.4 million doors in the campaign's final four weeks, arguing the effort will blunt Republican attempts to shift focus away from kitchen-table issues.
They are counting on voters like one resident in his 20s who answered the door in Livonia and, when asked whom he planned to vote for, replied simply, "Not Mike Rogers," before closing it.

Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:39:00 UTC
00:39:00 KST

Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
September 26, 2026
Just a few months ago, Russia's war was an distant reality for many people in Europe outside of Ukraine. If Russian drones occasionally entered the airspace of countries like Poland or Romania, even official statements seemed strangely dismissive and abstract. Even after a Russian drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the eastern Romanian city of Galati in late May this year, many EU and NATO representatives hesitated to accuse Russia of intentional action. At most, there was discussion of hybrid warfare.
The situation has changed radically since the summer. Drone overflights have become almost daily in certain parts of central and southeastern Europe, and there have even been crashes and explosions, particularly in countries bordering Ukraine. Alerts are becoming more frequent, with authorities increasingly having to close airspace or suspend operations at airports, as unauthorized flights are detected. Russia has been bombing border crossings, infrastructure and trains in Ukraine, but very close to other borders. Acts of sabotage are also increasingly common.
For the Baltic states, Poland, Moldova and Romania in particular, the war has long ceased to be "hybrid." More and more, politicians in these countries are saying that Russia is acting deliberately.
Drones violate Moldovan and Romanian airspace
This became evident this week in an unprecedented manner. Moldova recorded four drones entering Moldovan airspace, two of which exploded in Moldovan territory. Wreckage of another was also found. The country's northern airspace was closed temporarily.
Two drones also violated Romanian airspace; with one crashing near the northern town of Solca. A nearby border crossing with Ukraine a few dozen kilometers away was closed as a result. NATO aircraft were scrambled near the Danube Delta.
The scrambling of NATO aircraft has become more common in response to Russian air attacks in Ukraine.
In Poland, NATO fighter jets were scrambled twice in response to Russian attacks near the border with Ukraine. Two Polish border crossings were evacuated after a fire broke out at a Starlink ground station near the village of Wola Krobowska, 40 kilomters (ca. 25 miles) south of the Polish capital Warsaw, on Wednesday night. The station is used to route internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine.
On the same day, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds according to the Polish military.
Polish Prime Minister Tusk says Europe needs to prepare
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke very bluntly in Krakow on Thursday and said that Russia was refining its "disgusting forms of pressure" and Poland must be prepared for them.
Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to exhaust Ukraine by destroying its industrial and energy infrastructure, but he also wants to exhaust Europe," Tusk said. He added that there was a suspicion that the fire at the Starlink ground station had been deliberate.
Earlier this month, Tusk had already warned the Polish parliament that there might be Russian drone and even missile attacks against those who supported Ukraine.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu also reacted very strongly on Thursday, saying that Russia's war was a danger to all of Europe and reasserting Moldova's support for Ukraine.
In Romania, reactions were less clear. Defense Minister Radu Miruta said that not more than a "diplomatic protest" was needed, though he acknowledged that the drone that had crashed in Solca had new technical features, which suggested it could be a newer type of Russian jet-powered drone. 
In New York on Wednesday, in his address to the United Nations General Assembly, Romanian President Nicusor Dan had said: "We are in the fifth year of the illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression waged on a large scale against Ukraine by a permanent member of the Security Council." He had added that as the "EU member state with the longest border with Ukraine, Romania has directly felt the effects of this war through repeated violations of our airspace."
And he too reasserted support for Ukraine: "We have said it before, and we say it again: Romania will stand with Ukraine and its people, who are acting in legitimate self-defense, for as long as it takes."
Attacks on western Europe from the Mediterranean?
Meanwhile, there is growing speculation that Russia could expand its war to Western Europe. On Thursday, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo published information about a CIA report warning that Russia could be preparing drone attacks on Italy, France and Spain. The attacks could be launched from international waters in the Mediterranean and from vessels that were part of Russia's shadow fleet.
There has been no official confirmation so far. French President Emmanuel Macron said that that the CIA had not informed France of this information, but he did say that the possibility Russia could launch an attack against Europe was "plausible."
At a press conference in Denmark on Thursday, politicians and military officials warned that Russia was expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months. The situation is currently the most serious since the end of the Cold War," said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus.
This article was originally published in German.

Czech Republic's 6,500-year-old sanctuary found to predate Stonehenge by 1,000 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
20:24:52 UTC
05:24:52 KST

A prehistoric sanctuary discovered near Chelby in the Czech Republic is one of Central Europe’s oldest monuments, according to research shared earlier this summer from the University of West Bohemia (UWB).
The site has been dated to be over 6,500 years old, making it 1,000 years older than Stonehenge.
The circular enclosure measures to 230 meters in diameter, featuring an over 2.5 meters deep ditch and twelve irregularly spaced entrances.
"Circular enclosures are completely unknown in our region for this period, which already makes the site exceptional,” explained Petr Krišt of UWB’s Archaeology Department who is leading the research.
“But when we began to analyze the positioning of the entrances in detail, it became clear that their arrangement was not random,” he said. “Their geometry creates a system that made it possible to observe the most significant moments of the solar and lunar cycles.”
While similar to Stonehenge in function, Czech site is older
Archaeologists have found two main observation points at the Czech structure, connecting the sunrise at the summer solstice with sunset at the winter solstice in one, while the other is set in elation with the moon’s extreme positions on the horizon during its approximately 18-year cycle.
A similar arrangement can be seen at Stonehenge.
However, according to the research team’s latest findings, the Czech structure is significantly older than the famed British site.
“For prehistoric farming communities, the connection between sunrise and the summer solstice symbolized a beginning, while sunset and the winter solstice represented an ending,” stated Krištuf. “The same principle can be seen along Stonehenge’s main axis. We can now see that the sanctuary at Chleby was designed similarly, more than a thousand years earlier.”
Krištuf explained that the millennium older date came from radiocarbon dating of materials found at Chelby.
“We assume that they may originally have decorated monumental gateways leading into the enclosure,” added archaeologist Jan Turek, who is involved in the research on behalf of Charles University. “The cult of the bull was an important religious symbol among the first farming communities and is known from many parts of prehistoric Europe.”
Remains of Bronze Age burials also found at site
Previous excavations at the site uncovered the remains of approximately 18 people in the ditch, later identified as a Bronze Age Únětice culture burial. Current research, however, indicates that the site's role later changed.
“While Stonehenge experienced repeated periods of renewed use and is still associated, for example, with Celtic druids, the first results from Chleby suggest the opposite development,” noted Krištuf. “By the Iron Age, the monument appears to have definitively lost its original significance. The ditch was gradually filled in, and an ordinary settlement was established on the site of the former sanctuary.”
The research will from now focus on analyzing soil from the site to aid in the understanding of how it was used during different eras, explained Jan Fišer of the University of Hradec Králové, who is also participating in the research.
“In addition to artifacts and the remains of the dead, people leave chemical traces in the soil. These can help us understand how this exceptional site was used during different periods of prehistory,” said Fišer.
The research is part of the international Long-term Land Use Dynamics within the Areas of Prehistoric Ritual Places project. It is being carried out in cooperation with the University of West Bohemia in Pilsen, Charles University and the University of Hradec Králové.
