Turkey uncovers new fragment of oldest known peace treaty between Egypt and Hittites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
20:24:07 UTC
05:24:07 KST

A fragment of a cuneiform tablet found last year at Hattusha belongs to the ancient Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty, the Turkish Culture and Tourism Ministry announced on Monday.
“We have discovered the millennia-old traces of peace in the soil of Anatolia,” wrote Turkish Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy in a post to X/Twitter. “This valuable discovery, which we shared with the public on September 21, World Peace Day, once again highlights Anatolia's deep-rooted place in the history of peace and diplomacy.”
The fragment was unearthed during excavations at the Bogazkoy/Hattusha archaeological site, where the Hittite royal palace is believed to have stood, in Çorum's Boğazkale district in 2025.
Hattusha served as the Bronze Age capital of the Hittite Empire.
Since its discovery, researchers have been examining its cuneiform text and recently determined that it belongs to the front side of one of the treaty's Akkadian cuneiform copies.
The new fragment contains lines from the treaty's provisions regulating the treatment of people fleeing from one country to another, explained Ersoy.
Legible portions of the text mention people fleeing from Egypt and the land of Hatti, along with statements concerning the protection of homes from destruction.
Ersoy also congratulated the site’s excavation team and the researchers who contributed to the discovery.
The new discovery contributes to Turkey's efforts in completing the clay tablet copies of the treaty found at Hattusa, and future excavations at the site aim to uncover the remainder of the missing fragments.
What is the Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty?
The treaty, known also as the Eternal Treaty, or Silver Treaty, is the oldest known surviving peace treaty. It was signed between the Hittite King Hattusili III and the Egyptian Pharaoh Ramesses II in approximately 1259 BCE to end a centuries-long war between the two nations.
It is sometimes also called the Treaty of Kadesh, even though the Battle of Kadesh, which took place in 1274 BCE, is not mentioned.
The Egyptian-language text of the treaty was inscribed in hieroglyphs on the walls of two buildings belonging to Ramesses II in Thebes: the Ramesseum and the Precinct of Amun-Re at the Temple of Karnak.
Baked clay tablet fragments of its Akkadian text were uncovered at Hattusha during the earliest excavations of the site, between 1906 and 1912.
Previously found fragments are held in the collections of the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, the Berlin Museum of the Ancient Near East, and the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg.
A copy of the treaty is prominently displayed on a wall at the United Nations’ headquarters.

Saudi Arabia has not ruled out nuclear weapons: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:35:40 UTC
00:35:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia has not ruled out nuclear weapons: report
US intelligence agencies have assessed that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons programme, according to classified documents provided to Congress and described to The Washington Post by US officials.
The assessment is raising fresh questions about US President Donald Trump’s agreement to help Riyadh establish a civilian nuclear industry. Some US lawmakers fear the deal could give Saudi Arabia the means to produce nuclear material that might eventually be used as a weapon, although the intelligence finding does not say the kingdom has decided to build one.
The agreement, announced in July, would allow US companies to pursue nuclear energy projects in Saudi Arabia. The Trump administration says the partnership will strengthen ties with Riyadh, uphold non-proliferation standards, and reduce the prospect of the kingdom turning to Russia or China for nuclear technology.
But Democratic lawmakers say the deal's restrictions do not go far enough. Under the agreement, Saudi uranium enrichment would initially be limited to less than five percent. That ceiling could rise to 20% following a further study and written agreement, according to The Washington Post.
The agreement also does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which would give inspectors broader access to nuclear sites and information.
In a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday, senators led by Ed Markey and Jeff Merkley accused the administration of accepting weaker safeguards that could enable Riyadh to acquire uranium-enrichment capabilities.
Their concerns have been sharpened by the intelligence assessment, which officials said was among classified material sent to Congress last month. The State Department’s contribution to those documents appeared more confident in the deal’s safeguards and Saudi assurances, the officials told the newspaper.
Saudi Arabia did not answer the newspaper’s questions directly. Instead, it referred to an earlier statement by Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman saying its nuclear programme would be peaceful and pursued with responsibility and transparency. The State Department said the US "does not and will not support a Saudi nuclear weapon program".
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman said in 2018 that Saudi Arabia would seek a nuclear weapon if Iran developed one. That conditional statement has long fuelled concern that an Iranian bomb could trigger a regional arms race.
Congress is reviewing the agreement and could move to block it, though opponents would need sufficient votes to overcome a possible presidential veto.
Its future may also depend on diplomacy over Israel: a senior US administration official told The Washington Post that Saudi normalisation with Israel remains a condition of the deal, while analysts said Riyadh is unlikely to take that step as long as Israel rules out a Palestinian state.

Trump says he rejected Iranian proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz and end hostilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:34:00 UTC
00:34:00 KST

Trump rejects Iran proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
September 26, 2026
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and bring about an end to hostilities.
"I reject their proposal ... I rejected their deal," Trump told reporters at the White House in Washington, DC.
Iran had proposed an initiative aimed at reopening the strategic waterway at the UN General Assembly in New York, which it said could put an end to fighting within seven days.
Tehran said the proposal had been transmitted to Washington via Qatari mediators.
What did Trump say?
"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," said Trump, claiming: "We're winning tremendously."
Earlier, a US official had told Reuters that discussions with Iran, conducted through mediators, were "positive and constructive."
But the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was skeptical that Tehran would meet his demands. He reportedly told staff that a renewed bombing campaign is likely following the November US midterm elections.
"They want to make a deal and I think that's fine," said Trump. "What they want to do is immediately open the Hormuz Strait ... because they have no money coming in, because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait."
Iranian ports are currently under a US blockade as Washington attempts to pressure Tehran into lifting its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. The key waterway remains largely closed to international shipping despite claims by Trump that the US is control of it.
"I'd like to make a deal, too," said Trump. "But that deal would not be acceptable."
Hours earlier, the US President had posted an image on social media calling the Strait of Hormuz the "Trump Strait."
Strait of Hormuz: What was the Iranian proposal?
Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who was on his way back to Tehran after attending the UN General Assembly in New York, told CBS News the proposal had been developed "in coordination" with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
He said the process would have begun "from the very day they accept it."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who met with Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff earlier in the week, said the plan had foreseen a cessation of all hostilities across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, with the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened on the seventh day of the truce.
He said the conditions were the same as those laid out in a memorandum of understanding signed with the US earlier this year, which called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.

"Serious women in long skirts": Tajani under fire in memes and international media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:27:11 UTC
00:27:11 KST

Italian Foreign Minister Tajani sparked outrage after saying he prefers 'respectable' women in long skirts. Opposition women senators donned skirts in protest, and memes of the minister spread well beyond Italy on social networks.
Despite having apologised and despite Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's attempts to put an end to the controversy that erupted during the week, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani's comments about choosing a life partner on the basis of criteria such as the length of the skirt she should wear continue to spark negative reactions against the minister, crossing national borders and turning him into the subject of memes shared on social media.
During a speech at an event organised last week, Tajani said he would advise marrying serious women who wear "longer skirts". "Perhaps less eye-catching, but more reliable, more serious, someone who will be a good mother, who will remain faithful to the love she seals with marriage," the foreign minister went on, explaining that he would always choose "the pretty, serious, credible one, who keeps the family together, who is there, who you know will always have an answer and is there when you call."
After facing a torrent of criticism, Tajani apologised. "I am very sorry that some of my remarks, taken out of a much more wide-ranging speech, have been misunderstood. I apologise if some people felt offended by what I said, but I have never intended to offend women, I have never done so in my life, either in private life or in public," Tajani said on the sidelines of his visit to New York for the UN General Assembly. But it was not enough.
The criticism of Tajani
The minister's remarks have been roundly condemned by opposition parties, trade unions and the Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI). Female senators from the Democratic Party, Italia Viva, the Greens and Left Alliance, the Five Star Movement and the Autonomies group gathered at Palazzo Madama wearing skirts.
"This is an act of freedom to say that we are free to dress as we wish. We believe that women's freedom is measured by every act of freedom, including the length of a skirt or any other choice that women want to make without being judged by men," said Italia Viva group leader Raffaella Paita, who came up with the idea.
"His words are proof of the intrinsic and unconscious patriarchy, so much so that Minister Tajani then tried to justify himself and apologised, but his justification is even worse. They do not realise what they are saying because it is ingrained in them. Instead we need to show that those remarks are unacceptable," said Simona Malpezzi of the Democratic Party, who posted the group's photo.
The initiative also came in response to comments by the leader of Futuro Nazionale, Roberto Vannacci, who, weighing in on Tajani's words, said: "Between a woman in a long skirt and a woman in a short skirt, I always prefer a woman without a skirt," added the former general. "I do not care about silly criticism. I love women, a gift of the universe," Vannacci later wrote on social media, posting images of the statues of the Venus de Milo and the Venus of Candia, both half-naked.
Many other opposition MPs also posted pictures of themselves wearing skirts, as did some men, including Florence city councillor and Democratic Party member Andrea Ciulli, who shared a photo of himself created with artificial intelligence in which he is wearing a skirt, with the caption "The length of a skirt does not measure a woman's worth, her freedom does".
"Tajani is now a meme, he is no longer a minister," said former prime minister and Italia Viva leader Matteo Renzi, piling on the pressure. Memes depicting the minister in women's clothing have been circulating, and have also been picked up by international media including CNN and the BBC.
Unions and CEI against Tajani's comments
The CGIL union also issued a stinging response. "Pitting the 'flashy' woman against the 'serious', 'reliable' and 'good mother', even invoking the length of her skirt, revives an old model of society in which it is still men who decide how women have to be in order to be considered respectable," the union said, adding: "Institutions have a responsibility: to remove stereotypes and obstacles to the full participation of women, not to reproduce the former and weaken the safeguards against the latter. Starting with making the full right to work effective by overcoming existing pay and career disparities. The quality of democracy is also measured by the power that women can really exercise."
The CEI's secretary, Monsignor Giuseppe Batur, responding to a question about the remarks made by Tajani and Vannacci, said: "Every word, every way of looking at women must be filled with respect and admiration; for us Christians the first place where the Word became flesh is a woman's womb, and for those who have faith this forever shapes the way we look at women." "Through our gaze we enter into a relationship with others; towards men, women, children and older people we must show respect, and towards women that respect must be at its highest, given the extent to which they can be the object of superficial glances," Batur added.
Meloni and the majority defend Tajani
Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein in recent days called on Prime Minister Meloni to comment, but Meloni downplayed Tajani's words and urged people not to "blow them out of proportion", saying they were just an "awkward phrase". "I have already answered, I would not exaggerate and I do not think we should make it the main topic of Milan Fashion Week," Meloni said while attending an event during Fashion Week in Milan.
Tajani was later defended by other members of the government, including Defence Minister Guido Crosetto, who wrote on X: "Tajani did not tell women how they should dress, he explained, as a father, what kind of partner he would recommend to his son, on the basis of his own upbringing and values. Anyone who feels offended, in one case or the other, is naturally free to say so. But the fact that an opinion jars with someone does not necessarily mean that it limits their freedom. Deciding instead to silence someone else means failing to respect their freedom."
"You talk about women's freedom, but why not fight for those women who are prisoners of their husbands and cannot take part in the life of the country? For religious reasons you accept that there are slaves in Italy, including polygamy. Consistency would require you to join us in fighting against the burqa," said Stefania Pucciarelli of the League.

Zelensky sanctions more than 40 people involved in elections in Russian-occupied Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:26:52 UTC
00:26:52 KST

Zelensky sanctions more than 40 people involved in elections in Russian-occupied Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky imposed sanctions on 44 individuals who took part in elections for Russia's State Duma, the lower house of parliament, in occupied Ukrainian territories, the Presidential Office reported on Sept. 26.
Russia held its State Duma elections from Sept. 18 to 20, while voting in occupied Ukrainian territories began in late August. Eleven electoral districts were established in the occupied territories.
By signing the decree, Zelensky enacted a decision by Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council. The sanctions package includes 44 individuals "who act in Russia's interests and facilitate the occupation of parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, as well as Crimea and Sevastopol," the statement said.
read also
Some of those sanctioned had previously been "elected" to so-called local councils established by Russian-installed authorities in Ukraine's occupied territories. Others include alleged collaborators and individuals accused of aiding Russia's occupation.
Among those sanctioned are Russian propagandist and collaborator Irina Kuksenkova and former Ukrainian lawmaker Yurii Onyshchuk, who began cooperating with Russian authorities after Russian forces occupied Melitopol.
The Russian State Duma elections were the first elections for Russia's lower house of parliament to be held in the occupied Ukrainian territories after Russia had issued Russian passports en masse to Ukrainians there, requiring them to renounce their Ukrainian citizenship.
However, they were not the first Russian-organized votes held in the occupied territories.
In September 2022, Russian occupation authorities held sham referendums in the occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts.
Russia organized so-called regional elections in the occupied territories in 2023 and held presidential elections there in 2024, in which Vladimir Putin was again declared the winner.
Ukrainian Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk said that international humanitarian law, including the Hague Regulations and the Geneva Convention, requires an occupying power to respect the laws in force in the occupied territory.
"Occupation does not confer any sovereignty. The U.N. General Assembly has repeatedly reaffirmed Ukraine's territorial integrity, including in 2014 regarding Crimea and in 2022, when 143 countries condemned Russia's attempted illegal annexation of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts and declared it invalid," Vlasiuk said.
"Neither 'elections,' 'referendums,' nor 'electoral districts' change that status," Vlasiuk added.
United Russia, the ruling party, won more than 57% of the vote, while voter turnout stood at 59%, according to Russian authorities.
Yabloko, the only party to openly oppose Russia's war against Ukraine, was barred from the elections following a ruling by Russia's Supreme Court. The court acted on a lawsuit filed by the Rodina party, which accused Yabloko of extremism and copyright violations.
The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) was also not allowed to send an independent mission to monitor the vote.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry called the vote a "farce" and said Kyiv would not recognize its results. The EU, the U.K., Switzerland, Norway, Australia, Canada, and New Zealand also condemned the so-called elections.

UN Alliance of Civilizations Group of Friends holds high-level meeting in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:26:38 UTC
00:26:38 KST

Tugba Altun and Merve Berker
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
The UN Alliance of Civilizations (UNAOC) Group of Friends held a high-level meeting on Saturday in New York with the participation of representatives from Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and the International Organization of Turkic Culture (TURKSOY).
According to a written statement by TURKSOY, the meeting was chaired by Miguel Angel Moratinos, the high representative for the UNAOC.
Officials addressing the meeting included Turkish Deputy Foreign Minister Ambassador Levent Gumrukcu, TURKSOY Secretary General Sultan Raev, Azerbaijani Deputy Foreign Minister Yalcin Rafiyev, Kazakhstan's First Deputy Foreign Minister Yerzhan Ashikbayev, and Turkmenistan's UN Ambassador Vepa Hajiyev.
Gumrukcu, representing Türkiye as a co-sponsor of the UNAOC, said cultural diversity should be viewed not as a threat but as a source of strength, pointing to the importance of dialogue among civilizations amid growing intolerance and polarization.
Raev stressed that cultural diplomacy is not merely a complementary element of international relations but also one of the powerful tools of preventive diplomacy.
Noting that the world faces serious challenges including wars, forced migration, hate speech, and social polarization, Raev highlighted the importance of protecting cultural heritage and building mutual trust among societies for lasting peace.
'Protecting human life, cultural heritage is shared responsibility of all humanity'
Raev said that every war destroys not only human lives but also the memory of cities, sacred sites, historical artifacts, and the accumulated heritage of civilizations built over generations.
"The humanitarian tragedy taking place in Palestine once again reminds us that protecting human life and cultural heritage is the shared responsibility of all humanity," he said.
Raev said the shared cultural heritage of the Turkic world is integrated with the universal values of humanity, adding that TURKSOY has worked for more than 30 years to preserve, sustain and promote the common cultural heritage of Turkic peoples worldwide.
He said TURKSOY is ready to share its experience in cultural diplomacy with UNAOC.
Raev said TURKSOY and the UNAOC could develop new projects in areas including youth exchanges, cultural dialogue programs, literature and arts gatherings, protecting shared cultural heritage, and preventive diplomacy through culture.
Rafiyev said the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue, to be held in Azerbaijan’s capital Baku on Oct. 27-29, would make an important contribution to the UNAOC's work.
Also speaking, Ashikbayev emphasized the importance of strengthening interfaith harmony and promoting a culture of peaceful coexistence.
Hajiyev highlighted the role of dialogue, mutual respect, and adherence to international law in preventing conflicts, saying Turkmenistan is ready to further develop cooperation with the UNAOC.

====================================================================================================

From Russia with “Russophobia”: Kremlin propaganda accounts are posing as “angry Latvians” to influence the country’s Telegram communities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:24:30 UTC
00:24:30 KST

After Latvia banned broadcasts by Russian federal television channels, Telegram became a key platform for Kremlin propaganda in the country. The Insider estimates that around one-third of socio-political channels in Latvia’s Telegram ecosystem are controlled by Russian propagandists posing as “angry Latvians” — and the figure rises to upwards of 65% when only Russian-language channels are included in the count. The channels portray life in Latvia as getting worse, blaming anti-Russian sanctions for harming the Baltic states while calling for an end to support for Ukraine.
Methodology
The Insider collected data from 72 Latvian socio-political channels (353,000 posts from January 1, 2025) and analyzed the network of reposts from these channels. Of the 93,000 shares, 30.3% were reposts between the channels themselves, while 43.7% came from Russian state media, official government channels, military bloggers, and pro-war “Z-channels.” Together, these account for three-quarters of all shared content. For content analysis, a sample of up to 200 posts — stratified by month — was taken from each channel, totaling more than 12,000 posts. Each post was examined for pro-Kremlin and anti-Ukrainian narratives. These narratives were identified in 65 Telegram channels.
All of the channels analyzed by The Insider publish in Russian, and some operate anonymously. The largest are linked to the state-run media group Rossiya Segodnya, which includes RT. They are run by RT editorial staff, in-house RT journalists, or frequent contributors to the channel. At least one channel was previously part of the disinformation network overseen by the late Wagner Group co-founder Yevgeny Prigozhin.
None of the people behind the five largest channels have actually lived in Latvia in recent years. Some have left for Russia and others for Belarus. From abroad, they criticize Latvian government policies while presenting themselves as voices of the country’s “outraged citizens.”
The channels regularly repost one another’s content and amplify material from other Russian propagandists, including RT head Margarita Simonyan. They also promote pro-government Belarusian social media accounts.
The channels repeat a common set of narratives that closely mirror Kremlin messaging: that Russian speakers in Latvia are being persecuted, that Nazism is on the rise in the Baltic states, and that ordinary people in the country are becoming poorer. The channels blame these problems on Riga’s support for Ukraine, arguing that public money is being diverted to the war.
Aleksejs Rosļikovs’ channel
The largest channel, with about 30,000 subscribers, is run by Aleksejs Rosļikovs, a former member of Latvia’s parliament, the Saeima.
Rosļikovs, 42, is a controversial figure in Latvian politics. Before entering public life, he spent years in business, running a confectionery company and later owning several private security firms, a taxi dispatch service, and a car rental company. He went on to serve in the Saeima and later on the Riga City Council.
Latvian authorities have opened a criminal case against him on suspicion of inciting ethnic hatred. The case stems from a June 5, 2025, speech in parliament in which Rosļikovs made an obscene gesture toward fellow lawmakers and ended his remarks in Russian by saying, “There are more of us; Russian is our language.”
In the spring of 2026, Rosļikovs left Latvia for Belarus. From there, he continues to run his Telegram channel and says he plans to run again for the Saeima with his Stability! party. He has told potential voters that if elected, parliamentary immunity would allow him to return to Latvia and that he would seek to lift sanctions on Russia.
Over the past month, Rosļikovs’ Telegram channel gained several thousand subscribers, and in early September,he unexpectedly made the platform private, limiting access to subscribers only. Rosļikovs also runs personal accounts on Facebook (where he has about 16,000 followers) and Instagram (where he has around 109,000). Alongside political commentary, he posts videos of himself working out and taking ice plunges, a Russian Orthodox tradition in which participants immerse themselves in near-freezing water in January to mark the baptism of Jesus.
Baltnews
The second most significant channel, Baltnews (@baltnews), is run by the editorial staff of the “Russia Today” International Information Agency — as is explicitly stated on the publication’s website. The channel has 24,000 subscribers.
Its editorial team publishes dozens of posts a day, quotes Russian and Belarusian propaganda outlets, and reposts content from other channels in the network. In the past year alone, Baltnews reposted content from the BelVPO channel 149 times and from the “Belvestnik” channel 107 times.
The publication also claims that due to ongoing financial aid to Ukraine, the standard of living for Latvians has declined, and that Russophobia is so rampant in the country that it has forced Russian speakers to emigrate. Particular emphasis is placed on the idea that neighboring countries do not respect Latvia and openly mock it.
Even positive news, such as falling prices in stores, are presented in a negative light: “According to estimates by Latvian retail chains, a basket of groceries that used to cost 50 euros now costs 46.28 euros. Savings of 3.72 euros are hardly going to save the local poor or those rapidly approaching poverty.”
Even positive news, such as falling prices in stores, are presented in a negative light
The channel’s editor-in-chief is 34-year-old Riga native Andrejs Starikovs. After Latvian authorities banned the publication in 2018 and opened criminal cases against its staff, Starikovs moved to Moscow.
In addition to running his propaganda page, Starikovs also produces films commissioned by the Russian authorities.
The “Baltic Antifascists” page
The third most significant page in the pro-Russian network is the channel of the organization “Baltic Antifascists,” which has nearly 20,000 subscribers. The organization and the channel were created in November 2022 and are led by 62-year-old Sergejs Vasiļjevs, a native of Latvia.
The “Baltic Antifascists” page actively accuses the Latvian authorities of Nazism and Russophobia. Vasilyev refers to Latvia itself exclusively as a territory “temporarily occupied by NATO troops.”
Vasiļjevs refers to Latvia exclusively as a territory “temporarily occupied by NATO troops”
Criminal cases have now been opened against him and several others for gathering intelligence on behalf of the FSB.
Vasiļjevs himself does not deny gathering data for Russian security agencies, speaking openly about it during live broadcasts. For example, one of the organization’s tasks was to gather information on the bulldozer operators who demolished Soviet monuments.
“We launched a poll [via a Telegram channel] and a flood of opinions came in. We collected all these files and forwarded them to the Investigative Committee of Russia. Now we have a number of suspects in the vandalism case [on Russian territory],” Vasilyev openly boasted in an interview.
The administrators also used the “Baltic Antifascists” group to gather information about Russian opposition events, Latvian volunteers fighting on the side of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, as well as NATO equipment and facilities in the Baltic states.
Vasilyev also has a co-defendant in his criminal case over the collection of information for Russia’s security services: 26-year-old Latvian citizen and St. Petersburg State University student Tatiana Andriets. In 2022, Andriets traveled to Riga for vacation and participated in a protest against the demolition of Soviet monuments. Latvian authorities charged her with “aiding a foreign state” and forming a criminal group. She spent nine months in pretrial detention and is currently under house arrest while her trial is ongoing.
Although Andriets is not a Russian citizen, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has repeatedly commented on her case, calling the trial “political” in nature.
Alexei Stefanov, Ruslan Pankratov, and Nikolai Mezhevich
Three other major public pages are run by journalists and political analysts associated with Russia Today who appear as regular guests on Russian television programs such as Solovyov Live, Zvezda, and REN TV. These include the personal channel of “Russia Today” special correspondent Alexei Stefanov, with 16,000 subscribers; the channel of political scientist Ruslan Pankratov from the Institute of CIS Countries (12,000 subscribers); and the channel of Nikolai Mezhevich, a researcher at the Institute of Europe of the Russian Academy of Sciences (12,000 subscribers).
They regularly repost each other’s content. For example, over the past year, Mezhevich’s channel has mentioned Stefanov’s channel 200 times. Stefanov himself constantly cites the channel “Latviyskaya Kochka” (lit. “Latvian Bump”) which reposts content from Margarita Simonyan’s public pages and those of other Russian propagandists.
In addition to narratives about the oppression of Russians in Latvia, the channels offer advice on how to move to Russia, promote content about the “horrible Nazis in Kyiv,” and scare their audience by claiming that war will soon break out on Latvian territory if the country does not change its attitude towards Moscow.
The network also includes smaller public channels with notable backgrounds. One is “Zloi Pribalt” (@wagner_baltika), whose name and logo match channels from Yevgeny Prigozhin’s former Wagner-linked media network. It has only about 1,200 subscribers but is the most prolific channel in the network, publishing about 66,000 posts since Jan. 1, 2025.

USC ends sale of dead bodies to US Navy for Israeli military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:24:07 UTC
00:24:07 KST

Breadcrumb
USC ends sale of cadavers to US Navy for Israeli military training
The University of Southern California (USC) ended the sale of human cadavers for Israeli military training on Thursday, closing a programme that ran for over five years.
A report by Annenberg Media in 2024 revealed that the University of California San Diego (UCSD) supplied bodies to the University of California (USC), which were then sold to the US Navy and used for training Israeli army medics.
The revelation sparked public outcry, with protests demanding an end to the programme.
USC's medical school said it would not renew its cadaver contracts because it would no longer supply bodies for the US Navy programme.
The Keck School of Medicine emphasised that the contract did not end because of the protests.
Annenberg revealed in 2024 that the institution received over $860,000 from the US Navy to provide at least 89 human cadavers, including 32 specifically used for medical training for Israeli forces at Los Angeles General Medical Centre.
The training used "fresh cadaver bodies" and "perfused cadavers", bodies pumped with artificial blood to mimic living patients, to prepare the Israeli military's surgical teams.
Many of the cadavers are believed to have been unclaimed bodies.
Families who donated the bodies of their loved ones were not told the bodies could be used by the US, while others were only made aware after the reporting by Annenberg Media and The UCSD Guardian.
An AJ+ documentary also revealed that donor consent forms at USC/UCSD did not explicitly state that bodies could be used to train a foreign military.
The Keck School of Medicine wrote: "USC did not profit off donated bodies provided through UCSD. The Navy was charged at cost for obtaining bodies, plus fees for our surgeon expertise and oversight, the time of skilled technicians, and marginal overhead cost."
USC earned over $1 million through the contract.
USDC said they decided to stop supplying cadavers because the surgical skills laboratory did not meet the required standards in courses involving human remains.
Since at least 2023, the Israeli military's medical personnel have attended a recurring "combat trauma surgery skills" course at the Navy Trauma Training Centre (NTTC) based at Los Angeles General Medical Centre.
In its current genocidal war on Gaza, the Israeli military has continued its policy of taking and withholding Palestinian bodies, including cemeteries and hospitals, with some bodies being returned with missing organs.
Israeli forces have stolen at least 2,300 bodies from more than 20 cemeteries during the war, according to Gaza's Government Media Office.

Unknown

2026-09-26

Awad Rjoob and Rania Abushamala
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
 Israeli occupiers began establishing a new settlement outpost near the town of Adh Dhahiriya, south of Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian rights group said Saturday.
In a statement, the Al-Baidar Organization said the move was part of continued illegal settlement expansion in the area. It warned that the outpost threatened Palestinian land and could restrict residents’ movement and access to their property.
The group said occupiers also raided the area around the home of Palestinian resident Khairi Mohammed Abu Tuhfa in Khallat al-Hummus, in the Masafer Yatta area south of Hebron, and frightened members of his family.
Near the village of Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, a settlement outpost established about two months ago has developed into an inhabited site, the group said. It reported rapid construction and preparations there, warning that the outpost could expand onto more Palestinian land.
The group said occupiers living at the site have displayed extremist behavior toward Palestinians. The pace of construction, it added, “was creating new conditions on the ground and threatening residents’ land and property.”
In August, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee described Israelis involved in violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank as “terrorists” and warned that their actions were seriously damaging Israel’s image.
About 750,000 occupiers live in 156 illegal settlements and 360 outposts across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, according to Palestinian figures. The Palestinian government’s Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 628 occupier attacks in August.
Separately, Palestinian news agency Wafa said Israeli forces raided the village of Yabrud, northeast of Ramallah, as occupiers stormed a sheep farm there. The forces blocked the passage of several Palestinian vehicles in the area, the agency said.
In the northern West Bank, Israeli forces bulldozed land and uprooted dozens of olive trees near the village of Haddad in Jenin governorate, according to Wafa.
Israeli military and occupier attacks in the West Bank have intensified since the Gaza war began in October 2023. At least 1,206 Palestinians, including 254 children, have been killed, about 13,350 wounded and more than 24,600 arrested during that period, according to Palestinian official figures.
The UN has repeatedly affirmed that Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories are illegal under international law, warning that they undermine prospects for a two-state solution.

One year on, the UK’s recognition of Palestinian statehood is bearing fruit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:20:24 UTC
00:20:24 KST

One year on, the UK’s recognition of Palestinian statehood is bearing fruit
The British government is moving to translate rhetoric into policy.
This week marks one year since the United Kingdom, along with nine other Western countries, recognised the State of Palestine. What shifted was politics, not policy: overwhelming support for the Palestinian cause by the British public finally persuaded the government to align with the law.
For decades, the UK backed a two-state solution in words only. Its logic was twisted: recognise statehood only after a final peace agreement, handing Israel a veto over the very policy it claimed to support, even as successive Israeli governments worked – through words, bulldozers and bombs – to render Palestinian statehood impossible.
This approach treated Palestinian self-determination as conditional, not an inalienable right — earned through reform, “good governance” and benchmarks no other people have been made to meet.
The British recognition of Palestinian statehood marked a turning point – one that is already bearing fruit a year later. Upgrading relations with Palestine has allowed the UK to turn rhetoric into policy.
From words to policy
Almost a year after the UK formally recognised the State of Palestine, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced that the British government now regards the Israeli occupation of Palestinian lands as unlawful.
He then set out bans on settlement goods, services, advertising and arms licences, as well as sanctions on companies that build, finance or sell settlement homes. This move is a logical next step after the British recognition of Palestinian statehood.
The British foreign secretary, to his credit, acknowledged Britain should have acted sooner. Prime Minister Andy Burnham put it plainly: support for two states is “meaningless unless we back it up with action”.
The legal groundwork for these measures was laid in July 2024, when the International Court of Justice declared Israel’s occupation unlawful, along with the separation wall and settlements, and its near-total separation of settlers to be equivalent to racial segregation and apartheid. The court ruled the occupation must end “as rapidly as possible”.
After Miliband’s announcement, 11 other governments, including Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden, joined a parallel statement on sanctions and trade with settlements.
These measures matter because the occupation runs on an ecosystem of contractors, lenders, estate agents and Israeli state institutions sponsoring the settlements — and the new rules must reach every part of it. For decades, words on Palestine cost nothing while settlements multiplied; now there are consequences.
Israel has responded. It has ordered London to close its consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, which it cannot legally do since it holds no sovereignty there. The punitive measures unleashed onto the Palestinian population are worse still.
Since September 2, Israeli forces have demolished every home in Khirbet al-Tabban and northern al-Fakhit in the occupied West Bank, leaving roughly 70 people, 28 of them children, without shelter.
Settlement activities have also accelerated. Earlier this month, the occupation authorities issued tenders for 3,401 planned housing units as part of the E1 project, which would cut off occupied East Jerusalem from the occupied West Bank.
In Gaza, where two million of our people are confined to less than 30 percent of the Strip’s territory, Israel continues to bomb and kill civilians. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called ceasefire began last October last year. Meanwhile, more than 140,000 tarpaulins and 7,500 tents meant to provide shelter for the winter for homeless Palestinians sit blocked in the Jordan corridor.
The way forward
For too long, countries like the UK exercised caution and hesitation, sending the wrong signal to Israel, inviting more aggressive action and solidifying its culture of impunity.
For that to change, the announced sanction measures need to be followed by action.
First, there needs to be immediate and full implementation. The sanctions must be put into practice and the 12 governments should agree on how they will respond to pressure to reverse course. Unity can help withstand coercion.
Second, there needs to be protection for the people these measures exist for. The olive harvest begins next month in Palestine. During last year’s harvest, the United Nations recorded 126 settler attacks in 70 towns and villages within its first three weeks. This year’s harvest is the first real test of whether settler sanctions carry weight on the ground.
Collective action should not be limited to the occupied West Bank. There must be efforts to end the ongoing genocide in Gaza and Israel’s continuing violations of the ceasefire. Urgently, there needs to be pressure to secure the delivery of aid, particularly the much-needed shelter materials held in the Jordan corridor.
Moving forward, we must remember the example of apartheid South Africa. The boycott and sanctions campaign was resisted by Western governments, including the British one, and their action is remembered now as lagging behind their people.
This time, the UK can lead and be judged differently, if it holds its nerve, moving together with a growing number of partners, as it did with the 11 other governments two weeks ago.
Next year marks 110 years since the Balfour Declaration, 80 since the UN partition vote, and 60 since the occupation began. Palestine has had enough beginnings. What it needs now is an ending.
For the first time in a generation, law, politics and sentiment in London are beginning to point the same way. This is Britain’s chance to lead a better future and redeem the past.
When the occupation ends, and it will, the path to a peace rooted in justice, dignity and equality can finally be laid.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Iran denies plans for military retaliation over aviation restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:18:47 UTC
00:18:47 KST

Mohammad Sio
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
Iran’s Supreme National Security Council on Saturday denied reports that Tehran plans to respond militarily to recent restrictions imposed on Iranian aviation, according to Press TV.
In a statement, the council rejected reports that Iran will retaliate militarily over the aviation measures, saying negotiations are underway with the countries concerned to remove some of the “unlawfully imposed” restrictions on Iranian air travel.
It said Iran has “numerous non-military options” that can be used against some airports, if necessary.
The statement came after the council’s secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, warned neighboring countries on Wednesday against cooperating with US restrictions on Iranian aviation. Speaking to Iranian state television, Rezaei said that if countries prevented Iranian aircraft from operating, their own airports would also be unable to operate flights.
On Friday, Mohammad Mokhber, a senior adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, said that “either air travel in the region is available to everyone or to no one,” adding that if Iran could not fly or receive airport services, other countries in the region would not be able to do so either.
Early this week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said operations of Iranian airlines worldwide will come to a halt as of Sept. 23 under new sanctions. As part of the measure, Iranian flights were barred from regional countries, including Oman, the UAE, and Iraq.
The aviation dispute has unfolded amid stalled efforts to end the US war on Iran, despite a June memorandum aimed at reaching a final agreement, with negotiations deadlocked in part over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

Germany's FM Wadephul meets Lavrov on UNGA sidelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26

Germany's FM Wadephul meets Lavrov on UNGA sidelines
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 26, 2026
What you need to know
- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul meets Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on sidelines of the UN General Assembly debate
- Wadephul addressed the UN later on Saturday and urged regulation on AI
- India urges de-escalation in regards to Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
- Chinese VP Han Zheng slams 'unilateral military actions,' says big countries should follow rules
We are continuing our coverage of the 81st UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Wadephul: Russia's war in Ukraine 'shows contempt' for UN charter
Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia's war in Ukraine targets the lives of millions of innocent civilians, Ukraine and its culture, as well as the "European peace order."
"It puts vital grain deliveries for millions of people at risk, particularly in Africa, Asia and the Middle East," Wadephul said in his speech to the UN General Assembly, adding that Russia's actions "show contempt" for the UN charter and for the "common order on which we stand."
The minister also said Germany's support with Ukraine was consistent with UN values.
"Today Germany is the largest supporter of Ukraine and its defense against Russian aggression. This aggression has been condemned consistently by an overwhelming majority here in the General Assembly," Wadephul said.
He said Germany would continue to call on Russia to come to the negotiation table.
"I call on every member state to join us in convincing Russia that the future is built at the negotiation table, not on dead bodies in cities and villages," he added.
Prior to his speech, Wadephul met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the UNGA, in the first of such meetings since 2022.
The talks come in the midst of tensions between Berlin and Moscow, after Germany accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.
"Wadephul called on the Russian Federation to abandon its dangerous path of escalation vis-a-vis Germany, Europe, and NATO," a German diplomat said of the talks in comments to AFP news agency.
"He made it clear: incidents such as the recent attempted attack in Leipzig or further hybrid assaults would not shake Germany's resolve to support Ukraine, which has come under attack," the diplomat added.
"The German foreign minister condemned Russia's ongoing and increasingly targeted aggression against the Ukrainian civilian population. This attempt to increase pressure does nothing to change Russia's untenable situation: every month, tens of thousands of Russian soldiers die in a hopeless war of positions, while the Russian economy continues to collapse," the diplomat said.
Germany calls for AI regulation, urges 'profound' UN reform
Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul opened his UN General Assembly speech by warning about the extraordinary power of artificial intelligence and its implications for the world. He also addressed the erosion of international institutions in a world of rising nationalism.
"When a technology has the power to fundamentally change the world, we need to ask who controls it, who sets the rules, who is accountable," Wadephul said, adding that AI has the potential to upend the economy and "endanger the infrastructure that keeps our societies running."
"AI holds extraordinary promise," Wadephul said. But he warned that a "critical tension" exists when the technology is concentrated in two countries and a few companies. Such power holds great responsibility to humanity, Wadephul said, saying that as power becomes global, so must the responsibilites.
"AI is not waiting for our institutions to catch up, our institutions have to catch up with AI" Wadephul said.
"We need to make sure that tech progress is guided by a framework that we all have a say in shaping," he added, calling effectively for global regulation of AI.
"Germany calls on UN member states to work towards common safety requirements for the most capable models," he said.
On the weakening of UN institutions, Wadephul warned of a UN "under pressure."
"There are great powers that believe that they fare better if they ignore the rules enshrined in the UN charter,"
Wadephul said that "the overwhelming majority of the 193 states represented in this assembly" are harmed when international institutions are under attack.
"If this erosion contitnues, we all stand to lose," he added.
Germany's foreign minister urged for the the new UN Secretary General to lead "a profound process of reform," as the world needs "a functioning UN that plays an active role in conflicts, rather than managing."
"Germany stands up for peace and security," Wadephul said, citing his country's commitment to support Ukraine.
A new nationalism is not the path for nations, Wadephul said, adding that "it would makes our lives narrower, poorer and less secure"
India urges de-escalation amid Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
India's Minister for External Affairs, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, addressed the UN General Assembly, urging de-escalation and restraint from those involved in conflicts that have caused disruption to world navigation, in reference to the current crises in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea.
"In a globalized world, the effects of war are felt worldwide," Jaishankar said.
"Countries far from conflicts are being penalized for no fault in this. Those most impacted often have the least say," he added.
Jaishankar also denounced the security of seafarers caught in conflicts.
"We must ensure that the safety and security of shipping and seafarers is never compromised," he said.
Saudi Arabia says international community 'absent' in Gulf crisis
At UN, the Foreign Minister of Saudi Arabia, Prince Faisal bin Farhan al Saud, called for the defense of freedom of navigation in all international waterways.
"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," bin Farhan told the United Nations General Assembly.
The Saudi foreign minister called for the restoration of the Strait of Hormuz to its "pre-28th February status." The US and Israel began their military operations against Iran on that date.
He condemned the fact that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf nations "have been subjected to flagrant Iranian attacks" targeting their security, resources, and civilians.
Saudi FM also denounced Israel's war in Gaza, saying it opposed the "continuing suffering of the Palestinian people."
"We stress that a just and lasting peace can only be achieved through the implementation of a two-state solution and the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital."
Russia offers to help with Strait of Hormuz crisis
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that Moscow can help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov said in his speech to the UNGA.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region," he added.
Lavrov claims Europe 'thwarts' Ukraine talks
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addressed the UNGA, shortly after meeting with his German counterpart Johann Wadephul.
In his speech to the general assembly, Lavrov accused European countries of "doing everything" to thwart talks to help end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
Russia's unprovoked invasion of its neighbor will soon mark its fifth anniversary next February.
"Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the (Donald) Trump administration is interested," he said, referring to the US government and the various rounds of talks it has held with the Russian and Ukrainian government, led by Trump's son in law Jared Kushner and adviser Steve Witkoff.
German FM Wadephul meets Russia's Lavrov during UN assembly
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
A correspondent for the Russian Interfax news agency reported Wadephul and Lavrov, followed by aides, shaking hands before the press was asked to leave.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the meeting took place at the German initiative.
Moscow has been sanctioned by the EU over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine which the Kremlin launched in February 2022.
The last meeting between on this level was held in January of that year, between veteran diplomat Lavrov and Germany's then-top diplomat, Annalena Baerbock, who was on a visit to Moscow.
Lavrov and Wadephul's meeting was held as tensions between Berlin and Moscow have been high in recent weeks.
Germany has accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.
Moldova PM offers his country as testing ground for AI rules
Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan used part of his time before the General Assembly to present a vision of small nations serving as "regulatory sandboxes" for new technologies.
"Technology is moving faster than regulation almost everywhere, and artificial intelligence is widening that gap," said Tofan, who worked as an investor and businessman before becoming the head of Moldovan government two months ago.
"We want Moldova to become a place where emergent technologies can be tested responsibly through regulatory sandboxes, where regulators learn alongside companies, rules adjust with evidence, and good ideas do not wait years to reach the real economy."
"When an entrepreneur arrives with a technology for which the law has not caught up yet, the answer should not simply be 'There is no rule for this.' It should be 'Let us find a safe way to test it'," he said.
China cast itself as source of stability in changing world
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng called for safeguarding the post-WWII order, saying the world wanted "peace, not war."
"We should turn into action the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, and reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation," Han said.
"Major countries shoulder special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding the rule of law, and doing what's right."
"No matter how international dynamics evolve, China remains unchanged in its pursuit of peace and development, in its dedication to safeguarding fairness and justice and in its commitment to multilateralism," said the Chinese vice president.
"China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity, and make the world a better place for all of us."
China takes indirect swipes at US over Iran
Speaking at the UN on Saturday, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng said the world should reject "unilateral military actions that violate the UN charter and circumvent the Security Council authorization," in an apparent reference to the US attack on Iran.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of the countries in the Middle east, including the Gulf, should be respected, international industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded," he said.
In his speech, Han also spoke out against the US blockade of Cuba, albeit without explicitly mentioning the US.
He said China called on "the relevant country" to lift its blockade against Cuba and stop using the threat of force against the island nation.
In regards to Israel and the Palestinians, the Chinese official urged bringing the two-state solution back "on the right track" and "at an early date."

We are pausing our coverage
As the fourth day of the 81st UN General Assembly comes to a halt, we are pausing this blog for the night.
Today was another address-packed day, with several small island nations stressing the urgent need to address climate change, as they are most vulnerable to its consequences.
Norway and Sweden stressed the importance of continuing to support the UN, including with funds, as well as making it more representative by giving Africa a permanent seat on the Security Council.
Meanwhile, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took aim at India, rehashing in his address a short-lived conflict between the two countries last year. Small island states take aim at world leaders for inaction on climate change
The speakers for the small island nations of St. Kitts and Nevis, Samoa and Tonga called to attention the inaction of world leaders on climate change.
The island nations are disproportionately vulnerable to the climate crisis, with the deputy prime minister of Samoa, Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo, calling climate change "the single greatest threat" facing the country and the world.
Molioo stressed the need to scale up climate financing so small island nations weren't the ones bearing the burden of climate change.
Fatafehi Fakafanua, Prime Minister of Tonga, said Pacific leaders have been warning about the climate crisis, with little support for years.
Fakafanua said the question was not whether the world has heard the message of climate change but rather, he asked, "why has it still not acted?"
The deputy prime minister of St. Kitts and Nevis, Geoffrey Hanley, outlined some of the solutions his country has undertaken, such as investing in desalination and improving food security.
Hanley said that small states, who stand most at risk from the consequences of climate change, were still delivering big solutions.
But he said, because no small island state can perpetually adapt to the climate crisis, "adaptation cannot excuse inaction elsewhere."
Iran says it gave US 7-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has given the US a seven-day plan that would involve reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday.
Speaking to reporters at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, Araghchi said the plan was delivered via Qatar and the choice now rests with Washington to meet the conditions Tehran has laid out.
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he said.

Technological advances are allowing police to review old CCTV footage in the unsolved murder of the BBC broadcaster Jill Dando, Scotland Yard has revealed.
Advances in CCTV enhancement technology have allowed detectives to return to 27-year-old footage of Putney Bridge Underground station, Scotland Yard said. But detectives stressed that the review was part of existing inquiries – not a new investigation.
The former Crimewatch presenter was 37 years old when she was shot and killed outside her home in Fulham, west London, on 26 April 1999. An unidentified person, referred to as “Man X”, was captured on camera near Putney Bridge station – about a mile from Dando’s home – shortly after the attack.
A driver had seen a man “running for his life” on Fulham Palace Road around the time of the shooting, the Mirror reported. She later picked out Man X in the station CCTV as the person who had been sprinting.
A Met spokesperson said: “In the 27 years since Jill Dando’s murder, the investigation has been subject to numerous reviews, aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.
“Recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology have provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station.
“The review of CCTV footage forms part of ongoing inquiries and should not be interpreted as a significant line of inquiry nor as a new investigation being opened on this matter.”
Outside her work on Crimewatch, Dando was also seen during the 1980s and 1990s on BBC shows including travel show Holiday and The Antiques Inspectors.
She began as a reporter at her local paper The Weston Mercury in Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, before moving to the morning programme Breakfast Time, which later became BBC Breakfast.
In 2019, the detective who led the inquiry into Dando’s murder expressed doubt the case would ever be solved. Speaking in a BBC documentary to mark 20 years since the television presenter’s shooting, Hamish Campbell said he did not think any new suspects would ever be brought to court.
“Do I think somebody will come back to court? Probably not, no. Sometimes, I felt we were a day away from solving it and other times, I thought: ‘No, we’re a long way away’. Senior officers were asking: ‘What are the likelihoods of this case being resolved?’
“We had over 2,000 people named as potential suspects or responsible. Some actions to trace and eliminate one person might take a day. One action might take two weeks. But there’s thousands of them and that’s the issue of managing stranger homicides.”

Pentagon brings in Ukrainian jamming maker to do to its candidate drones what Russia does to Ukraine’s, and see which survives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:11:11 UTC
00:11:11 KST

A Ukrainian jamming-systems maker went to a US Army base to do to candidate drones what Russia does to Ukraine's: flood them with electronic warfare (EW) and see which survives. Unwave company has tested four of its EW systems at Fort Carson in Colorado as part of the Pentagon's Drone Dominance program and has been asked to continue supporting it.
The Pentagon is using Drone Dominance to choose the drones it will buy at scale, more than 200,000 by 2027, and it needs to know they work under jamming, the condition that decides most drone fights in Ukraine.
So it brought in a Ukrainian electronic-warfare maker to supply that jamming, turning Ukraine's hard-won counter-drone experience into the test bench for American hardware. It follows a pattern in which US defense efforts adopt Ukrainian battlefield models.
Ukraine brings the jamming
From 24 August to 2 September, Unwave's team worked at the base, running scenarios that pitted its jammers against drones tasked with protecting fixed positions, moving vehicles, and infrastructure.
The crews operated from three separate positionsat short and long range to compare how drones from different manufacturers held up.
"Our mission was to create conditions as close to the real battlefield as possible," the company said, adding that it judged the tasks successfully completed but could not detail the scenarios for security reasons.
In all, 14 drone makers and three electronic-warfare firms took part.
Four systems on show
Unwave brought four:
- VIHA, which it calls Ukraine's first tactical-operational jammer for directed suppression of drones
- BOOMBOX, built to shield troops and positions from FPV and drop-drones
- SHATRO, for vehicles
- CHOVEN-2, a multi-frequency amplifier for cars.
Its participation was organized by Revenant Technologies, a US firm that specializes in bringing combat-proven defense tech to the American market, and helped design the scenarios using its ties to Ukraine and frontline experience.
A foothold in the US market
For Unwave, the value is a door into the alliance's security architecture. The event showed the importance of Ukrainian, American, and European specialists testing together, the company said, and "such interaction will help integrate Ukrainian technologies into the security architecture of our allies."

Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of sabotaging efforts to reach a peace agreement in the Gaza Strip in an interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour on Saturday.
“It’s very simply for one person’s gain, ... the (Israeli) prime minister and his far-right government,” said Al Thani. “That’s the whole thing.”
Al Thani claimed that Israel has not fulfilled their commitment under the agreement reached in Sharm el-Sheikh in October 2025, in which Egypt mediated between Israeli and Hamas representatives to achieve a ceasefire and the release of Israeli hostages.
“When every aspect of that move is ousted … they just deny it, and they move on in the opposite direction,” Al Thani said. “They now occupy more than 70% of the strip; instead of withdrawing, they are continuing the killing while this agreement called for a ceasefire, and the targeting of the population over there.”
He added that on average, 150 humanitarian trucks enter the strip daily, despite claiming the agreement requires a minimum average of 600 per day.
“We have a long list of violations that, unfortunately, Netanyahu’s government are committing, and basically we have seen that he is the biggest obstacle right now in progressing this peace plan, while everyone among the mediators is trying to work very hard to make sure this agreement is upheld,” he said.
Al Thani: 'No single penny' from Qatar has reached Hamas's military wing

Israel’s elections committee votes to bar Arab-majority parties from election but not far-right ones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:03:34 UTC
00:03:34 KST

Israel’s elections committee votes to bar Arab-majority parties from election but not far-right ones
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has voted to bar the country’s two main Arab-majority political lists from next month’s parliamentary election, potentially leaving Palestinian citizens of Israel without their principal representatives in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, Al Jazeera reported.
The committee also voted to disqualify Ofer Cassif, a Jewish politician from the Arab-Jewish Hadash party, and Sami Abu Shehadeh, the leader of the Palestinian nationalist Balad party.
The votes are not the final word on who can run in the October 27 election. The Supreme Court is expected to review the decisions next week and has overturned previous attempts to exclude Arab parties and candidates.
But the committee’s decision has already prompted accusations of double standards, with Palestinian-led parties facing exclusion while parties led by far-right ministers, some of whom have been sanctioned internationally, remaining on the ballot. Here is what the decision means.
Which parties have been barred?
The committee voted to disqualify two separate groups. The first is the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Balad and Ta’al. The second is Ra’am, also called the United Arab List, which is running on its own. Both rely on support from Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about one-fifth of the country’s population.
The Joint List
This brings together three parties. Hadash is a left-wing party with Jewish and Arab members, Ta’al campaigns primarily for the rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Balad calls for a state with equal rights for all its citizens. They agreed to contest this election on a single list, meaning their candidates would appear together on the ballot.
It is an electoral tactic used to not split votes among parties that are similar ideologically. A list must also win at least 3.25 percent of the national vote to enter the Knesset, so by joining forces, smaller parties combine their votes and reduce the risk that each falls below the threshold – in which case none of them would win seats.
In the current 120-seat Knesset, the Hadash-Ta’al alliance holds five seats. Of the Hadash-Ta’al seats, three belong to Hadash politicians and two to Ta’al. Balad has no seats.
Ra’am
Led by Mansour Abbas, it is running separately. It has been more willing to negotiate with other parties over funding and services for Arab communities. Ra’am joined the broad coalition that governed Israel from 2021 to 2022. The Joint List did not join that government.
In the current Knesset, Ra’am holds five seats.
Why have these parties been barred?
The decision followed petitions by the right-wing parties, Likud and Otzma Yehudit, which accused the parties and candidates of denying Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, supporting armed struggle against Israel or inciting racism.
The committee is chaired by a Supreme Court justice, but its voting members represent parties in the outgoing Knesset. Politicians therefore vote on whether rival parties and candidates can contest the election, although the Supreme Court has the final say.
The committee voted 18-5 to bar Ra’am and, in a separate vote, 18-5 to bar the Joint List. It also voted 18-5 to bar Cassif and 31-4 to bar Abu Shehadeh, according to Adalah, the Palestinian legal rights group representing the lists and candidates.
Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara opposed the disqualification of the two lists and Cassif, saying the evidence did not meet the legal threshold. She took a different position on Abu Shehadeh, however. The case against him centres in part on an article he wrote on October 8, 2023, the day after Hamas’s attacks on Israel.
The article was published on the Arab 48 website and referred to the attack as “an important historic event militarily, politically and strategically”.
The attorney general claimed its wording could amount to support for armed struggle.
Abu Shehadeh rejects that reading. He said on X that he opposed armed struggle and supported a “political and civil struggle for peace, justice, and equality”.
Other opposition parties in Israel support the disqualification of Abu Shehadeh. Yair Golan, leader of the opposition Democrats party, said of Abu Shehadeh: “Whoever wants a Jewish-Arab partnership does not speak this way, period,” he said, calling any legitimacy given to armed struggle or harm to civilians “a red line”.
Adalah disputes the case against Abu Shehadeh. It says the article contains no call for violence and argues that the petitions against the Joint List largely rely on old material or positions previously examined by the courts. It plans to challenge the decisions in the Supreme Court.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, remains eligible to run, despite being the subject of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, and a corruption trial that began in 2020 and remains ongoing. Netanyahu denies the allegations against him.
Cassif, whose disqualification from a previous election was overturned by the Supreme Court in 2019, called Wednesday’s decisions “another nail in the coffin of the remnants of democracy” in Israel. He said he and the Joint List would be in the next Knesset.
Attempts to exclude Arab candidates are not new. Adalah has documented challenges in elections in 2003, 2013, 2015, 2020 and 2022. The Supreme Court has repeatedly reversed committee decisions, but that history offers no guarantee of what it will do this time.
What about the far right?
Petitions which sought to disqualify the two far-right ministers in Netanyahu’s cabinet, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party, were rejected by the election committee.
Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have both advocated the displacement of Palestinians from Gaza and the annexation of the occupied West Bank, and face international sanctions over their actions and rhetoric towards Palestinians.
Attorney General Baharav-Miara, who has repeatedly clashed with Netanyahu’s government, said the bids to bar the far-right parties lacked a legal basis, according to Haaretz. However, for his part, Golan has said he supported disqualifying Ben-Gvir as well.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, remains eligible to run, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, and a corruption trial that began in 2020 and remains ongoing. Netanyahu denies the allegations against him.
Human rights advocate Ubai Al-Aboudi condemned the decision. The committee, he told Al Jazeera, has decided “not to bar Israeli politicians, parties or lists that are openly calling for the ethnic cleansing and genocide of Palestinians”.
“It has not even decided to view their statements as extreme.
“This shows that the current Israeli political structure still views Palestinians as a demographic threat, is still vilifying Palestinians.”
What happens now?
About one-fifth of Israel’s population is Palestinian. If the Supreme Court upholds the votes against both Ra’am and the Joint List, voters could still cast ballots for other parties, but neither of the two main Arab-majority lists would be able to contest the election. The court will also decide whether Cassif and Abu Shehadeh can stand.
Al-Aboudi said earlier attempts to bar Arab representatives had been overturned, but this vote went further. “It is the first time that all representation has been barred,” he said, describing it as a sign of “the mentality and extremism of the current Israeli political structure”.
The final decision rests with the Supreme Court. Al-Aboudi said its past rulings offer some grounds for hope, but added that, given the present political atmosphere, it is unclear whether it would overturn “part, all or none” of the committee’s decisions.
