Feature: Lesotho's "Mother of Hard Enduro" roars on as villagers seek lasting legacy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
21:58:58 CST
22:58:58 KST

by Silence Charumbira
MASERU, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- For three days this week, Tello Mahooe has a job. The resident of Ha Monyooe, a village near the Ha Lebamang section of the Roof of Africa off-road motorcycle race in Roma, works as a track marshal, earning 150 maloti (about 9 U.S. dollars) a day.
"We are happy to have the event here because some of us get piece jobs and get some money as we are not working," Mahooe said. He and fellow villagers have been deployed as marshals, cleaners and setup helpers for an event that, while little known outside motorsport circles, is among the most celebrated in off-road racing.
First held in 1967, the Roof of Africa is billed as the world's oldest hard enduro, a demanding form of off-road motorcycle racing over steep mountain tracks, rock faces and river crossings where simply completing the course is considered a major achievement.
Within the sport, it is widely referred to as the "Mother of Hard Enduro."
BORN ON "THE WORLD'S WORST ROAD"
The race takes its name from its geography. Lesotho, entirely surrounded by South Africa, is the only country in the world whose entire territory lies above 1,000 meters in elevation. The course climbs from approximately 1,400 meters to more than 3,000 meters in the Maluti Mountains.
The competition originated from an informal challenge. In the 1960s, road builder Bob Phillips constructed a route over the Moteng Pass in Lesotho's northern highlands and remarked to a friend, Louis Duffet, that he had built "the world's worst road." Duffet proposed holding a rally along the route.
The proposal evolved into an off-road race. In 1967, organizer Mike Reid dispatched the first group of participants from the Sani Pass Hotel, at the foot of the Drakensberg escarpment in South Africa, toward Maseru. Heavy rain resulted in few finishers, with South African driver Jan Hettema winning the inaugural event in a Volvo. Frequent wet weather during early editions earned the race the nickname "The Rainmaker."
Motorcycles joined the event in 1969, and over the following decades, the Roof of Africa shifted entirely to a motorcycle competition. Past winners include American Malcolm Smith in 1975 and Italian Elio Andreoletti in 1978 and 1981. South Africans Alfie Cox and Wade Young hold the record with nine victories each, with Young becoming the youngest winner at age 16 in 2012.
Today, the race covers 250 to 350 kilometers over three days and features four rider categories: Gold (elite), Silver, Bronze and Iron (entry level). The event has also gained international championship status. Last year's edition served as the final round of the FIM Hard Enduro World Championship, while this year's event was moved to September as the sixth round of the global series.
"At the Roof of Africa, not everyone is expected to finish," said Mopeli Ntabe, chairperson of the Lesotho Off-Road Association (LORA), organizer of the event. "That is the nature of the race."
EXPANDING LOCAL PARTICIPATION
For Lesotho, the event serves as a major international showcase, but organizers acknowledge that public awareness across the host country remains a work in progress. Ntabe noted that several visiting government officials attended the event for the first time this week, underlining the need for broader local engagement.
"We need all the help we can get from the media to educate Basotho about what the Roof of Africa is," Ntabe said.
Historically dominated by international competitors, the profile of the race is gradually changing. This year, 11 riders from Lesotho entered the competition, marking a significant increase from earlier years when the country was represented by only a single competitor.
"A few years ago, the Roof of Africa was purely a white man's sport. Only individuals from South Africa would come in and enjoy the Roof of Africa," Ntabe noted. "But we have seen a change over the last couple of years, with more and more Basotho coming in."
Despite the progress, Ntabe believes local participation has the potential to grow much further. Given recent competitive performances, he estimated that Lesotho should ideally field 20 to 30 riders, noting that two local participants currently competing in the Silver class have the ability to step up to the elite Gold category.
HIGH BARRIERS TO ENTRY
The primary obstacle to broader participation remains the high financial cost. A competitive motorcycle costs approximately 150,000 maloti, while essential safety gear, including helmets and boots, requires an additional 25,000 to 30,000 maloti.
Factoring in fuel, logistics and mechanical preparation, total expenditure for a single participant can reach 200,000 maloti. Ntabe, himself an active rider, is unable to compete this year because of the financial demands.
"There is only so much that LORA can do," Ntabe said, adding that the association plans to begin reaching out to corporate partners next week to secure sponsorship for both the event and prospective local athletes.
Parents and riders feel the strain directly. Edward Nko spent over 60,000 maloti preparing his 15-year-old son for his event debut, only for the teenager's bike to suffer damage midway through the course after falling into a ditch.
"It is too expensive, and it would help if there was support for local riders," Nko said, while adding that the opportunity for his son to compete alongside elite international athletes remains an invaluable learning experience.
The physical and financial toll is felt across categories. In the Iron class, local participant Lesekele Hlaoli, competing in his third Roof of Africa, placed ninth in Thursday's time trial before slipping to 16th on Friday following a crash. "Tomorrow I will be out in full force, and I am hoping for an improved showing," Hlaoli said.
SEEKING A LASTING LEGACY
While the immediate economic boost from temporary employment and visitor spending is welcomed in host communities such as Ha Monyooe, local residents are calling for longer-term benefits that endure beyond the race weekend.
"We still pray that in the future more can be done to see that the event leaves some legacy, such as community projects," Mahooe said.
Chief among local concerns is the condition of transport infrastructure. Heavy traffic and harsh terrain during the three-day event often leave unpaved mountain roads damaged, a problem exacerbated by seasonal rains.
"After the event, the roads are left in bad condition, and when it rains it becomes worse," Mahooe said. "It would be good if organizers could at least assist in rehabilitating our roads." ■

Asian Games | 2-time Olympic champion fencer Cheung Ka Long leaves door open on future after hard-fought final
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
21:58:54 CST
22:58:54 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Hong Kong, China lost to host Japan in the men's team foil final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Friday, with two-time Olympic champion Cheung Ka Long mounting a strong fightback before his team ultimately fell short.
Cheung fenced three bouts and scored 18 points in total, at one stage helping Hong Kong, China cut Japan's lead to three points. However, his team was unable to complete the comeback.
"I just wanted to take it one point at a time. I didn't think about tying the score. I just wanted to chase one point at a time and make things more comfortable for my teammates, without putting too much pressure on them," Cheung said after the final.
He said he had "not fenced very well" at the beginning but gradually found his rhythm and ways to deal with his opponent, adding that his form "got better and better" as the match progressed.
That was in sharp contrast to his state just three days earlier.
On Tuesday, Cheung suffered a shock 15-13 defeat to Daniil Kravtsov of Uzbekistan in the round of 32 of the individual event, ending his hopes of defending his Asian Games title.
After the defeat, the 29-year-old took off his mask, crouched beside the piste, covered his face with one hand and rested the other on the floor, remaining there for some time. In the mixed zone, he said in disappointment that this "could be my last Asian Games."
Asked after the team final whether he had changed his mind, Cheung paused for a moment, smiled and said, "That's a very good question. I don't think so. But I said 'could be.'"
Cheung said his body had gradually become less able to cope with high-intensity training as he has grown older. During the Games, his hand was wrapped in bandages and he repeatedly used treatment spray after physical problems emerged several days before his competition, leaving little time to make adjustments.
"But since I came here to compete, I had to give 100 percent," he said. "I did everything I could, so I have no regrets."
As a two-time Olympic gold medalist in men's individual foil, Cheung has achieved many of the goals he once pursued. Now, new questions have emerged.
"I lost my motivation and started repeatedly asking myself what else I could pursue," he said.
Cheung said he had tried to rediscover the simple joy of competing, telling himself to step onto the piste and enjoy the experience. But when results failed to meet his expectations, disappointment would return, leaving him caught in a struggle with himself.
"I cherish my time as an athlete very much, but I think every sporting career has to come to an end one day," he said. "But I'm not afraid of having a different kind of life."
Cheung is the oldest member of his team. In the team final, the responsibility of fencing in the last leg was put on 17-year-old Ho Shing Him Harris.
Once entrusted with the final leg himself, Cheung is now supporting the team in a different role as a younger generation begins to take on greater responsibility.
From the disappointment of his individual defeat to the enjoyment of competing alongside his teammates in the team event, and from pursuing his Olympic ambitions to contemplating life beyond competitive sport, Cheung is still considering whether to continue.
But at least at these Asian Games, he made sure to fight for every point he could. ■

4th Russian Fuel Plant Shut Down in One Week Following Drone Attacks
A major Russian oil processing facility halted operations on September 25 following a Ukrainian drone attack, Reuters reported, citing two industry sources. This is the fourth Russian oil refinery to halt operations in less than a week.
The strike triggered a fire on the site, inflicting damage on pipelines, storage tanks, and processing units.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Situated over 1,500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, the Perm processing plant ranks as the seventh largest facility of its kind in Russia by volume.
The plant processed approximately 12.6 million tons of crude oil in 2024, producing various fuel types, including motor gasoline, diesel, and aviation fuel.
Ukraine’s sustained drone campaign against Russia’s largest oil refineries, which Ukraine enacted in response to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, has disrupted Moscow’s energy sector, knocking out roughly a third of its refining output and pushing crude processing down to its lowest levels in over a decade.
On September 25, 2026, the LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest processing facilities, was targeted in a drone attack.
Perm regional Governor Dmitry Makhonin confirmed the strike on the region, noting that emergency and operational services were working at the scene.
The plant, which served as a critical component of the LUKOIL group, processed more than 13 million tons of crude oil annually.

Russell holds off Verstappen to win Azerbaijan Grand Prix
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
21:58:42 CST
22:58:42 KST

by F1 correspondent Michael Butterworth
BAKU, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Mercedes' George Russell converted pole position into victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on Saturday, holding off a late charge from Max Verstappen to cut Kimi Antonelli's Formula 1 championship lead.
Russell led every lap and set the fastest lap to complete a grand slam, but crossed the line just 0.1 seconds ahead of Red Bull's Verstappen after two safety-car periods wiped out a commanding advantage and set up a tense finish.
Isack Hadjar finished third on his return from a three-race injury absence, giving Red Bull two cars on the podium for the first time this year, while Charles Leclerc was fourth for Ferrari.
Antonelli recovered from 16th on the grid to take fifth and limit the damage to his championship lead, with Russell cutting his teammate's lead by 15 points. Antonelli now has 302 points to Russell's 236.
"It's amazing to be back on the top step of the podium. I want to say a big thanks to the team for continuing to believe in me through the tough moments and helped me come through it. I'm really proud to have had this weekend," said Russell, whose win was his third of the season, and his first since the Austrian Grand Prix seven races ago.
"The first half of the race felt pretty plain sailing, getting the gap. At the safety car restart with Max behind, I thought 'this is not going to be easy,' and he drove incredibly at the end of the race."
Russell had been in control from the start, quickly moving clear of McLaren's Oscar Piastri after starting on medium tyres and stretching his advantage to more than nine seconds by lap 23.
Behind him, Verstappen made rapid progress after starting eighth following a difficult qualifying session in which a power-unit problem had left his Red Bull down on power. Red Bull changed the engine ahead of the race without incurring a grid penalty.
Starting on medium tyres, Verstappen passed Lewis Hamilton and Leclerc before Hadjar allowed his teammate through into third on lap seven. But the Dutchman then spent much of the opening stint bottled up behind Piastri, with the McLaren quicker through Baku's tight middle sector and the Red Bull gaining ground on the long straight.
The complexion of the race changed on lap 31 when Alex Albon crashed at Turn 6, bringing out the safety car and allowing the leaders to make their pit stops.
Verstappen took advantage at the restart to pass Piastri for second, but the race was immediately neutralized again after a multi-car collision involving Franco Colapinto, Pierre Gasly and Lando Norris.
Colapinto locked up at Turn 1 and hit Gasly, who was sent into Norris, eliminating all three. Liam Lawson also spun in the incident but was able to continue.
Russell retained the lead at the second restart, but Piastri's race unraveled on lap 40 when he locked up while defending third place from Hadjar at Turn 1 and was forced down the escape road, dropping to the rear of the field.
Hadjar inherited third, while Antonelli continued his recovery through the field and passed Hamilton for fifth on lap 43.
Verstappen, much happier after switching to soft tyres, then closed rapidly on Russell and was within half a second by lap 46. Russell briefly rebuilt his advantage to around a second before Verstappen closed again over the final laps, but the Mercedes driver held on by the narrowest of margins.
Hadjar's third place capped an impressive comeback weekend after missing the previous three races with a wrist injury.
Leclerc finished fourth ahead of Antonelli and Hamilton, while Arvid Lindblad took seventh after pipping Esteban Ocon at the line. Ocon and Ollie Bearman finished eighth and ninth, giving Haas its first double-points finish of the season, while Carlos Sainz took 10th for Williams.
The race marked the 10th edition of Formula 1 racing in Baku, which first joined the calendar as the European Grand Prix in 2016.
The championship continues next weekend with the rescheduled Bahrain Grand Prix at Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit, which will host Formula 1 for the first time since 2017. ■

Seminar in Kenya highlights China-proposed global initiatives for shared future
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
21:58:35 CST
22:58:35 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- The China-proposed Global Development Initiative (GDI) and Global Governance Initiative (GGI) have the potential to reshape multilateralism and foster people-centered growth, equality, peace and stability, a seminar held in Kenya's resort town of Naivasha heard on Thursday.
The seminar, co-organized by Kenya's Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs and the Chinese Embassy in Kenya, with the Africa Policy Institute (API), a pan-African think tank, as implementing partner, brought together senior officials, diplomats, scholars, industry executives and representatives of UN agencies.
Themed "Jointly Advance Global Development and Governance: China and Kenya Usher in a New Chapter of a Shared Future", the seminar assessed the impact of the two initiatives on the realization of the Sustainable Development Goals and on global governance cooperation.
Abraham Korir Sing'Oei, principal secretary of the State Department for Foreign Affairs in the Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs, said Kenya and China share common views on global governance.
In a speech read on his behalf by Jane Makori, deputy director general of the Asia and the Pacific Directorate in the ministry, Sing'Oei said Kenya joined the Belt and Road Initiative, the GDI, the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative and the GGI. He said relations between the two countries are based on mutual respect, trust and the principles of South-South cooperation.
Under the GDI, China has supported Kenya in implementing priority national development projects in sectors including health, education, finance, tourism, culture and trade, Sing'Oei said.
Participants discussed how the GDI, five years after it was proposed by China, has contributed to a more equitable, prosperous and greener world. They also examined the impact of the GGI, which China proposed in September 2025 to help build a more just and equitable global governance system.
Guo Haiyan, Chinese ambassador to Kenya, said the four global initiatives on development, security, civilization and governance complement one another, promoting prosperity through development, safeguarding stability through security, enhancing mutual trust through civilizational exchanges, and pursuing justice through governance.
Amid a volatile international situation, China is ready to work with Kenya and other African countries, as well as international organizations and think tanks in Africa, to advance global development and improve global governance, Guo said.
She noted that September marks the fifth anniversary of the GDI and the first anniversary of the GGI. More than 130 countries and international organizations have expressed support for and participated in GDI cooperation, and the Group of Friends of the GDI has grown to 88 countries, including Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Rwanda and Uganda, she said.
The GGI has been welcomed and supported by nearly 160 countries and international organizations, and more than 60 countries have joined the Group of Friends for Global Governance, the envoy added.
In July, China and 28 countries, including Kenya, the Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia and Tanzania, jointly initiated the establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, Guo said.
"This is a major step taken by China to respond to the call of the Global South and actively advance the development and governance of artificial intelligence," she said.
According to API, both the GDI and GGI are global public goods critical to realizing the UN 2030 Agenda and to ensuring a functioning and inclusive multilateral order that reflects the aspirations of people worldwide. The think tank stressed that the two initiatives should serve as a platform for deeper cooperation among China, African countries and multilateral institutions to achieve long-term development and stable governance.
Erastus Mwencha, former deputy chairperson of the African Union Commission, said multilateralism, which has underpinned decades of shared growth since the end of World War II, is under strain from trade wars, supply chain disruptions and protectionism.
Mwencha described the GDI and GGI as "practical correctives anchored firmly in multilateralism."
"GDI asks us to put people, not geopolitics, at the center of the development agenda," he said, adding that the GGI "asks the international community to recommit to sovereign equality and the rule of law in global affairs, rather than power alone dictating outcomes."
Shaheen Nilofer, UNICEF representative to Kenya, said cooperation with China has advanced maternal and child health in the East African nation, citing a program launched with 3 million U.S. dollars from the China International Development Cooperation Agency and 1 million dollars from UNICEF.
Guo said that since the beginning of this year, UNICEF and the UN Industrial Development Organization have been approved to use the Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund to implement projects in Kenya that promote the health and well-being of women and children and support the development of agro-industrial parks. ■

Asian Games | Six world records fall in men's 70kg, 75kg weightlifting
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
21:58:16 CST
22:58:16 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Six world records were rewritten on Saturday in the men's 70kg and 75kg weightlifting divisions at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, with lifters from the DPR Korea and Indonesia claiming one gold apiece.
Ri Won-ju of the DPR Korea set world records in the clean and jerk at 198kg and the total at 349kg on his way to winning the men's 70kg weightlifting title, while host Japan's Masanori Miyamoto had a snatch world record with a lift of 154kg to secure the silver in the same category.
Ri Won-ju trailed Miyamoto by three kilograms in the snatch, but overtook his rival in the clean and jerk to claim the victory with a 7kg margin. Albert Ian Delos Santos of the Philippines took bronze with a total of 324kg.
Delos Santos hails from a weightlifting family. His father, a former lifter with the Philippines national team, was his first coach. Speaking of this special family legacy, Delos Santos could barely contain his excitement.
"My sister competed at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, and now being here is like a full circle. And my dad back in the 90s, this is a legacy given to me," he said.
Later in the men's 75kg final, Rahmat Erwin Abdullah of Indonesia also created world records in the clean and jerk at 206kg and the total at 366kg on his way to the title.
In the snatch, Ri Chong-song from DPR Korea saw a world record with a lift of 162kg, but failed his second and third attempts in the clean and jerk, settling for the bronze medal in the division. Thailand's Weeraphon Wichuma took silver, narrowly missing out on gold by just one kilogram.
Wichuma said in a post-match interview that he was delighted with his performance.
"I'm happy for silver. It's so good," he said. "The level here was quite high, this is a competitive field full of good competitors."
The women's 69kg and 77kg divisions will take place on Sunday. ■

China and the United States reach eight deliverables and understandings
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
21:58:09 CST
22:58:09 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- From Sept. 23 to 25 local time, Chinese President Xi Jinping paid a state visit to the United States. During the visit, the two heads of state had in-depth discussions on the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability and major international and regional issues, and reached eight deliverables and understandings:
1. The two sides agree to build "a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."
2. China and the United States support each other in successfully hosting the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and the G20 Summit. The two heads of state intend to attend each other's meetings.
3. The two heads of state agree that Iran should honor its commitment to not developing nuclear weapons, and no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways.
4. The two heads of state recall that China and the U.S. were allies in World War II and fought side by side to win the war.
5. The two heads of state recognize the positive role of the China-U.S. economic and trade consultation mechanism, endorse the outcomes of the consultations between the two economic and trade teams, including establishing and taking forward the Board of Trade and other mechanisms, reaching an arrangement for a 30-billion-U.S.-dollar reciprocal tariff reduction, and the extension of the outcomes of economic and trade consultations in Kuala Lumpur, and give instructions that they be implemented.
6. The two sides note that cooperation between the counter-narcotics and law enforcement agencies of China and the U.S. has produced visible outcomes. Recently, the two sides working closely together have jointly cracked multiple cases involving New Psychoactive Substances (NPS) and precursor chemicals, and apprehended dozens of relevant criminal suspects in the two countries.
7. The two sides agree on the establishment of the China-U.S. AI Dialogue to exchange views on risks and benefits related to AI. The next exchange will occur in November 2026. China and the U.S. also agree to establish a bilateral communication channel for AI incidents.
8. The United States welcomes the arrival of two giant pandas, leased by China to Zoo Atlanta.
In addition, the Chinese and U.S. militaries agree to conclude a memorandum of understanding on crisis communication and prevention as soon as possible, and continue their cooperation to search for the remains of missing U.S. servicemembers in China. ■

Bulgarians in Riga showcase their homeland at European Languages Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:54:37 UTC
22:54:37 KST

Author
Elena Karkalanova
News
With Cyrillic letters and Folklore
Bulgarians in Riga showcase their homeland at European Languages Festival
Dicho Chumov on his role as a “guardian of the roots” and his unfulfilled dream of seeing a Bulgarian Embassy in Riga
Saturday 26 September 2026 15:25
Saturday, 26 September 2026, 15:25
PHOTO Iskra Boneva
Font size
For the third consecutive year, the Bulgarian language has resounded in the heart of Latvia, as the Latvian-Bulgarian Cultural Society “Sts. Cyril and Methodius” presented Bulgaria at the European Languages Festival in Riga. The participation of the Bulgarian community in the event on September 18 was dedicated to two landmark anniversaries: the 1,200th anniversary of the birth of St Constantine-Cyril the Philosopher and the 1,140th anniversary of the arrival of his disciples in Bulgaria.
At a specially prepared stand, information panels were displayed in three languages: Bulgarian, Latvian and English.
PHOTO Iskra Boneva
“They presented, in an accessible and visually engaging way, the significance of the work of the holy brothers Cyril and Methodius, the overcoming of the three-language dogma, and Bulgaria’s role in the creation and consolidation of the Cyrillic alphabet, a writing system still used by millions of people around the world. The historical narrative was complemented by facsimile editions of some of the most valuable literary monuments of the Bulgarian literary school. These included the Gospel of Tsar Ivan Alexander, preserved at the British Library in London; the Asseman Gospel (Codex Assemanius), the oldest Glagolitic Old Bulgarian manuscript known to scholars, kept at the Vatican Apostolic Library; Paisii Hilendarski’s Slavonic-Bulgarian History, preserved at Zograf Monastery on Mount Athos; the collected works of Clement of Ohrid, as well as other publications,” Iskra Boneva, a member of the “Sts Cyril and Methodius” society team, told Radio Bulgaria.
Visitors were also able to take home contemporary bilingual and trilingual books devoted to Bulgarian culture. For children, too, the encounter with Bulgaria at the Language Festival in Riga proved a memorable experience, with the youngest guests receiving books of Bulgarian poetry and educational publications.
“Alongside history and literary heritage, the Bulgarian participation also stood out for its vibrant cultural atmosphere. At the end of the festival day, the Bulgarian Folk Dance Group in Riga invited the audience to join a Bulgarian horo to the sound of popular folk songs. The northerner-style rachenitsa also attracted particular interest, with the most enthusiastic participants putting their dancing skills to the test and adding to the festive atmosphere of the event,” Iskra Boneva told us.
PHOTO Lauma Kalninya
For Bulgarians in Latvia, expressing their national identity is more than a symbolic gesture. It is an inner need to preserve their sense of identity and pride. Some time ago, the coordinator of the Bulgarian participation, Iskra Boneva, told Radio Bulgaria how wearing traditional Bulgarian dress has become a bridge to her roots:
“I am proud to be Bulgarian. I use every opportunity to attend official events wearing Bulgarian traditional dress or clothing featuring Bulgarian embroidery. We even go to the opera in Bulgarian traditional costumes. Bulgarian traditional dress is formal attire, and you can wear it even to a reception hosted by a king, queen or president. I also wear it to corporate events and at my workplace, and everyone is always delighted because our traditional costumes are exceptionally beautiful.”
Iskra Boneva
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
For more than three decades, Dicho Chumov, chairman of the society, has been at the heart of Bulgarian community life in Latvia. His journey to the Baltic began in aviation. Having worked in a helicopter aviation services unit, he moved to Riga to study engineering at one of Europe’s leading institutes. Following the political changes in 1991, he went on to build a successful business. He is the driving force and chairman of the Latvian-Bulgarian Cultural Society “Sts Cyril and Methodius”, founded on April 13, 1993. During one of his visits to Sofia some time ago, he explained how it all came about:
“With love and enthusiasm. The longer version is that man is a social animal and always looks for others who share his or her way of thinking, mood and so on. Bulgarians are no different. Naturally, besides everything else, Bulgarians also have hopes, which is perhaps the greatest punishment: hope. I always advise people not to live in expectation. If God gives, I thank Him and move boldly forward. If He does not, then accept it as a lesson from God and continue boldly along your path, like a samurai.”
Chumov makes no secret of what he considers his greatest disappointment: the absence of a Bulgarian Embassy in Riga.
Dicho Chumov
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
“For all these years, our greatest achievement is that we survived, despite the state. Throughout these 37 years, we have had the desire and the hope that Bulgaria would fulfil its obligations and establish an embassy in Riga. Not that it would help us all that much, but at least that way we would have our country behind us. We need consular and embassy services, and when you do not have that support behind you, you feel cast aside,” Mr Chumov explains. He adds that so far, his efforts to help turn this dream into reality, including contacts at the highest levels, have produced no result.
Speaking about his role as a source of inspiration, his personal freedom and his attitude towards his homeland, he adds:
“I have no other people but my own, and I do everything I can to make sure  that we do not forget our roots. I wish everyone that when they reach my age, and go much further beyond it, they can look back and have no regrets.”
PHOTO Elena Karkalanova
Thanks to people like Dicho Chumov, Iskra Boneva and the other volunteers who contributed to yet another presentation of Bulgaria in Riga, including Vasil Tsalta, Miglena Ivankova, Vladimir Zikov and the society’s co-chair Benita Skrodere, the Bulgarian spirit in Latvia continues to live on and inspire the new generations.

Iran makes diplomatic push at UN with 24 meetings and Trump envoy talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:53:03 UTC
22:53:03 KST

While Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit and speech at the UN General Assembly this week will be remembered mainly for the walkout by members of numerous delegations as he began speaking and for the relatively few diplomatic meetings he held during his stay in New York, the Iranian delegation sent to the gathering appears to have had a far busier diplomatic agenda.
Representing Iran at the gathering were President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who is still in New York and, according to sources, is expected to remain there for the next several days.
According to a CNN review of Araghchi’s visit to New York, he met with representatives of at least 24 countries, including the foreign ministers of leading European powers. Netanyahu, by comparison, met with nine leaders during the General Assembly, including Argentine President Javier Milei, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Slovenia’s new prime minister, Janez Janša.
Among others, Araghchi met with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and his counterparts from Britain, France, Germany, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Poland, Russia and Ukraine. Araghchi also met with his Jordanian counterpart, Ayman Safadi, shortly after Iran attacked U.S. targets on the territory of the Hashemite Kingdom. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met with UN Secretary-General António Guterres and spoke with representatives of Western media outlets.
But the highlight of Iran’s diplomatic activity during the General Assembly was Araghchi’s meeting with Steve Witkoff, U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy. After the meeting, Araghchi told Western journalists that he had put a new proposal on the negotiating table between Tehran and Washington. Although reports overnight said Trump had rejected the proposal and was preparing for further military strikes, from the Iranian perspective, the significance lay in the fact that the meeting took place at all.
Araghchi also heard tough messages directed at his country in other meetings. According to a BBC report, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told his Iranian counterpart: “The Foreign Secretary reiterated the UK’s unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups on UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community.”
CNN, which has been engaged in an ongoing dispute with the Trump administration, wrote of the Iranian delegation’s arrival at the General Assembly: “Seven months after escaping with his life from a U.S.-coordinated Israeli airstrike that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s top diplomat walked the streets of Manhattan this week under the protection of the U.S. Secret Service.”
US economic pressure intensifies
Alongside Iran’s efforts to renew ties with Western countries, Washington appears to be seeking to use additional pressure to deepen Tehran’s isolation. According to a Wall Street Journal report, a senior U.S. Treasury official recently traveled to several countries in Europe and the Middle East that trade with Iran and delivered a message: “You either trade with Tehran or Washington.”
The newspaper noted that in recent days, Iranian airlines have been cut off from vital regional routes while the Islamic Republic’s leading commercial bank has been prevented from conducting transactions in the United Arab Emirates and Turkey. The measures come on top of sanctions imposed on Iran in recent years and the continuing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian seaports.
British lawyer Nigel Kushner, who has advised companies on Iran sanctions for two decades, told The Wall Street Journal that he had never seen such intense pressure brought to bear on Iran’s banking and aviation sectors.
“The U.S. has achieved greater impact in a matter of weeks than during the lengthier campaigns commenced from 2010” he said.
During his address to the General Assembly, Iranian President Pezeshkian acknowledged that U.S. sanctions posed a problem for his country but said they would ultimately have the opposite effect.
“The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying," Pezeshkian said. “We will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”

Germany's FM Wadephul meets Lavrov on UNGA sidelines

We are continuing our coverage of the 81st UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Wadephul: Russia's war in Ukraine 'shows contempt' for UN charter
Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia's war in Ukraine targets the lives of millions of innocent civilians, Ukraine and its culture, as well as the "European peace order."
"It puts vital grain deliveries for millions of people at risk, particularly in Africa, Asia and the Middle East," Wadephul said in his speech to the UN General Assembly, adding that Russia's actions "show contempt" for the UN charter and for the "common order on which we stand."
The minister also said Germany's support with Ukraine was consistent with UN values.
"Today Germany is the largest supporter of Ukraine and its defense against Russian aggression. This aggression has been condemned consistently by an overwhelming majority here in the General Assembly," Wadephul said.
He said Germany would continue to call on Russia to come to the negotiation table.
"I call on every member state to join us in convincing Russia that the future is built at the negotiation table, not on dead bodies in cities and villages," he added.
Prior to his speech, Wadephul met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the UNGA, in the first of such meetings since 2022.
The talks come in the midst of tensions between Berlin and Moscow, after Germany accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.
"Wadephul called on the Russian Federation to abandon its dangerous path of escalation vis-a-vis Germany, Europe, and NATO," a German diplomat said of the talks in comments to AFP news agency.
"He made it clear: incidents such as the recent attempted attack in Leipzig or further hybrid assaults would not shake Germany's resolve to support Ukraine, which has come under attack," the diplomat added.
"The German foreign minister condemned Russia's ongoing and increasingly targeted aggression against the Ukrainian civilian population. This attempt to increase pressure does nothing to change Russia's untenable situation: every month, tens of thousands of Russian soldiers die in a hopeless war of positions, while the Russian economy continues to collapse," the diplomat said.
Germany calls for AI regulation, urges 'profound' UN reform
Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul opened his UN General Assembly speech by warning about the extraordinary power of artificial intelligence and its implications for the world. He also addressed the erosion of international institutions in a world of rising nationalism.
"When a technology has the power to fundamentally change the world, we need to ask who controls it, who sets the rules, who is accountable," Wadephul said, adding that AI has the potential to upend the economy and "endanger the infrastructure that keeps our societies running."
"AI holds extraordinary promise," Wadephul said. But he warned that a "critical tension" exists when the technology is concentrated in two countries and a few companies. Such power holds great responsibility to humanity, Wadephul said, saying that as power becomes global, so must the responsibilites.
"AI is not waiting for our institutions to catch up, our institutions have to catch up with AI" Wadephul said.
"We need to make sure that tech progress is guided by a framework that we all have a say in shaping," he added, calling effectively for global regulation of AI.
"Germany calls on UN member states to work towards common safety requirements for the most capable models," he said.
On the weakening of UN institutions, Wadephul warned of a UN "under pressure."
"There are great powers that believe that they fare better if they ignore the rules enshrined in the UN charter,"
Wadephul said that "the overwhelming majority of the 193 states represented in this assembly" are harmed when international institutions are under attack.
"If this erosion contitnues, we all stand to lose," he added.
Germany's foreign minister urged for the the new UN Secretary General to lead "a profound process of reform," as the world needs "a functioning UN that plays an active role in conflicts, rather than managing."
"Germany stands up for peace and security," Wadephul said, citing his country's commitment to support Ukraine.
A new nationalism is not the path for nations, Wadephul said, adding that "it would makes our lives narrower, poorer and less secure"
India urges de-escalation amid Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea crises
India's Minister for External Affairs, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, addressed the UN General Assembly, urging de-escalation and restraint from those involved in conflicts that have caused disruption to world navigation, in reference to the current crises in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea.
"In a globalized world, the effects of war are felt worldwide," Jaishankar said.
"Countries far from conflicts are being penalized for no fault in this. Those most impacted often have the least say," he added.
Jaishankar also denounced the security of seafarers caught in conflicts.
"We must ensure that the safety and security of shipping and seafarers is never compromised," he said.
Saudi Arabia says international community 'absent' in Gulf crisis
At UN, the Foreign Minister of Saudi Arabia, Prince Faisal bin Farhan al Saud, called for the defense of freedom of navigation in all international waterways.
"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," bin Farhan told the United Nations General Assembly.
The Saudi foreign minister called for the restoration of the Strait of Hormuz to its "pre-28th February status." The US and Israel began their military operations against Iran on that date.
He condemned the fact that Saudi Arabia and other Gulf nations "have been subjected to flagrant Iranian attacks" targeting their security, resources, and civilians.
Saudi FM also denounced Israel's war in Gaza, saying it opposed the "continuing suffering of the Palestinian people."
"We stress that a just and lasting peace can only be achieved through the implementation of a two-state solution and the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital."
Russia offers to help with Strait of Hormuz crisis
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that Moscow can help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov said in his speech to the UNGA.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region," he added.
Lavrov claims Europe 'thwarts' Ukraine talks
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addressed the UNGA, shortly after meeting with his German counterpart Johann Wadephul.
In his speech to the general assembly, Lavrov accused European countries of "doing everything" to thwart talks to help end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
Russia's unprovoked invasion of its neighbor will soon mark its fifth anniversary next February.
"Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the (Donald) Trump administration is interested," he said, referring to the US government and the various rounds of talks it has held with the Russian and Ukrainian government, led by Trump's son in law Jared Kushner and adviser Steve Witkoff.
German FM Wadephul meets Russia's Lavrov during UN assembly
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
A correspondent for the Russian Interfax news agency reported Wadephul and Lavrov, followed by aides, shaking hands before the press was asked to leave.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the meeting took place at the German initiative.
Moscow has been sanctioned by the EU over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine which the Kremlin launched in February 2022.
The last meeting between on this level was held in January of that year, between veteran diplomat Lavrov and Germany's then-top diplomat, Annalena Baerbock, who was on a visit to Moscow.
Lavrov and Wadephul's meeting was held as tensions between Berlin and Moscow have been high in recent weeks.
Germany has accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport, with each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.
Moldova PM offers his country as testing ground for AI rules
Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan used part of his time before the General Assembly to present a vision of small nations serving as "regulatory sandboxes" for new technologies.
"Technology is moving faster than regulation almost everywhere, and artificial intelligence is widening that gap," said Tofan, who worked as an investor and businessman before becoming the head of Moldovan government two months ago.
"We want Moldova to become a place where emergent technologies can be tested responsibly through regulatory sandboxes, where regulators learn alongside companies, rules adjust with evidence, and good ideas do not wait years to reach the real economy."
"When an entrepreneur arrives with a technology for which the law has not caught up yet, the answer should not simply be 'There is no rule for this.' It should be 'Let us find a safe way to test it'," he said.
China cast itself as source of stability in changing world
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng called for safeguarding the post-WWII order, saying the world wanted "peace, not war."
"We should turn into action the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, and reject the Cold War mindset and bloc confrontation," Han said.
"Major countries shoulder special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding the rule of law, and doing what's right."
"No matter how international dynamics evolve, China remains unchanged in its pursuit of peace and development, in its dedication to safeguarding fairness and justice and in its commitment to multilateralism," said the Chinese vice president.
"China will join hands with all other countries to build a community with a shared future for humanity, and make the world a better place for all of us."
China takes indirect swipes at US over Iran
Speaking at the UN on Saturday, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng said the world should reject "unilateral military actions that violate the UN charter and circumvent the Security Council authorization," in an apparent reference to the US attack on Iran.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of the countries in the Middle east, including the Gulf, should be respected, international industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded," he said.
In his speech, Han also spoke out against the US blockade of Cuba, albeit without explicitly mentioning the US.
He said China called on "the relevant country" to lift its blockade against Cuba and stop using the threat of force against the island nation.
In regards to Israel and the Palestinians, the Chinese official urged bringing the two-state solution back "on the right track" and "at an early date."

Small island states take aim at world leaders for inaction on climate change
The speakers for the small island nations of St. Kitts and Nevis, Samoa and Tonga called to attention the inaction of world leaders on climate change.
The island nations are disproportionately vulnerable to the climate crisis, with the deputy prime minister of Samoa, Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo, calling climate change "the single greatest threat" facing the country and the world.
Molioo stressed the need to scale up climate financing so small island nations weren't the ones bearing the burden of climate change.
Fatafehi Fakafanua, Prime Minister of Tonga, said Pacific leaders have been warning about the climate crisis, with little support for years.
Fakafanua said the question was not whether the world has heard the message of climate change but rather, he asked, "why has it still not acted?"
The deputy prime minister of St. Kitts and Nevis, Geoffrey Hanley, outlined some of the solutions his country has undertaken, such as investing in desalination and improving food security.
Hanley said that small states, who stand most at risk from the consequences of climate change, were still delivering big solutions.
But he said, because no small island state can perpetually adapt to the climate crisis, "adaptation cannot excuse inaction elsewhere."
Iran says it gave US 7-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has given the US a seven-day plan that would involve reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday.
Speaking to reporters at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, Araghchi said the plan was delivered via Qatar and the choice now rests with Washington to meet the conditions Tehran has laid out.
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he said.

Quantum computer simulates matter “popping into existence”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:47:38 UTC
22:47:38 KST

Quantum computer simulates matter “popping into existence”
Scientists used a quantum computer to simulate particles seemingly “popping into existence,” opening a new window into the physics of the early universe.
- Date:
- September 26, 2026
- Source:
- Duke University
- Summary:
- Scientists recreated a particle-forming process linked to the extreme physics of the early universe using a 13-ion quantum simulator. The breakthrough suggests quantum computers could eventually help researchers investigate how matter formed and evolved after the Big Bang.
- Share:
Researchers led by the Duke Quantum Center (DQC) have used a quantum simulator to observe string breaking dynamics connected to particle antiparticle formation, marking one of the earliest demonstrations of its kind in quantum physics.
The work, published September 23 in Nature Physics, shows how trapped ion quantum computers could become powerful tools for exploring some of the deepest questions in fundamental physics. The experiment simulated a process known as string breaking, in which two connected building blocks of matter are pulled apart until so much energy accumulates that new particles can effectively "pop into existence" when the connection breaks.
"Quantum computer simulations provide the best platform to investigate complex questions like matter formation, short of having witnessed the Big Bang itself," said Christopher Monroe, the Gilhuly Family Presidential Distinguished Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering and Physics at Duke, who led this research. "These findings signal a marked development in the quantum science field and open new avenues for us to understand string-breaking dynamics."
The study was carried out by an international collaboration that included researchers from the University of Maryland (UMD), Oxford University, California Institute of Technology, Cornell University and KU Leuven. The findings appear alongside two other recently published studies from separate teams that reproduced similar physics using different types of quantum computing hardware.
Why Quarks Cannot Simply Be Pulled Apart
Quarks are among the most fundamental known building blocks of matter. They are found inside particles such as protons and neutrons and are roughly a billion times smaller than an atom. Scientists cannot currently observe isolated quarks directly because quarks normally remain tightly bound together.
One way to picture this is to imagine two tiny charged particles connected by a tightly stretched string. The farther apart they are pulled, the more energy is stored in the connection between them.
Eventually, enough energy can accumulate to create additional charged particles. This is possible because mass and energy are related through Einstein's famous equation E=mc2. Rather than ending with one separated pair, the original connection breaks and new particle pairs form.
Such processes require enormous amounts of energy and normally occur only under extreme conditions, such as those created inside the Large Hadron Collider or those believed to have existed shortly after the Big Bang.
Recreating String Breaking in a Quantum Machine
In the new experiment, the Duke-led team reproduced analogous string breaking behavior using a trapped-ion quantum platform. Quantum simulators are especially useful for this kind of work because researchers can precisely control them and program them to imitate physical processes that occur at atomic and subatomic scales.
"Working at the intersection of quantum simulation and high-energy physics is incredibly exciting," said Arinjoy De, first author on the paper, former PhD student in Monroe's lab and now production machine lead at QuEra Computing. "By simulating quark confinement and string-breaking phenomena in a controlled lab environment, we're opening up new pathways for experimental investigations into the behavior of matter at its most fundamental level."
To build the simulation, the researchers encoded a string breaking model into a chain of 13 trapped ions. Carefully controlled laser beams were then used to adjust how the ions interacted with one another.
Those interactions allowed the team to control the system's energy in a way that reproduced the stretching and eventual breaking of a particle like string.
Watching the Quantum System Evolve
The researchers prepared the system in an out of equilibrium state and then followed how it changed over time. This allowed them to detect the appearance of effective charges and reconstruct the dynamics associated with the simulated string breaking process.
To check the results, the team also modeled the same process using a classical computer. The classical calculations agreed with the experimental results produced by the quantum simulator.
For simulations at this relatively small scale, classical computers can still perform the calculations. The researchers expect that as future experiments become larger and more complicated, however, quantum computers will eventually be able to solve versions of these problems that classical machines cannot handle.
Other research groups have recently reached similar milestones using different forms of quantum hardware. Teams led by Google and QuEra Computing recreated related string breaking models using superconducting circuits and neutral atoms, respectively. Each approach comes with its own strengths and limitations.
"These are the three platforms leading the charge in quantum computing, so it's a nice benchmark and comparison for the quantum community," added Monroe.
Toward Simulations Beyond Supercomputers
The trapped ion results represent another step toward quantum simulations that are too complex for even the world's most powerful conventional supercomputers.
If quantum systems continue to scale up, researchers could eventually use them to investigate questions that are difficult or impossible to reproduce directly in the laboratory, including how matter behaved and evolved shortly after the Big Bang.
"As a physicist, it is incredibly exciting to investigate the conditions of the early universe in an atomic-level computing machine," said Zohreh Davoudi, associate professor of physics at UMD, who was part of the research team. "Even the slightest insights from an out-of-equilibrium physics model will guide us in the future."
The research was supported by the Department of Energy (DE-SC0020312, DE-SC0025341, DESC0019040, DE-SC0024220, DE-SC0020271), National Science Foundation (OMA-2120757), Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and Amazon Web Services.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Duke University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Arinjoy De, Alessio Lerose, De Luo, Federica M. Surace, Alexander Schuckert, Elizabeth R. Bennewitz, Brayden Ware, William Morong, Kate S. Collins, Zohreh Davoudi, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Or Katz, Christopher Monroe. String-breaking dynamics in a quantum simulator. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03422-0

Angad Singh Dhillon appointed as Canada’s ambassador to the UAE
BATHINDA: Hailing from Ludhiana village in Punjab, Angad Singh Dhillon has been appointed as Canada’s next ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the United Arab Emirates. Dhillon, whose appointment has been announced by Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand on September 25, will succeed Radha Krishna Panday as Canada’s ambassador to the UAE.As per official website of global affairs Canada, Angad Singh Dhillon has only recently served as Director of Operations and Stakeholder Relations in the Office of Prime Minister Mark Carney and has previously served as Chief of Staff to two federal cabinet ministers handling the small business and transport portfolios.
In these roles, he supported Canada’s engagements at the G7, G20, UN General Assembly, Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, International Transport Forum and Conference of the Parties.As one of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s closest advisers, he supported the Prime Minister in re-engaging Canada’s diplomatic relationships with key bilateral partners, including India and China, by helping restore high-level channels of communication and cooperation. He also led stakeholder coordination to secure incoming investment commitments into Canada, including the development and planning of Canada’s inaugural national Investment Summit.He had joined the liberal party as a field organizer in 2015. Angad Singh Dhillon family traces its roots in Ghungrana village in Ludhiana as his grandfather Jagjit Singh Ghungrana was a farmer and known figure in the area.
An engineer by training but a journalist at heart, Neel Kamal writes about sustainable agriculture, environment, climate change and peace initiatives between India and Pakistan by peace groups on both sides.

China opposes 'unilateral military actions' amid US-Iran war, calls for 2-state Palestine solution track

Saadet Gökce
26 September 2026•Update: 26 September 2026
 China’s vice president on Saturday voiced Beijing's opposition to "unilateral military actions" amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict, also using his address to the UN General Assembly to urge a two-state solution to the Palestinian issue.
"We should settle differences and disputes through dialogue and consultation, and oppose unilateral military actions that violate the UN Charter and circumvent Security Council authorization," Han Zheng said, urging major countries to shoulder "special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security," and take the lead in "complying with the rules, upholding rule of law, and doing what's right."
He also said China believes the sovereignty and security of Middle Eastern countries, including Gulf states, should be respected.
"International industrial and supply chains should be kept stable and unimpeded, and global trade should be safeguarded," said Han.
He called for advancing governance in the West Bank and post-conflict reconstruction in Gaza in line with the principle of Palestinians governing Palestine.
China also calls for "bringing the Palestinian question back onto the right track of the two-state solution at an early date," he said.
On Ukraine, he said China plays a continued "constructive role in its own way" to achieve a political settlement of the crisis, also urging "the relevant country to immediately stop using the threat of force against Cuba and immediately and completely lift the blockade and sanctions against Cuba."
On tech advances, he said the world should take a people-centered approach and ensure positive AI development amid the rapid development of new technologies and industrial transformation, while narrowing the digital divide and promoting development that is universally beneficial.

Ex-defense minister Fedorov announces new 'Army of Robots' initiative in latest move since leaving office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:45:39 UTC
22:45:39 KST

Ex-defense minister Fedorov announces new 'Army of Robots' initiative in latest move since leaving office
A screenshot from an AI-generated video showing hypothetical military robots, posted by former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov on Sept. 26, 2026. (Mykhailo Fedorov / Telegram)
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has announced the launch of a new defense tech initiative called the "Army of Robots," which will look to replace human beings on the battlefield.
The announcement — made simultaneously on social media and in a presentation at this years's IT Arena conference in Lviv on Sept. 26, in Fedorov's latest move into defense tech after he was controversially dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July.
According to Fedorov, the initiative, modeled on the success of his Army of Drones project launched in 2022 while Digital Transformation Minister, will be not one company, but an "ecosystem."
"We will invest in defense tech companies, launch our own technology projects, create R&D capabilities, test solutions together with the military, and scale up as quickly as possible the things that actually work on the battlefield," the minister said.
After his dismissal from the post of Defense Minister, Fedorov did not initially make clear what his next move would be, as thousands of Ukrainians protested across the country for weeks, calling for the reinstatement of the popular tech-minded reformer.
After delivering a major challenge to Ukraine's wartime political order by calling for elections in mid-August, Fedorov has since turned his attention to defense tech.
During a much-publicized trip to the United States at the end of August to meet with supporters, donors, and tech leaders, Fedorov announced the creation of a fund to help drive innovation and scale up production to meet Ukraine's most important defense needs.
Just days later, the ex-minister said he would launch his own defense-tech company, one of the first investors of which would be Alex Karp, CEO of controversial tech company Palantir, whose products are used in the Ukrainian war effort.
In his announcement of the Army of Robots, Fedorov didn't specify what organization was behind the initiative.
"Even outside government, now from the private sector, we are continuing to work on our vision of technological warfare — Air. Land. Economy. — and on our main mission: to create technologies that help Ukraine win and save the lives of our service members," Fedorov said.
Asked by the Kyiv Independent to specify, Fedorov's press team did not reply at the time of publication.
Fedorov also called for skilled robotics engineers to join the Army of Robots team.
Fedorov's vision for the Army of Robots initiative places a particular focus on the advancement of humanoid robots to replace infantrymen in trenches.
According to Ukrainian media watching his presentation at IT Arena in person, Fedorov said that the initiative aims to achieve the first enemy soldier killed by a humanoid robot in six months, and the first successful assault of an enemy position with no infantry involved in twelve months.
Even in famous cases of all-UGV "assaults," described by some of Ukraine's top units, ground was not yet considered taken until it is done so by human boots on the ground.
On social media, the announcement came accompanied with an AI-generated video showing fancifully designed robots of different shapes and sizes fighting in trenches and fields. The video shows soldiers with Ukrainian uniforms and patches, but the English-language voiceover doesn't mention Ukraine.
"Robots intercept the enemy, defend against attacks, destroy targets, move on to enemy positions first;" the voiceover said, "people control the systems from a safe distance and enter the cleared position only when it is safe."
"Yeah, it sounds like the war of the future, but we are already there."
Unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) — known as "ground robotic complexes" in Ukraine — have come to play an increasingly important role for both sides on the battlefield, especially in logistics roles, as the saturation of enemy first-person view (FPV) drones makes conducting supply runs or casualty evacuation on vehicles close to the front line a near-suicidal task.
These machines, while unmanned, are almost never autonomous robots in the true sense, instead being directly piloted by human operator, usually via Starlink internet connection.
While more capable units sometimes use UGVs to fire upon the enemy directly or assault positions on the ground, the practical experience of "robots fighting instead of people" on the ground in Ukraine is still in its early stages, and held back by multiple complicating factors.
Ground drones, like any other combat vehicle, have a finite store of energy and ammunition, and need to be serviced, recharged, and reloaded by humans in the field.
Even though they are smaller and less noticeable than larger manned vehicles, UGVs also have a high rate of loss from enemy drones when operating close to the front line all the same.
Most of the robot designs featured in Fedorov's video, including humanoid, spherical, as well as dog and spider-like robots, are not currently used in combat in Ukraine.

Opposition parties Pro and Volt team up to force budget deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26

Opposition parties Pro and Volt team up to force budget deal
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Opposition parties Pro and Volt have joined forces for the next round of budget negotiations as they try to step up the pressure on the cabinet to make further concessions on social security.
Prime minister Rob Jetten said ministers had spent the last week drawing up “a new and attractive offer” addressing opposition parties’ concerns on welfare, the cost of living and replacing the “Box 3” asset tax mechanism.
Pro leader Jesse Klaver said the combined votes of his left-wing party and the pro-European Volt would give the government a “stable majority” in both houses of parliament.
An agreement with both Pro and Volt would give the coalition parties a comfortable majority in the lower house and the 16 seats it needs in the Senate, where Pro is the largest group but still needs Volt’s two seats to get over the line.
But the right-wing liberal VVD, the party of finance minister Eelco Heinen, is anxious not to make too many concessions to Pro, which would risk driving its voters away to its rivals such as JA21 and Geert Wilders’ far-right PVV.
Pick a side
“We are fighting for progress for ordinary people and a fair contribution from the super-rich,” Klaver said. “We believe in progressive co-operation.”
Volt leader Laurens Dassen said: “The world is changing rapidly. People expect politicians to work together towards a sustainable and innovative future.”
Jetten has been under pressure from the opposition on left and right to choose a side after all parties poured cold water on his hopes of finding a route through the middle.
The prime minister argued he would be “short-changing the country” if he excluded one side from the talks, but JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans said a broad approach “isn’t going to work” while Klaver warned his party would block the entire budget if the cabinet tried to do separate deals for each department.
Welfare cuts
Heinen has already agreed to postpone or cancel around half of the €6 billion cuts to welfare spending that were in the coalition agreement in February, but Pro wants the cabinet to go further.
Parties such as JA21, on the other hand, want to see even bigger welfare cuts, arguing that lower taxes are the best way to relieve the pressure on households and businesses.
Jetten and Heinen held talks on Saturday with Pro, Volt and the ChristenUnie, whose leader, Mirjam Bikker, said there had been “movement” from the coalition parties.
The ChristenUnie’s priorities are to ensure households are able to pay for essentials through the winter as energy and grocery bills rise. Bikker said it was “high time” that the coalition parties “feel the urgency” to make a deal.
BBB back on board
Later on Saturday the two ministers are due to talk to JA21 and the orthodox-protestant SGP, who have formed a right-wing alliance with 12 seats in the lower house.
Jetten and Heinen will also speak to Jan Struijs, leader of pensioners’ party 50Plus, and Henk Vermeer of the farmers’ party BBB, who are the second largest party in the Senate.
Jetten had initially said the BBB were no longer an option after the party backed a motion of no confidence during the budget debate, but he and Vermeer patched up their differences in a phone call last week.

Polish president “doesn’t like” Trump inviting Putin to G20 but will still attend summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26

22:40:41 KST

Polish President Karol Nawrocki “does not like” the fact that the Trump administration has invited Vladimir Putin to this year’s G20 summit in the United States, says his chief foreign policy aide.
However, Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Donald Trump, still plans to attend the event – which Poland has been invited to as a guest rather than a full G20 member – in order to represent Polish interests and push for full membership of the group.
🔴 "Nie podoba nam się to". Nawrocki ma problem po decyzji Trumpa
Prezydent Karol Nawrocki weźmie udział w grudniowym szczycie G20 w Miami, na który zaproszono również Władimira Putina. Szef Biura Polityki Międzynarodowej Kancelarii Prezydenta Marcin Przydacz przyznał na antenie…
— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 26, 2026
The G20, a major intergovernmental forum, holds an annual summit whose location rotates among members. This year’s event will take place in December at a golf resort in Miami owned by Trump.
On Wednesday this week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Trump has invited Putin to attend the summit, saying that “we think it’s an opportunity for him to engage…with other world leaders” and “we hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept”.
“If you only meet with people that you agree with, then these are very nice meetings but nothing happens,” added Rubio. “In order to solve problems, you have to meet with people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with.”
Marco Rubio on Russia:

We hope that’s an invitation he will accept. pic.twitter.com/e0GSz7Y8gm
— Clash Report (@clashreport) September 23, 2026
Last December, Rubio also announced Poland’s invitation to the summit as a guest, saying that it would be “assuming its rightful place in the G20”. In May this year, the US also “expressed its strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member”.
Poland will be represented by Nawrocki, who is a vocal critic of Putin and Russia, and is himself on a Russian wanted list for his work leading efforts to demolish Soviet-era monuments in Poland.
In an interview on Sunday with news website Wirtualna Polska, the head of Nawrocki’s international policy office, Marcin Przydacz, was asked if the US was right to invite Putin. “We don’t like it,” he replied.
“But we were invited to the G20 summit as guests, and it’s not our role to tell the participants who should be part of it,” he added, noting that Russia is a founding member of the G20. However, “if it were up to us, Russia should be isolated in all international forums.”
Nevertheless, “President [Nawrocki] is going to Miami and doesn’t intend to change his plans at this stage”, confirmed Przydacz. “Poland will be at the G20 summit because it’s in our interest…This isn’t the only format in which we sit with countries we disagree with.”
However, he also added that, “if the Russian leader actually intends to come, and is not just invited, we will discuss this with our European and Euro-Atlantic allies”.
Putin has not attended a G20 summit in person since 2019, initially due to the COVID-19 pandemic and later amid the fallout from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant against him. The US is not a member of the ICC, so the arrest warrant does not apply on its territory.
Przydacz told Wirtualna Polska that Putin “should be held accountable for his crimes”. Asked if Nawrocki would shake hands with the Russian president at the G20, Przydacz said that he “doesn’t think any interactions will occur”.

He also emphasised that Poland’s invitation to the summit was a “major success, demonstrating our growing role”. He said that Nawrocki would use the event to push its ambition to become a full member of the group.
He added that it would also seek to “bring a Central European perspective” to the event, representing its entire region, which has so far been excluded from the G20.
Earlier this week, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said that, in his opinion, the US should make Putin’s invitation to the G20 conditional upon Russia implementing a ceasefire in Ukraine, reported news website Interia.
However, he noted that, when a G20 meeting of finance ministers took place in the US earlier this year, Poland had attended alongside Russia.
