Turkiye calls for UN Security Council veto to end: Could it happen?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:17:05 UTC
22:17:05 KST

Turkiye calls for UN Security Council veto to end: Could it happen?
Fully abolishing the veto would require the unlikely agreement of all five permanent Security Council members.
Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has called for the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) to lose their veto power, arguing that the current veto system is “unjust” and hinders “global stability and peace”.
The call comes as the UNSC, which has five permanent members and 10 rotating, non-permanent members, remains deadlocked on many issues – from Israel’s war on Gaza to Russia’s war in Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3UNGA81: Why has Africa’s Security Council reform push remained unresolved?
- list 2 of 3Did Germany lose its UNSC seat because of support for Israel?
- list 3 of 3Trump invites Putin to Miami G20: Why that matters
The US, one of the five permanent members, has vetoed seven resolutions related to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict over the past three years, including five calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.
Russian vetoes have prevented the UNSC from passing any firm resolutions on the war in Ukraine.
Speaking to journalists in New York on Thursday, Erdogan said, “Let the veto mechanism be abolished… Let us move from a UN model that protects only five members to a mechanism that encompasses all members”.
So, could Erdogan’s call become a reality and what would abolishing the veto mean for the UNSC?
What is the UNSC veto and who can exercise it?
It is a special power to veto any substantive resolution, granted to the body’s five permanent members – the US, the UK, France, Russia and China.
It means that even if 14 of 15 UNSC members vote in favour of a resolution, just one veto from any of the five permanent members (P5) can tank it.
What has Turkiye called for?
Erdogan has called for a complete overhaul of the UNSC. That includes ending permanent membership of the council and eliminating the veto power.
Laying out his case in a September 22 article published by Bloomberg, Erdogan wrote that the UNSC’s current structure, developed eight decades ago, no longer meets the needs of a changing world and that a single country should not be able to block the wishes of the broader international community.
“Leaving the resolution of global crises to the will of a handful of capitals is no longer compatible with the realities of today’s world,” he wrote.
Erdogan also called for greater powers for the UN General Assembly (UNGA), which he said should elect all UNSC members for set terms. Countries seeking to serve on the council would therefore have to “regain the confidence of the majority of member states through elections”, he said.
Erdogan lobbied for this initiative during his recent address to the UNGA, saying “a system in which the will of more than 190 countries is subject to the whims of five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully establishing trust”.
What would it take for the UNSC to decide to end the veto?
Formally ending the veto would require an amendment to the UN Charter.
Under Article 108, that requires approval by two-thirds of the UNGA and ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent members. In other words, the P5 would have to sign off on giving up their own veto power.
What is the France-Mexico proposal that is gaining ground?
In 2015, France and Mexico tabled a proposal urging the P5 to suspend their vetoes on resolutions involving mass atrocities, such as genocide and crimes against humanity.
The initiative would rely on a “collective and voluntary agreement” among P5 states.
The initiative has recently gained renewed traction, with 21 states, including P5 member the UK, backing it within the last four months.
That brings the total number of UN members states supporting it to 128, according to the French government, just one short of the number needed to pass a resolution in the UNGA.
While such a resolution would be non-binding, advocates hope it would exert more pressure on P5 states to withhold their votes in emergency situations.
What is most likely to happen?
Any formal effort to abolish P5 members’ veto power is likely to fail, as it would inevitably face resistance from most, if not all, P5 members.
Russia has already responded to the Turkish initiative by saying it believes permanent UNSC members should retain their veto power, though it did say it supports expanding the number of permanent members on the council.
The US and China have previously strongly defended their veto privileges.
Expanding the UNSC, as Russia proposed, is more likely, though that would also come with challenges.
The US and China have both previously said they would support modest increases to the council’s composition, including by adding seats for African nations, none of which hold permanent membership. The UK and France have also backed expansion, including permanent seats for Brazil, Germany, India and Japan, as well as African countries.
But expanding the UNSC would also require an amendment to the UN Charter, which again requires the backing of all P5 states. Getting the P5 to agree on which countries to share their power with – and whether to extend new members the veto power – has long proved difficult.
“The status quo is not really interested in change,” Professor Ibrahim Gambari, a former Nigerian foreign minister and former Nigerian permanent representative to the UN, told Al Jazeera.
As for the France-Mexico initiative, analysts say its impact would be limited because the commitments are voluntary and non-binding.
Writing in a 2022 article for US publication Lawfare, analysts John Ramming Chappell and Emma Svoboda noted that the France-Mexico initiative and others like it are “couched in voluntary language” and lack consensus “from the most frequent veto-users (Russia, the United States and China)”.
As a result, “the principles advanced in the initiatives remain aspirational”, they wrote.
Who has exercised the veto most in the past?
Historically, Russia (or the Soviet Union prior to 1991) has cast the most vetoes by far, with nearly half of all vetoes ever recorded (163 out of 331).
The US is second, with 95 vetoes – around 28 percent of those cast.
In recent years, the US has vetoed numerous resolutions concerning the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including five calling for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it has vetoed three resolutions relating to that conflict.
When have France and the UK exercised the veto?
France and the UK – the two permanent members calling for suspension of the veto in resolutions relating to humanitarian atrocities – have exercised their veto far more sparingly, with a combined 50 vetoes. Neither country has used a veto since 1989 and most of their earlier vetoes were cast alongside the US.
The UK has only been the sole veto on a resolution a handful of times, all related to its former colony Rhodesia, which later became independent as Zimbabwe.
France has only vetoed a resolution on its own twice, once in connection with a territorial dispute with Comoros and the other related to the Indonesian conflict in 1947.

The Evolution of New York Times Opinion on Gaza: From Unconditional Support to Bounded Criticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:16:00 UTC
22:16:00 KST

Much has been written about the coverage of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in legacy western media, and most of it points to a clear bias towards Israel.
Scholars and journalists have highlighted language bias in major US newspapers, the failure to maintain accuracy and provide context, and internal newsroom pressures at institutions like the BBC and CNN designed to curtail critical reporting on Israel.
However, less attention has been dedicated to the evolution of this coverage as the war on Gaza progressed. Examining this evolution allows us to identify some of the forces that appear to shape mainstream media discourse on Palestine and Israel, and to consider whether the changes observed during the height of the war are likely to endure.
To trace whether and how elite American media discourse evolved alongside the U.S. public discourse around support for Israel, I conducted a qualitative content analysis of The New York Times Opinion section across two years of intense hostilities. The core sample comprised 40 articles (dataset available here) distributed evenly across five time periods—eight articles every six months, starting October 7, 2023, and concluding October 14, 2025.
I focus on opinion pieces rather than news coverage because opinion writers are less constrained by journalistic conventions of objectivity and therefore provide a clearer window into shifts in elite discourse.
The analysis reveals that while sympathy for Palestinians and criticism of Israel’s conduct grew over time, opinion articles in the New York Times remained markedly late in acknowledging the scale of devastation in Gaza. Palestinian agency remained largely absent, and while discourse evolved to allow some critique of the Israeli political system and society, influential voices within the New York Times Opinion section remained faithful to an idealized vision of Israel. Moreover, the analysis considers several factors that may help explain this change — limited and slow as it was — allowing us to reflect on which aspects of the shift may prove lasting and which may be merely transitory.
October 2023: Total Absence of Palestinian Context
Articles published in the immediate aftermath of the 7 October attacks were dominated by shock.
When an interpretation of the attack was offered, it was always first and foremost that Hamas is a terrorist organization intent on the destruction of Israel. The New York Times Editorial Board described the attack as occurring “without warning or any immediate provocation” and noted “how vulnerable Israel has always been — and continues to be, at a time of rising global antisemitism”.
Conspicuously absent were discussions of Palestinian grievances that formed part of the broader context in which the attack occurred. The occupation, the blockade of Gaza, Palestinian prisoners, and settler violence were virtually absent from the sample.
Most writers accepted that an Israeli military response was inevitable. Differences emerged primarily over strategy. Bret Stephens denounced calls for an immediate ceasefire, arguing that they would “shield the killers from consequences and deny their victims the right to effective self-defense”. More cautious voices, such as David Harden, warned against a ground invasion, but mainly because it would benefit Hamas and prove costly for Israel.
Only Nicholas Kristof made a sustained moral argument concerning the Palestinian civilian casualties that would likely result from a large-scale Israeli assault.
April 2024: Frustration with Netanyahu, but Palestinian Suffering Sidelined
By April 2024 criticism of the Israeli government is beginning to emerge as a theme in NYTimes opinion articles, but in most cases this criticism is not framed in terms of what it is doing to the Palestinians. Instead, the government is criticized for failing to bring back the Israeli captives, showing poor leadership, following a futile military strategy and for its handling of relations with the US.
The emergence of criticism toward Benjamin Netanyahu’s government should be understood in its political context. By April 2024, opposition to the Israeli prime minister was growing not only among segments of the Israeli public but also within the Biden administration, which was facing increasing domestic pressure. As Bret Stephens put it, “Wishing Netanyahu gone is the most mainstream position possible.”
Yet most articles fail to reflect the scale of global outrage over the war. By this point, the International Court of Justice had found a plausible case of genocide, the UN was warning of imminent famine in northern Gaza, and thousands of protests had been taking place globally. Soon they were to reach a crescendo in the United States with the wave of encampments on US campuses.
More than 33,000 Palestinians had already been killed and much of Gaza had been destroyed, but in most of the articles, Palestinian suffering is mentioned only in passing. Stephens lamented the displacement of Israelis in the north while omitting Palestinian casualties altogether. David French referred to Gaza’s civilian toll as “a human tragedy,” yet employed far more direct language in reference to Israeli deaths, describing “Hamas’s massacre of Israeli civilians.” Benny Morris argued that Israel must go ahead with the proposed invasion of Rafah, even as he professed concern for the civilian casualties that will result from it.
However, this batch of articles does include two pieces that made forceful arguments about Israel’s moral and legal failures. Spencer Ackerman argued that “International law is unambiguously against what Israel is doing in Gaza” and highlighted the International Court of Justice’s finding that genocide allegations were plausible. David Wallace-Wells, writing about the Israeli military’s use of artificial intelligence, argued that the devastation in Gaza should not be understood as an automated process but as the product of human choices: “a man behind a curtain, fiddling the switches.”
October 2024: Taking Stock on the First Anniversary
Articles marking the first anniversary of October 7 included a moving personal account from Yaffa Adar, an 86-year old resident of Kibbutz Nir Oz, who was abducted by Hamas and remained in captivity for 49 days.
At the same time, it included another personal account from Mohammed Aghaalkurdi, a Palestinian humanitarian worker displaced in Khan Younis. He argued that Israel’s recent consent to a polio vaccination campaign in Gaza should not be allowed to whitewash its conduct in the war.
A noticeable shift had begun to emerge. After a year of continuous bombardment and mass death in Gaza, some articles paid greater attention to Palestinian suffering and offered more forceful criticism of Israel.
Indeed, for the first time in the sample, criticism extended beyond the Israeli government to broader features of Israeli society. Peter Beinart described Israel’s political system as one “explicitly based on religion and ethnicity.” Mairav Zonszein lamented widespread Israeli indifference to Palestinian suffering, writing that “[t]here is almost no outrage over the indiscriminate destruction of Gaza and the killing of over 40,000 people.”
These developments should not be overstated. Strongly pro-Israel perspectives remained present in the sample. Bret Stephens argued that the “world had better hope that Israel wins its wars against Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and their masters in Tehran”.
Thomas Friedman, while disapproving of the Israeli government’s excessive use of force, reaffirmed his commitment to Zionism, portraying Israel as a unique democratic haven.
Spring 2025: Discontent with Israel Reaches Its Peak
Eighteen months into the war, criticism of Israel reached its highest level in the sample, with seven of the eight articles faulting either Israel, Netanyahu, or both.
By this stage, Israel had ended a six-week ceasefire, blocked aid deliveries, and overseen a death toll exceeding 50,000 Palestinians. Much of the criticism focused on the humanitarian catastrophe and the starvation of Palestinians. Sean Carroll, argued that “Israel is now openly exploiting aid as a tool of war”.
The trend toward broader critiques of Israeli policy beyond the war in Gaza also continued. Nicholas Kristof highlighted the long-standing oppression of Palestinian Christians in the West Bank, while Mohsen Mahdawi described growing up under what he called “Israel’s apartheid system,” recounting the deaths of family members and friends at the hands of Israeli forces.
Yet even amid stronger criticism, some writers continued to distinguish between opposition to Netanyahu and opposition to Israel itself. Thomas Friedman sharply criticized the prime minister while continuing to assert his own belief in Israel’s “core identity — that of a proudly proclaimed rule-of-law democracy in a region of strongmen”.
Another important factor shaping discourse was Donald Trump’s return to power. Six of the eight articles connected criticism of Israel to concerns about Trump. Mahdawi, who was detained by ICE during his U.S. citizenship process drew parallels between his suppression in Trump’s America and his family’s suppression in Israel. Friedman argued that Trump and Netanyahu shared a similar political trajectory: “Each is a wannabe autocrat.”
He also criticized both governments’ “weaponization of antisemitism as a way to silence or delegitimize critics”. This theme appears for the first time in the sample as the Trump administration intensified its attacks on universities in the name of combating antisemitism. Peter Beinart railed against the suppression of pro-Palestinian Jewish voices on campus, and Michelle Goldberg denounced “the way Israel’s defenders conflate all but the mildest criticism of Israel with antisemitism”.
October 2025: Who Won? What Next?
The final sample, published after the ceasefire agreement, was dominated by cautious celebration. Writers generally welcomed the end of hostilities while warning that major obstacles remained, including Hamas’s future, Israeli withdrawal, and governance arrangements for Gaza.
Some proposed solutions continued to deny full Palestinian agency. Friedman, for example, envisioned a new mandate over Palestine “that combines Palestinian, Arab and international stewardship over Gaza’s future. If it works, the arrangement might one day be extended to the West Bank.”
There was no consensus regarding who had “won”. Bret Stephens argued that “Israelis rallied and won,” praising Israel’s refusal to “buckle to unceasing international pressure”.
Other writers contended that Netanyahu had squandered military gains by repeatedly rejecting political solutions.
Israeli author Shira Efron argued that the ceasefire represented the collapse of the government’s central promise. “This ‘victory’ is actually a defeat — a necessary and blessed defeat,” she wrote, because the agreement ultimately contradicted the goal of “total victory” that the prime minister had promised for two years.
The Authors: Who sets the tone?
In addition to the qualitative analysis of the core sample, a quantitative review was conducted of the authors of 816 articles published over the full two years in the Opinion Section of the New York Times (dataset available here). .
The most prolific contributors to these articles are NYTimes columnists Thomas Friedman (75 articles), followed by Nicholas Kristof (66 articles) and Bret Stephens (64 articles).
While Friedman is a critic of Netanyahu’s far-right government and its conduct of the war, he is a strong supporter of liberal Zionism. Kristof is critical of both Hamas and Likud and is seen as being sympathetic to Palestinian grievances while still committed to Israel’s legitimacy. Stephens, a former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post and defender of Israeli settlements in the West Bank, describes himself as “a stalwart defender” of Israel.
By virtue of the volume of their contributions alone, these writers played a significant role in shaping discourse in the New York Times opinion section. Despite their differences, it is a discourse that allows for criticism of Netanyahu’s policies but is generally committed to Israel.
The corpus also includes 339 contributions from guest authors, of which 45 are contributions from writers who are explicitly identified as Israelis or Israel-based (excluding one author who is identified as a Palestinian citizen of Israel), and 19 contributions from writers who are identified as Palestinians or based in Gaza or the West Bank or East Jerusalem.
While nationality is not a reliable indicator of political position, the disparity suggests that Israeli perspectives were afforded substantially greater visibility than Palestinian ones.
Conclusion: What Drives the Change in Discourse?
While the analysis shows that the tone of New York Times Opinion articles shifted over time to become, within limits, more sympathetic to Palestinians and more critical of Israel, an important question remains: what drove this change, and should we expect it to last?
One possible factor is the degree of domestic support enjoyed by the Israeli leadership. The growing criticism of Netanyahu and his government in the spring of 2024 articles coincided with a decline in his popularity inside Israel, suggesting that the domestic legitimacy of an Israeli government may influence how readily American opinion writers criticize it.
Relations between the Israeli and American governments also appear to affect the tone of coverage. Tensions between Netanyahu and the Biden administration coincided with stronger criticism of the Israeli government in the same period. This is perhaps unsurprising given the New York Times’ broadly liberal political orientation and its generally more sympathetic stance toward the Biden administration. Conversely, its critical stance toward Donald Trump appears to have carried over into its coverage of Netanyahu in the spring of 2025, as the two leaders grew increasingly politically aligned.
Furthermore, the tactics used by Israel may have also contributed to the shift in discourse. The harshest criticism of Israel was around its deliberate use of starvation as a weapon, particularly visible after March 2025 when it fully blocked all humanitarian aid deliveries to Gaza. While Israel-sympathetic writers could attempt to explain away the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinians in military strikes as unfortunate but necessary collateral damage, the starving of Gaza’s population may have been too cruel to stomach.
Underlying all these factors, however, was the sheer scale of destruction of Palestinian life and property. It is difficult to imagine that the discourse of unconditional support for Israel that prevailed in the immediate aftermath of October 7 could have remained unchanged as the subsequent genocide unfolded.
While the previous factors are connected to specific developments over the course of the two years of war, one further factor that may prove more enduring is the sharp decline in support for Israel among the American public. The above analysis does not examine the correlation between New York Times discourse and opinion polls, however, one can make the general observation that, although the Times’ discourse lagged behind and remained far more restrained than many voices critical of Israel in the United States, its general trajectory evolved in the same direction: toward rising sympathy for Palestinians and declining sympathy for Israel. Opinion polls indicate that this shift in public sentiment has persisted, and in some cases accelerated, beyond the period under study (2023–2025). This suggests that at least some of the changes in elite media discourse documented here may prove more lasting than transitory.
Additional contribution to research by Kawthar Ali, Marta M. Asencio, Hugo Bajas, Benjamin Fultz, Omnya Khalil and Alia Sabry

The Silent Battle in Ukraine: How Drug Resistant Infections Could Become a Global Threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:14:00 UTC
22:14:00 KST

On the front line, a Ukrainian soldier survives a drone strike. He, unlike so many Ukrainian soldiers since the full-scale invasion in 2022, survives the explosion. He survives the trench, and the days-long evacuation. He finally reaches a hospital where he should be able to breathe a sigh of relief. But instead of healing, he dies alone, in an overburdened hospital, from an infection that drugs can no longer fight.
This is the reality for some Ukrainian soldiers right now. While the world’s attention is focused on the front line, a silent battle is raging in the country’s hospitals: infections are becoming increasingly difficult to treat and people are losing limbs and dying unnecessary deaths.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In Ukraine today, unlike other recent wars in the 21st century, infections have days, weeks, and sometimes even months to spread. Many soldiers endure a long and complicated evacuation pathway – from point of injury to stabilization points to hospitals – where every transfer creates new risk of the infection spreading.
Ukrainian medical workers are operating under extraordinary circumstances. Every day they save lives in unimaginably stressful conditions. But they are also extraordinarily well-positioned to become leaders in fighting multi-drug resistant organisms, also known as MDROs.
Treating these recalcitrant infections requires more than developing new drugs. Ukraine needs to understand and contain them by learning how they emerge and how they move between patients and hospitals. That means funders and stakeholders investing in laboratory capacity, data collection systems, outbreak tracking, and improving complex wound management. Infection mitigation and management is one of the less visible needs created by the war. It doesn’t photograph well. And solutions aren’t simple. But it is crucial – not just for the patients surviving today, but for patients who haven’t been born yet, in hospitals nowhere near this war.
Why the Baltics Are Right to Worry About Putin’s Latest Reassurances
These infections can easily emerge in a hospital in Denmark, Germany, or even the United States. Resistant organisms are an immediate issue in Ukraine, but they’re by no means exclusively confined to its borders.
MDROs have long been a top priority of the World Health Organization and other global health organizations – it is not a new issue, but a crisis that experts have been warning about for years. No modern healthcare system has ever been forced to address wartime infections on such a scale, under such pressure, and in real time.
Acknowledging the problem creates an opportunity to solve it. We must see this hardship as a necessary way to save lives, and also a unique opportunity to transform medicine for the patients, doctors, and hospitals of tomorrow. The world will remember the drone strikes. It should also remember the infections that killed the soldiers who survived them. Ukraine didn’t have years to figure out drones. It won’t have years to figure this out either.

US-China: Carving up the World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:13:00 UTC
22:13:00 KST

The recent United Nations gathering showcased Donald Trump, who completely rejected the institution’s founding concept by suggesting he may “annihilate” Iran, keep Venezuela’s oil because “to the victor belong the spoils,” and then gloated about his security arrangement in Greenland.
Fortunately, he displayed a new, positive attitude toward Ukraine and its President Zelensky. This is because he likes winners, and Ukrainians are decimating Russia’s military and oil industry.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In his speech, he predicted that war will end “more quickly than people understand,” good news if true. But geopolitically speaking, the UN has become irrelevant and was overshadowed by a more consequential gathering that took place this week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Unlike the UN with all its flaws and complications, these two giants’ negotiations will shape the world order because of their unmatched economic, technological, and military leverage.
Washington rolls out the red carpet for China’s leader, starting with a state dinner for 125 that includes the first ladies and business leaders from both nations. Their last bilateral summit was in Beijing in May, when they agreed to establish a “Constructive Strategic and Stable Relationship” and concentrated on stabilizing trade relations.
Now on the table are: AI guardrails, Taiwan, Iran, impending sanctions on China’s purchases of Russian oil, North Korea, critical minerals, rare earths, semiconductors, a delayed $14-billion arms sale to Taiwan, and China’s commitments to buying American oil, agricultural products, and planes, notably 200 Boeing jets worth up to $19 billion.
Bipartisan Senators Urge Trump Not to Bring Putin to Miami
Both sides have plenty of economic and geopolitical leverage over one another, and here’s the state of play:
- China’s biggest bargaining chip is rare earths and critical minerals, which it controls globally in terms of production. These are essential to the manufacture of modern electronics, weaponry, defense systems, and clean energy systems, namely batteries and solar panels.
- China also has geopolitical “cards” because of its relationships with Iran and Russia. Americans and Europeans have been asking it to put pressure on both regimes to stop their hostilities, but unfortunately the leverage works in reverse. China is a big customer and supplier to both. Even so, Trump has lately pushed China more than once to use his leverage over Vladimir Putin. Xi publicly supports a “fair, lasting and binding peace agreement” and stated China’s readiness to promote this, but is against penalizing or coercing Moscow.
- On the other hand, America’s biggest bargaining chip is access to its gigantic market as well as to its advanced semiconductors and related technologies. China cannot afford to lose this and is aware that an angry Trump can deploy trade weapons such as tariffs, export bans, and restrictive legislation.
- America’s other leverage is that in May it delayed arms sales to Taiwan to please Beijing. In return, America was able to sell China more oil, defense, aviation, and farm products.
- According to a Chinese expert, Beijing recently gained leverage by cutting back on Russian and Iranian oil, which has kept prices (and US gasoline costs) down. “I see that restraint partly as a favour to Trump – reciprocity for Trump’s restraint on issues that Beijing cares about,” said the expert in The South China Morning Post. The quid pro quo Beijijng wants would be that the US president continues to put on hold arms sales to Taiwan. This wouldn’t be difficult, given the Pentagon’s weapons shortages because of the Iran war.
The two superpowers have opposite approaches and strategies when it comes to international diplomacy and nation-state relationships. Trump doesn’t want, or believe he needs, partnerships. As a result, he doesn’t work well with traditional allies in Europe and around the world. He pushes them around, belittles them, and makes one-sided demands.
“That came as a surprise… that has come as a profound opportunity for Beijing,” said Julian Gewirtz in Foreign Policy, who worked on China policy under President Joe Biden. Trump the politician is the same as Trump the businessman. He was always a sole proprietor and remains that way as President.
By contrast, Xi has been on a hectic “road show” for weeks in the lead-up to this summit, garnering attention, support, and making new alliances.
“Beijing can deepen and expand its influence across Eurasia and across the Global South, and can build institutions around its own priorities, and then arrive in Washington to have the American president throw him a lavish reception,” said Gewirtz.
In other words, Xi is a better “marketer,” crisscrossing the globe from Egypt to India and other countries that have been contested between the superpowers for years. Between his campaign and China’s Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing is beating Washington at the superpower game.
However, the most important issue is not popularity but how the world’s two technological superpowers will devise safety and monitoring systems to prevent “catastrophic misuse or loss of control” in the future.
Trump’s finance and China “expert,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, met for days with China’s vice premier before the summit to start the process of devising a system of goals, threat reduction measures, and setting up a hotline for crises.
Arguably, these are critical diplomatic discussions for humanity, and Trump, as usual, is not gracious or accommodating when it comes to AI. He recently told reporters: “We’re leading China in AI very substantially. By the way, we have the president of China coming on the 24th. That’ll be very exciting. Great, love to have him. A lot of good things to discuss, very, very productive things to discuss with President Xi.”
American and Chinese summitry ripples through the global economy and politics more than any negotiations or actions taken by the United Nations, with its cumbersome and useless rules and regulations.
All 193 UN members realize the organization no longer works but don’t know how to repair it. But in this session, Turkey’s President Erdogan called for the abolition of the veto power held by the five nations in the Security Council that created the organization: The US, UK, France, China, and Russia. This privilege has completely crippled the Security Council and the organization, preventing it from sending peacekeepers to regions to prevent full-scale wars, to stop fighting, or to save victims.
A case in point is that Ukraine this week asked the UN to intervene to save the lives of 2,000 Ukrainians held in a frontline city where Russia has blocked food, water, or aid. They will die without help, but their rescue by the UN won’t happen because Russia will veto it.
The organization is not only irrelevant but damaging unless reformed or replaced. The reality is that there are only two sheriffs “in town,” and neither one is worried about the rest.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine’s Drone Offensive Gives Kyiv a 3-to-1 Edge Over Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:12:00 UTC
22:12:00 KST

Ukraine has conducted approximately three times more long-range drone strikes against targets in Russia than the Kremlin has launched in the opposite direction over the past 100 days, according to a Kyiv Post analysis of open-source strike data.
The analysis found that even when Russia’s cruise, ballistic, hypersonic, and anti-ship missiles are included, the cumulative explosive payload delivered by Ukraine’s long-range drone campaign often matches, and at times exceeds, the total weight of warheads launched by Russia against Ukraine on a given night.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The study was based on open-source data tracking long-range strikes from the Ukrainian Air Force documenting Russian drones and missiles detected in Ukrainian airspace, alongside daily statements from Russia’s defense ministry reporting Ukrainian drones and missiles it claimed to have intercepted.
Those databases, to some degree, undercount strike-weapon totals for Russia as not all launched weapons are detected by Ukrainian air defenses. For Ukraine, even if all Russian shootdown claims are accurate, some Ukrainian drones and missiles are not stopped and go on to hit targets in Russia.
One problem with the Russian official data is that it is incomplete. On some days, Russia’s defense ministry publishes shootdown claims covering a full 24-hour period, while on others it reports figures for only 12 hours or less. Another challenge is the tendency to overcount. By the Kremlin’s own figures, Russia has destroyed 17,936 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), yet an independent Western analysis estimates that Ukraine has likely launched only about 4,620 UAVs at Russian.
Serbia Hopes for Gas Deal Extension After Vucic-Putin Call
Still, based on that imperfect but extensive dataset, one figure stands out. During the 100-day period from June 17 to Sept. 24, official Ukrainian data recorded the launch of around 16,000 Russian drones of various types against Ukraine. Kyiv Post estimates, assisted by AI analysis, suggest the actual number was likely closer to 16,200, though an exact total is impossible to determine.
Over the same three-month period, Russian defense ministry claims, compiled from daily reports published by state-run news agency RIA Novosti, indicated that Russian forces had shot down or otherwise neutralized between 48,000-55,000 Ukrainian long-range drones. Those figures suggest Ukraine was launching more than three times as many explosives-toting robot aircraft at targets in Russia compared to what Moscow was sending the other direction.
Records of peak long-range strike activity also point to a roughly 3-to-1 Ukrainian advantage in large-scale aerial attacks. During the past 100 days, Russia launched more than 400 drones against Ukraine on two occasions, July 2 and Sept. 12, and more than 250 drones on five occasions: Sept. 24, Sept. 23, Sept. 12, Aug. 29, and Aug. 27. Three of those attacks were directed at Kyiv, striking civilian homes and infrastructure in the capital, while two others hit railway, logistics, energy, and industrial targets across the country.
Based on Kremlin shootdown claims, Ukraine carried out drone attacks involving more than 1,000 aircraft on at least three occasions. The largest came on Aug. 19-20, when Russian authorities claimed to have destroyed 1,164 Ukrainian drones, the highest figure recorded during the period. Russia also reported intercepting that same amount during attacks on Aug. 17-18 and Aug. 15-16, with two additional large-scale strikes, on Aug. 18-19 and Sept. 22-23, involving more than 900 Ukrainian drones, per Russian claims.
Major Ukrainian drone raids have generally been broader in scope and less focused on harming civilians, as compared to Russian attacks. Instead, Ukrainian long-range strike aircraft have typically targeted Russian energy infrastructure, military manufacturing, military headquarters, and ammunition storage sites.
Direct comparisons of Russian and Ukrainian drone strike totals do not provide a complete picture of their impact or the damage inflicted. Russia, a nuclear power with one of the world’s oldest missile industries, regularly supplements its drone attacks with ballistic, cruise, hypersonic, and even anti-ship missiles launched against targets across Ukraine.
Ukraine, while owning a fairly advanced aerospace industry capable of building ballistic and cruise missiles throughout the war, has been unable to conduct large-scale missile strikes against Russia due to high costs and sustained attacks. Worse for the Ukrainians, stopping Russian ballistic missiles depends heavily on interceptor missiles controlled by the White House.
On July 2, Russia launched 496 drones and 74 missiles at Ukraine. Ukrainian air defenses shot down nearly 90% of the drones, but a number of missiles penetrated the defense shield, killing at least 30 people and damaging around 130 buildings in Kyiv. On July 6, Russia launched 23 ballistic missiles. None were intercepted, and at least 20 Ukrainians were killed, most of them when a ballistic missile strike caused the collapse of the apartment building where they lived.
During the first three weeks of September, Ukraine reported detecting 2,100 jet-powered drones and 136 missiles launched by Russian forces. Over the same period, civilian authorities recorded 288 deaths, most caused by weapons that Ukrainian air defenses had little or no ability to stop.That death and destruction notwithstanding, measured by the raw weight of warheads, the amount of explosives carried by Ukrainian drones into Russia is, on average, at least in part and probably greater than the amount of destructive force carried by Russian drones and missiles heading the other way.
Based on open-source descriptions of the types of drones spotted over Russia, and statements by Ukrainian military sources, a typical mix in a major Ukrainian one-night attack involving more than 1,000 aircraft would probably include 550-600 workhorse FP-1-type drones, each carrying a warhead of around 100 kilograms (220 pounds), 100-150 longer-range Sichen or Morok drones armed with lighter 30-40 kilogram (66-88 pound) warheads, and a similar number of jet-powered drones carrying similar payloads.
The total warhead weight of such a strike force, while hypothetical, would closely approximate that of actual large-scale Ukrainian drone attacks. Depending on the exact mix of aircraft and payloads, it could deliver between 55 and 75 tons of explosive warheads against targets in Russia. Actual components and warheads are not publicly disclosed.
In a maximum-effort Russian strike against Ukraine, there is better data and a number of well-documented examples. The Russian attack of July 29-30 included 74 missiles, among them 61 cruise missiles, nine ballistic missiles, and four anti-ship missiles, all carrying warheads in the 450-kilogram (992-pound) range. The missiles were accompanied by 284 drones, some armed with warheads weighing around 100 kilograms (220 pounds) and others operating as unarmed decoys designed to complicate Ukrainian air defenses.
A reasonable estimate of the total warhead weight delivered by those Russian missiles, in what was one of the largest missile attacks of the war, is around 38-40 tons of high explosives. Even if every accompanying Russian drone had also been armed with a warhead, and Russian strike tactics always employ decoys, the maximum additional warhead weight in the drones would have been 25-30 tons.
The outcome of that notional arithmetic is that, if total explosive payload delivered in a single maximum-effort raid is used as the benchmark, then Ukraine, despite lacking the capacity to manufacture cruise and ballistic missiles in large numbers, probably delivers more explosives to its targets in a peak attack than Russia does in a comparable strike, thanks to a 3-to-1 advantage in the number of drones Ukraine is typically able to launch.
A major qualification to that Ukrainian numerical advantage is that a single 450-kg (992-pound) missile warhead detonation will cause significantly more damage than three or four 100 kg (220 pound) drone warhead detonations. Because of its high speed, a ballistic missile can penetrate a target more deeply, with the explosion of its warhead taking place in a single location. This is a partial answer to the begged question of why Russian strikes against Ukraine seem so destructive: the missiles Russia is using, when and where they hit, are far more destructive individually.
However, quantity matters as well as quality in a large conventional war. Over the past three months, practically every Ukrainian strike has, according to open-source imagery and Kyiv Post’s daily tracking of those attacks, achieved at least some useful hits on Russian targets – roughly three times more often than Russia has managed against targets in Ukraine during the same period.

Artistic swimmers of team China greet the spectators after the mixed team acrobatic routine of Artistic Swimming at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Hamamatsu of Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan, Sept. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhou Mi)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- China made a strong start to the artistic swimming competition at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Saturday, ranking first in both the duet technical routine and mixed team acrobatic routine on the opening day.
The artistic swimming competition at the Games features two events -- duet and team. The former consists of technical and free routines, while the latter comprises acrobatic, technical and free routines.
In the duet technical routine, China's Lin Yanjun and Xu Huiyan performed "Warriors of moon shadow," incorporating elements of Chinese martial arts into their routine.
The pair brought the spirit of martial arts to the water, performing sharp kicks and dynamic movements in sync with the music. They scored 317.5108 points to take the lead, ahead of Japan's Moe Higa and Tomoka Sato on 309.8432 points.
"We performed quite steadily today and showed what we have practiced in training," Xu said after the event. "We hope to complete all the declared difficulty elements in the free routine and present what we want to express to everyone."
In the mixed team acrobatic routine, China performed "Soul of the Terracotta Army," a routine that previously won gold at the World Aquatics Artistic Swimming World Cup Super Final and the swimming worlds.
Dressed in armor-inspired costumes, the Chinese squad portrayed Terracotta Warriors in the water, showcasing a distinctive blend of strength and grace. They executed the routine smoothly to score 246.0977 points and rank first, while Japan finished second with 234.5992 points.
"Overall, we are quite satisfied with our performance today," said Chinese team captain Chang Hao. "The acrobatic routine is inherently full of uncertainty and risk. Unexpected situations and mistakes can also occur in training. Today's performance was probably our best-quality execution of this routine in recent times, so we brought our best form to the competition."
Head coach Zhang Xiaohuan also praised the team's performance. "The athletes performed well overall today. This was also the best I have seen them perform this routine," she said.
Zhang said that the new rules in artistic swimming have increased the uncertainty of competition, making it more important for China to focus on its own performance. "First of all, we need to execute our technical elements well. Only by doing our best, completing all the declared difficulty elements and then competing with our opponents can we do justice to all the effort and hard work we have put into our preparations," she added.
On Sunday, the duet event will award its gold medal after the free routine, while the team competition will feature the technical routine. ■

Palestinian election commission opens candidate registration for legislative elections

Unknown Publisher

21:08:41 CST
22:08:41 KST

RAMALLAH, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Palestinian Central Elections Commission (CEC) on Saturday opened registration for electoral lists seeking to participate in the upcoming legislative elections.
The CEC said in a press statement that it began accepting applications at 8:00 a.m. local time (0500 GMT) at its headquarters in Al-Bireh in the West Bank and its office in Deir al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip.
The registration period will last 12 days. The commission said a large number of electoral lists submitted applications on the first day in Ramallah and Deir al-Balah.
Under the applicable electoral law, candidates for the Legislative Council must run through electoral lists, and individual candidacies are not accepted. Each list must include between 16 and 132 candidates and meet the legal requirements for women's representation.
Applications must be submitted by the list's coordinator and authorized representative, along with all required forms, documents and supporting materials.
The CEC said all applications will be reviewed and verified to determine whether they meet the legal requirements, stressing that submitting an application does not constitute its acceptance or approval.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree in July setting Nov. 28 as the date for legislative elections, with presidential elections to be held in the first quarter of 2027.
Abbas had previously approved amendments to the electoral law, including increasing the number of seats in the Legislative Council to 200, lowering the minimum age for candidates to 23, increasing women's representation and requiring all candidates to recognize the Palestine Liberation Organization as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people.
The last Palestinian legislative elections were held in 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats in the Legislative Council. Subsequent tensions between Hamas and Fatah led to a political and geographical division between the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
In April, Palestinians voted in local elections in the West Bank and Deir al-Balah, marking the first voting process since the outbreak of the Gaza war in October 2023. ■

22:08:36 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Ahead of the 2026 Mid-Autumn Festival, dozens of residents from different ethnic groups in a Yinchuan community donned costumes featuring traditional paper-cutting designs and took to the runway for a festive celebration.
An ethnically diverse community in the capital of northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, Changcheng Huayuan is home to more than 19,000 residents, with members of 11 ethnic minority groups accounting for about 35 percent of the population.
In the living room of resident Zhao Shoucheng, who comes from a multi-ethnic family, two framed works hang prominently on the wall.
One is a photograph of President Xi Jinping's visit to the family home in June 2024, while the other is an ink painting of pomegranates, a fruit traditionally associated with unity and a flourishing family in Chinese culture.
On that summer day, Xi sat with the family beneath the pomegranates painting and chatted about their everyday lives, asking about everything from employment and income to medical insurance and education.
Xi also noticed that Zhao's grandson, then a fifth-grader, had finished first in his grade in a running event. He told the boy: "Children should attain a well-rounded development, with sound moral grounding, intellectual ability, physical vigor, aesthetic sensibility and work skills."
Over the years, Xi has set foot in a number of places inhabited by ethnic minority groups, discussed their development with national legislators and political advisors, and supported paired-assistance programs designed to help these less-developed regions catch up.
Backed by unprecedented support for infrastructure, industries, public services and more, all of the over 30 million people living in poverty in China's five autonomous regions of Inner Mongolia, Guangxi, Xizang, Ningxia and Xinjiang, as well as the three multi-ethnic provinces of Guizhou, Yunnan and Qinghai, had been lifted out of poverty by the end of 2020, along with the rest of the country.
This historic achievement embodied Xi's long-held conviction that "not a single ethnic group should be left behind" in China's efforts to build a moderately prosperous society in all respects.
The transformation of the Dulong people, with a population of just about 7,000, offers a vivid example. Mostly living deep in the mountains of southwest China's Yunnan Province, they endured generations of relative isolation and poverty, with rugged terrain making travel to the outside world a difficult undertaking.
Shortly before New Year's Day in 2014, residents of Gongshan County, home to most of the Dulong people, wrote to Xi to share the news that a highway tunnel through the Gaoligong Mountains was nearing completion. The tunnel promised to cut a journey that once took days to less than three hours.
During an inspection tour of Yunnan a year later, Xi met with the residents who had written to him, asking about the progress of the tunnel and changes in their lives.
"I'm here to encourage you to keep up the good work," Xi said, assuring them that the development of all ethnic groups was a matter of great importance to the central leadership.
Building on the gains of poverty elimination, Xi has pivoted to a broader vision -- common prosperity. For ethnic minority regions, this means advancing rural revitalization across the board, fostering coordinated regional development, and pursuing high-quality development in border areas.
In a village called Galai in the Xizang Autonomous Region in southwest China, locals have turned the annual peach blossom festival into a thriving tourist attraction with the support of a paired-assistance program involving south China's Guangdong Province. Notably, traditional folk customs like archery and horse riding, along with homestays, fruit-picking orchards and planting businesses, are helping to boost local incomes.
Five years ago, Xi visited this village located in the city of Nyingchi in Xizang, where he walked into the home of villager Dawa Gyaltsen and had a chat with his family.
Dawa Gyaltsen told Xi that the family had multiple sources of income, ranging from transportation services to tourism dividends generated by the peach blossom festival. "That adds up to several hundred thousand yuan -- a happy family indeed," Xi told the Tibetan villager.
Fueled by the "peach blossom economy," villagers in Galai now earn, on average, 20 times what they did at the beginning of the century.
Last year, Nyima Dorje, a village official, wrote a letter to Xi on behalf of the residents, detailing the latest changes in the village. Xi's reply delighted him. "I feel happy for you," Xi wrote back, encouraging the villagers to work together to safeguard ethnic unity and build happier, better lives.
To enhance law-based governance and promote unity and common prosperity among the country's 56 ethnic groups, Xi signed a presidential order promulgating the Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which took effect in July 2026.
The law designates the fourth week of September to highlight the promotion of unity and progress among ethnic groups. A range of activities have unfolded across the country to mark this occasion.
Xi has stressed the importance of ethnic unity and progress to realizing national rejuvenation, urging people of all ethnic groups to stay closely united like the seeds of a pomegranate.
First shared by a Uygur resident during his visit to Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, northwest China, more than a decade ago, this metaphor has since become a recurring theme in Xi's remarks on ethnic unity.
At the square of the Changcheng Huayuan community, Xi shared his view with residents who had gathered to greet him: "The 56 ethnic groups, united as one, form the community of the Chinese nation."
"Together, we will strive to advance Chinese modernization and realize the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation!" ■

ATHENS, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Six bodies have been recovered from the rubble of a building in central Athens, where a powerful explosion caused part of the building to collapse on Friday, Greek state broadcaster ERT reported Saturday.

The six bodies are believed to be those of four U.S. nationals staying in a first-floor short-term rental and an elderly Greek woman and her British husband who lived on the second floor, according to ERT.

Asian Games | China secures table tennis mixed doubles top two, Japanese star Harimoto suffers shock exit

Sun Yingsha of China hits a return during the women's singles quarterfinal match of table tennis against Joo Cheonhui of South Korea at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Toyota of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Sept. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Cheong Kam Ka)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Lin Shidong and Kuai Man defeated fellow Chinese pair Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha 4-0 in the table tennis mixed doubles final at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games to win gold on Saturday.
Lin and Kuai won the first three games 11-9, 13-11 and 11-9 before recovering from a six-point deficit in the fourth to win 11-9 and complete the sweep.
"Actually, I had just finished the singles match, I was still in the rhythm of competition, so I probably didn't even need to prepare and could just go straight into the match," Lin said.
"We just fought for every point and kept battling. The match was very intense for both of us, so it wasn't easy to come away with the win," he added.
South Korea's Lim Jong-hoon and Shin Yu-bin, and India's Manush Shah and Diya Chitale, shared the bronze medals.
In the men's singles, the day's major upset went to Japan's star player Tomokazu Harimoto, ranked fourth in the world, who lost 4-3 to Iran's Noshad Alamiyan, ranked 344th, in the quarterfinal.
"If you only look at the content of the match, I think you can say it was almost a complete defeat. The only game I really played well and managed to win was probably the third," Harimoto said. "There were many reasons, but in competitive sport, the result is everything. I didn't win a medal, so I didn't win a medal. That's it."
Harimoto's 19-year-old teammate Sora Matsushima also lost in the quarterfinal, falling 4-2 to China's Lin. Japan was therefore eliminated from the men's singles competition.
In the semifinals, Wang will face Alamiyan, while Lin will take on Chinese Taipei's Lin Yun-ju.
In the women's singles, China's Sun and other leading players advanced to the semifinals. Sunday's semifinals will see Sun meet Japan's Hina Hayata, while China's Wang Manyu will encounter Japan's Miwa Harimoto.
In the women's doubles, China's Kuai Man and Wang Manyu defeated Japan's Miyu Nagasaki and Rin Mende 3-0 to reach the semifinal. Japan's Miwa Harimoto and Hina Hayata advanced with a 3-0 win over China's Fan Shuhan and Chen Yi.
In the men's doubles, China's Lin Shidong and Huang Youzheng will play against Japan's Tomokazu Harimoto and Hiroto Shinozuka on Sunday. The other semifinal will also be a China-Japan match-up, with Japan's Sora Matsushima and Shunsuke Togami taking on China's Wen Ruibo and Xiang Peng. ■

China consistently, firmly supports UN: VP
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
21:08:04 CST
22:08:04 KST

Chinese Vice President Han Zheng meets with UN General Assembly (UNGA) President Khalilur Rahman on the sidelines of the 81st UNGA session in New York, Sept. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Pang Xinglei)
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice President Han Zheng said Friday that China has consistently and firmly supported the United Nations (UN).
At a meeting with UN General Assembly (UNGA) President Khalilur Rahman in New York on the sidelines of the 81st UNGA session, Han congratulated Rahman on assuming the presidency.
In September 2025, Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed the Global Governance Initiative, sending a clear signal of China's firm commitment to safeguarding the authority and central role of the UN, Han said, adding that the initiative has been welcomed and supported by nearly 160 countries and international organizations.
The UNGA is the most representative deliberative and policymaking organ of the UN, as well as a key platform for upholding multilateralism and promoting global governance, Han said, adding that China will continue to support the work of the UNGA and its president.
Noting this year marks the 55th anniversary of the restoration of the lawful seat of the People's Republic of China at the UN, Han said that China-UN cooperation will embrace broader prospects from this new starting point.
China advocates for advancing UN reform and increasing its efficiency to better adapt to the changing times, Han said. China also supports making sustainable development a priority of the 81st UNGA session and delivering more inclusive development outcomes in response to the aspirations of people around the world, he said.
The one-China principle is the political foundation of China-UN cooperation, Han said, expressing his belief that the UNGA president and the assembly will continue to uphold the principle.
Rahman said that China is an important partner of the UN, thanking China for its support for the work of the UNGA.
At a time when unilateralism is prevalent, China has remained committed to multilateralism and put forward positive proposals for addressing challenges facing world peace, security and development, he said.
The four global initiatives proposed by Xi are closely aligned with the six priorities of the 81st UNGA session, Rahman said.
The UNGA president said he looks forward to maintaining close communication and coordination with China, deepening cooperation, and jointly promoting the cause of world peace and development.
He stressed that the UNGA will firmly adhere to the one-China principle. ■

Taiwan plans to procure 200 additional anti-ship missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:06:25 UTC
22:06:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of National Defense plans to procure an additional 200 anti-ship missiles from the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, reports said Saturday.
A budget of NT$22 billion (US$693.38 million) will launch the project next year for an eight-year period, per Liberty Times. The contract will cover upgraded versions of the Hsiung Feng II and Hsiung Feng III missiles.
Taiwan was already planning a total of more than 1,400 anti-ship missiles, including US-made land-based Harpoon systems. However, the military reasoned that in the face of China’s rapidly expanding and modernizing navy, the original plan was not ambitious enough, Liberty Times reported.
The new missiles will include the latest semiconductors allowing the systems to counter electronic jamming by China’s newest ships and amphibious vehicles and reach their intended targets.
The extra missiles would also help avoid the risk of depletion as shown by the wars in Ukraine and Iran. The likelihood existed that some missiles would be destroyed by the enemy, while each enemy ship would need to be hit by two to four missiles to guarantee its sinking, the report said. In this scenario, the 200 new missiles could serve as a backup.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:03:45 UTC
22:03:45 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has said that war criminals belong in courtrooms rather than at the UN rostrum, stressing that those committing genocide must be held accountable.
"War criminals belong not at the UN rostrum but in courtrooms where they will answer for the crimes they have committed and the blood they have shed," Erdogan said at the closing programme of the 21st MUSIAD EXPO International Trade Fair and 29th International Business Forum in Istanbul on Saturday.
"If those committing genocide are not held accountable before justice and history, the same atrocities will happen again," he warned.
Erdogan reiterated Türkiye's support for Palestinians, saying, "The Palestinian people are not alone or abandoned.”
“Our sisters and brothers in Gaza are not alone in their quest for rights and justice," he stressed.
"We will continue, to the best of our ability, to tell the truth and be the voice of the oppressed," he added.
Erdogan praised those who walked out of the UN General Assembly when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech began.
“The UN General Assembly responded to genocide perpetrators by walking out of the hall," he said.
Erdogan further said the region is experiencing a "full-blown storm of crises", while the global system is facing an impasse in terms of "legitimacy, representation and justice".
Turning to the economy, he said Türkiye has recorded uninterrupted growth for the past 24 quarters and is currently the world's 16th-largest and Europe's sixth-largest economy.
He added that the number of Turkish exporting companies increased from 33,000 in 2002 to 168,000 in 2025.
"With the new Medium-Term Programme we announced 20 days ago, we will continue resolutely in line with our sustainable and balanced growth targets," Erdogan said.

Belgium Contracts Specialized Drones and Boats for Ukrainian De-Mining Efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:02:57 UTC
22:02:57 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Belgium Contracts Specialized Drones and Boats for Ukrainian De-Mining Efforts
Belgium has ordered three specialized TRIDENT vessels designated for launching K-STER C underwater mine-countermeasure drones for Ukraine, according to Militarnyi on September 25.
The Belgian Ministry of Defense allocated €9.9 million ($11.3 million) for the procurement, with the contract officially awarded to Exail Robotics Belgium through a negotiated procedure without prior publication.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The TRIDENT (Tactical RHIB for Identification and Disposal of Explosive Naval Threats) serves as a tactical craft designed to locate and eliminate explosive naval hazards.
Manufactured by Belgian company Exail, the K-STER C is a lightweight underwater drone designed to destroy mines using a shaped charge integrated into its forward section.
Its swiveling warhead allows precise targeting of various submerged explosive devices, while its construction incorporates stealth technologies to minimize acoustic and magnetic signatures.
The device measures 1,500 mm in length, 445 mm in height, and weighs 55 kg in air. The head can tilt and rotate from +90° to −90°, enabling operators to neutralize targets from optimal angles.
Powered by a lithium-ion battery, the propulsion system relies on two horizontal and two vertical thrusters. It features a dual-frequency sonar for long-range detection and close-range targeting, along with a day/night camera and searchlight.
The drone operates autonomously for up to one hour, reaches top speeds of 5 knots (with operational speeds ranging from 0 to 3 knots), functions at depths down to 300 meters, and maintains an operational radius of up to 1,500 meters.
On June 18, 2026, Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken outlined new plans for the delivery of F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine, announcing an increase in both the number and operational status of aircraft to be transferred. Speaking to journalists ahead of the NATO Defense Ministers Meeting, Francken said Belgium had revised its earlier commitments and would provide more F-16s than previously pledged.

Ukraine streamlines permits for foreign service members
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
14:00:25 BST
22:00:25 KST

Ukraine has issued new guidance intended to make it easier for foreign nationals and stateless people serving under contract to obtain temporary residence permits, with military units taking on more of the administrative work involved in preparing applications, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
The guidance sets out how commanders and designated officers should manage the process, from checking how long an individual is legally entitled to remain in Ukraine to preparing documents, arranging appointments with the State Migration Service and collecting completed permits. The intention is to reduce the amount of time foreign service members spend away from duty dealing with paperwork themselves.
Deputy Defence Minister Liubov Halan said: “The guidelines draw on the best practices of units that have already set up the processing of temporary residence permits this way. The unit organises the preparation of the documents and the appointment, while the service member provides the documents that only they hold and goes through the necessary procedures in person. This cuts the administrative burden on the individual and the time they have to be taken away from duty.”
Under the process, a designated officer within each unit will maintain a list of foreign service members, check when contracts were signed and whether the individual already holds documentation confirming lawful residence, then identify which cases need to be handled first. The unit prepares the documents it can issue itself, checks the wider application package with the migration authorities and arranges the in-person appointment. Service members need attend only where their presence is required, including for photographs, biometric data and signatures.
The guidance also covers cases where normal travel is difficult. If a service member is in hospital and cannot attend a State Migration Service office, the unit can arrange for a mobile team to visit. Where combat tasks or the security situation prevent travel, the designated officer can apply for an extension to the individual’s lawful stay and arrange submission once movement can be undertaken safely.
The rules implement Law No. 4730-IX, which came into force on 10 May 2026 and requires foreign nationals and stateless persons serving under contract in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, National Guard or State Special Transport Service to obtain a temporary residence permit. The permit is valid for the duration of the service contract and, in most cases, for a further six months after it ends.
Those who signed contracts before 10 May 2026 and do not yet have a permit or other document confirming lawful residence must apply by 10 November 2026. Until then, their military registration document or service ID is sufficient to confirm lawful stay. For those who joined on or after 10 May, the filing deadline depends on when they entered Ukraine and how long they are otherwise entitled to remain in the country.
The State Migration Service is expected to issue a permit within 15 working days after accepting the documents, with the completed document collected in person by the service member. The new guidance follows earlier Ukrainian measures intended to standardise support for foreign volunteers serving in the country’s defence forces.

Large analysis connects specific personality traits to problematic internet pornography use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:00:12 UTC
22:00:12 KST

People who exhibit high levels of impulsivity, sexual compulsivity, and neuroticism are more likely to struggle with problematic internet pornography consumption, according to a recent review of past research. The large analysis also found that traits like conscientiousness and self-control correspond with lower rates of pornography use overall. The findings were published in the journal Communication Research.
Internet pornography is widely accessible and highly popular, with many adults consuming it for leisure, curiosity, or to enhance intimate relationships. While this consumption is casual for most viewers, a subset of people develop what psychologists call problematic use. This pattern of behavior is characterized by emotional distress, feelings of addiction, and negative impacts on a person’s daily life or relationships.
Understanding what drives someone toward problematic consumption can help clinicians identify at-risk individuals and design better treatment protocols. Mehdi Akbari, a clinical psychologist at Kharazmi University in Iran, led a team to investigate how various psychological profiles correspond with different viewing habits. The researchers aggregated data from dozens of past studies to paint a detailed picture of the psychological vulnerabilities associated with unregulated viewing.
Akbari and his colleagues conducted a meta-analysis, a statistical technique that combines the results of multiple independent studies to identify broad trends. They searched academic databases for previous research measuring internet pornography use alongside personality traits or relationship attachment styles. Attachment styles refer to how people emotionally bond with others, often categorized as secure, anxious, or avoidant.
The final analysis included 51 studies published between 2005 and 2024. These studies encompassed a large sample of 45,808 participants from various countries, with an average age of 38. The researchers divided the data into two categories based on how the original studies measured viewing habits: general internet pornography use and problematic internet pornography use.
The strongest psychological correlate across all the data was sexual compulsivity, which is defined as an intrusive, repetitive urge to engage in sexual behaviors. People scoring high in sexual compulsivity were heavily represented among those reporting problematic pornography habits. Impulsivity, or the tendency to act without planning or considering long-term consequences, showed the second strongest positive link to problematic consumption.
The researchers also found positive correlations between overall pornography use and traits like sensation-seeking and narcissism. Sensation-seeking involves a desire for novel and varied experiences, which the internet’s endless supply of adult content easily fulfills. Narcissism, which involves excessive self-focus and a desire for idealized experiences, might draw individuals to the highly curated and flawless sexual scenarios frequently depicted in commercial pornography.
The analysis also evaluated the “Big Five” personality traits, a standard psychological model that measures extraversion, agreeableness, openness, conscientiousness, and neuroticism. Neuroticism, which involves a tendency to experience negative emotions like anxiety and sadness, was positively correlated with both general and problematic pornography use. People with high neuroticism might turn to online sexual content as a coping mechanism to manage or escape their emotional distress.
Two other Big Five traits, extraversion and openness, were positively correlated with general pornography consumption. Extraversion measures a person’s sociability and preference for stimulation, while openness reflects curiosity and a willingness to try new things. Individuals high in these traits might be more inclined to explore diverse digital environments, though these specific measurements were not statistically significant in their relation to problematic or addictive viewing patterns.
Conversely, the analysis revealed that conscientiousness and self-control correspond with lower pornography consumption. Conscientiousness involves being goal-oriented, organized, and capable of delaying gratification. Individuals with high scores in these areas reported lower levels of both general and problematic viewing, suggesting that self-discipline acts as a protective buffer against developing behavioral addictions.
Agreeableness, a trait characterized by a cooperative and harmonious disposition toward others, was also linked to lower overall consumption. The researchers noted that highly agreeable people often maintain successful interpersonal relationships offline. This real-world social success might make them less likely to use online activities as a compensatory strategy for loneliness or unmet psychological needs.
When examining attachment styles, the team found a positive link between anxious attachment and problematic pornography use. Anxiously attached individuals tend to worry about being rejected or abandoned by their romantic partners. The researchers suggested that these individuals might prefer pornography because it provides sexual stimulation without the risk of interpersonal rejection.
The research team tested whether demographic factors like age and gender altered the strength of these psychological correlations. Although pornography consumption is generally higher among men than women, the statistical links between specific personality traits and viewing habits remained consistent regardless of gender. The associations also held steady across different age groups, indicating that these psychological vulnerabilities operate similarly in both young adults and older populations.
Because the analysis relies on observational data, the results only show correlations and cannot prove that certain personality traits cause problematic pornography use. It is possible that the relationship works in the opposite direction, where excessive viewing alters a person’s self-control or heightens their neuroticism over time. Both factors could also be driven by an unmeasured third variable, such as an underlying mood disorder or an environmental stressor.
Many of the included studies relied on participants from Western, industrialized nations, meaning the results might not perfectly reflect the habits of a global population. The researchers also noted that differing definitions of internet pornography across the original 51 studies made it difficult to establish perfectly uniform measurements. Small sample sizes for some specific traits, like the relationship between narcissism and problematic use, prevented the team from running deeper statistical comparisons.
Future investigations will need to look at specific clinical populations and explore how different genres of pornography interact with individual psychological differences. Tracking these viewing habits over a longer period would help clarify how specific personality traits influence digital media consumption as people age. In the meantime, clinical psychologists can use these behavioral profiles to better support individuals struggling with unregulated digital habits.
The study, “Personality, Attachment, and Pornography: A Meta-Analysis,” was authored by Mehdi Akbari, Shiva Jamshidi, Zahra Sadat Hosseini, Sonay Sheikhi, Rezvaneh Asadi Asadabad, Mahshid Zamani, and Paul J. Wright.

Thousands protest government in Madrid over Ceuta migrant crisis

Ceuta, a Spanish territory located in North Africa, has been embroiled in a humanitarian crisis since more than 70,000 migrants arrived from neighbouring Morocco on July 30 and 31.
Most returned in the following hours, but thousands have remained for weeks, many sleeping on the streets, straining the small city's resources and creating a political crisis for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
The protest was organised by right-leaning civil society platform Sociedad Civil Espanola and backed by the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox.
The central government's representative in Madrid put the turnout at around 20,000. The organisers of the protest said 180,000 participated.
A manifesto issued by the group called for an early general election by November 15, the return to Morocco of all migrants who entered Ceuta and for Sanchez to be tried for "treason".
"There is clear negligence," the PP's parliamentary spokesman Miguel Tellado told reporters at the demonstration, adding that "the majority of Spaniards are calling for an election now".
The next general election in Spain is due by August 2027.
The government plans to approve a decree at its Cabinet meeting on Tuesday to accelerate the return of migrants from Ceuta to Morocco, daily newspaper El País reported on Saturday.
The measure would shorten the time allowed to decide asylum applications and limit applicants' ability to remain in Spain while their cases are being considered, the report said.
But Vox leader Santiago Abascal said: "No one can trust this government to do anything."
"This government has done nothing throughout this time," he told reporters at the protest when asked about the report.
The government has increased capacity at temporary migrant shelters in Ceuta, deployed hundreds of police officers and soldiers and boosted funding for the territory's government.
But local groups and opposition parties say those measures fall short of what is needed to resolve the crisis.
