Your worldview might dictate how you perceive neutral faces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
11:00:11 UTC
20:00:11 KST

People who view the world as an inherently dangerous place consistently overestimate the likelihood of specific threats, from violent crimes to animal attacks. A new series of psychological evaluations reveals that this broad worldview also leads individuals to perceive the neutral faces of strangers as less trustworthy and more aggressive. The findings were published in the Journal of Individual Differences.
Psychologists categorize the fundamental ways people perceive their environment into a framework called primal world beliefs. These primal beliefs represent 26 broad dimensions that describe how an individual interprets reality, such as seeing the world as beautiful, abundant, or just. These beliefs cluster into four higher-order categories, one of which involves viewing reality as generally safe versus generally dangerous.
Researchers Nicholas C. G. Kerry and Jeremy D. W. Clifton wanted to understand how a generalized belief about danger influences the way people react to specific, everyday situations. Prior research has established that individuals who believe the world is inherently just will often perceive specific situations, like a workplace or a sports game, as fairer. Kerry and Clifton aimed to test if a similar pattern exists for dangerous world beliefs.
The researchers designed four studies to see whether individuals who see reality as generally threatening consistently overestimate objective physical risks and view unknown people with heightened suspicion. They wanted to determine if holding a broad belief that the world is dangerous translates to overestimating specific, proximate threats. They also sought to rule out alternative explanations, such as the possibility that clinical anxiety or underlying personality traits drive these threat perceptions.
In the first study, the researchers recruited 457 American adults through an online platform. Participants completed a survey measuring their primal world beliefs and then estimated the statistical frequency of 12 real-world dangers in the United States, such as the rate of murders, assaults, and bear attacks. The researchers also measured the participants’ personality traits and recent symptoms of anxiety and depression.
The researchers found that participants with a high dangerous world belief overestimated the prevalence of these specific threats at much higher rates than those with a low dangerous world belief. On average, individuals in the highest quintile for dangerous world beliefs estimated the incidence of these events to be more than four times higher than individuals in the lowest quintile. This broad belief predicted risk estimates better than a person’s underlying anxiety, depression, or general personality traits.
The second study expanded on these results to see if this heightened perception of risk applied to diseases and positive events. The researchers surveyed 881 American adults, asking them to estimate the likelihood of physical dangers, health risks like strokes or infectious illnesses, and positive events like winning money. Participants were randomly assigned to estimate these probabilities for themselves or for the average American.
Individuals with a strong dangerous world belief consistently predicted higher risks for physical dangers, just as they did in the first study. They showed only a weak tendency to overestimate health and disease risks, and they did not overestimate the likelihood of positive or neutral events. The results were similar whether participants estimated risks for themselves or for others, indicating a generalized pattern of threat perception rather than a specific personal fear.
For the third study, the researchers tested how dangerous world beliefs influence the perception of novel social situations. A group of 599 American adults viewed photographs of Caucasian strangers with neutral facial expressions. The participants rated the faces on various emotional and behavioral traits, including warmth, trustworthiness, and the likelihood that the person might commit a crime.
As part of the third study’s design, participants were randomly assigned to a threat condition or a control condition. In the threat condition, the photographs were accompanied by text claiming the person in the image had committed a crime. The researchers wanted to see if contextual cues would interact with dangerous world beliefs to amplify threat appraisals.
Participants who viewed the world as a dangerous place rated the neutral faces as less trustworthy, less warm, and less happy. They also perceived the strangers as more aggressive and more likely to pose a threat to society. The contextual manipulation of telling participants that the targets were criminals did not result in a statistically significant interaction with dangerous world beliefs. Once again, the participants’ generalized belief about the world predicted negative social evaluations better than their reported levels of anxiety or depression.
The fourth study sought to replicate the facial evaluation findings across different racial groups. The researchers recruited 979 American adults, evenly split between Black and White participants, who evaluated a series of neutral Black and White faces. The survey structure mirrored the previous experiment, focusing on traits like trustworthiness and perceived threat.
The evaluations matched the previous results, with dangerous world belief heavily associated with seeing societal threat and crime risk in the neutral faces. It was also linked to lower ratings of trust and warmth. In some instances, the association between dangerous world beliefs and evaluations of traits like warmth and happiness was stronger among Black participants than White participants, regardless of the target’s race.
While these four studies demonstrate a strong link between generalized worldviews and specific threat appraisals, the researchers noted several caveats. The data are cross-sectional and rely on surveys taken at a single point in time. Because of this, it is not possible to prove that holding a dangerous world belief directly causes someone to overestimate risks. It remains possible that an unknown third variable drives both the broad belief and the specific threat perceptions.
Another caveat is that the effects were observed in relatively ambiguous scenarios, such as guessing statistics or judging the faces of complete strangers. A person’s generalized belief about danger might not influence their judgment in environments that provide distinct safety cues, established relationships, or readily accessible facts. The researchers also found no evidence that dangerous world beliefs actually correlated with an individual’s history of participating in real-world risky behaviors, such as extreme sports or high-risk investments.
Future research will need to explore how these generalized beliefs might influence high-stakes professional decision-making. Medical professionals who view the world as highly dangerous might make different judgments regarding treatments than those who see the world as safe. Similarly, judges or jurors with high dangerous world beliefs might evaluate criminal sentencing in a more risk-averse manner.
Psychologists also hope to design experiments that attempt to alter a person’s primal world beliefs. If behavioral interventions can successfully change a person’s overarching worldview, scientists could test whether that shift leads to a lasting reduction in how they perceive everyday threats.
The study, “From Bear Attacks to Neutral Faces: Dangerous World Belief Predicts Specific Appraisals of Threat,” was authored by Nicholas C. G. Kerry and Jeremy D. W. Clifton.

====================================================================================================

K-pop, BTS, and What the Grammys Get Wrong About Asian Music
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
11:00:05 UTC
20:00:05 KST

In 2009, I moved to Middletown, Conn. from Seoul, South Korea to study ethnomusicology. At the time, I admittedly did not listen to K-pop, seeing it as largely teen pop, though I would soon realize how limited my view was. Over the next decade, as the genre became increasingly visible in the United States, it reshaped not only how American audiences encountered Korean popular music, but also how I understood its global significance.
That shift is still unfolding, and recent events have raised new questions about how K-pop is categorized and recognized within the American music industry. Those questions came into particularly sharp relief early this summer, when the Recording Academy announced a new category, Best Asian Pop Music Performance, for the 2027 Grammy Awards. In response, the world’s biggest boy band, BTS, announced that they would not submit their music for Grammy consideration.
The decision sparked heated debates among K-pop fans around the world, some of whom feared that the new category would sideline Asian artists by placing them in a separate “Asian Pop” category while reducing their chances of recognition in the Grammys’ prestigious General Fields awards.
Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. clarified that “The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity, and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia,” and that submitting music in a genre category would not exclude an artist from also submitting and being considered for Record of the Year, Album of the Year, and Song of the Year.
This controversy raises important questions. Is a category like “Best Asian Pop Music Performance” necessary? Does it risk creating a new form of segregation? Or can it provide greater visibility for Asian artists in American mainstream media?
The United States’ influence on Korean popular music
The first music cassette tape that I bought as a Korean kid living in Seoul in the 1990s was Mariah Carey’s compilation album, #1’s. Well into the 2000s, listening to Western pop was considered “cool” in South Korea. Koreans certainly listened to gayo, or Korean popular music, although Western pop often carried a different kind of cultural prestige. Western pop was typically described as more “intellectual,” “authentic,” and “meaningful.” Radio DJs and music critics did not hesitate to encourage young Koreans to listen to more Western pop rather than gayo.
The cultural hierarchy between Western and Korean popular music was shaped by South Korea’s postwar political and military relationship with the United States. South Korea’s commercial recording industry began to take shape in the early 20th century through the activities of Japanese and American record companies. Following liberation from Japanese colonial rule from 1910 to 1945, and the division of the peninsula, South Korea came increasingly under U.S. political and military influence.
In the years following the Korean War in the 1950s, the Eighth U.S. Army shows became an important site for the development of South Korean popular music, employing hundreds of Korean entertainers to perform American popular music and other forms of entertainment for U.S. soldiers. Korean performers would listen to the American Forces Korea Network (AFKN), transcribe music they heard on the radio, and memorize the latest American songs for performances at military bases.
For decades afterward, imported albums, AFKN, and MTV remained important sources through which Korean musicians and audiences encountered new musical trends from the United States.
U.S. military, media, and commercial networks became powerful channels through which American popular music entered South Korea and shaped the development of its contemporary popular music industry. Indeed, American pop was long considered more prestigious and trendier than Korean pop—until K-pop began to command international recognition of its own.
The K-pop universe
K-pop refers primarily to music performed by artists known as “idols,” whose careers are developed and managed by entertainment companies. This integrated system was first established in 1995 by Lee Soo Man, founder and producer of SM Entertainment, to bring artist recruitment, talent management, and music and visual production under one roof. Inspired by Motown’s Fordist model of music production and Japan’s idol industry, Lee developed a cultural industry in which idols could grow into professional artists and, eventually, entrepreneurs themselves.
Shortly after I moved to the U.S., I began encountering more and more American fans who asked me if I knew acts like Girls’ Generation or BIGBANG. These fans introduced me to the world of K-pop, and I gradually stopped listening to American pop. Around the same time, Korean music critics lamented that younger Koreans were no longer listening to Western pop as they once had. Perhaps I was not the only one.
Over the last decade, I have met hundreds of American K-pop fans as a K-pop ethnographer. My first question is always the same: “Why do you like K-pop?” The question carries an assumption: “If K-pop is merely a copy of American pop, as some critics dismissively claim, why listen to the replica rather than the original?”
Their responses were surprisingly similar, as if they had compared notes. K-pop was “magical” and “catchy,” while American pop was “boring” and “always the same.” According to these fans, while American pop stars sang “too much about sex, drugs, and parties,” K-pop offered “dreams, fantasies, and self-growth,” often through elaborate alternative “universes” in which idols developed distinct personas and narratives.
This idea of “universe” was first systematically introduced to K-pop in 2012, when SM Entertainment debuted EXO as extraterrestrial beings from “EXO Planet,” each endowed with a supernatural power. Since then, world-building has become increasingly intertwined with K-pop’s integration of music, dance, costume, stage design, fashion, beauty, digital media, and more recently, virtual idols and AI production, making K-pop an increasingly audiovisual, narrative, and participatory cultural form for audiences worldwide.
Parallel to the fantasy world presented on stage and through mass media, entertainment companies—especially those with smaller budgets and limited access to traditional media networks—began to use online platforms to communicate with fans by revealing more down-to-earth, behind-the-scenes moments. BTS became one of the most prominent examples through its YouTube series BANGTAN BOMB, which captured offstage moments that portrayed the members as humble, playful, and hardworking. Fans, in turn, voluntarily created subtitles in multiple languages, helping introduce BTS to international audiences and expand its global fanbase.
Few popular music industries have institutionalized fan participation as intensively as K-pop. Idol groups compete against one another every week on televised music chart shows, relying heavily on various forms of fan labor, including album purchases, song and music video streaming, and fan voting.
K-pop fans have developed highly coordinated strategies to influence chart performance, spending considerable time, energy, and money to push their favorite idols’ new releases to the top. The scale of this participation can be striking: In 2023, 19 of the top 20 albums on IFPI’s Global Album Sales Chart—which measures physical album sales and full-album downloads worldwide—were by South Korean acts. This collective fandom power became especially visible in 2017, when BTS won Billboard’s Top Social Artist award, a fan-voted prize that helped propel the group into the center of American mainstream attention—a kind of “fan-forced entry” into the American market, as ARMYs sometimes jokingly put it. BTS went on to win the award five consecutive times, from 2017 to 2021, until the category was discontinued the following year.
K-pop’s power in the modern music landscape
Today, people no longer rely on MTV to learn about new releases. Nor do they simply listen to music. They actively seek out new music on platforms such as Spotify and YouTube and participate in fan discussions on X and TikTok. Fans also use these platforms to pressure media and entertainment companies through organized protests, boycotts, and coordinated online campaigns.
Fan power certainly existed in the old media era, but digital media has made it more immediate, visible, and able to reach beyond the boundaries of individual fandoms. Organized fan communities directly influence entertainment companies’ decisions. This means that media industries—including the American music and entertainment industries, which have long served as powerful gatekeepers in the global music market—may not exercise the same degree of control over which artists gain visibility and recognition.
Why, then, is BTS refusing to submit its music for Grammy consideration? The Recording Academy presents Best Asian Pop Music Performance as a genre category determined by musical style, yet its eligibility rules make language a crucial condition of entry.
The Academy states, “The musical style is determinative of eligibility, not the ethnicity or nationality of the performer(s).” Yet it also requires that “an Asian language should play a significant role within the song,” while “incidental or minimal use of an Asian language” does not qualify. A recording performed entirely in English is therefore ineligible for the category. The Academy also prohibits artists from entering different language versions of the same recording in separate performance categories.
For K-pop artists who often release both Korean- and English-language versions of the same song, submitting the English version in another performance category means they cannot separately submit the Korean version for Best Asian Pop Music Performance.
This creates a dilemma. An English-language recording cannot qualify as Asian Pop, while recordings primarily performed in Asian languages have historically had little presence among the Grammy General Field winners.
But before considering this dilemma, a more fundamental question arises: If eligibility is determined by musical style, what does language have to do with it? Why should a K-pop act’s music be labeled “Asian” on the basis of language—and if a recording is performed entirely in English, does it somehow cease to be “Asian pop”? More importantly, why must Asian artists prove their Asianness, rather than simply being recognized as individual musicians, as Western artists often are?
What is ‘Asian pop?’
This raises another question: What, exactly, constitutes “Asianness” in music? K-pop, J-pop, and C-pop, for instance, are only a few of the many musical cultures that may be grouped under the label “Asian,” yet they use different languages and emerge from distinct musical industries and cultural histories. On what musical grounds, then, are they grouped together under a single category called “Asian Pop”?
BTS’s decision not to submit its music for Grammy consideration was a bold one. At the same time, the group can afford to say no. We now live in a world where BTS can walk away from the Grammys and filmmaker Bong Joon Ho can famously call the Oscars “very local.” Artists like BTS can turn instead to other mainstream platforms and reach audiences around the world. The Grammys remain prestigious, but they are no longer the only institution capable of conferring global recognition.
Other K-pop acts will likely continue to submit their work to the Grammys’ Asian Pop category, but not necessarily in pursuit of the symbolic recognition historically attached to the award. They may instead regard it as one among many opportunities for media exposure and broader audience reach.
This leaves us with one last lingering question: Can every “Asian” musician afford to say no to the Grammys? BTS can walk away and still remain mainstream artists in South Korea, receiving recognition through platforms such as the Melon Music Awards and MAMA Awards. But what about Asian American musicians in the United States, for whom the American music industry is not a foreign market they can simply leave behind, but their own domestic mainstream?
The Recording Academy says it wants to celebrate an Asianness that is “widely recognized within Asian markets, including K-Pop, J-Pop, and C-Pop.” But where, then, does that leave Asian American artists whose music may be rooted in the United States rather than in an “Asian market”? For them, the United States is not a foreign market, but home.
The larger question, then, is whether “Asian” can meaningfully function as a cultural category. The Grammys have bet that it will.
My concern is that this framing threatens to collapse distinct cultures into one. A label as broad as “Asian” does not by itself imply a shared language, culture, or musical tradition. Pop music may be more global than ever, but not every artist gets to be just pop.

When the referee fumbles: Election Commission row explained in 7 key questions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
10:57:20 UTC
19:57:20 KST

The CEC can have a distinct role within the institution, but the law does not provide for a system in which the CEC's view automatically prevails over the other two commissioners.
NEW DELHI: Elections are, by their very nature, a contest.Political parties fight for ground, candidates wage fierce campaigns and voters ultimately decide whom to trust with their mandate.Through it all, the Election Commission is meant to stand apart and monitor the process. Its role is to frame the rules, enforce them fairly and ensure that the contest remains even-handed.Yet, in recent days, the spotlight has moved away from those fighting the election and towards the institution meant to referee it.The players are no longer the only ones under scrutiny. Increasingly, the referee itself has become the subject of the debate.A report in The Indian Express claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi repeatedly raised objections with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over decisions and communications that they said were issued without their knowledge or approval.The Election Commission has rejected the suggestion that the episode points to a breakdown in its functioning. It has maintained that differences of opinion are a normal part of institutional deliberation and that all final decisions of the Commission have been unanimous.
That leaves a larger constitutional question at the heart of the controversy: how is India's election watchdog actually supposed to function?Is the Chief Election Commissioner the boss of the Election Commission, or simply the first among three equals? What happens when the three commissioners disagree? And why has the law governing their appointment become a subject of such intense controversy?
What triggered the latest EC controversy?
On September 23, The Indian Express reported that Sandhu and Joshi had, on multiple occasions, objected to decisions and communications they said were taken or issued without their prior knowledge.According to the report, the two commissioners recorded such objections on at least 14 occasions over the past 10 months.The issues reportedly ranged from changes to electoral forms and access to the voter database to the allocation of work within the Commission and the filing of appeals involving electoral rolls.The report has since triggered a wider debate over whether the Election Commission's three members are exercising their powers collectively, as the law envisages, or whether the CEC has acquired a greater role in practice.
What did the two ECs object to?
According to the Indian Express report, the concerns raised by Sandhu and Joshi covered several aspects of the Commission's functioning.
Changes to Form 6: The two commissioners reportedly objected to changes made to Form 6, the application citizens use to register as new electors, without following due process. In May, Joshi warned that the form could not be altered without an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. On August 13, Sandhu reportedly described the change as "unauthorised and illegal" and called for its immediate removal.
Access to electoral roll data: The commissioners also reportedly raised concerns about whether statutory authorities responsible for maintaining electoral rolls had complete access to voter data on the ERONet portal. Joshi flagged what he described as the "gradual centralisation of the electoral roll database" and proposed an audit to establish that only authorised officials had credentials to modify voter data. Sandhu, separately, recorded that state-level election officials had complained of not having "proper and complete access" to ERONet. He also questioned whether the Commission's director general of IT, Seema Khanna, had the legal authority to restrict access for statutory officials such as Electoral Registration Officers.
Reasons for objection by the other two election commissioners over the decision taken by CEC Gyanesh Kumar
Changes in work allocation: Joshi and Sandhu reportedly wrote separately to the cabinet secretary objecting to changes in the allocation of work that removed a layer of oversight over the Commission's IT infrastructure. They said the changes had been made without their knowledge.
West Bengal SIR appeals: During the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in West Bengal, the Election Commission filed around 16.10 lakh appeals involving voters whose names judicial officers had added. The appeals were heard by tribunals headed by retired high court judges appointed by the Supreme Court. According to the report, neither the two election commissioners nor West Bengal's chief electoral officer were informed about the basis or process for filing these appeals.
Restoration of voters in Goa: Another concern reportedly involved 97 eligible voters whose names had to be restored to Goa's electoral rolls. Despite repeated requests from Electoral Registration Officers, the voters could not initially be restored because the ECI's software did not have an option for reinstatement.
Communications issued in the ECI's name: The two commissioners also reportedly objected to communications being issued in the Election Commission's name without what they considered to be the Commission's full approval. They cited Article 324 of the Constitution as well as the 2023 law governing the poll panel.
Taken together, the reported objections raise a question that goes beyond any individual decision: how does a three-member constitutional body exercise collective authority when its members do not initially agree?
What did the Election Commission say?
The Election Commission strongly rejected the suggestion that its internal differences amount to a breakdown in decision-making, and added that all official orders and administrative directions had been issued unanimously."Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the ECI said in a statement."In recent months, the Commission has taken numerous decisions, issued instructions, introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms, including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year," the poll body added.It also criticised the media report, saying that highlighting specific internal notes over a period of 10 months gives only one part of the picture."Highlighting certain specific internal notes/observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives give only one part of the picture," it said.
The Election Commission stated that internal disagreements and suggestions from officers were a routine part of its decision-making process before reaching a final verdict.
The disagreement, therefore, is not simply over whether commissioners have expressed reservations. It is over what those reservations mean for the functioning of the institution as a whole.
CEC or ECs: Who has the final say?
This is where the 2023 law becomes important.Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, provides that the Commission may, by unanimous decision, regulate how its business is conducted and allocate work among the CEC and the other Election Commissioners.It also says that, as far as possible, the Commission's business should be transacted unanimously.But it makes an important provision for situations in which consensus is not possible.
The opposition objected over the 2023 EC law alleging that the panel arrangement is made to 'favour' the government in power
If the CEC and the other Election Commissioners differ on a matter, the issue is to be decided according to the opinion of the majority.In other words, the statutory framework does not make the CEC an executive superior to the other two commissioners. The three constitute the Commission collectively, while the CEC is the "first among equals".The CEC can have a distinct role within the institution, but the law does not provide for a system in which the CEC's view automatically prevails over the other two commissioners.Where the three disagree, the majority view is the deciding view.The controversy now centres on whether some of the decisions cited in the recent report were, in practice, implemented despite objections from the other two commissioners, and if so, how that squares with the statutory scheme governing the Commission's decision-making.
Why is the 2023 EC law controversial?
The current controversy also brings back an older and deeper question: Who should appoint the people who conduct India's elections?In March 2023, the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament had not yet enacted a law governing appointments to the Election Commission, despite Article 324 of the Constitution envisaging such a framework.Until Parliament enacted such a law, a Constitution bench prescribed an interim selection mechanism comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India.The court stressed that an independent Election Commission was essential for democracy and observed that those entrusted with conducting elections must be insulated from executive influence.
The Constitution outlines the removal guidelines for the CEC and details about the conditions of service as a CEC
Parliament subsequently enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.But the new law changed the composition of the selection committee.Instead of the Chief Justice of India, it provided for a Union Cabinet minister nominated by the Prime Minister. The committee therefore consists of the Prime Minister, a Union minister nominated by him and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.The opposition has alleged that the 2023 Act gives the executive “overwhelming” control over the appointment of Election Commissioners. The government, meanwhile, has defended the law and its institutional framework.
Matter in Supreme Court
The dispute has now reached the Supreme Court, where a challenge to the validity of the appointment law produced a split verdict.A two-judge SC bench differed over whether the matter should immediately be referred to a Constitution bench. Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma disagreed on that question, although both agreed that the matter should ultimately be placed before the Chief Justice of India for consideration by a larger bench.
Section 18 of the CEC and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, outlines that the EC should ideally conduct business unanimously, but allows a majority opinion to decide matters when members disagree.
They also agreed that sending the case first to a three-judge bench would be of "little worth" and could further delay a final determination of the constitutional questions involved. The matter is likely to be heard by a 5-judge bench soon.The issue is vital as it extends beyond the current dispute inside the Election Commission. It touches a larger institutional question: How independent should the body conducting India's elections be from the executive, and what safeguards should govern the appointment of those who head it?
Can a CEC actually be removed?
The latest controversy has also acquired a political dimension, with opposition parties preparing fresh notices seeking the removal of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.According to media reports, the notices, being drafted and vetted by experts, are expected to be submitted in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha next week. The proposed notices are expected to include issues raised in the Indian Express report.This would not be the opposition's first attempt.On April 7, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairperson CP Radhakrishnan rejected an earlier notice seeking Kumar's removal. That notice had been signed by 130 Lok Sabha members and 63 Rajya Sabha members and alleged partisanship and arbitrariness in the conduct of the SIR exercise.
The CEC can be removed by the same procedure as a Supreme Court judge and requires a majority vote from both the Houses.
Separately, a notice submitted by 73 opposition MPs in the Rajya Sabha on April 24 seeking Kumar's removal remains pending in the Upper House.But removing a CEC is deliberately difficult.Article 324(5) of the Constitution provides that the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only "in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court".The same protection is incorporated into Section 11(2) of the 2023 Act.The other Election Commissioners enjoy a different safeguard: they cannot be removed from office except on the recommendation of the CEC.The higher threshold for removing a CEC is intended to protect the office from arbitrary or politically motivated removal.
What does it take to remove a CEC?
The removal process is rooted in the constitutional procedure applicable to Supreme Court judges.Article 124(4) of the Constitution, which lays down the procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge, states that a judge can be removed only by an order of the President following an address by each House of Parliament.Such an address must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of at least two-thirds of members present and voting, in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.The process begins with a notice of motion in either House of Parliament alleging misbehaviour or incapacity. The notice must be signed by at least 100 MPs in the Lok Sabha or 50 MPs in the Rajya Sabha.The presiding officer of the concerned House can admit or refuse the motion after considering the material and information available. If the motion is admitted, an inquiry is conducted into the charges by a committee constituted for the purpose.If the charges are established, the motion must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in both Houses.Once both Houses pass the motion in accordance with these requirements, an address is made to the President, who then issues the order removing the CEC.The President's role at this stage is constitutional and formal once Parliament has passed the required address.
How the EC evolved
The current structure of the Election Commission is itself the product of an institutional evolution.When the ECI was established in 1950, it was a single-member body, with the Chief Election Commissioner as its sole member.It became a three-member body for the first time in 1989, but that arrangement was short-lived. In January 1990, the VP Singh government reverted the Commission to a single-member structure.The system changed again in October 1993, when the PV Narasimha Rao government appointed MS Gill and GVG Krishnamurthy as Election Commissioners alongside CEC TN Seshan.Seshan challenged the appointments in the Supreme Court, arguing that the addition of commissioners diluted the authority of the CEC.In its 1995 judgment, a Constitution bench upheld the multi-member structure.The court made clear that the CEC was not institutionally superior to the other Election Commissioners. The three were intended to function collectively, with differences being resolved through the decision-making mechanism of the Commission.That judgment established the broad institutional framework that exists today.
The big picture
The Election Commission is not designed as a hierarchy in which one person commands and two others merely assist. Nor is it simply three independent offices operating in parallel. It is a constitutional body meant to function collectively.The law provides for unanimity where possible and a majority where consensus fails.The CEC occupies the position of first among equals, rather than that of a superior authority.The significance of the current controversy, therefore, lies not merely in the existence of disagreements within the Commission. Differences are inevitable in any institution exercising such enormous constitutional responsibility.The larger question is what happens after those differences arise: whether they remain part of an internal deliberative process, as the ECI maintains, or whether they reflect a deeper dispute over how collective authority is being exercised.
The credibility of an election does not rest only on the final tally of votes.It also rests on whether voters believe that the rules were applied fairly, the institutions enforcing them remained above the contest and the process was conducted without favour or hidden influence.The Election Commission, therefore, carries a burden that goes beyond administering polls: it must command confidence across the political spectrum and among voters themselves. Any perception that the referee is divided, opaque or partisan can cast a shadow over the process, even when the electoral machinery continues to function formally within the law.In the end, public trust is not built merely by declaring an election free and fair; it is built by ensuring that voters have little reason to doubt that verdict.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Sukkot 2026: Faith and prayer can protect us, but Israel still needs a strong IDF - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
10:53:10 UTC
19:53:10 KST

Even as our heads spin from a dizzying array of consecutive holidays, the parade of crises focusing on the IDF marches on and on.
The latest (at least of this writing) is the fallout from the dastardly film, NAZA (a title loved by global Jew-haters because it sounds so much like the monsters they think we are).
Wanna get your movie in an avant-garde film festival, be hailed as a hero, and snatch a ton of moola to boot? Just trash Israel and catalogue/concoct our atrocities, while studiously avoiding any mention of the other side’s abhorrent sins.
Before this story broke, there was the hullabaloo over who knew what, and when did they know it, on Oct. 7. Did the prime minister oversleep, or was he purposely not woken up when the fighting began? Did Yair Golan really rush to Gaza and slay several of the terrorists, and if so, how did he get there so fast? And will there ever be – now three years and counting – an independent investigation into what actually happened on that dark day?
The balagan that is known as Israeli elections
Not to mention the balagan that is known as Israeli elections, where the central issue this year – once again – is who must serve in the armed forces, and for how long.
And the deepest point of turmoil, from my religious perspective, is the ongoing debate as to who is the guardian of Israel and its citizens. Whom do we depend on for our safety: our military, or our Maker?
Sources abound on both sides. King David’s 121st Psalm flatly proclaims that “God is our guardian,” yet David himself was a brilliant military strategist who finally overcame the Jebusites and conquered Jerusalem. Our recent Torah portion of Ha’azinu portrays God as “an eagle hovering above, carrying us, His young, to safety,” and our daily prayers proclaim that “God is a Man of War, God is His name.”
But at the same time, the Torah includes extensive censuses specifically of those who were eligible for military service, starting at age 20. And while Deuteronomy 20 lists those who are exempt from military service, Torah study is pointedly not one of those exemptions.
And this is just for optional wars, such as wars of expansion. For obligatory wars, the well-known source in Sotah 44b rules that even a groom is taken from his wedding to fight; and according to Maimonides (Melachim 5:1), a defensive war is in the category of an obligatory war.
As we all know, the religious-Zionist community subscribes to both opinions, representing the best of both worlds. These young men (and an increasing number of young women) combine Torah study with military service through a multitude of programs for both Israelis and foreign lone soldiers. They have served with amazing distinction, suffering an inordinate, even excessive number of deaths and injuries in defense of this country.
IT SEEMS to me that Sukkot sends a clear message on this very same subject.
The Talmud in tractate Sukkah discusses a difference of opinion as to why we build a sukkah and dwell in it for a week.
Rabbi Eliezer says the sukkot mimic the real booths, or huts, in which the Israelites lived in the desert during their 40-year journey to Israel. The desert can be a brutal environment, with burning heat and intense cold, sandstorms, and dangerous snakes and scorpions as daily threats. And so each family had to build their own sukkah to protect themselves from the elements.
Rabbi Akiva – though himself one of the principal leaders of the ill-fated armed rebellion against the Romans – has a very different viewpoint. He maintains that the “booths” described in the Torah were actually miraculous, Heaven-sent clouds that enveloped us and shielded us from harm as we traveled. We build the sukkah merely to represent the impenetrable safety that God provided then and always.
Sukkot accentuates the metaphysical and the spiritual
One sage emphasizes the Heavens and Divine protection. The other stresses Earth and the need to use our resources to secure our safety.
This same dichotomy accompanies the ritual acts of Sukkot.
On the one hand, this festival requires us to touch the physical. With our own hands, we build a sukkah, one that must be walled and may not be open to the sky. We grasp the Four Species, waving the lulav (palm branch) and smelling the etrog (citron). We acknowledge our dependence on water in the Simchat Beit Hashoeva ceremony, even as we thank God for this life-giving necessity.
Yet Sukkot also accentuates the metaphysical, when we sing the Hallel’s praises of God, when we nightly “invite” invisible biblical heroes into our sukkot, and when we daily march in the synagogue around a Torah scroll as we chant, “Hoshana; Save us, our Creator; save us, our Redeemer.”
Both sides get equal representation, as they should.
Living in two worlds
IN OUR history, we have been blessed with unique individuals who were able to live, and live beautifully, in two distinct worlds.
David Ben-Gurion, our first prime minister, often quoted the Tanach, which he studied extensively. Yigal Yadin, Israel’s second IDF chief of staff, who excavated Masada, was a brilliant biblical scholar.
At the same time, MK Avraham Verdiger, who studied at the Mir Yeshiva and served as general secretary of Poalei Agudat Yisrael, fought in the 1948 War of Independence and actively worked to promote haredi integration into both the workforce and the military.
MK Avraham Ravitz, longtime chairman of Degel HaTorah, joined the Lehi (Stern Group) pre-state underground movement in 1947 at just 13, enlisted in the newly formed IDF in 1948, and fought throughout the war. His wife, Avigail, once told me how proud he was of his military service.
These are the kind of heroes – lovers of Heaven and Earth – that I will be thinking of both on Sukkot and when I cast my ballot in the coming election. They are the best – and we deserve the best.
Chag Sameach to all.■

An unexpected welcome: Syrian Kurds return to their homes in Afrin
Syrian Kurds who were forced to flee their homes in Afrin in 2018 are beginning to return home.
Afrin, Syria – When Dilshad Hamdo walked into the home his father built 30 years ago, there was no place to sit. The stone walls were intact, but the rooms had been stripped bare. Yet, standing in the empty space, there was still a strong sense of relief at being back home.
“I have a lot of memories in this house with my extended family. There is nothing like the house and the land,” Hamdo told Al Jazeera.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Syria’s president appoints ex-commander of Kurdish-led SDF as advisor
- list 2 of 4As SDF disband in Syria, Kurds ponder how to secure their rights
- list 3 of 4Syria abolishes al-Assad-era ‘terrorism’ court as Kurdish tensions flare
- list 4 of 4Syrian army offensive overjoys some, leaves others with ‘existential’ fear
Hamdo fled Afrin as a young man in early 2018, during a Turkish-led military offensive, dubbed “Operation Olive Branch”, against the Kurdish-dominated People’s Protection Units (YPG) of the Syrian Democratic Forces.
In the ensuing chaos, tens of thousands of Syrian Kurds were displaced. Vacant properties across Afrin were soon occupied by other displaced Syrians, most of them Arabs fleeing the intense Syrian government bombardments of opposition areas in Homs and Damascus.
For the Hamdos, exile meant drifting ever eastwards – from Aleppo to Raqqa of Syria, and finally to a camp for the displaced in Qamishli.
“We heard that there are people returning to Afrin, and that there is registration in order to return,” Hamdo recalled. “We told them we want to return to our land. We cannot live here. Because a person can only rest in his house and his land, and we suffered greatly outside our land.”
Following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Syria’s newly formed transitional government announced it would facilitate the safe return of those who had fled Afrin in 2018.
Internal security forces assisted the return of hundreds of Syrian Kurdish families from Hasakah to Afrin in April and May.
Hamdo’s father travelled ahead to check on their property, only to find a displaced family from Homs living inside. Rather than a confrontation, the encounter between the two displaced families ended in a quiet negotiation.
“The people who were living in our house asked for a period of several months until they left. After several months, we paid them 300 American dollars so they would leave the house, travel money so they could return to Homs, and we got our house,” he said.
“After Syria was liberated, we wanted to return to our land. We do not see any distinction between the Arab and the Kurd, and all of us are one people. And we only want peace and safety.”
Rebuilding trust
The transitional government in Damascus is heavily promoting the return of families such as the Hamdos.
Khayro Dawood, the director of the Afrin region, said the state’s priority is to “completely stop the Syrian bleeding” by reaching out to those languishing in camps.
“The state was trying to understand and to receive with an open heart,” Dawood told Al Jazeera, describing government delegations sent to camps in the northeast. “Our visit to the Hasakah region gave a positive impression in the hearts of the people there … and this visit had a positive result in rebuilding trust anew.”
What started as a trial run of 400 families has grown into a wave of roughly 12,000 families returning to Afrin via state-organised convoys.
Dawood pointed to the implementation of Decree 13 – a transitional law recognising the cultural and political rights of Syria’s Kurdish community – as proof of a new era between Arabs and Kurds in Syria.
‘A house for human beings’
But government decrees offer little comfort to those returning to homes that lie in ruins.
Zeina Sido boarded one of the recent state-sponsored convoys back to Afrin. “It was a wonderful feeling when they told us, ‘Pack your belongings; you will return to your homes,'” she recalled. “Their treatment was excellent.”
That joy vanished the moment she arrived at her property. Her four-room house had been gutted, looted, and repurposed.
“We went and saw our house completely destroyed,” Sido said. “We found it had turned into a house for sheep. This house was for a human being and it should not turn into a house for animals. Did they not take into consideration that the people of these houses would return to them?”
With no money to rebuild, Sido now lives in a nearby displacement camp – a facility recently vacated by those fleeing the former regime, which is now filling up again with Afrin’s native residents.
“Every time we are able to establish something, we are forced into displacement and we repeat the cycle,” she said,
While Sido has bitter feelings about returning home to find nothing as it was, being surrounded by the wreckage of her old life, she refuses to leave the region again.
“My wish is that we establish our family in our house and in our land, and this is a beautiful feeling that we are able to do that,” Sido said. “I still have hope to do that. Were it not for hope, we would not have been able to return here in the first place.”

2 American tourists dead after building explosion in Greece

4 American tourists dead after building explosion and collapse in Athens
Four Americans were among the six people who died after an explosion and building collapse in Athens' tourist district of Plaka near the Acropolis on Friday, officials said.
A U.S. State Department spokesperson confirmed to CBS News on Saturday that their deaths were a result of a gas explosion.
"I am deeply saddened to learn of the death of four American citizens in yesterday's explosion in central Athens," Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to the Hellenic Republic, said on X.
"I extend my deepest appreciation to the Greek first responders who worked tirelessly at the scene. The U.S. Embassy is providing consular assistance and support to the victims' families."
The two other people killed were an elderly British man and his Greek wife who lived on the second floor of the three-story building, Greece's state broadcaster ERT reported.
The American family of four had been renting an apartment on the first floor and were preparing to go to the airport hours later Friday for their return to the United States when the blast occurred, according to the Kathimerini newspaper.
The explosion brought down the residential building and damaged properties and vehicles along the street. Two other women were injured from an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, fire brigades said, according to the Associated Press.
The New York Times reported that the U.S. family was composed of a couple, their son and his girlfriend. Greek authorities did not immediately give their identities, ages or where in the U.S. they came from.
On Saturday, AFP reporters saw mechanical diggers moving debris at the site and thermal-imaging cameras deployed.
"We are talking about an incredible disaster," Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said.
Two nearby buildings were left in a dangerous state, he added, with inspections underway "to determine if they can remain standing or if they also have to be demolished."
The owner of the ground-floor apartment, Mathaios Artavanis, told the Kathimerini daily he was absent at the time of the blast. He said he had tried afterward to contact the U.K.-Greek couple who lived there, without success.
Video footage from the scene showed rubble strewn across the street, with parked cars smashed by falling debris. The people rescued by the fire department from the adjacent building were all tourists, resident Andreas Martzaklis said.
The pastor of a nearby church said this Sunday's service would be held outdoors because of damage to the church.
A year ago, locals in the Plaka neighborhood had warned the city and utility companies about the risk of gas leaks or short circuits, according to a letter by the residents' association published by Kathimerini.
The residents had urged a fire drill to identify possible weaknesses in the emergency response plans for the district.
A citizens' group said on social media that one resident in the street where the explosion happened had alerted authorities after smelling a possible gas leak.
The neighborhood is one of Athens' most popular tourist areas. The nearby Acropolis, one of Greece's best-known landmarks, welcomed 4.6 million visitors last year.

British tourist sparks backlash with Auschwitz cafe rant (VIDEO)
A British tourist has drawn widespread online backlash after a viral TikTok video complaining about drink prices and menu options at a cafe near the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial and Museum in Poland, the site of a former Nazi death camp.
At least 1.1 million people were murdered by Nazis at Auschwitz between 1940 and 1945, most of them Jews. Other victims included Poles, Roma and Soviet prisoners of war. Many were murdered in gas chambers, while others died from starvation, disease, brutal forced labor and other forms of persecution. The museum explicitly requires visitors to behave with “due solemnity and respect” while visiting.
However, in a video posted on TikTok on Wednesday and captioned “Prices at Auschwitz,” a woman named Lynne and her daughter made flippant complaints about drinks at a cafe near the memorial.
“Here’s a tip if you’re going to Auschwitz,” Lynne tells followers, pronouncing it like “Oswitch,” before adding: “Take a drink with you. I got a strawberry smoothie which tasted very watered down.” The two then bemoan the lack of decaf and alternative milk and lemonade that tasted “a bit like Dettol,” a toilet cleaner. The pair also complain that the two drinks cost £9 ($12), calling the price “very expensive.”

A spokesman for the museum told The Times that the cafe is outside the visitor services center, independently operated, and displays its prices clearly.
“The essential point remains that people come to the Auschwitz Memorial to learn about the history of the German Nazi concentration and extermination camp, to confront the fate of its victims and to commemorate them,” the spokesman argued.
The museum repeatedly reminds visitors that Auschwitz is a memorial rather than a conventional tourist attraction, urging them to behave with respect and to avoid conduct that undermines the memory of its victims.
Still, it has faced controversies over visitors and businesses treating the site in ways critics regard as inappropriate. In 2020, a TikTok trend drew condemnation after users role-played as Holocaust victims. A year later, TripAdvisor removed an offensive review of Auschwitz after initially saying it complied with its guidelines. In 2023, an “Ice Love” ice-cream stand installed near the camp prompted another outcry.
Russian officials, meanwhile, have repeatedly accused Western countries of distorting the history of World War II, including diminishing the Soviet Union’s role in defeating Nazi Germany. Last month, Moscow condemned plans for a supermarket and logistics facility at the site of the former Hirtenberg women’s concentration camp in Austria, accusing Vienna of erasing the memory of its victims. South Korea's gender pay gap grows as women get older
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
10:44:00 UTC
19:44:00 KST

South Korea's gender pay gap grows as women get older
September 26, 2026
At 27, a woman in South Korea earns 8% less than male peers. By her late 50s, she earns 50% less. This is according to government wage data published in a recent Human Rights Watch (HRW) report.
South Korea is a global technology and industrial powerhouse, but its gender pay gap has remained the highest in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) since comparable records began in 1992.
"The gender division of labor inside the home leads directly to a gender division of labor in the labor market," Min Hee Kim, a Korean activist for women labor struggles, told DW.
The problem, she argues, is not simply that women are paid less than men. As women age, the kinds of work available to them narrows and the consequences of lower pay, career breaks and precarious jobs accumulate.
For the report, "Too Old and a Woman," HRW interviewed 41 South Korean women aged 28 to 87 about their working lives.
Structural barriers to women's careers
Discrimination has changed form rather than disappeared, Kim said. Until the 1980s, it was legal for employers to fire women simply for getting married, a practice known as "marriage-based dismissal," where employers assumed a married woman would soon leave to raise children anyway.
Today, "it is difficult to openly say, 'We won't hire you because you're a woman,'" Kim added. But caregiving responsibilities still fall on women, pushing them into lower-paid jobs when they try to return to work.
According to the HRW report, women's university attainment has passed men's since the 1980s. Higher education would suggest equal opportunity after graduation, but the job market says otherwise.
One year after graduating, women already earn 22% less than men, according to a 2024 study.
Many women told HRW that after leaving work for marriage or children, chances of returning to the workforce were limited to a handful of jobs such as call centers, cleaning or caregiving.
Women who opt to focus on their career told HRW they hit a glass ceiling at work. Women held 18% of manager jobs in 2024, and only five of 38 senior civil servants were women.
Wages peak and drop off
Women's wages peak in their late 30s and then steadily decline, according to Labor Ministry survey data cited by HRW.
South Korea's Gender Ministry told HRW that career interruptions, along with occupational segregation and discrimination within organizations, drive the gap.
J. Mi-sook, 53, told HRW that her three years of experience weren't recognized by her next employer, so she started at entry level on a lower salary.
The longer women spend outside the workforce, the less experience they accumulate on their resumes, which results in less pay and less work stability.
Kim pointed to structural discrimination, a concept from the report that HRW describes as discrimination so embedded in social practices and institutions that even the people harmed by it may not recognize it as a problem.
"When you are alone, it is easy to think, 'It's because I'm not capable enough,' or 'It's because I'm getting older,'" she said. It's only when women who've had similar experiences meet and talk, she added, that they realize, "this wasn't just my problem."
It gets harder as you get older
Park Jae-soon, 61, was forced to retire at 60 from a utility company and now works part-time as a care worker. Her annual income fell from 55 million won ($40,500/€35,600) to 15.6 million won, a 72% drop.
HRW argues the mandatory retirement age and the "peak wage" system, which lets employers cut older workers' pay in the years before retirement, should both be abolished.
According to data cited in the report, women received 53% of men's National Old Age Pension on average in October 2025, a 47% gap.
"I think what is important here is that this is not simply a problem of middle-aged women having difficulty finding jobs," Kim said.
"The work that women have traditionally done inside the home, like cleaning, cooking, caregiving and managing other people's emotions, is classified as 'work suitable for women' when it enters the labor market, and then low wages are assigned to it," she added.
From first paycheck to pension
HRW argues the disadvantage builds stage by stage, from a woman's first paycheck up until her pension.
"Career interruption among women in their 30s is already a pension issue," Kim said. "Part-time work among women in their 40s is a pension issue, and low wages among women in their 50s are already a pension issue," she added.
South Korea's government has said it will pursue a phased increase in the statutory retirement age from 60 to 65.
"This cannot be solved with just one policy. Equal pay for equal work needs to be actually implemented, wage structures need to be transparent, and care needs to be treated as a public responsibility rather than something that is pushed onto individual families and women," Kim said.
The rights activist said the report is an important starting point, but believes its picture is incomplete.
Most interviewees were recruited through civic organizations and largely in Seoul, she noted, while disabled women, migrant workers and others may experience a different combination of age and gender discrimination.
"The important question is not simply, 'How much discrimination do women face?'" she said. "It is which women, in what positions, become increasingly distanced from which resources and rights as they grow older."

Zelenskyy confirms strike on plant in Russia's Rostov Oblast producing missile components – video
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian plant in Rostov Oblast where components for missiles and other weapons are produced. Ukraine's defence forces attacked the facility on the night of 25-26 September.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter); Security Service of Ukraine (SSU); Ukrainian Exilenova+ OSINT project
Details: Zelenskyy described the strike on the plant in Azov as one of "our warriors' long-range responses" to Russian attacks on civilians.
Quote from Zelenskyy: "Our long-range capabilities were also effective in Rostov Oblast: a plant supplying the occupiers with components for missiles and artillery, as well as a Pantsir-S2 system, was struck."
More details: Ukraine's military struck the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in the Russian city of Azov, SSU reported. The strike was carried out by personnel from the SSU's Special Group Alpha jointly with the Ukrainian Navy.
The plant was attacked using Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles as well as Ruta, Palianytsia and Bars jet-powered drone missiles.
Quote from SSU: "Early reports indicate that optical and foundry production facilities, an assembly section, an electroplating workshop and a printed circuit board production facility have been damaged."
More details: Earlier, analysts from a Ukrainian Exilenova+ OSINT project reported that explosions were recorded overnight in Azov, Rostov Oblast, and that the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant, which works for Russia's defence industry, had likely been targeted.
NASA's FIRMS satellite fire-monitoring system recorded a fire near the plant. Exilenova+ analysts also released footage showing the moment the facility in Azov was attacked.
Strike on plant in Azov/Exilenova+
The Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant is part of the Tactical Missiles Corporation. It manufactures electronic systems for high-precision artillery, missile and anti-tank weapons, radar homing heads for tactical guided missiles, airborne thermal imaging and heat-detection equipment,as well as optical-mechanical and optoelectronic products, according to Defence Intelligence of Ukraine's War&Sanctions database.
The plant in Rostov Oblast is subject to sanctions imposed by the United States, Canada, Switzerland, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Japan and Ukraine.
Background: On 25 September, Ukraine's defence forces struck three facilities in Russia's Ulyanovsk, Tula and Voronezh oblasts.

'Only those who elected us can dissolve us': J&amp;K dy CM on BJP's demand for Omar govt dismissal

Unknown Publisher

J&K deputy CM comments came a day after BJP MLAs, led by Sham Lal Sharma, demanded the immediate dismissal of the National Conference-led government.
NEW DELHI: Jammu and Kashmir deputy chief minister Surinder Choudhary hit out at the BJP over its demand for the dismissal of the Omar Abdullah-led government, saying any attempt to interfere with an elected government would amount to an assault on democracy and the Constitution.Choudhary made the remarks after reviewing the progress of ongoing work at the new legislative assembly complex in Jammu. His comments came a day after BJP MLAs, led by Sham Lal Sharma, demanded the immediate dismissal of the National Conference-led government.
Questioning the BJP's demand, Choudhary said the government had been elected by the people and asked what right the BJP had to seek its removal."If anyone can dissolve us, it is only those who elected us," Choudhary told reporters.He was responding to the BJP's criticism of the government after Chief Minister Omar Abdullah moved a resolution in the assembly demanding the restoration of full statehood to Jammu and Kashmir.
BJP accuses government of overstepping constitutional domain
Sharma had accused the National Conference government of attempting to revive an earlier political arrangement and challenge the constitutional framework.He alleged that the assembly resolution on statehood and related issues sought to revive matters linked to autonomy and the pre-1953 constitutional arrangement.
Reacting to the demand for the government's dismissal, Choudhary said, "...this means you want to resort to hooliganism and use force and coercion. That is exactly what we have been saying -- that the BJP resorts to such tactics."He added that any attempt by the BJP to interfere with the functioning of the Jammu and Kashmir government or "block our freedom would amount to an assault on democracy and the Constitution".Choudhary also accused the BJP of being "anti-democracy, anti-constitutional and anti-public", alleging that its actions and statements were against the interests of the people."When you oppose a government elected by the people, you are going against those who voted for it," he said, adding that such conduct amounted to "treason".
Deputy CM attacks BJP over assembly proceedings
Choudhary also criticised the BJP's conduct during the ongoing autumn session of the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly.He said the government wanted to focus on its work, while accusing the opposition party of prioritising political confrontation."They kept saying, we will corner them. But what did they actually corner? Instead, they themselves ended up in trouble after coming to the assembly," he said.Choudhary challenged the BJP to explain what it had done during the first three days of the session for the people."If the BJP is honest, let it tell us what work it has done in the last three days of the assembly session in the interest of the people," he said, accusing the party of carrying "bundles of lies".He alleged that the BJP had attempted to corner the government on social media but had failed to do so on the floor of the House, where issues could be debated through the constitutional process.
Statehood restoration remains key issue
On the demand for restoration of statehood, Choudhary said the absence of statehood had weakened the ability of ordinary people to have their grievances addressed.
He also accused the BJP of using police action against sections of society, including poor people, shopkeepers and journalists. He alleged that shops had been demolished and journalists who sought to publish reports critical of the government had faced pressure."If statehood is restored, I can say with confidence that these things will not continue," he said.Choudhary further alleged that journalists, employees, farmers and students were being prevented from speaking freely."If it were up to the BJP, they would impose Army rule across the entire country," he said, while alleging that the party's approach amounted to "hooliganism".

Meta’s Muse Is Adults-Only. Why Does It Look Like a Kids’ Toy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Meta’s Muse mascot is named Jolly. It's an adorable, cuddly representation of Meta’s AI agent that you can dress however you want—like a doll. At the company’s recent Meta Connect event, CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s furry Muse donned a toga and laurel wreath. In Instagram ads I saw for Muse, the mascot wore exercise gear and boasted about helping with my fitness goals. Later this year, Meta plans to sell a Tamagotchi-style device for your Muse character. It’s all very kawaii-coded.
Although Muse’s ability to complete digital tasks rocketed it to the top of the app charts, its Labubu-adjacent mascot latched this agent onto the cultural zeitgeist. Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, recently posted nonstop memes of Jolly, sometimes in suggestive situations. What remains perplexing to me is why a product for adults—Muse is restricted to those 18 and over—looks just like a well-designed children’s toy.
"This is a story in search of a story,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts tells WIRED. “People want to be able to create their own avatar with personality and unique style, because it's fun and brings them joy. We require everyone using the Muse app to provide their date of birth, we block people we detect may be under 18 from creating an account, and we do additional checks to help ensure people who say they're adults are actually over 18.”
Mona Sarantakos, vice president of Product Management at Meta Superintelligence Labs, describes the design process for Muse as leaning into “delightful” elements and meant to feel less awkward than chatting with “a corporate logo or entity," in a blog post she co-authored around Muse's release.
Youth advocates are already pushing back against Meta’s Muse mascot. “Oh my God, it looks like a Teletubby,” says Josh Golin, an executive director at Fairplay, a nonprofit that previously lobbied against Meta’s targeting of children. “It’s so clearly a character that would appeal to very young children,” he says. “People who study children’s media understand that those rounded shapes particularly appeal to kids in the preschool age.”
Jolly’s appeal is not limited to those in diapers. The adorable aesthetic of Muse’s mascot also draws me in, a 32-year-old man living in San Francisco. The branding may disarm people of all ages, especially since the backlash against Meta and generative AI continues to resonate with many Americans.
“These types of cute factors can make the product seem warm and less threatening,” says Julian De Freitas, an associate professor of marketing at Harvard who focuses on AI companions. “There’s a high bar that they have to overcome here, because attitudes toward Meta are quite negative after the social addiction rulings.” In August, Meta settled claims regarding social media addiction, agreeing to add restrictive features for teens on Instagram and Facebook as well as paying out up to $16.7 billion.
Some experts I spoke with were less convinced this design was meant to appeal to children, comparing Muse’s mascot to Japan’s long history of broadly relying on adorable characters to market technology. Meta’s approach is not unique either. From the annoying chirping of Microsoft’s Clippy to the more recent red-shelled OpenClaw lobster, AI assistants often revolve around anthropomorphized characters.
No matter your age, a cuddly creature representing an AI tool can be disarming, even to the point where you might forget about privacy concerns. For example, Meta trains its AI models on your Muse interactions unless you opt out.
“Design features like being cute and frictionless, or tapping into nostalgia for devices that didn’t constantly surveil and intervene in our lives, are sly ways to make people drop their guard, stop asking critical questions, and slip into being passive users,” says Jathan Sadowski, an associate professor with the Emerging Technologies Research Lab at Australia’s Monash University. “Agents like Muse are trying to convince us they’re just a cute little guy who lives in your pocket, and definitely not an always-open portal into the servers of a major surveillance company.” Research suggests that adopting AI agents could make you more passive.
Meta says it will release a “confidential” version of its virtual machine that helps power Muse later in 2026. This option could “cryptographically and verifiably prevent” Meta from accessing a user’s data.
Even so, a level of risk remains when adults decide to trust an AI agent, going beyond potential privacy concerns. Ryan Calo, a professor at the University of Washington and faculty cofounder of its Tech Policy Lab, compares using agents to hiring a tour guide when you’re on vacation. You’re relying on them as the intermediary between you and the experience, without necessarily knowing who they are getting kickbacks from and which restaurant the group is visiting only because the guide and the owners are friends.
As the holidays roll around soon and Meta launches Muse Charm, its Tamagotchi-like device, youth advocates are remaining on red alert.
“This really feels like a completely inappropriate attempt by Meta to get young kids hooked on Muse,” Golin says. “This is something that families should say no to, and I think it's something that regulators should take a hard look at.”
