Journalist Mariia Yizhvenko, 29, killed in Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:00:00 EEST
18:00:00 KST

Journalist Mariia Yizhvenko, 29, killed in Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre
Journalist Mariia Yizhvenko, 29, has been killed in a Russian strike on a business centre in Kyiv. She had only recently left NV Business, the business news section of a Ukrainian media holding company, and was planning to start a family with her husband.
Source: Mariia's husband, combat medic Danylo Yizhvenko; Mariia's former colleague Oleksandra Nekrashchuk
Details: Reporting Mariia's death, Danylo said the couple had had big plans for their future. At the end of last year, they took out a loan to buy an apartment and planned to start a family this winter.
About two weeks ago they bought Mariia a car so she could get around the city more easily with their future child. She had taken two driving lessons to refresh her skills.
"The car burned out, Masha was killed. I have lost my friend, my girlfriend, my wife, and the mother of my future children, who will now never be born," Danylo wrote.
"Masha was a wonderful, intelligent person who cared deeply about Ukraine. She was my voice of reason and the person who always showed me what true care looked like."
Oleksandra Nekrashchuk, deputy editor-in-chief of NV Business, said Mariia covered defence tech, Ukraine's IT sector and military technology. Several months ago, she left journalism to pursue a career in the corporate sector.
"She was not just a talented journalist but an incredible person – cheerful, intelligent and deeply thoughtful [...] She could explain the most complicated things simply and genuinely wanted to help her country. Her kindness and smile will remain in the memory of everyone who had the privilege of knowing her," Nekrashchuk added.
Danylo has set up a fundraiser for Mariia's funeral. He said any remaining money will go to the Ukrainian military. Mariia's family will announce the time and venue of the ceremony later.
Russian forces have attacked Ukraine with almost 300 attack drones of various types since the evening of 24 September, 267 of which were destroyed by Ukrainian air defence.
In Kyiv, a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the Pecherskyi district, killing a 14-year-old boy. Debris fell onto a 25-storey residential building in the Solomianskyi district, while another drone struck an office building.
Four people were killed in the strike on the business centre. Two were outside at the time. One person was found dead in a car in the car park, and one inside the building.
Daria Kulchytska, who owns a nearby flower shop, told Suspilne Kyiv, a branch of Ukraine's national broadcaster, that she had arrived early that morning to inspect the damage from the overnight attack. By the time the area was struck again, workers had cleared up and boarded up the windows with plywood.
"We were relieved that we'd got off lightly. Then someone called me over to talk about where to take the broken glass. I went outside, my partner arrived – and then there was this explosion," she said.
Daria was knocked to the ground and her partner was also injured.
"I don't know how I survived, because there was a dead body lying next to me. I went over to the woman – she wasn't breathing. It was horrific on the other side of the road. There was a dead person in a car, and the guys were pulling her out," she said.
Another eyewitness, Nataliia Potiuk, said there had been no information that Russian aerial assets were heading towards the area.
"I turned towards the window and saw a Shahed [drone] fly past. A few seconds later there was a plume of smoke. A lot of people were injured. They were taking people away with shrapnel wounds," she said.

Iran submits seven-day Hormuz plan; Yemen forces advance in Taiz

Hello and welcome to today's coverage of the Middle East and beyond. Here is the latest:
US President Donald Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's latest proposal put forward by Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi during a visit to New York, which outlined a seven-day proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
In Yemen, government forces advance towards the Taiz and Lahaj governorates, coinciding with a call for "mobilisation" to confront Houthi troops. At least 13 Houthi militants have been killed and dozens others injured in the past 24 hours of fighting, according to Aden-based government figures.
Meanwhile, Israeli strikes have continued in southern Lebanon, with attacks reported in Mansouri, Majdal Zoun and Wadi Hassan overnight.
The natural springs and ancient pools of the occupied West Bank have long provided a respite from the oppressive summer heat. They also have been a lifeline for Palestinian communities, which rely on them for tourism and irrigation for their farmland.
But for the 2.8 million Palestinians who live in the territory, those springs and the stone reservoirs they fill are increasingly out of reach as Israeli settlers — encouraged by a hard-line government facing reelection — have stepped up efforts both to seize the springs and other heritage sites.
In one case this summer, water from a natural spring to the Palestinian village of Fasayil was illegally diverted to an ancient pool nearby. Whoever siphoned the water used it to fill up that pool, declaring it a new tourist attraction named after Herod, the Roman-appointed king of Judea.
Read the full story here.
Oscar-nominated actor Florence Pugh has said she was never "scared" to speak up for Palestine, while promoting her new movie East of Eden.
In an exclusive interview with Variety, the actor said no one ever advised her to keep quiet on the issue, and she was confused about why so many weren't voicing their support.
"I don't know why it took so long for people to start talking and for people to actually feel sympathy," Pugh told Vanity Fair.
ussian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said at the UN Saturday that Moscow is ready to help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region, as the US-Iran conflict drags on.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states, and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov told leaders at the UN General Assembly.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region."
Attacks targeting Libya's energy infrastructure, or any actions that could undermine it, may constitute grounds for sanctions under relevant UN Security Council resolutions, the UN Support Mission in Libya said on Saturday.
The warning comes as the Sharara-Zawiya oil pipeline remains closed, causing losses in crude production and public revenues and raising risks to fuel supplies and electricity generation, the mission said in a statement.
US intelligence agencies have assessed that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons programme, according to classified documents provided to Congress and described to The Washington Post by US officials.
The assessment is raising fresh questions about US President Donald Trump’s agreement to help Riyadh establish a civilian nuclear industry. Some US lawmakers fear the deal could give Saudi Arabia the means to produce nuclear material that might eventually be used as a weapon, although the intelligence finding does not say the kingdom has decided to build one.
The agreement, announced in July, would allow US companies to pursue nuclear energy projects in Saudi Arabia. The Trump administration says the partnership will strengthen ties with Riyadh, uphold non-proliferation standards, and reduce the prospect of the kingdom turning to Russia or China for nuclear technology.
The University of Southern California (USC) ended the sale of human cadavers for Israeli military training on Thursday, closing a programme that ran for over five years.
A report by Annenberg Media in 2024 revealed that the University of California San Diego (UCSD) supplied bodies to the University of California (USC), which were then sold to the US Navy and used for training Israeli army medics.
The revelation sparked public outcry, with protests demanding an end to the programme.
USC's medical school said it would not renew its cadaver contracts because it would no longer supply bodies for the US Navy programme.
Israeli drone strike inside the so-called "ceasefire" zone in west Nuseirat, Gaza, kills at least one Palestinian and injured multiple others, according to local media.
US President Donald Trump said Saturday that he had rejected a plan proposed by Iran on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran says would have opened the waterway within seven days.
"I reject their proposal," Trump told reporters outside the White House.
"They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," he said. "They want to make a deal and I think that's fine. I like making a deal too."
Players from Ireland's football team voted on Saturday to fulfil a Nations League tie with Israel despite player unease over the war in Gaza.
"We carried out a vote amongst the squad to establish their sentiment on fulfilling the (Israel) fixtures," Football Association of Ireland head David Courell told reporters in Debrecen, Hungary, where the game will take place on Sunday.
"It was a significant majority that was returned with the intention to continue," he said.
Egypt’s then-intelligence chief travelled to Israel 11 days before Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack and warned that the group appeared to be preparing a major assault, according to an investigation by The Atlantic.
The report comes amid intensifying pressure on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to allow an independent inquiry into Israel’s failures ahead of the attack, as the country approaches an election next month.
Abbas Kamel arrived in Israel on 26 September 2023 aboard a plane linked to Egyptian intelligence, The Atlantic reported on Friday, citing an Israeli airport flight log and officials from Israel, Egypt and other countries who were briefed on the visit after the attack. The plane spent 67 minutes on the ground before returning to Cairo.
Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti Saleh bin Fawzan al-Fawzan has exhorted the coalition forces fighting against Yemen's Houthis to be ready to sacrifice their lives in the conflict, the Saudi Press Agency reported on Friday.
Addressing soldiers on the frontlines of the conflict and in stationed along the country's borders, the mufti's statement comes as Yemen slides further back into civil war, with the Houthis advancing on government-held territory.
Ireland cancelled their pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, and their training session has also been delayed, the Israeli FA press officer said on Saturday.
The game has been under the spotlight since the sides were drawn together in February, with Ireland one of Europe's most outspoken critics of Israel's genocidal war in Gaza. There have been numerous protests in Ireland asking for the team not to fulfil the fixtures with Israel.
Ireland were due to hold the press conference on Saturday but shortly before the scheduled start at 10:15 a.m. local time (0815 GMT), reporters were informed that this would now take place following the team's training session at the stadium in Debrecen.
Iran's top security body denies that Iran is planning for military moves over bans on Iranian flights, according to state media.
Thousands of people rallied in Madrid on Saturday to protest the Spanish government's handling of a recent migrant influx into Ceuta, accusing it of failing to protect the country's borders and calling for an early general election.
Demonstrators, many waving red and yellow Spanish flags, chanted "Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended" as they marched through the centre of the Spanish capital.
Ceuta, a Spanish territory located in North Africa, has been embroiled in a humanitarian crisis since more than 70,000 migrants arrived from neighbouring Morocco on July 30 and 31.
Most returned in the following hours, but thousands have remained for weeks, many sleeping on the streets, straining the small city's resources and creating a political crisis for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
The protest was organised by right-leaning civil society platform Sociedad Civil Espanola and backed by the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox.
US actor Adam Brody said he wants a "free Palestine" on Friday while promoting his show Nobody Wants This, after several Hollywood actors were arrested during a protest against the arrival of Israel's ICC fugitive Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
In an interview with GQ, Brody, known for his breakout role in the series The O.C., said he wants to noted as being among those who believe a genocide is occurring in Gaza.
“Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” Brody said when asked if he would like to speak about the topic.
One person injured following reported Israeli fire in the Beit Lahia area of northern Gaza, according to Palestinian media.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran's new plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz was coordinated with supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, state media reported Saturday, quoting an interview with US media.
Pezeshkian also told broadcaster CBS that the Islamic republic would fulfil its obligations were the United States to agree to the proposal, according to excerpts released by state news agency IRNA.
The strait is crucial for the world's oil supply and central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which remains deadlocked after nearly seven months.
"Coordination with the leader of the revolution (the supreme leader)... has been carried out," Pezeshkian said.
"If the US accepts it and fulfils its obligations, we will do the same, and there will be no issue in this regard," he added.
Pezeshkian said that a six-member team in Iran has been meeting for discussions and has "the authority to make decisions".
This team includes representatives from "various organisations and bodies, including the military, the parliament and the government".
The Ireland team’s press conference the day before the first of its Nations League games against Israel has been delayed as pressure to boycott the matches grows.
Journalists in Debrecen, Hungary — where Israel’s "home" game is to be played Sunday — were left waiting Saturday after being told the press conference was being pushed back until after training. That was 15 minutes before it was supposed to begin.
Training was also delayed, however, with Irish broadcaster RTÉ reporting the players were still in their hotel when it was supposed to begin.
The team has been coming under increasing pressure in Ireland, where affinity with Palestinians is strong, to boycott the two games — the first on Sunday and the second, Ireland’s “home” game, in Backa Topola, Serbia on Oct. 4.
Ireland midfielder Jason Knight said after Thursday’s 1-0 loss in Kosovo that the players were in a difficult situation and that he didn’t think the matches should be going ahead.
The Iraqi government said Saturday it was holding talks with the United States to secure an exemption from the ban on Iranian airlines, which has disrupted travel for patients, students and pilgrims.
All Iraqi airports enforced the ban this week, resulting in major disruption at the airport of the holy city of Najaf, the main destination for Iranian flights to Iraq.
"The Iraqi government is holding direct talks with the American side to exempt certain Iraqi airports from these measures," the prime minister's media office said.
An exemption would allow flights to resume "for humanitarian reasons, including medical treatment, education, religious visits, and for the interest of civilians," it added.
Israeli forces use artillery shelling to target the outskirts of Yater in southern Lebanon, according to local media.
Israeli forces and military vehicles are stationed by Birzeit University north of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian media.
The university, meanwhile, has condemned the Israeli military raid, claiming "intimidation" of students during final exams is "flagrant and explicit violation" of conventions and laws that protect education.
Saudi Arabia's military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, claimed early Saturday that a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen was intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Maliki said the missile was fired toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
There was no immediate statement of responsibility, though it can take days for the Houthis to issue one.
A regional body representing Arab Gulf states, the Gulf Cooperation Council, condemned the latest Houthi attacks as a "grave escalation and threat to regional security" and urged the international community to respond.
A passenger bus overturned in Iran, killing 11 people and injuring 24 others, state television reported Saturday.
The crash occurred on the Saveh-Hamedan freeway in central Markazi province. Provincial traffic police said driver fatigue and drowsiness caused the crash.
Authorities did not immediately say where the bus was headed.
Iran has one of the world’s worst traffic safety records. Crashes kill more than 17,000 people a year. Experts blame the high toll on unsafe vehicles, widespread disregard for traffic regulations and inadequate emergency services.
Earlier this month, a fuel tanker crashed into other vehicles and exploded near the western city of Sanandaj, killing 11 people and injuring seven others.
Libya's National Oil Corporation said on Saturday it has shut down one of the refining units at the Zawiya refinery due to the continued forced closure of the Sharara crude pipeline valve by armed groups belonging to the Petroleum Facilities Guard.
The corporation warned that ongoing disruptions to the flow of crude could directly impact state oil revenue, increase fuel import costs and harm the national economy.
The closure has reduced cumulative production at the Sharara field by 942,376 barrels over five days through Friday, causing direct financial losses of about $95 million, the NOC said.
Lost output on Friday alone totalled 222,014 barrels, according to NOC.

The closure has reduced cumulative production at the Sharara field by 942,376 barrels over five days through Friday, causing direct financial losses of about $95 million, the NOC said.
Lost output on Friday alone totalled 222,014 barrels, according to NOC.

U.S. Army drone-killing system tested in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
08:37:45 UTC
17:37:45 KST

- U.S. Army soldiers of the 11th Airborne Division operated the M-LIDS counter-drone system during exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026 in Rajasthan, India.
- Indian Army personnel observed the system and discussed counter-drone tactics but did not operate it, the U.S. Army said.
U.S. Army soldiers from the 11th Airborne Division took a mobile counter-drone system to India’s Rajasthan desert during exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, showing Indian Army troops how it finds and defeats small drones.
The system, the Mobile Low, Slow, Small Unmanned Aircraft Integrated Defeat System, or M-LIDS, was set up at the Mahajan Field Firing Range. U.S. soldiers operated it throughout. Indian Army personnel were shown its external components and discussed counter-drone tactics with their U.S. counterparts but did not operate the system, the U.S. Army said.
M-LIDS is a set of sensors, command software and weapons mounted on mobile tactical vehicles. A Ku-band radar and electro-optical and infrared cameras detect, track and identify incoming drones. The Forward Area Air Defense Command and Control system combines that sensor data into one air picture. Crews can then choose between electronic warfare to jam a drone or kinetic weapons to shoot it down.
During the exercise, soldiers practiced setting up the system quickly and moving from spotting a drone to choosing a response. Because it rides on vehicles, M-LIDS can move with the troops it protects. The Army said the Rajasthan heat, dust and heat shimmer tested both personnel and equipment.
“Defeating the small UAS threat is not a single-nation fight; it requires interoperable forces that can share information, integrate capabilities, and act as one,” said Chief Warrant Officer 3 Mark Giauque, the division’s air and missile defense systems integrator.
Yudh Abhyas is an annual exercise between the U.S. and Indian armies. The 2026 edition, the 22nd, opened Sept. 15 and brings together about 600 soldiers from each side. It is running at two sites at once: the Mahajan range in Rajasthan and the Auli training area in the Himalayan state of Uttarakhand. U.S. forces come from the 1st Infantry Brigade Combat Team, 11th Airborne Division, based in Alaska. The exercise is scheduled to end Sept. 28.
Elsewhere at Mahajan, U.S. and Indian artillery crews trained together on the M777 lightweight howitzer, including live fire, rapid moves to alternate positions and “shoot-and-scoot” drills to avoid counter-battery fire. The Army said U.S. and Indian gunners served together in combined M777 crews, while other units rehearsed aviation, maneuver, medical and force protection tasks.

U.S. Navy’s new sub-launched warhead enters development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
08:32:59 UTC
17:32:59 KST

- The U.S. Navy's W93 warhead and Mk7 reentry body entered engineering and manufacturing development after passing Milestone B this year.
- It is the first new U.S. nuclear warhead and reentry system program started in nearly four decades.
The U.S. Navy’s new submarine-launched nuclear warhead, the W93, has moved into full-scale development, the first U.S. nuclear warhead and reentry body program started in nearly 40 years.
The Navy’s Strategic Systems Programs office said the W93 and its Mk7 reentry body, the cone-shaped shell that carries the warhead back through the atmosphere to its target, passed Milestone B this year and have entered engineering and manufacturing development. In this phase, engineers finish the production design and prove the weapon can be built in the numbers the Navy needs. The office did not say when the milestone was reached or give a date for first production.
“W93/Mk7 will provide flexibility and adaptability to meet future Warfighter needs and ensure an uninterrupted at sea deterrent for the sea-based leg of the nuclear triad,” said Vice Adm. Douglas Williams, director of Strategic Systems Programs. “We were able to accelerate our entry into this next phase because of the dedicated partnership between PAE SSP, National Nuclear Security Administration, and our industry base. This is what working at hyper-speed looks like.”
The Navy runs the program with the National Nuclear Security Administration, the Department of Energy agency that designs and builds U.S. nuclear warheads, and its national laboratories. Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico is designing the warhead.
“Credible deterrence demands that we move with urgency, and the progress we’re making on W93/Mk7 demonstrates exactly that,” said Brandon Williams, administrator of the National Nuclear Security Administration.
The W93 will arm the Trident II D5 ballistic missiles carried by U.S. Navy ballistic missile submarines, the part of the U.S. nuclear force that stays hidden at sea. Those missiles now carry two warheads: the W76, in service since 1978, and the W88, which entered the stockpile in 1988. The W76 rides in the Mk4 reentry body and the W88 in the Mk5.
Los Alamos said the W93 design uses nuclear components that were tested before the United States stopped explosive nuclear testing, updated with modern materials. The lab said the warhead is expected to go aboard Ohio-class submarines, likely starting in the mid-2030s, and later move to the new Columbia-class submarines as they replace the Ohio class.
The program completed its feasibility and design options phase in March 2025, according to Los Alamos, producing draft military requirements and a description of the conditions the weapon must survive from storage to detonation.
Britain is tied to the program through the Mk7. The United Kingdom will use the same reentry body for its own new warhead, the A21, known as Astraea. The British Ministry of Defence says Astraea is a sovereign design developed in parallel with the W93 and will arm the Royal Navy’s future Dreadnought-class submarines.
Strategic Systems Programs also maintains the Trident missile system on the Ohio-class boats and is integrating a life-extended version of the D5 on the Columbia class. The office is developing a follow-on missile, the D5LE2, as well as a nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missile known as SLCM-N and the non-nuclear Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic weapon.

Pro-Palestine Action group to rally at Labour conference led by Burnham
Unknown

Pro-Palestine Action group to rally at Labour conference led by Burnham
Defend Our Juries say Sunday’s action is an ‘integrity test’ for the UK’s new premier.
London, United Kingdom – Protesters are planning to gather in support of Palestine Action at the first Labour Party conference Prime Minister Andy Burnham will preside over.
Sunday’s “mass, silent sign-holding vigil” in Liverpool, close to the conference centre, is in response to the proscription of Palestine Action as a “terrorist” group, said Defend Our Juries, a rights group that organises rallies calling for the government to drop the ban.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Declassified documents show UK aware of Israeli war crimes for 24 years
- list 2 of 4UK lawmakers vote against bill to legalise assisted dying
- list 3 of 4Burnham defends UK ban on Israeli settlement trade
- list 4 of 4‘They told me to go back to my country’: Inside the UK’s wave of racism
Since it was outlawed in July 2025, a civil disobedience campaign has seen more than 3,600 people arrested for showing their support for the group, often while holding signs reading, “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action”.
Organisers at Defend Our Juries expect further arrests, saying several hundred people are likely to attend.
The protest is designed as an “integrity test of the new leadership’s commitment to ending Britain’s complicity in Israel’s ethnic cleansing and war crimes”, they said.
Burnham faced further scrutiny on Friday as Declassified UK, an investigative outlet focused on foreign policy, reported that it had been denied media passes to cover the Labour conference, which runs from Sunday to Wednesday.
Where does Labour stand on Palestine?
Compared with his predecessors, Burnham has taken a stronger stance against illegal Israeli settlements and settler violence in the occupied West Bank, announcing sanctions earlier this month.
But rights groups and activists have called on Labour to suspend all arms sales to Israel in order to stop the bloodshed in Gaza and the West Bank.
They also want the UK to reverse the ban on Palestine Action, whose main target is Israel’s largest weapons maker, Elbit Systems.
“If [prime minister] Burnham means what he says, that he plans to end Britain’s complicity in Israel’s horrific crimes, then he would stop the arrests of people peacefully demonstrating against the genocide and the authoritarian attempts to crush its opponents,” Defend Our Juries said. “We urge PM Burnham to do the only sensible thing and lift the ban on Palestine Action, the very people in the UK actually trying to prevent British complicity in Israel’s war crimes.”
Labour’s past positions on Palestine
In recent years, the Labour Party has faced waves of criticism over its positions on Israel and Palestine.
“I think the interests of a Labour leader who wants to keep the Labour Party together, and keep a broad electoral bloc together too in a first-past-the-post system, is to try and defang this issue as much as possible,” Colm Murphy, a senior lecturer in British politics at Queen Mary University, told Al Jazeera.
He explained that “we’ve seen a series of gradual steps” on Palestine by party leaders, but the shift has been a “slow, painful evolution”.
“Recognition of the Palestinian state by [former Prime Minister Keir] Starmer was the culmination of a process really begun by Ed Miliband,” he said, referring to the current Foreign Secretary who was Labour’s leader from 2010 until 2015.
Starmer was prime minister when the UK proscribed Palestine Action under the Terrorism Act.
Days after Israel attacked Gaza following the Hamas attacks of October 2023, then-PM Starmer said Israel had the “right” to cut off the strip’s water supply, adding, “Obviously, everything should be done within international law.”
Although he later walked back his statement, for many, the damage was done.
“The legacy of Starmer is actually worsened by the fact that Burnham and Miliband were able to act, because it shows that they could act and they had the political will, they had the personal and public will, and they actually did do something,” said Joseph Willits, head of Parliamentary Affairs at the Council for Arab-British Understanding.
The new sanctions announced under Burnham’s Labour highlight the “inadequacies and the lack of will from the previous government”, he said.
Before Starmer, Jeremy Corbyn, a leftist and lifelong supporter of Palestinian rights, led Labour.
But his era was marred by allegations of anti-Semitism and in late 2019, he announced his resignation as the party’s head.
Under Miliband’s tenure, Labour’s stance on Palestine was supportive of a two-state solution and Palestinian statehood.
He has since reflected on how his Jewish mother, a Holocaust survivor, shaped the principles that have guided him.
The question remains whether Burnham’s Labour could reverse the ban on Palestine Action, especially after United States President Donald Trump recently outlawed the group.
“I think it’s too early to say,” Willits said. “If this is also a battle line with Trump and the Trump administration, do they pick that battle line or the others? Has he already picked other battle lines when it comes to Palestine and therefore does he just leave this one?”
Murphy said Burnham’s Labour may address issues around Palestine Action if they become “salient in British politics again”.
“I’m not so sure it will, but we shall see. A protest might raise the profile a bit.”

U.S. Navy creates new command to master drone warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
08:22:37 UTC
17:22:37 KST

- The U.S. Navy established the Robotic and Autonomous Systems Warfighting Development Center at Little Creek-Fort Story under Rear Adm. Melvin Smith.
- The center will test unmanned systems, develop tactics and training, and feed results to the Navy's new robotic systems acquisition office.
The U.S. Navy has set up a new command to turn its growing collection of drones, unmanned boats and robotic submarines into tools sailors can actually fight with, naming Rear Adm. Melvin Smith as its first commander.
The Robotic and Autonomous Systems Warfighting Development Center, known as RASWDC, is headquartered at Joint Expeditionary Base Little Creek-Fort Story in Virginia and falls under U.S. Fleet Forces Command. The Secretary of the Navy and the Chief of Naval Operations formally established it this week. The Navy said the center will be the fleet’s single operational home for robotic and autonomous systems in the air, on the surface and under the sea.
“This is just day one,” said Rear Adm. Melvin Smith. “Our purpose here is to consolidate the Navy’s autonomous efforts across air, surface, and undersea domains, and give them a single home here at Little Creek. Our mandate is straightforward: educate our warfighters, equip the Fleet with tools that actually survive the environment, and develop the combined tactics to employ them decisively. We are here to make sure our forces don’t just field unmanned systems, but dominate with them.”
The center will test unmanned systems in realistic conditions, write the doctrine and tactics for using them, and build the training needed to certify sailors to operate them. It will also send performance data from testing, experiments and training back to the engineers and program managers who design and buy the systems.
“To maintain our decisive maritime advantage, we must rapidly integrate robotic and autonomous systems into how we operate, train, and deploy,” said Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle. “The establishment of RASWDC ensures our Sailors are equipped with the tactical edge, advanced training, and specialized doctrine required to win the high-end fight.”
The center is the operational half of a reorganization that began over the summer. On Aug. 5, the Navy created a Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Robotic and Autonomous Systems, a single office responsible for buying, budgeting, setting technical standards and fielding unmanned systems across the Navy and U.S. Marine Corps. The office is modeled on the one the Navy uses to manage submarine programs.
Christopher Miller, who also leads the Navy’s maritime acquisition portfolio, is serving as acting head of that office and reports directly to William Toti, who is performing the duties of Under Secretary of the Navy. The move replaced the head of the Navy’s previous drone acquisition office eight months after it was set up. The Navy said at the time it was reviewing whether to move the office’s staff out of Washington and closer to the fleet.
The new Navy office works alongside a Department of War-wide portfolio manager for unmanned offensive and defensive systems that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth established in late June. That office reports to Deputy Secretary Steve Feinberg.
“RASWDC is the critical bridge between capability development and operational employment,” said Adm. Daryl Caudle. “By forging a direct feedback loop, we are accelerating the delivery of unmanned capabilities from the foundry directly to the Fleet, ensuring our forces are postured to meet any challenge.”
The Navy said RASWDC will not take over work done by its existing warfighting development centers, type commanders or systems commands. It will coordinate with them to share lessons and feed in new requirements.

“Postponing the protest is part of our strategy. We have to wear down the federal government,” said Afridi, whose province is governed by Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
The announcement came after authorities blocked main access routes to Islamabad with double-stacked shipping containers ahead of the protest originally scheduled for Sunday, disrupting traffic and public transport.
Police deployed 22,000 security personnel to lock down Islamabad, officials told AFP, barring entry and exit to neighbouring Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.
Key highways, entry points, and major intersections were obstructed, completely severing transport links and bringing movement to a virtual standstill.
The government's preemptive crackdown ahead of the planned protest expanded earlier this week with the detention of Khan's sisters Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan, and Noreen Niazi.
Khan, 73, has been in jail since August 2023 following convictions in several cases that he and his PTI party have branded politically motivated.
Some of his convictions have been suspended or overturned, while several appeals remain pending before higher courts.

Iran war squeezes Iraq’s economy as oil revenues fall and prices rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
08:13:06 UTC
17:13:06 KST

Iran war squeezes Iraq’s economy as oil revenues fall and prices rise
Disrupted oil exports, costlier imports, and a weaker dinar expose Iraq’s economic dependence on oil, foreign goods.
Iraq is a state heavily dependent on imports, from food and medicines to appliances, as well as raw materials for its industries. Its one big export is oil, but it sits on such a huge supply of the natural resource that revenues from the sale of oil abroad offset the imports and ensured that the country had a positive trade surplus.
Things have changed, however, since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February, and the subsequent end to the free flow of trade through the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of the country’s trade with the rest of the world passed. Now, Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has described the country as “facing extraordinary economic challenges”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Netanyahu’s UN belligerence wins cheers at home as world walks out
- list 2 of 3The Trump-Xi summit exposes a US disadvantage in the Global South
- list 3 of 3UAE bars Iranian airlines as US sanctions squeeze Iran’s aviation sector
Al-Zaidi said earlier this week that Iraq had lost about $60bn in oil revenues as a result of the war, the result of being, for a period, unable to export about 90 percent of its oil through its usual Gulf routes, which have become central to negotiations between Washington and Tehran, with the latter linking free passage through the strait to an easing of US pressure and the lifting of a blockade on Iranian ports.
That’s a massive blow to Iraq: oil revenues account for more than 90 percent of Iraq’s federal budget.
The disruption to shipping routes has also affected supply chains, increasing transport times and costs for Iraqi businesses and consumers, in addition to reducing imports.
One supermarket owner in Baghdad, Alaa-Eddin Sulaibi, estimated that the percentage of imported goods sold at his store was now 70 percent, down from 90 percent before the war started.
“We have no choice but to sell local products, even if they are not of the same quality as imported ones,” he said.
He added that the price of the imported goods had risen by between 25 and 30 percent.
“The reasons [for the price increase] extend beyond disruptions in the Gulf, but also longer delivery times for goods arriving from China, and higher fuel and transportation costs, particularly for trade with Turkiye,” he said.
Several merchants who spoke to Al Jazeera said goods imported from China were now facing significant delays, in some cases taking up to three months to arrive because of the increase in transportation costs as a result of importers being forced to take more circuitous routes to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, or being delayed at the maritime chokepoint.
Dollar rises against Iraqi dinar
The crisis has put pressure on the Iraqi dinar, which has dropped against the US dollar, in a development that has triggered concern among Iraqis.
The dollar rose to about 1,600 Iraqi dinars on the parallel market last week, before easing to about 1,575 this week. Prior to the war, it had been about 1,540 Iraqi dinars to the dollar.
The widening gap between the official exchange rate – approximately 1,300 dinars to the dollar – and the parallel market rate has also created uncertainty for businesses and added to the financial burden on consumers. The official market rate is largely not available to everyday people, and the divergence in rates allows for some businesses to obtain dollars at the cheaper official rate, while others are forced to use the parallel market and pay more.
At the same time, the Iraqi government is also dealing with concerns about the availability and transfer of dollars that Baghdad receives through arrangements linked to its oil revenues.
Following the fall of the regime of President Saddam Hussein after the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, the country’s oil revenues were placed in a special account in the US, with money then transferred to Baghdad. This transfer is renewed annually by the US president, with the stated purpose of safeguarding Iraq’s financial resources. But the system also gives Washington a large degree of oversight over the flow of dollars from the account to Iraq.
In April, the Trump administration began halting the shipment of physical cash from the account to Iraq, releasing only electronic dollar transfers, with some reporting indicating that the halt in physical cash transfers was linked to pressure over the activities of Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
Some physical cash shipments resumed in July, but the US has also accused several private Iraqi banks of being involved in large-scale dollar smuggling operations to Iran.
Local reports have suggested that the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) is facing difficulties supplying commercial banks with sufficient dollars, particularly for financing imports, potentially leading to higher prices in local markets.
The CBI has denied that it is facing a shortage, saying in a statement on Saturday that it “has sufficient foreign reserves to meet all demands for foreign currency”, adding that included “financing foreign trade”.
The central bank blamed the rise in the parallel market dollar exchange rate on “speculation, expectations, and the misuse of regional geopolitical conditions by certain parties seeking to disrupt Iraq’s economic and financial stability”.
‘Deep imbalances’ in the economy
The pressure on Iraq’s finances is nevertheless intensifying as the war continues and oil revenues fall.
Mudher Mohammed Salih, the Iraqi prime minister’s financial adviser, said in a television interview this week that the CBI’s foreign reserves had fallen from about $106bn before the war began, to roughly $80bn by late August.
Economists say the crisis has exposed longstanding structural weaknesses in Iraq’s economy, particularly its dependence on oil revenues and imported goods.
“This crisis has revealed the deep imbalances within the structure of the Iraqi economy, most notably the absence of safeguards capable of protecting the economy during times of turmoil,” Ziad al-Hashimi, a PhD researcher in international economics at Anglia Ruskin University, told Al Jazeera.
“The crisis has also shown that the Iraqi government lacks genuine solutions or effective measures that could bring about the kind of structural change needed to overcome the situation,” he added.
Al-Hashimi said that the government’s immediate options were limited.
“All the Iraqi government can do are short-term measures that may have only limited the impact in the coming period, such as resorting to borrowing, which is not a genuine solution,” he said. “Real solutions require a long time before results can be seen. They include diversifying Iraq’s oil export markets abroad, managing public spending in a more systematic way to avoid unnecessary expenditures, and continuing efforts to combat corruption.”

U.S. Air Force moves to upgrade aging E-3 AWACS planes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
08:06:45 UTC
17:06:45 KST

- The U.S. Air Force is seeking contractors to replace the DAR-400 encryption unit on its 15 operational E-3G AWACS aircraft.
- General Dynamics Mission Systems told the U.S. Air Force the DAR-400 cannot be upgraded to meet changing NSA requirements.
The U.S. Air Force is looking for a contractor to replace an aging encryption unit on its E-3G AWACS radar planes after the manufacturer warned it can no longer keep up with changing National Security Agency security requirements, according to a sources-sought notice posted Sept. 25 on the federal contracting website.
The part, known as the DAR-400, is a data-at-rest unit that stores encrypted mission data on board the aircraft. The Air Force called it mission-critical and said it is in critical need of an obsolescence fix to avoid disrupting operations. Its maker, General Dynamics Mission Systems, told the service the DAR-400 cannot support or be upgraded to meet new NSA requirements.
Because the unit holds encrypted data for several of the plane’s mission and computing systems, the notice said, a failure would directly affect both operations and data security.
The Air Force already has a replacement. It is providing a government-owned solution based on the KG-204, which it said complies with current Department of War and NSA mandates. The contractor would install and integrate that equipment across the fleet. The notice did not give a cost estimate, schedule or number of units.
The notice is market research, not a solicitation. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and special operations directorate is asking companies of all sizes, including small businesses, to describe their capabilities by Oct. 12. The responses will help decide whether the work is set aside for small businesses.
The Air Force listed its operational E-3G fleet at 15 aircraft. The Boeing 707-based planes carry a large rotating radar dome on top of the fuselage and serve as airborne command posts, tracking aircraft and directing U.S. and allied forces. The fleet is based at Tinker Air Force Base, Oklahoma.
One E-3G was destroyed in a drone and missile attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia on March 27, 2026, during the war with Iran.
Air Force leaders have said for years that the E-3 is increasingly difficult to keep flying and that its Cold War-era radar is outdated. The radar dome takes 10 seconds to complete one rotation and refresh its picture of the sky.
Its planned replacement, Boeing’s E-7 Wedgetail, remains in dispute between the Pentagon and Congress. The Department of War tried to cancel the E-7 in its fiscal 2026 budget, but lawmakers blocked the move. The fiscal 2026 defense policy law also barred the Air Force from retiring any of its E-3s if the fleet would fall below 16. In March 2026, the Air Force signed about $2.4 billion in contracts to buy developmental E-7s.
The department then requested no money for the E-7 in its fiscal 2027 budget. Congressional committees have since written about $1.55 billion for the program into their bills, but the final amount has not been settled.
With the E-7’s future unresolved, the Air Force plans to keep the E-3G flying, and the DAR-400 replacement is one of the upgrades needed to do that.

Ohio steelmaker gets $995M deal for artillery shell steel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:56:29 UTC
16:56:29 KST

- The Defense Logistics Agency awarded Metallus a sole-source contract worth up to $995 million for HF-1 steel used in 155 mm artillery shells.
- The five-year contract runs through Sept. 24, 2031, and covers the U.S. Army, U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Navy, U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force.
The Defense Logistics Agency has awarded Ohio steelmaker Metallus a contract worth up to $995 million for High Fragmentation 1 steel, the special alloy used to make the bodies of U.S. 155 mm artillery shells, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The five-year, firm-fixed-price contract runs through Sept. 24, 2031, and has no option periods. The U.S. Army, U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Navy, U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force are listed as the using services. The $995 million figure is a ceiling; the announcement did not say how much steel will be bought or how much will be spent in the first year. Funding will come from fiscal 2025 through 2029 accounts. The Defense Logistics Agency’s contracting office in Columbus, Ohio, is managing the contract.
The agency awarded it without competition under a federal rule that allows sole-source deals to keep a producer available for industrial mobilization or a national emergency.
The steel, known as HF-1, is formulated to break into lethal fragments when a shell explodes. It forms the body of the 155 mm M795 high-explosive round and the M1128 extended-range round, the main artillery shells fired by U.S. howitzers. An M795 weighs about 47 kg (103 pounds) and carries 10.8 kg (23.8 pounds) of TNT or IMX-101 explosive inside its HF-1 casing.
Metallus, formerly TimkenSteel, is based in Canton and has produced HF-1 steel for the U.S. military continuously since 1993. It normally sells the steel as a subcontractor, supplying billets to companies such as General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems, which forge them into shell bodies.
The U.S. Army has spent the past two years expanding Metallus’ output as part of its push to build 100,000 155 mm shells a month. In February 2024, the Army signed an agreement worth up to $99 million with Metallus, funded by Ukraine supplemental appropriations, to raise HF-1 capacity from 1,500 to 6,720 tons a month. It was the first time Metallus had held a prime contract with the U.S. military.
On Aug. 26, the Army and Metallus commissioned a new bloom reheat furnace, a roller furnace and supporting equipment at the company’s Canton facilities. The Army said that at full capacity the plant will make enough HF-1 steel for more than 120,000 155 mm shell bodies a month.
The Army says its ammunition enterprise has opened 16 new facilities over the last two years as part of nearly $6 billion in investments in the defense industrial base.

CCPA penalises Amazon, Flipkart, JioMart for selling unregistered herbicide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:53:45 UTC
16:53:45 KST

Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed penalties of Rs 10 lakh
NEW DELHI: Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed penalties of Rs 10 lakh each on Amazon and Flipkart, and Rs 5 lakh on JioMart, for selling and advertising an unregistered agrochemical product, Cyclosinone Herbicide.Cyclosinone Herbicide is marketed as a granular weed-control product used to prevent and eliminate broadleaf and grassy weeds in lawns, gardens and agricultural fields.In separate orders issued recently, the consumer watchdog directed the e-commerce marketplaces to immediately discontinue the false and misleading advertisements and conduct a self-audit of their platforms to identify and remove products that violate the law or pose a risk to consumers’ life and safety.The CCPA initiated proceedings after the department of agriculture and farmers’ welfare forwarded a complaint it had received from the Crop Care Federation of India (CCFI) regarding the sale and advertisement of the unregistered herbicide through e-commerce and digital media platforms.During the investigation, the agriculture department informed CCPA that the import, manufacture, sale, transport, distribution and use of insecticides and pesticides are regulated under the Insecticides Act, 1968, and the Insecticides Rules to safeguard human beings and animals from potential risks.
The department told the authority that no chemical named Cyclosinone is included in the Schedule to the Insecticides Act. However, a product marketed as “Cyclosinone Herbicide” was being sold through online platforms without disclosing the chemical name of its active ingredient or its composition.
“It is currently being marketed illegally because it bypasses the mandatory safety, bio-efficacy, quality and legal checks required under the Insecticides Act,” the department said in its submission to CCPA.The authority rejected the e-commerce companies’ argument that they could not be held responsible for products listed by third-party sellers. The CCPA said online marketplaces cannot disown their statutory obligation to protect consumers and are required to exercise due diligence to prevent the sale of products that are illegal or hazardous.

U.S. Marine Corps buys more anti-ship missile launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:51:19 UTC
16:51:19 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps awarded Kongsberg a contract worth up to $404.4 million for full-rate production of Naval Strike Missile launchers and fire control systems.
- Work will take place in Norway and Pennsylvania through September 2034, with funds obligated only as individual orders are placed.
The U.S. Marine Corps has awarded Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace a contract worth up to $404.4 million for full-rate production and support of Naval Strike Missile launchers and the fire control system that aims them, the U.S. Department of War announced Sept. 25.
The firm-fixed-price contract covers the Naval Strike Missile Launcher Unit, its Weapon Control System and related support equipment. Kongsberg will do 85% of the work in Kongsberg, Norway, and 15% in Johnstown, Pennsylvania, through Sept. 24, 2034. No money was obligated at award. The Marine Corps will fund the work through individual orders as it places them, so the final amount spent depends on how much it buys.
The Marine Corps did not compete the award, citing a federal rule that allows sole-source contracts when only one company can meet the requirement. The Marine Corps’ Portfolio Acquisition Executive at Quantico, Virginia, is managing the contract. The announcement did not say how many launchers or control systems the Marine Corps plans to order.
The Marine Corps fires the Naval Strike Missile from the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, or NMESIS. Each NMESIS launcher carries two missiles on an unmanned, remotely driven version of the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle built by Oshkosh Defense, called ROGUE-Fires. With no crew cab, the vehicle can hide among coastal terrain and move between firing positions while its operators stay out of the target area.
The Naval Strike Missile is a stealthy, sea-skimming anti-ship missile that flies at high subsonic speed and weighs 407 kg (897 pounds). It finds its target with an imaging infrared seeker and an onboard database that lets it pick out the right ship on its own. Kongsberg lists its range as more than 300 km (186 miles). The Marine Corps has described NMESIS as having a striking range of about 185 km (115 miles). Raytheon is Kongsberg’s U.S. production partner, and the U.S. Navy also carries the missile on its warships.
The 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment received the first NMESIS launchers in November 2024. Marines took the system to the Philippines for Balikatan 2025, flying launchers across northern Luzon and the Batanes Islands, and to Okinawa, Japan, that summer for its first training there. During Balikatan 2026, they moved NMESIS by C-130J to the island of Itbayat and landed it by ship on Calayan, both in the Luzon Strait north of the Philippine main islands.
The Marine Corps has made NMESIS its main long-range anti-ship weapon and dropped plans for a ground-launched Tomahawk. Its fiscal 2027 budget request includes 32 NMESIS launchers and 103 Naval Strike Missiles. In May, Oshkosh received a delivery order for more ROGUE-Fires vehicles, due through September 2028. In July, Kongsberg received a $50.3 million modification for launcher missile modules for the program.

Disaster zone declared across Bangkok as heavy rain triggers flooding
Nonstop rain since Thursday has submerged Thai capital’s roads and canals, sending water into many homes and stores.
Bangkok authorities have declared a disaster zone across all 50 districts of Thailand’s capital after three consecutive days of rainfall caused heavy flooding.
The disaster designation, which gives local organisations authority to take action, came on Saturday after Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said almost 300mm (11.8 inches) of rain had fallen since Thursday afternoon.

The nonstop rain inundated roads and canals with water, sending water into many homes and stores alongside them, according to reports. Photos and videos showed major roads submerged and cars abandoned after drivers were unable to move through the rising water.
Chadchart said the east of the city was most impacted and warned that more rain was forecast again on Saturday. He added that flooding should recede once the rain subsides, as city officials work to drain floodwaters as quickly as possible.
“The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full,” he said on social media. “The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled.”
Later on Saturday, the government said the flooding situation had “stabilised” but added it would still take two or three days for the water to drain, as long as the rain held off. “If more rainwater doesn’t fall in the area, it will be solved,” he said.
Chadchart also advised residents to move their cars to higher ground, as Bangkok’s public transport authority offered free access to MRT train “park and ride” carparks to store their vehicles until October 2.
Reporting from a flooded street in Bangkok, Al Jazeera’s Tony Cheng said the Thai capital is no stranger to heavy rain during the monsoon season, but the continuous rainfall had locals worried.
“What usually happens is we get heavy downpours for a couple of hours, then you’ll see the street often flooded but it would flow away into the drains quickly, and it would only happen in isolated areas too,” he said.
“What’s happening here is … happening all across the city. This is not a flash flood; this is persistent heavy rain since Thursday evening, and it shows no sign of letting up.”
Somkid Pheuk-ngam, 67, a vendor who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, said she had to close her shop for two days.
“The water keeps coming in. It’s hard to go out now. It’s at my waist level,” she told the AFP news agency. “I cannot go anywhere,” she said, adding that this was “worse than the 2011 flood.”
Widespread flooding across Thailand in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes.
The Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation has warned of low pressure across eastern, northeastern and central Thailand until Sunday, saying there was a risk of flash floods, forest runoff, mudslides and river overflow.

Could AI firms be held responsible for mass shootings?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:46:45 UTC
16:46:45 KST

Could AI firms be held responsible for mass shootings?
A new lawsuit against OpenAI raises questions about liability and duty to warn in the AI industry, say experts.
A series of Canadian lawsuits against OpenAI over its failure to alert authorities to threats made on its ChatGPT platform ahead of one of the worst mass shootings in Canada’s history has renewed scrutiny of AI firms’ privacy and security practices.
The lawsuits have also prompted questions about potential legal accountability over how AI firms’ platforms are used.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How an OpenAI ‘agent’ hacked Australia’s Medicare and what that means
- list 2 of 3What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
- list 3 of 320 countries propose global oversight body to manage AI dangers
The most recent case to be filed is by the province of British Columbia, seven months after 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar – whose ChatGPT account was flagged for conversations that reportedly included gun violence – killed eight people in the small Canadian town of Tumbler Ridge. Victims included Van Rootselaar’s mother and half-brother, as well as five children and an educator at a secondary school. Van Rootselaar died by suicide.
British Columbia Attorney General Niki Sharma said the lawsuit is “an important step toward seeking justice”. It follows about 30 lawsuits filed earlier by the family members of victims.
In April, OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman apologised to the victims’ families.
“I am deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement,” Altman wrote in an open letter.
Here’s what we know about the cases and what they could mean for accountability in the fast-changing AI industry.
What lawsuits have been filed?
This week, the Canadian province of British Columbia filed its case in the San Francisco federal court in California, US, alleging that OpenAI failed to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT ahead of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.
The British Columbia lawsuit accuses OpenAI of “aiding and abetting a mass shooting” and product defect liability. It also names CEO Sam Altman as a defendant.
It asks for financial compensation from OpenAI to cover costs tied to emergency response and community recovery efforts, including rebuilding the school where the shooting took place, which is to be demolished.
The lawsuit also wants the court to force OpenAI to revamp its policies for identifying and addressing user conversations that threaten violence.
Jean-Christophe Belisle-Pipon, assistant professor in health ethics at Simon Fraser University, said British Columbia is likely pursuing the case in a US court rather than a Canadian court because it has a greater chance of recovering higher damages there.
“That speaks to how restrictive Canadian law is on damages. Awards for pain and suffering are capped, and punitive damages are rare and modest,” Belisle-Pipon told Al Jazeera. “A Canadian judgement is unlikely to offset what the province now has to cover.”
Victims and their families also filed 30 lawsuits against OpenAI in the Northern District of California in the San Francisco division at the start of September, alleging that “ChatGPT played a role in the mass shooting and OpenAI could have, and should have, prevented it”.
What happened at Tumbler Ridge?
Eighteen-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar shot and killed eight people at a high school and residence in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, in February this year.
Tumbler Ridge is a remote municipality with a population of about 2,400. It is located in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains in northern British Columbia, approximately 1,155km (718 miles) northeast of Vancouver.
Tumbler Ridge Secondary School is a Grade 7-12 school with 160 students, according to its website.
Officers found the suspected attacker dead at the school. Two victims’ bodies were found at a nearby house, which police have said were those of the attacker’s 39-year-old mother and 11-year-old half-brother.
Victims included a 39-year-old female educator, three 12-year-old female students, and two male students aged 12 and 13.
What do we know about the attacker’s ChatGPT use?
After the mass shooting, OpenAI disclosed that it had flagged a ChatGPT account linked to Van Rootselaar for abuse eight months earlier and deactivated it.
The account had been banned for “misuses of our models in furtherance of violent activities”, it said.
However, OpenAI said it did not alert police at the time because the user’s content “did not meet the higher threshold required for referral” – meaning the company did not believe it indicated a credible, imminent risk of a plan for violent acts.
The Wall Street Journal, quoting people familiar with the matter, reported that about a dozen OpenAI employees had discussed whether to alert authorities about the conversations, in which Van Rootselaar described scenarios involving gun violence. Some employees urged the company to refer the matter to authorities, but OpenAI leadership decided against doing so, according to the Journal.
US publication Mother Jones reported that after Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT account was banned, she opened a second account on the platform used in the months leading up to the shooting. During that time, the chatbot gave Van Rootselaar “tips on how to evade its own safeguards” to avoid another ban, such as presenting violent content as “fictional or hypothetical”, reported the publication, citing informed sources and material from Van Rootselaar’s chat history.
OpenAI says it has shared chat logs with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), but British Columbia says it has not received them.
Why do parents and local officials blame OpenAI?
They say the company failed to take action that could have prevented the mass shooting and configured ChatGPT in an unsafe way.
“One telephone call to the RCMP could have prevented the tragedy,” says British Columbia’s lawsuit against OpenAI, filed in San Francisco federal court on September 21.
That lawsuit also notes that OpenAI failed to implement a user-level ban that would have stopped Van Rootselaar from opening a second account on the platform. It further alleges that ChatGPT’s safety features were weakened to prioritise engagement.
The platform is “not a passive conduit for the speech of others but a content-generating product that manufactured scenarios involving gun violence”, says the lawsuit.
“Feasible, safer design alternatives existed and were not adopted or effectively implemented,” it adds.
Tiffany Li, associate professor of law at Southwestern Law School, said OpenAI’s alleged disregard for its safety guardrails could strengthen British Columbia’s legal claims.
“This puts this case in contrast with other AI death cases where the companies did not have sophisticated flagging and reporting safety workflows in place,” Li told Al Jazeera. “There is a stronger case for claims related to negligence and failure to warn.”
What has OpenAI said?
In an open letter in April, OpenAI’s Altman apologised to the Canadian community at Tumbler Ridge for his company’s failure to notify authorities about the flagged account.
“While I know words can never be enough, I believe an apology is necessary to recognise the harm and irreversible loss your community has suffered,” Altman wrote.
Altman also said he would work to “find ways to prevent tragedies like this in the future”, including by working with governments.
Earlier, OpenAI had pledged to the Canadian government that it would carry out a series of safety reforms. Those reforms were to include strengthening protocols for referring matters to law enforcement, establishing a direct line with Canadian law enforcement, incorporating “country and community context” into its de-escalation work and improving its systems to better detect users who repeatedly violate its policies.
However, Sharma said OpenAI has still not “taken meaningful steps to address the concerns raised by survivors, families and the Tumbler Ridge community”.
OpenAI has filed motions to dismiss the lawsuits filed against it in California related to the Tumbler Ridge shooting, arguing those cases should instead be addressed in British Columbia.
Could society really hold AI chatbots responsible for real-life tragedies?
Calls have been growing for digital platforms to take greater responsibility for their impact on users, specifically children, who parents and campaigners say are particularly susceptible to addiction and other harms.
In March, A Los Angeles jury found Alphabet’s Google and Meta liable for damages in a landmark civil trial over youth social media addiction, saying the companies intentionally built addictive platforms that harmed mental health.
Experts say the British Columbia lawsuit against OpenAI could also be an important test case for how the law treats digital platforms. They say it raises largely unresolved questions about when an AI company can be held responsible for violence carried out by a user, including under what circumstances it owes a duty of care and when it breaches such a duty.
Anat Lior, associate professor of law at Drexel University in Pennsylvania, US, said the question of whether OpenAI had a duty to warn the authorities about the shooting will likely hinge on factors such as the company’s ability to anticipate danger and “to some extent control the potential harm”.
“If courts recognise such a duty, it could impose affirmative obligations on AI companies, based on their exposure to user information, to alert authorities or take other protective measures on behalf of potential victims,” said Lior. “We are still very much in the early stages of AI liability from a practical standpoint, and much remains to be worked out.”
Belisle-Pipon said ChatGPT’s reported content advising Van Rootselaar on how to evade safeguards could also affect the case.
“Failing to call the police is one thing. Teaching a user how to slip past your own safeguards is another,” Belisle-Pipon said. “If those facts are validated in court, this is no longer only a failure to warn. It becomes a question of what the product itself contributed, and I think the claimants will have a very strong case.”
Li added: “This case raises many unanswered questions in US law. There are many ongoing cases on deaths related to use of AI applications, but there is no clear law on the topic yet.
“This could also be an opportunity for this lawsuit to make a strong impact on how AI law develops,” Li said.

====================================================================================================

the runway tells you where to look: 10 fashion shows that rewrote the catwalk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:45:56 UTC
16:45:56 KST

the path of the runway rewritten
Fashion shows typically begin with a straightforward diagram. Models move along a prescribed path, its edges lined with spectators, and everyone knows where to look. In general this basic layout has remained consistent across time. Yet some of the strongest runway sets begin by disturbing that diagram.
Across four decades, designers and scenographers have buried the catwalk beneath the floor, broken it into a grid, or removed the act of walking all together. In these shows, set design shapes much more than just a decorative backdrop. It determines when a model appears and how long they stay visible. It can even determine whether two viewers sitting a few feet apart experience the same sequence. During this season of fashion weeks, we return to ten examples where the runway itself became part of the choreography.
thierry mugler turns the catwalk into an arena
For Thierry Mugler’s fall 1984 show at Le Zénith in Paris, the runway unfolded through the concert venue like a pair of wings. It was one of the first examples of a runway show dreaming beyond the quiet, standard setup. More than 6,000 people filled the room, including paying members of the public, pushing the fashion show beyond the scale of the usual industry presentation. Models could appear at different points across the extended stage, and the audience watched from a wide field instead of a narrow strip beside the garments.
The plan suited Mugler’s theatrical language, but its effect was spatial first. Distance became part of the show. A figure could register as a silhouette from across the arena before moving closer into view, while the runway reached outward toward spectators instead of holding them along one straight edge. The traditional catwalk had been stretched into something closer to a diagram for a crowd.
Thierry Mugler Fall/Winter 1984, Paris | image © Paul van Riel / HH
maison martin margiela shares the runway with its audience
Maison Martin Margiela’s spring/summer 1990 show, presented in fall 1989, moved fashion onto a playground in Paris’s 20th arrondissement. Local children sat along the dirt paths, then began moving among the models as the show continued. The route never hardened into a polished runway. It remained part of the ground everyone was already occupying.
The photographs are completely changed because of that looseness. Models pass close to seated guests, children enter the frame, and the edge between watcher and participant keeps shifting. The runway becomes shared territory. Instead of a protected corridor cut through an audience, Margiela works with a path that can be crossed, crowded, and briefly taken over.
Martin Margiela Spring/Summer 1990, Paris | image © Jean-Claude Coutausse
viktor & rolf stop the runway entirely
Viktor & Rolf pushed the idea in another direction for their fall 1999 couture collection, Russian Doll. Maggie Rizer stood on a rotating platform while Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren dressed her layer by layer, building the collection onto a single body. There was no procession of models moving past the audience. The audience kept returning its gaze to the same point.
The rotating platform turns the usual relationship between clothing and movement inside out. Rizer stays almost fixed while the silhouette expands around her, and the show advances through accumulation instead of distance. The catwalk has effectively collapsed into a circle a few feet wide.
Viktor & Rolf, Russian Doll, Fall/Winter 1999–2000 | video still
alexander mcqueen turns the gaze back on the room
Alexander McQueen’s spring/summer 2001 show, Voss, begins before a model appears. Guests sit around a huge two-way mirrored box and see their own reflections staring back at them. Once the lights shift, the interior becomes visible from outside, while the models inside remain unable to see the audience.
McQueen takes the separation already built into a runway and makes it physical. The model route is contained inside the box, the spectators stay outside it, and the glass controls who gets to see whom. The audience moves from watching itself to observing bodies that cannot return the gaze. Few runway designs make the mechanics of spectatorship so visible.
Alexander McQueen, Voss, Spring/Summer 2001 | image courtesy Alexander McQueen
prada breaks the front row into a field
For Prada men’s spring/summer 2012, AMO treated seating and catwalk as a single plan. Six hundred guests sat on individual blue foam blocks spaced across a 1.5-by-1.5-meter grid, while models followed several choreographed routes through the gaps. Artificial grass covered the floor, turning the hall into a strangely ordered field.
There is no single runway edge to claim. A model might pass directly beside one spectator, then turn through the grid and move toward another. From above, the set reads almost like graph paper filled with people. At eye level, it creates a sequence of brief encounters. The audience is no longer arranged around the route. It helps form the route.
Prada, Field, Men’s Spring/Summer 2012, set design by OMA / AMO, Prada Fondazione, Milan © OMA | image by Agostino Osio
anya hindmarch hides a spiral beneath the floor
At first glance, Anya Hindmarch’s spring/summer 2017 set looked almost empty. A white circular platform sat in the Royal Horticultural Halls in London. When the show began, the platform lifted to reveal a sunken amphitheater and a spiral path beneath it, with a model ascending through the newly opened center. Above, a circular canopy rotated and tilted as the show progressed.
The surprise works because the runway begins as concealed architecture. Its route appears only once the floor moves, turning an apparently flat stage into a section of ramps and levels. Models circle upward through the space, and spectators read their movement across depth as well as distance. The runway is discovered during the show.
Anya Hindmarch, Circulus, Spring/Summer 2017 | image © Neil Mason
dior puts the runway itself in motion
For Dior Men’s fall 2019 show, Kim Jones replaced the conventional catwalk with a 76-meter moving walkway inside a dark box. The models stood still as the belt carried them past the audience, posed almost like figures in a long moving frieze. Jones linked the format to couture salon presentations, where clothing could be observed on relatively stationary bodies.
It is a small reversal with a strange effect. Walking, usually the basic action of a runway, disappears. The floor controls speed and direction instead, sending each look past the same line of viewers at an even pace. The model becomes stationary and the architecture takes over the choreography.
Dior Men’s, Fall/Winter 2019-2020 | video still
balenciaga winds the audience into a double spiral
Balenciaga’s spring/summer 2020 show filled a 2,000-square-meter room with around 500 seats arranged as an elliptical double spiral. Guests sat in a single row that climbed across five levels, all inside a field of saturated blue conceived in reference to a parliamentary chamber. The corridors created by that seating system became the catwalk.
The spiral removes the easy distinction between runway center and audience edge. Spectators face across the room toward one another, while models wind through the same geometry at changing distances. A person several turns away can enter your sightline long before reaching your section. The show becomes something seen across layers of other spectators.
Balenciaga Spring/Summer 2020, set design by SUB | image © Boris Camaca
dior opens the floor beneath the entire cast
Dior Men’s summer 2024 presentation initially offered a broad field of polished metal tiles. Then 51 panels slid open in a three-by-seventeen grid and the full cast rose from beneath the runway on individual lifts. For a few seconds, the collection appeared all at once across the floor before the models began moving through the show.
The entrance usually sits at the end of a runway, somewhere backstage and outside the audience’s view. Here, every point on the floor becomes an entrance. The first image is spatial as much as sartorial: 51 bodies distributed across a precise grid, each occupying a position that had appeared empty seconds earlier.
Dior Men’s summer 2024, set design by Villa Eugénie | image © Adrien Dirand
willo perron sends chanel across two crossing ramps
For Chanel’s spring/summer 2025 haute couture show, Willo Perron laid two broad curving ramps through the Grand Palais. Together they traced Chanel’s double C into a figure-eight path, with the walkways rising and crossing over one another like bridges. The runway became a continuous loop with models moving through changing heights and directions.
Seen from above, the structure reads immediately as geometry. From a seat beside it, that geometry becomes circulation. One model climbs while another passes through a different section of the curve, and the crossing ramps create views above and across the audience’s usual eye line. Perron turns the catwalk from a strip of floor into a route with elevation and overlap.
Chanel Spring/Summer 2025, set design by Willo Perron | image courtesy Chanel

Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

China's gold-medal tally stood at 98 at the end of Friday. Its 99th gold came in the women's synchronized 10m platform on Saturday, before Han, Zhang and Wang's team victory brought the delegation to the 100-gold milestone. ■
