Tracked storks from northern Türkiye reach Egypt, Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:17:28 UTC
16:17:28 KST

Migratory white storks stand resting inside their large, stick-built nest positioned securely on top of a tall wooden pole against a partly cloudy sky. (AA photo)
Two storks tracked with satellite transmitters from Türkiye’s northern province of Sinop reached Egypt and a third arrived in Syria as part of a multi-agency conservation project mapping migration routes.
The birds began their journeys in August. A stork departing on Aug. 27 traveled 650 kilometers to reach the Syrian city of Aleppo. The other two, leaving on Aug. 11 and Aug. 17, flew 1,500 and 1,200 kilometers respectively to Egypt, where they are currently resting to feed and regain strength.
The Agriculture and Forestry Ministry’s Nature Conservation and National Parks General Directorate attached the devices to three chicks hatched this year in the Cuma Plain. The effort falls under a population monitoring project launched in 2022 led by Sinop University. The project features contributions from Ondokuz Mayıs University, Ankara University and Saraydüzü Mehmet Akif Ersoy Anatolian High School.
Nature Conservation and National Parks 10th Regional Director Ali Bozkurt said his directorate has made significant contributions to the 5-year project, tracking the birds daily to gather vital information on their movements.
“We will be able to instantly see what routes our storks take, how long they stay and where they stop,” he said. “We will have obtained important data on this subject.”
Türkiye serves as a primary transit corridor for migratory birds traveling between Europe and Africa each year, with millions of birds passing over the Anatolian peninsula. Storks typically migrate south in late summer to escape plunging temperatures and find abundant food sources before returning in the spring to breed. Tracking helps officials protect habitats across international borders.

Egyptian intelligence chief visited Israel days before Oct. 7 to issue security warning - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:17:18 UTC
16:17:18 KST

Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel secretly visited Israel 11 days before the October 7 attack and delivered a warning that Hamas was preparing for a significant attack and that time to prevent further escalation was running out, an investigation by The Atlantic revealed Saturday.
The investigation found that on September 26, 2023, as senior Israeli officials gathered in Jerusalem to mark the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War, a chartered Cessna aircraft linked to Egyptian intelligence services landed at Ben-Gurion Airport.
The aircraft stopped in an isolated area of the airport used, the report said, for sensitive diplomatic and security missions.
On board was Kamel, who served at the time as head of Egypt’s General Intelligence Service and was one of the closest figures to Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
The aircraft reportedly remained in Israel for only 67 minutes before returning to Cairo, with The Atlantic saying that the timing appears in Israel Airports Authority flight logs and is also documented by independent flight-tracking services.
Israeli, Arab, American, and European officials briefed after October 7 on the visit said Kamel warned that Hamas appeared to be preparing for a major attack, the report mentioned, adding that he urged Israel to take economic steps to reduce tensions in the Gaza Strip.
A former Israeli official briefed on the meeting described the Egyptian message this way: “If you don’t change course, Gaza is going to explode in your face.”
The warning did not include a specific attack plan
The investigation noted that Kamel did not provide a date for a possible attack, identify targets, or share concrete details about the nature of the threat. It remains unclear who exactly he met with during his hour-long visit to Israel.
At the time, most warnings focused on the possibility of escalation, rocket fire, or renewed violence in Gaza, rather than the coordinated, multi-front assault Hamas carried out on October 7.
Despite this, officials from seven countries who spoke with The Atlantic argued that the fact that the head of Egyptian intelligence personally traveled to Israel for such a short and urgent visit should have drawn the attention of Israel’s political and security leadership.
“The messenger was the message,” a former Israeli official said, adding that no scenario existed in which senior Israeli officials met with the head of Egyptian intelligence without Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu being aware of it.
An Egyptian official told The Atlantic that Kamel’s brief visit to Israel indicated that Sisi believed he needed to travel personally to deliver the message.
Egyptian warnings continued until days before the attack
Several days after the October 7 attack, the Prime Minister’s Office rejected reports that Egypt had issued a warning before the attack.
It said that Netanyahu “has not spoken or met with the head of Egyptian intelligence since the establishment of the government, neither directly nor indirectly.”
The Atlantic said Netanyahu’s and Sisi’s offices did not respond to inquiries regarding the newly revealed details about Kamel’s visit.
Tzachi Hanegbi, who served as head of the National Security Council at the time, told the magazine this past week that Kamel did not visit Israel and that no Egyptian warning was delivered.
Israeli, Egyptian, and American officials said Egyptian warnings continued until two days before the attack.
On October 5, Egypt sent another message to Israel warning that the situation could not continue and expressing urgency over the possibility of an attack. That message also did not include a date or method of operation.
The investigation noted that on the same day Kamel landed in Israel, Netanyahu attended a ceremony marking the anniversary of the Yom Kippur War.
In his speech, he referred to the intelligence failure of 1973 and said Israel does not take any threat lightly. His public schedule showed that he later attended a classified briefing that day.
PMO rejects allegations, says 'recycled' report being used to 'manipulate' Israelis
Later on Saturday, the PMO rejected the allegations, saying the report in The Atlantic "was denied at the time and is being recycled to manipulate the Israeli public."
"On October 11, 2023, Egypt officially denied that it had warned Israel of the October 7 attack," the PMO stated. "In the months preceding October 7, Prime Minister Netanyahu neither met nor spoke with Abbas Kamel, then head of Egypt’s General Intelligence Service. No Israeli intelligence official conveyed such a warning to the prime minister."
"Recycled lies will not become true, no matter how often they are repeated," the PMO added.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Six takeaways from a turbulent week of United Nations diplomacy - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:17:18 UTC
16:17:18 KST

Limousines whisked world leaders away from the United Nations on Friday after a week of speeches, meetings, and hallway diplomacy.
While they reached no breakthroughs on the world's most intractable conflicts, talks on the Iran and Ukraine wars inched forward, and global powers used the venue to debate AI risks with industry leaders.
Here are the big takeaways from scores of panels, hundreds of meetings, hours spent in lines and listening to speeches – and countless cups of coffee:
Reboot of US-Iran diplomacy
The UN was probably most useful for facilitating the first shuttle talks between American and Iranian officials since the collapse of a ceasefire in July. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicated through mediators.
The efforts must continue, a senior Iranian official told Reuters, even as Iranian and American leaders exchanged sharp words at the General Assembly hall, with the US threatening to "annihilate" Iran and Iran accusing the US of a "bullying mentality."
The senior Iranian official said Tehran was reviewing Washington's response to its proposals, which include lifting a US naval blockade on Iranian ports and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
But no agreement appeared imminent. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio cautioned that a deal would involve hard work over time.
Ukraine, grain, and energy
Rubio also held talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, after which he said Ukraine and Russia had both voiced an interest in a limited ceasefire involving grain and energy-related targets.
Ukraine and its allies are racing to secure limited agreements on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping before winter, fearing renewed Russian strikes on power and heating facilities.
But hours after Rubio spoke on Wednesday, Lavrov addressed the Security Council meeting on Ukraine, showing no indication Russia was prepared to engage on any subject. "Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause, and it wants to use it to pump the Kyiv regime with weapons," Lavrov said.
AI steals climate change's spotlight
Climate change - a focus of UN discussions in recent years - was largely pushed aside by debate over artificial intelligence.
The festival of diplomacy coincided with an unprecedented outpouring of concern around AI after several safety breaches, and as top researchers warned it could destroy humanity.
The UN convened a Security Council meeting featuring OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who made an appearance in person, as well as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. The industry leaders appealed for governments to work together to manage AI.
Underscoring the concerns, just as they spoke, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that an AI agent developed by OpenAI infiltrated an Australian government website in June, accessing public and non-public files.
US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed AI risks as a "hoax" and "sick conspiracy," told the UN he "rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control" AI, describing it as amazing while promising the US would be careful.
Surprise arrival of Venezuela's interim president
The biggest surprise arrival at the UN was Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who used her trip to hold first in-person talks with Trump since coming to power after US forces grabbed then-President Nicolas Maduro in a dramatic nighttime raid.
The Venezuelan delegation's focus was on restructuring its billions of dollars in sovereign debt as it met US officials, multilateral lenders and companies.
Trump used his speech to the body dedicated to global peace to declare that in Venezuela: "to the victor belong the spoils," and called an oil deal the US signed with Caracas last month "perhaps the biggest deal ever made."
As Rodriguez and Trump met in New York, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado made three unsuccessful bids to return to her country.
Surprise absence of Sudanese army chief
The biggest surprise absence was the Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. The US withheld his visa in a move that Sudanese and other sources said was linked to a US-backed ceasefire proposal that Khartoum has resisted.
The dispute, first reported by Reuters, threatened to deepen tensions between Washington and Sudan's army at a critical moment in the civil war, which the UN calls the world's largest humanitarian crisis.
Burhan had represented Sudan at the General Assembly since the coup. Another notable absentee was Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, who addressed delegates by video and condemned US curbs on the Palestinian mission's access to the UN.
UN's future uncertain as funding crisis continues
The cash-strapped United Nations may no longer be in "freefall," but it remains stuck in an "open-ended crisis," International Crisis Group analyst Richard Gowan said. The organization is grappling with shrinking budgets, waning influence and mounting geopolitical conflicts.
Wars in Ukraine and Iran rage on, while Trump has denounced the 193-member body as bloated and globalist, slashed US funding and withdrawn from dozens of UN agencies.
As UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres received a standing ovation after his final General Assembly speech, a small group of politicians and former UN officials lobbied publicly and behind closed doors to succeed him. His second five-year term ends on December 31, leaving little time for the world's major powers to agree on a replacement.
The race, conducted according to an arcane multi-step process involving "straw polls," has no clear frontrunner, but former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan and Guyana's UN Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett are leading the pack.
Whoever gets the world's most difficult job will inherit an organization buffeted by crises, low morale, and declining political relevance. That person, too, will welcome the leaders to New York for next year's summit.

Aspendos excavations reveal 6,000-year-old settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:17:15 UTC
16:17:15 KST

The ancient city is best known for its nearly 2,000-year-old Roman theater, considered among the best-preserved ancient theaters in Anatolia.
Recent excavations at Aspendos have revealed that the site was inhabited as early as 6,000 years ago.
Located in the Serik district of the southern province of Antalya, Aspendos, an ancient city known for its exceptionally well-preserved theater and aqueducts, was one of the important cities of ancient Pamphylia. Excavations are being conducted under the direction of Mustafa Bilgin, an associate professor at Afyon Kocatepe University, as part of the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Heritage for the Future Project.
The ancient city is best known for its nearly 2,000-year-old Roman theater, considered among the best-preserved ancient theaters in Anatolia. It also features aqueducts, an agora, a monumental fountain, a temple, a stadium, a council building and an ancient theater street. Recent excavations have also uncovered a depiction of the river god Eurymedon dating to the third century, adding to the site’s archaeological significance.
The discoveries have pushed the known history of settlement at Aspendos back well before the Iron Age.
Bilgin told state-run Anadolu that the ancient theater was a rare example in Anatolian and Mediterranean archaeology because it has retained nearly all of its architectural elements.
He said most of the structures are standing almost to roof level, while monumental structures reflecting the landscape of the period can still be seen on the acropolis.
“Through our recent excavations, we understood that the history of the ancient city dates back 6,000 years from today,” Bilgin said.
“This fertile geography was not an area that had only been settled from the Iron Age onward. We realized this, and it was an important archaeological finding for us,” he said.
Archaeologists found evidence dating to the Late Chalcolithic Period in soundings beneath the floors of two-story shops, Bilgin said.
“Plates, bowls and various tools from that period revealed that the historical past of Aspendos’ acropolis dates back to 3500-4000 B.C.,” he said.
Bilgin described Aspendos as a “multilayered archaeological site,” noting that most of its structures have survived in a form consistent with their identity in antiquity.
“This makes Aspendos an important destination in terms of tourism and archaeology,” he said.
The site has also drawn increased visitor interest since the Culture and Tourism Ministry introduced night museum visits.
“Visiting the ancient theater and monumental structures at night, in that atmosphere, is very enjoyable for visitors,” he said.

====================================================================================================

Israel’s October 7 lesson: How a state can survive in a volatile Middle East - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:17:05 UTC
16:17:05 KST

In the Middle East, a state that desires peace cannot assume it will live in peace, and a state that avoids war cannot assume war will avoid it.
Alliances in this region change rapidly. Stable states sit beside fragile states, militias, and ideological groups. The interests of major powers tangle with the conflicts of regional powers. A state may find itself pulled into a confrontation it did not choose, or watch its territory, economy, and infrastructure become a tool for one party to pressure another.
The question of national security therefore goes beyond preventing a war. It concerns stopping danger before it fully forms, discouraging an adversary from exploiting it, and ensuring the state can still function if all safeguards fail and the blow lands.
Israel offers the clearest example of this dynamic, given its location, geography, and the history of conflict around it.
Since its founding, the country has contended with limited strategic depth. The history of confrontation on its borders means a major security failure carries different consequences than the same failure would in states with more territory and greater distance from front lines.
Israel’s security doctrine has historically rested on deterrence, warning, decisiveness, and defense. Prevention later gained a larger role.
The October 7, 2023, Hamas-led massacre did more than add a new element to that doctrine. It exposed the danger of trusting an adversary to remain deterred, and the danger of treating an assessment of intentions as a security guarantee.
It revived an old truth in Israeli thinking: the latitude you grant your enemy today may become tomorrow the danger that catches your state unprepared.
Permanent preparedness or repeated failure
After that day, the entire cost calculus changed. For Israel, the question was no longer a simple tradeoff between high military readiness and a calm period that allows lower spending. It became a choice between the cost of permanent preparedness and the risk of repeating a failure whose consequences could far outweigh the money saved during quiet years.
Deterrence stays essential, intelligence more so, and military readiness cannot drop to a level that would require months to rebuild when a crisis starts. This carries a heavy economic, social, and political price. It has come to be seen as the cost of lowering the chance of surprise, rather than a burden that can be put off indefinitely.
Prevention by definition does not begin after danger strikes or a breach occurs. At that point, the state has already moved from stopping danger to managing its aftermath.
Prevention begins much earlier, before rockets launch and before fighters cross borders. It begins when capability takes shape in weapons stockpiles, smuggling routes, command and funding structures, training sites and positioning areas, and in rocket and drone systems that build up under cover of waiting.
Prevention, in this sense, does not mean unlimited use of force. It means targeting a specific capability that poses an operational danger before it matures into a full threat.
The lessons from Israel’s experience apply elsewhere. The same geopolitical conditions, in varying degrees, impose a similar logic on other states in the region.
The recent Gulf war demonstrated that location, wealth, international ties, and balanced policies offer no complete immunity when the region erupts. Iran targeted Gulf states and their vital economic infrastructure as part of a broader confrontation with the United States and Israel.
The Gulf, in one aspect of this strategy, became an area that could be hurt so that political and economic pain would reach Washington, the West, and global markets.
The lesson is stark. A state can declare it wants no confrontation, open channels for mediation, and maintain relations with opposing parties. That does not force its adversary to read the situation the same way.
If the adversary believes striking it will pressure a larger power or raise the cost of war for others, the state may become a target despite having no role in starting the conflict.
Iran has specifically shown its calculations change when the cost of action becomes tangible, and when it believes the other side can reach its centers of gravity and inflict damage hard to absorb. Deterrence here does not come from good intentions. It comes from a capability the adversary knows exists and must account for in its planning.
Even so, deterrence offers no complete protection. What happens if one rocket gets through defenses and hits a major power station? What if a desalination plant, data center, or port central to trade movement goes offline?
At that moment, another test appears that aircraft and missiles alone cannot settle: the state’s ability to continue after receiving the blow.
Here, the meaning of strength also changes. What matters is not only keeping the adversary from reaching its target, but making the adversary know that hitting the target will not produce the desired result. The more alternatives and backup capacity a state has, the less effective any single blow becomes.
Inflicting damage differs from paralyzing a state. Real preparation starts years before a crisis, with sufficient stockpiles, repair capacity, and institutions that know how to operate when basic services fail.
No matter how strong domestic capacity grows, international alliances remain an important part of the security equation.
Alliances carry weight. They cannot replace domestic capacity, however. An ally may supply weapons and intelligence. It cannot manage a state’s internal crises or restart systems that have broken down inside it.
In this sense, Israel’s experience amounts to more than a special case. It serves as an early testing ground for questions that states across the region have begun to face in their own ways.
The requirement is not to copy Israel. Differences in geography, society, and politics make that pointless. The requirement is to grasp the lesson that its environment forced on it decades ago, and that October 7 brought forcefully back to attention.
Security costs money. Intelligence costs money. Ready armies cost money. Creating alternatives, stockpiles, and redundant vital structures also costs money. Discovering the need for these things after war begins, however, usually proves the costliest option of all.
The Middle East grants its states no permanent guarantees. This is not a call for militarization of the region or for treating war as unavoidable fate. It is a call for understanding the region as it is, not as we wish it were.
The most durable peace requires a state that resists blackmail and paralysis, and whose adversary knows that striking one of its assets will neither break its will nor disable its ability to continue.
This is the doctrine of the survivable state. In a region like ours, a state may not get to choose when the next crisis arrives.
It can decide today, however, whether to enter that crisis counting on it never happening, or prepared for it to happen and able to endure afterward without the adversary robbing it of its capacity to carry on.
The writer is a UAE political analyst and former Federal National Council candidate.

Why Israel must distinguish Iran’s Kurds from separatist movements - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:16:57 UTC
16:16:57 KST

As a journalist who spent years in newsrooms monitoring global geopolitical shifts, I do not doubt that Gideon Sa’ar is one of the most capable, accomplished, and strategically minded foreign ministers in the world today.
From Fiji to Kazakhstan and Colombia, his record reflects a profound understanding of diplomacy.
However, his recent remarks at a Jewish-Kurdish conference in London on September 6-7, 2026, regarding Iran’s Kurds represent a strategic error and a factual miscalculation, indicating that his advisers fail to comprehend the complex internal realities of Iran.
The problem is Israel’s failure to distinguish between the patriotic majority of Iranian Kurds and transnational Kurdish separatist movements.
Kermanshah: Largest Kurdish city and citadel of Iranian patriotism
Kermanshah, the most populous Kurdish city in Iran, is the undisputed citadel of Iranian patriotism, boasting a history filled with pride.
The Bisotun inscription, the masterpiece of Darius the Great and one of Iran’s oldest written historical records, stands proudly near Kermanshah.
This 2,500-year-old monument stands as living testimony that this land has been at the heart of Iran’s national sovereignty and identity since antiquity. Bisotun is a powerful symbol of Iran’s unity and grandeur.
Kermanshah’s centrality to Iranian national identity runs so deep that more than eight centuries after Darius carved Bisotun, the Sasanian monarchs chose Kermanshah to carve Taq-e Bostan.
Located in the heart of the modern city, this masterpiece remains one of the most precious and enduring jewels of Sasanian heritage.
While transnational separatist movements deliberately obscure the reality of major regions like Kermanshah and Ilam to overstate their own influence, the truth remains that the patriotic Kurdish majority across Iran consists of people deeply rooted in Iranian soil with an unbreakable bond of loyalty.
The Iranian-Jewish bond: A strategic asset for Israel
Through my daily work, I am in regular contact with Iranians from diverse regions, socio-economic backgrounds, and walks of life.
Despite not knowing one another, these individuals consistently echo a striking trend: rapidly growing trust in Israel.
Many Iranians now view Israel as the only actor with the determination and strategic clarity to directly confront the core of the regime’s power.
They see Israel’s approach as fundamentally different from powers that can simply pack up and leave the region; it is a strategy focused on confronting threats at their source.
This deep trust is not arbitrary. It is rooted in 2,500 years of shared history between Iran and the Jewish people, stretching back to the era of Cyrus the Great.
This civilizational bond remains strong to this day. A powerful modern testament to this civilizational solidarity occurred in the wake of the October 7 attacks.
As massive antisemitic demonstrations surged across Western cities, the Iranian diaspora stood firmly and courageously alongside Jews and Israelis.
In defiance of the hostile Left-Islamist crowds, the Iranian Lion and Sun flag was proudly raised side-by-side with the Star of David on Western streets, proving that the ancient alliance between these two peoples remains unbroken.
This profound bond is a priceless strategic asset for the State of Israel, one that must be continuously protected, defended, and nurtured against deliberate subversion.
By including Iran’s Kurds in rhetoric that flirts with separatist undertones, Sa’ar is stepping onto a psychological landmine.
This language triggers painful memories of the immediate aftermath of the 1979 revolution, when armed separatist Kurdish factions launched violent clashes in western Iran.
Crucially, this rhetoric causes the greatest outrage among Iran’s patriotic Kurdish majority. It was these patriotic Kurds who fought against the separatists after 1979, sacrificing their lives to preserve Iran’s territorial integrity.
Historically, Iran’s Kurdish population has been a bedrock of Iranian national identity and cultural heritage, consistently rejecting the regime’s attempts to question their loyalty to Iran’s territorial integrity.
To be Kurdish is to embody the most authentic narrative of being Iranian.
Transnational Kurdish separatist movements: PKK, Öcalan, Assad, and the Palestinian cause
Sa’ar’s advisers must understand that the separatist minority in Iran’s Kurdish regions largely views Abdullah Öcalan as the “Father of the Kurdish Nation.” A segment of these separatists operates as the Iranian branch of the PKK.
Let us look at the history: in the 1980s and 1990s, Hafez al-Assad utilized the PKK as a proxy, hosting Öcalan and establishing the group’s training camps in the Syrian-controlled Bekaa Valley in Lebanon.
During this era, the PKK operated as a Marxist-Leninist movement with direct organizational and training links to Palestinian militant factions. In 1982, PKK fighters deployed to the Bekaa front to fight directly against Israel.
This historical backdrop instilled an enduring anti-Western and anti-Israel paradigm within the movement’s DNA.
Even Öcalan’s recently reported stance in August 2026 has descended into structural antisemitism and conspiracy theories, framing Zionism as the barrier that prevented the formation of an independent Kurdish state following the fall of the Ottoman Empire.
This is historically absurd, given that World War I ended in 1918, while the State of Israel was established three decades later, in 1948.
This deeply rooted anti-Israel history of the PKK and its Syrian affiliate could have been a contributing factor in the Israeli government’s decision not to intervene during the collapse of the Syrian autonomous Kurdish administration in January 2026.
Civilizational continuity of Iran
Iran is not a manufactured twentieth-century state like Iraq or Syria.
As Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel famously observed, Iran is the first historical state in the world. It is a society with a deep institutional memory, a potent national consciousness, and a shared, deep-seated understanding of sovereignty.
The nationwide demonstrations of 2026 cut entirely across religion, language, and regional lines, completely shattering these divisive geopolitical calculations.
What emerged was not fragmentation, but a powerful “re-nationalisation,” a shared political identity centered squarely on the idea of Iran itself. One of the regime’s longest-standing strategies, dividing society through identity politics, has collapsed.
In that very same Kurdish city of Kermanshah, mass protests openly expressed support for Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, directly contradicting decades of state propaganda claiming that national unity was fragile.
Investing in marginal, discredited separatist factions will not enhance Israel’s security. Instead, it severely jeopardizes Jerusalem’s greatest strategic asset inside Iran: the trust of patriotic Iranians.
It is time for Sa’ar’s advisers to put on the lens of reality.
The writer is the communications director to Prince Reza Pahlavi and an Iranian journalist who previously served as editor-in-chief of news at Manoto TV, a UK-based Persian-language television network.

Aslanbay described Cappadocia as a major tourism destination, saying the region receives 4.5 million visitors and generates $2.5 billion in tourism revenue.
He said the Culture and Tourism Ministry believed Cappadocia had the potential to attract more visitors and generate greater tourism value.
“We believe we are achieving this by improving the valleys and introducing night museum visits,” Aslanbay said. “When we also repair the churches and incorporate a faith route, Cappadocia will receive the recognition it deserves in the world.”
The Cappadocia Area Presidency had previously carried out maintenance and restoration work on two other fairy chimneys.

Sometimes a chef’s greatest skill is knowing when not to intervene
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
07:16:33 UTC
16:16:33 KST

Chef Çiğdem Seferoğlu brings traditional recipes into the present at Hodan while taking care to preserve their original character with minimal intervention.
Hodan has moved from Beyoğlu to Nişantaşı. But the real change is not in its address; it is in the kitchen. Today, Çiğdem Seferoğlu is pursuing a cuisine that intervenes less and listens more. So is bringing a cuisine into the present about how much we can change a dish — or about knowing when to stop?
There is a story behind the bread currently arriving at the table at Hodan that is far more interesting than a chef-created recipe. On one of her visits to a garden outside Istanbul where she goes to buy vegetables, Çiğdem Seferoğlu was offered some bread the local women had made for themselves. The dough had been baked between vine leaves. Here, the leaves are not decorative: They form a layer between the dough and the heat, imparting a gently tart, vegetal aroma to the bread. Seferoğlu tasted it, was struck by it and brought the bread back to Hodan.
But this is where the important part of the story begins. Once she brought it into the restaurant, she resisted the temptation to turn it into a “chef’s creation.” What she had encountered, she felt, was less a recipe than a way of doing things, and she wanted to carry that knowledge to her own table with as little distortion as possible. Because sometimes, in her view, the best intervention a cook can make is not to intervene too much. She describes Hodan as “a cuisine of Istanbul and Anatolia with a memory, expressed in the language of today.”
After four and a half years in its historic Beyoğlu building, Hodan moved to Nişantaşı around two months ago. Yet the change at the new Hodan strikes me as more philosophical than physical. The early urge to say everything at once has given way to a desire to say less, but say it more clearly. To me, that is one of the clearest signs of a restaurant coming of age.
Part of that refinement lies in listening more carefully to the sources from which the kitchen draws its knowledge. In traditional cuisines, it is often impossible to identify the true author of a dish. Hodan’s içli köfte is a perfect example. The filling carries the knowledge of the Gaziantep family of Hasan, who has worked alongside Çiğdem for more than 15 years; the outer shell bears traces of Çiğdem’s own family and the Central Anatolian tradition of boiled içli köfte. Two families and two geographical memories meet in a single dish.
This is why one of Çiğdem’s favourite questions in the kitchen is: “How did you make this at home?” One cook’s mother fries the onions differently; another’s grandmother uses a different spice; in someone else’s hometown, the same ingredient is prepared using an entirely different technique. That knowledge enters the kitchen, where it is discussed, tested and eventually translated into the language of the restaurant. Seen this way, the chef ceases to be the person who creates everything and becomes part curator, part researcher and part custodian of inherited knowledge.
At a special dinner Hodan recently hosted with Miele, a brand the restaurant has worked with for years, Çiğdem spoke about the dishes that have become Hodan’s “masterpieces” over time. But what constitutes a restaurant masterpiece? Is it the dish made with the most expensive ingredients, the most technically accomplished plate, or the one that, years later, you still cannot bring yourself to remove from the menu because it has become inseparable from the identity of the restaurant? At Hodan, the answer is closer to the third.
The artichoke is one of them. It is first cooked in the simplest, most traditional way, then breaded and fried. The memory of the ingredient remains intact while another layer of technique is added. Tarama opens another door into the cuisine of Istanbul: Served on cornbread with truffle purée, it brings together flavours that might initially seem distant without erasing the character of the tarama itself. Vegetables, meanwhile, have always been Hodan’s quieter masterpieces. Artichokes, chard, borage and fennel are not garnishes placed beside meat; they are ingredients considered important enough to command the centre of the plate in their own right.
It is here that Hodan’s understanding of what it means to be contemporary becomes clearest. “Bringing something into the present does not mean correcting what came before,” Çiğdem says. It is an important distinction. Traditional cuisines are sometimes approached with a curious sense of superiority, as though a dish made for centuries is finally going to be “improved” once it passes through the hands of a contemporary chef. Yet many of these recipes are the result of geography, climate, scarcity and abundance, the need to preserve food and generations of trial and error.
So where is the line? How far can you change an içli köfte, an artichoke or a tarama before it ceases to be itself? For Çiğdem, the answer lies in taste memory. The recipe can change, as can the technique, the presentation and even some of the ingredients. But if someone who grew up eating that dish tastes it and feels no sense of recognition, then you have made something else. Sometimes the entire memory of a dish is held in the smell of onions browning in a pan; sometimes in the acidity of yoghurt or the lingering flavour of butter. Once the memory disappears, all that remains is technique.
The direction Hodan is now taking is really an extension of the same idea. Its kitchen garden in Beykoz has transformed the restaurant’s relationship with produce: Fennel root and fronds, chard, cabbage, borage… The future promises more plants, more producers and greater sensitivity to the seasons — but, conversely, a little less intervention. Because innovation does not always mean adding something. Sometimes it means understanding the history of a dish well enough to remove what it does not need; sometimes it means genuinely listening to someone else’s knowledge; and sometimes it means having the restraint to encounter a loaf of bread baked between vine leaves and leave it largely as it is.
Perhaps this is where a chef truly comes of age: Not when they learn to make their signature more visible on every plate, but when they become confident enough to step back and let it disappear from some of them.

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday addressed for the first time European concerns that Russia could escalate its confrontation with Western European countries, categorically rejecting the possibility. Responding to warnings voiced in Europe over the past week about the possibility of a direct military confrontation with Russia, Putin said: "Many in Europe say they expect an attack by the Russian Federation and therefore must prepare for military action, for war with Russia. I want to emphasize once again that we are not preparing for any military action against Europe. We have no such plans. Most importantly, there is no reason for it."
Putin nevertheless heightened tensions with the Baltic states by mocking a statement by Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem, who said his country must be prepared to repel any attack and "destroy anyone who crosses the border."
"This is a provocation," Putin said. "The circus has already left, but the clowns remain."
Putin's remarks came hours after Russia's state-run RIA Novosti news agency removed an opinion column in which the author threatened another Baltic state, Lithuania, with a blitzkrieg and nuclear strike. The column was removed after several hours, with the agency saying it did not conform to its editorial position or the official policy of the Russian Federation.
One scenario raised in the West this week is that Russia and its ally Belarus could attempt to seize the Suwalki Gap, the strip of territory between Poland and Lithuania that separates Belarus from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and provides the Baltic states' only land connection to the rest of NATO.
The deleted column was written by commentator Alexander Nosovich after Lithuania's parliament moved this week to advance a proposal that would lift the country's ban on stationing nuclear weapons on its territory.
The column, headlined "Russia is in for another special military operation. It will be very short," said in part: "European countries continue to push the issue of moving unconventional weapons to Russia's borders and have chosen a country willing to become a nuclear depot."
Nosovich went on to threaten Lithuania with an invasion and even a nuclear strike.
"Russia can even afford to forgo deploying ground troops. Just missiles with the appropriate warheads," he wrote. "The solution is not merely quick, it is lightning-fast. Don't think too much about seconds."
Elsewhere in the column, Nosovich described Lithuania as "a suicidal country with no brains whatsoever," a "useful idiot" and "a small but proud kamikaze in Russia's near abroad."
Shortly after publication, however, the column was deleted. Anyone visiting the original link on RIA Novosti's website encountered an editor's note saying: "The article by freelance author Alexander Nosovich was removed from the website because it did not correspond to the editorial board's views, editorial policy or the official policy of the Russian Federation."
Before it was removed, the threatening column circulated on social media and caused alarm among parts of the Lithuanian public. An official Lithuanian military spokesperson issued a statement seeking to reassure the public: "In light of Russia's propaganda statement, we remind you that Russia routinely tries to intimidate its neighbors using hostile rhetoric. This is a common Russian practice, and no additional action should be taken as a result of these remarks."
Over the past roughly 35 years, Russia has lost much of its strategic position around the Baltic Sea. The former Soviet republics of Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia joined NATO in the early 2000s. About two decades later, Finland and Sweden abandoned decades of military nonalignment and joined the alliance. Russia's Baltic Sea coastline now includes the Kaliningrad exclave, whose land connections to the rest of Russia require transit through neighboring countries.
'Ukraine as cannon fodder'
Turning to the war in Ukraine, Putin said Friday that before there could be progress toward a settlement, Kyiv must "feel the power of Russia's retaliatory strikes" following Ukraine's massive drone attack on Moscow this week.
The Ukrainian attack came on the final day of Russia's parliamentary "elections," in which Putin's United Russia party won as expected.
"Polling stations were attacked," Putin said. "One of the attacks targeted a school where there was a polling station. They began attacking the homes of regional election commission chairs. In one case, a regional commission chair was wounded, her husband was wounded and her child was wounded. In another case, unfortunately, it ended in tragedy and an election commission chair was killed. We must make Kyiv understand that strikes deep inside Russian territory will only make the situation worse."
Addressing the role of Western European countries in the war in Ukraine, Putin said: "They want Ukraine to continue serving as cannon fodder, as a tool in the struggle against Russia."
Putin also showed no willingness to accept a proposal to halt reciprocal attacks on energy facilities in Russia and Ukraine.
"They have no means to counter our advanced weapons or to end the blockade we have imposed on their Black Sea coast," he said. "They need to remember that they are the ones who started all of this."

"The conclusion of the agreement would create the necessary legal conditions for further development of joint control, including for Ukrainian border and customs services to operate on Polish territory.
This issue is becoming particularly relevant amid constant Russian attacks on the Ukrainian border and transport infrastructure," the ministry said.

Bangkok authorities have declared a flood disaster across the Thai capital after almost 48 hours of heavy rain overwhelmed canals, submerged roads and flooded homes and businesses.
The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) declared all 50 districts disaster zones on Saturday, giving local organisations special powers to respond.
The governor urged residents to stay home after almost 300 millimetres of rain fell since Thursday afternoon, while Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said he was cutting short a trip to London to return.
Almost continuous rain has swollen Bangkok’s network of canals, sending murky water into surrounding homes, restaurants, shops and alleyways.
Numerous major roads were flooded on Saturday, AFP reporters saw, with residents forced to wade through knee- or sometimes thigh-deep water in several neighbourhoods.
“The water keeps coming in. It’s hard to go out now. It’s like at my waist level now,” said Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old vendor who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok.
“I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now,” she said.
Although her neighbourhood often floods, she said: “I think this time is worse than the 2011 flood.”
Widespread flooding across Thailand in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes.
In Bangkok’s Ari neighbourhood, motorbike rider Samruay Nakkamnueng said the flooding had disrupted his journey to work.
“I woke up to go to work and the street in front of my house was flooded,” he said. “I worried if my motorbike would be able to wade through this much floodwater.”
In On Nut neighbourhood, an AFP reporter saw residents filling sandbags to protect their homes and businesses.
Authorities said they had prepared one million sandbags for distribution and opened several temporary shelters in schools.
'Every canal filled'
Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said the east of the city had been hardest hit and warned that more rain was forecast.
“The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out,” he said on social media on Saturday morning.
“The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled.”
Water levels later began to stabilise as the city’s pumping stations operated at full capacity, moving a combined 1,200 cubic metres of water per second, the BMA said.
“If there is no additional rainfall, the situation is expected to improve within six hours,” it said in a lunchtime update.
Chadchart urged bedridden patients who depend on life-saving medical equipment to consider temporarily moving to hospital and advised residents to move their cars to higher ground.
Bangkok’s public transport authority offered free parking at MRT park-and-ride facilities until October 2 so residents could protect their vehicles.
Once dubbed the “Venice of the East” for its canals, Bangkok is built on former marshland and sits about 1.5 metres above sea level.
Wetter than usual
Municipal workers were out on Saturday clearing rubbish to keep drains flowing.
“Our job is to make sure rubbish along the road doesn’t block the drains, so the water can drain away quickly,” said Kwan Nobnom, one of a group wearing bright orange raincoats.
“We thought this year would be dry, so we didn’t expect the flooding to be this bad.”
September marks the peak of Bangkok’s rainy season, but rainfall has been heavier than usual, according to the city’s drainage and sewage department.
The capital recorded 487 millimetres of rain between September 1 and 25, compared with an average of almost 269 millimetres for the same period between 1991 and 2020.
The Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation warned that low pressure would affect eastern, northeastern and central Thailand until Sunday, bringing a risk of flash floods, forest runoff, mudslides and overflowing rivers.
Scientists warn that extreme weather events will become more frequent and intense as fossil fuel emissions continue to heat the planet.

====================================================================================================

Palestinian family dismantles 40-year-old farm under Israeli demolition threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
06:36:55 UTC
15:36:55 KST

More than 500 volunteers have helped dismantle structures at a Palestinian farm in the occupied West Bank after Israeli authorities ordered their demolition, threatening to charge the owners if the army carried out the work.
The volunteers worked over three days at Hakoortna farm in western Tulkarem before the Al-Tanib family obtained a temporary court order suspending the demolition pending a hearing.
Established more than 40 years ago, the farm lies near Israel’s separation wall in the northern occupied West Bank and is surrounded by Israeli industrial facilities.
For decades, it has supported the family’s livelihood while serving as a site for agricultural training and student visits.
Short deadline before demolition
Farm owner Fayez Awad al-Tanib said that Israeli authorities issued a demolition order on September 16, giving the family a deadline to dismantle the structures themselves.
“The family was told that if it failed to comply, the Israeli army would carry out the demolition using its machinery and charge the family for the cost,” he said.
The order followed an August 2025 notice directing the family to halt work on several agricultural structures ahead of their removal. With assistance from the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center, the family began legal proceedings to challenge the measures.
Al-Tanib said Israeli authorities cited “security grounds” related to the farm’s proximity to the separation wall, arguing that some structures obstructed visibility and others had been built without permits.
The family disputed any suggestion that the structures were new, saying many dated from between 1984 and 1995.
Three days of dismantling before freeze
As the deadline approached, more than 500 volunteers spent three days dismantling greenhouses and other agricultural structures, emptying fish ponds and moving beehives and tree-cultivation equipment to save what they could before demolition machinery arrived.
“The work continued into the evening, while the family emptied fish ponds and moved whatever equipment and structures could be dismantled,” al-Tanib said.
Most of the structures covered by the demolition order had already been taken apart when the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center informed the family that it had obtained a temporary court order suspending the demolition.
“We dismantled everything out of fear of the demolition, and then we received a decision freezing it,” he said.
The centre said the Jerusalem District Court issued the temporary order following an urgent petition by its lawyers and scheduled a hearing for December 17.
The order does not cancel the demolition decision but temporarily suspends the implementation until the court considers the petition.
Four decades of farming and education
Al-Tanib began working and managing the land in 1984 after his father’s death. Together with his family, he later developed it into a farm using organic agricultural methods and reducing its reliance on fertilisers and chemicals.
According to al-Tanib, Hakoortna covers around 32 dunams, equivalent to 32,000 square metres or 7.9 acres. Around 10 dunams are planted with citrus trees and another 10 with other fruit trees.
The farm also includes greenhouses, fish ponds, beehives and a two-storey agricultural house, with each floor covering around 120 square metres.
Over the decades, Hakoortna grew into a centre for agricultural training and education as well as food production.
“Tens of thousands of children had visited the farm, along with university students specialising in agriculture who sometimes spent up to four months a year training there,” said al-Tanib.
Separation wall, industrial facilities
The family said conditions at the farm changed significantly after Israel began constructing the separation wall in 2002, leading to the loss of part of its land and restrictions on access and agricultural work.
Hakoortna now lies between the wall and Israeli industrial facilities. Al-Tanib said repeated measures against the farm threaten his family’s ability to remain on the land.
“They want to uproot us from the farm and remove us from it to clear the way for the chemical factories,” he said.
Israeli authorities, according to what the family was told, said the measures concerning the farm are based on security and planning considerations as well as permit-related issues.
The family also blames nearby factories for environmental damage to its land and crops over the years.
Most of the wall’s route runs inside the occupied West Bank rather than along the Green Line separating it from Israel. An Israeli system of permits and gates regulates farmers’ access to agricultural land isolated by the barrier.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has documented how these restrictions disrupt essential agricultural work, including plowing, pruning, fertilising and harvesting, particularly in the northern West Bank’s Tulkarem governorate.
In a 2004 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found that Israel’s construction of the wall within the occupied Palestinian territory and its associated regime violated international law. Israel contends that the wall was built for security reasons to prevent attacks.
Demolitions accelerate across occupied West Bank
Since the beginning of 2026,, Israeli authorities have demolished or forced Palestinians to demolish 1,164 structures for lacking Israeli-issued permits, displacing more than 1,500 people, according to OCHA. The agency says such permits are nearly impossible for Palestinians to obtain.
In August alone, Israeli authorities carried out 71 demolition operations affecting 155 Palestinian structures, including 61 agricultural structures and 33 used as sources of livelihood, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
According to OCHA, the average number of structures demolished each month in Area C and East Jerusalem since 2024 has been at least double the monthly average recorded during the previous 15 years, indicating an acceleration in demolitions.

Sustainable development impossible without peace: Iran FM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
06:27:42 UTC
15:27:42 KST

Addressing a high-level meeting of the Global Development Initiative on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Friday, Araghchi said the need to put development at the heart of international cooperation has never been more urgent.
“Developing countries continue to face persistent poverty and hunger, widening inequalities, rising debt burdens, gaps in financing and technology, and growing environmental challenges,” he said.
“These pressures have been further intensified by conflicts, protectionist policies, unilateral coercive measures, acts of aggression and the use of force, undermining development prospects and reversing hard-won development gains,” the Iranian foreign minister added.
Araghchi also noted that development cannot thrive in an environment shaped by war, coercion, and unilateralism.
“Developing countries need financial resources, technology, knowledge and cooperation, not more barriers,” he said.
He also censured the continued use of unilateral coercive measures as a tool of political pressure against developing countries.
“Iran has faced such measures for decades, and they have intensified over recent years and months,” he said, adding that US sanctions restricting trade, financial resources, medicine, technology, education and scientific cooperation directly affect the daily lives of the Iranian people.
“From our perspective, the devastating impact of these measures on ordinary people constitutes economic terrorism,” Araghchi said. “The United Nations must stand against such coercive measures and call for their complete and unconditional lifting.”
Araghchi also condemned the ongoing US-Israeli aggression against Iran as “a clear violation of international law and the UN Charter.”
He said the attacks have killed thousands, including women and children, and destroyed civilian and vital infrastructure, causing severe economic, social and environmental damage.
Referring to several sites hit during the attacks, including a primary school in the southern city of Minab where 168 students were killed, Iran’s Pasteur Institute and a sports complex in Lamerd, in Fars province, Araghchi said places representing “education, health and hope” have been turned into scenes of “blood, death and destruction.”

Italy charges three adults, 14 minors with neo-Nazi, white supremacist activity-linked offenses
Unknown

Three adults and 14 minors were charged with training for terrorist activities, incitement to commit hate crimes, and propaganda after an Italian General Investigations and Special Operations Division (DIGOS) investigation into online neo-Nazi and white supremacist groups, the Italian state police announced on Friday.
DIGOS officers in multiple areas of Italy executed search warrants on the suspects' computers and belongings. They uncovered bladed weapons, paraphernalia with Nazi symbolism, and electronic devices used to spread propaganda.
Italian authorities launched the investigation after monitoring online channels linked to accelerationist, white supremacist, and neo-Nazi ideologies.
According to the police, the suspects actively participated in two groups on a private social network.
Suspects engaged in Holocaust denial, discussed white supremacist attacks
One group was active chatrooms tied to the “New European Order,” a movement based on Nazi propaganda, white supremacy, and antisemitism. The chatrooms focused on Holocaust denial, Nazi ideology, and the dissemination of instructions for making explosive devices.
The other suspects engaged in online communities for the Italian Fascist Front, a group that promotes hatred and violence towards Jewish people, people of color, and the LGBTQ+ community, according to the DIGOS investigation.
In the online groups and chatrooms, the suspects praised Adolf Hitler and discussed details of attacks carried out by white supremacist extremists, including weapons and tactics used.
The suspects also shared instructions for handling guns and knives, as well as manuals for making and detonating homemade explosives designed to maximize lethal impact.
The suspects also played online games together in which they recreated simulations of violence and attacks against minority groups.

====================================================================================================

Saudi Arabia’s security needs expose limits of diplomacy, give Israel an opportunity - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
06:24:47 UTC
15:24:47 KST

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has weapons and enough money to buy more, but the crisis with the Houthis is showing him how difficult it is to buy something else: a country willing to use force to defend him from Iran and its proxies.
Twice on the same day at the beginning of the month, bin Salman called US President Donald Trump and asked him to attack the Houthis. The American president refused, agreeing instead to provide intelligence assistance and targeting information. Ten days later, he came much closer to intervention: targets had been selected, bombs had been loaded onto American aircraft, and a strike in Yemen was about to begin. At the last moment, Trump halted it.
The Saudis returned to bombing Yemen. It did not solve the problem. Britain sent a refueling aircraft to temporarily support the defensive operations of the Saudi Air Force; Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s Turkey and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s Pakistan expressed support for Riyadh, and Ankara announced that it was prepared to assist with technical military needs under the defense agreement signed between the countries.
Riyadh has no shortage of friends willing to stand beside it. Far fewer are willing to enter a war themselves.
The limits of Saudi Arabia’s security strategy
Three and a half years ago, it appeared that bin Salman had found a formula. After years of confrontation with Iran, Saudi Arabia reached a reconciliation agreement with Tehran mediated by China. The logic was simple: since there was no certainty that the US would aid it in every crisis, Riyadh sought to reduce the number of crises it might face in the first place.
At the same time, it expanded ties with China, Russia, Turkey and Pakistan. On August 7, it signed a joint defense agreement in Mecca with Ankara and Islamabad, stating that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be considered an attack against all three.
America remained the main security pillar. Saudi Arabia continued buying weapons from Washington and relying on it, while simultaneously acquiring several additional insurance policies of its own.
Now comes the moment of reckoning. The question is what each of these policies is worth when missiles begin falling: weapons and intelligence, air defense, soldiers, or a statement of support. During peacetime, it is easier to blur the differences. During war, they are exposed quickly.
The Houthis are targeting Saudi Arabia’s economic foundations
The reconciliation with Tehran did not stop the Houthis, and the Mecca defense agreement has so far not brought Turkey and Pakistan into the war. Riyadh is not necessarily expecting a Turkish division to race toward Sanaa. The more immediate problem is air defense: Saudi Arabia is seeking interceptors and assistance against Houthi missiles and drones from its allies, after prolonged fighting in the region has also depleted American stocks.
It also needs intelligence, early warning capabilities and protection for energy infrastructure. The practical value of its new alliances will be measured by this assistance.
For bin Salman, the insult is the less important part. The bill presented by the crisis to the kingdom is far more concerning. The Houthis threaten two of the foundations on which bin Salman has built his new Saudi Arabia: security and business.
The war brings back the old security risk precisely as the crown prince tries to convince the world that the new Saudi Arabia is a place where it is possible to invest for the long term. Ultimately, he needs investors, tourists and international company executives to continue viewing the kingdom as stable enough to invest in.
Vision 2030, the future cities, tourism, foreign investment, business centers and ports, the entire Saudi project of the past decade, is based on the assumption that the kingdom can transform itself from a country living from crisis to crisis into a place that is boring in the best sense of the word: stable, predictable and open to capital.
Missiles over Riyadh and war in Bab al-Mandab are a poor advertisement for that product.
Oil also returned to remind everyone who still pays the bills. For decades, Saudi Arabia invested in the East-West Pipeline, a roughly 1,200-km route built to let the kingdom bypass the Strait of Hormuz during a crisis and transport oil from the Gulf to Yanbu on the Red Sea.
The more Riyadh used it, the more important the western route became, and the more exposure it brought. In June, 92% of Saudi crude oil exports by sea passed through the Yanbu terminal. The East-West Pipeline, which became a central artery after disruptions in Hormuz, carried four million to five million barrels per day. Until September 11, when drones arriving from Iraq struck three of its pumping stations, temporarily halting oil flows through the pipeline.
At the same time, the Houthis are pressuring the western export route. In July, they announced a naval boycott against Saudi shipping, and the multinational maritime task force warned that they had moved from threats to active attacks against vessels identified with Saudi Arabia and its interests.
Riyadh was forced to reroute oil exports destined for Asia through the Suez Canal, significantly lengthening the journey compared with passage through Bab al-Mandab.
Shipowners, insurers and trading companies do not need a sinking vessel to change course. The possibility that the Houthis will choose them as targets is enough. The risk immediately enters the price: insurance becomes more expensive, voyages become longer, and the advantage of the shorter route through the Red Sea is eroded.
Sometimes the missile can remain on the launcher. The Houthis only need to create a credible and sustained risk to cause economic damage far greater than the force they invest.
Riyadh has found itself inside an almost perfect geographical trap: Hormuz is disrupted in the east, three pumping stations on the pipeline designed to bypass it have been hit, and in the west the Houthis are threatening the export route through the Red Sea.
The alternatives Saudi Arabia built over years to spread its risk are now exposed themselves.
Saudi Arabia does not lack oil. It is harder to guarantee the route that carries it to the market. Geography does not give bin Salman any favors. Saudi Arabia can buy more aircraft and interceptors, but it cannot move Hormuz or Bab al-Mandab.
Freedom of navigation largely determines how much of its economic power it can truly realize.
The Houthis' continued dependence on Tehran for weapons and funding still them. Control of the coast, ports and energy resources, alongside revenues and the millions of residents under their rule, would give them far greater freedom of action.
Their goals have long extended beyond another hill in Yemen. After taking control of Mocha and advancing along the coast, the fighting in Taiz is important because the province is a junction between areas controlled by the government and allows forces and supplies to move.
To the east lies Marib, a longstanding strategic target for the Houthis and one of the most important remaining strongholds held by their rivals. Yemen’s main oil and gas fields are located there. A future takeover would harm the government’s economic base and give the Houthis a more independent source of income.
Their achievements also stem from the weakness of the Yemeni forces fighting them and from Saudi Arabia and its partners’ reluctance to become entangled again in a long war.
In this asymmetric conflict, the Houthis do not need to conquer Riyadh, sink the Saudi navy, or defeat its air force. They only need to survive and exhaust their opponents. The longer the campaign continues, the more it works in their favor.
That is the story behind the renewed war in Yemen.
Israel sees an opportunity in intelligence and defense cooperation
Israel has something to offer in this situation. For years, Israel sought to convince the Saudis that the shared threat from Iran was more serious than the disagreements between them. Now Iran and its proxy in Yemen are providing a practical demonstration of that argument.
In Jerusalem, the potential is easy to identify. Saudi needs meet areas in which Israel has a clear advantage: intelligence on the Houthis, operational experience against them, detection and interception systems, and years of experience connecting intelligence with long-range strikes.
For years, a regional alliance was discussed in ceremonial terms: leaders, flags, signatures and ambassadors. In practice, it could begin in a much less ceremonial way: a system that detects a threat, an alert delivered in time, tracking a target, and an interceptor launched into the sky.
The diplomats can come later.
Jerusalem should only be careful not to fall in love with its own thesis. In Israel, there is sometimes a tendency to view every security-related convergence of interests with Saudi Arabia as a step toward diplomatic relations.
Bin Salman can benefit from Israeli capabilities against the Houthis while at the same time managing his relationship with Israel according to a much broader calculation: the Palestinians, public opinion, his standing in the Arab world and the price he seeks from Washington.
Riyadh is not simply sitting and waiting for better conditions for a deal with Israel. In recent months, it has identified more risks than opportunities in normalization.
In a poll published in August 2025, 99% of Saudi respondents described establishing “normal relations and peace” with Israel as a negative step. The Saudi leadership has also stated that it will not establish diplomatic relations with Israel without a Palestinian state along the 1967 lines with east Jerusalem as its capital.
At the same time, improved relations with the Trump administration allow Riyadh to seek significant American benefits without paying for them through normalization.
A Houthi missile could change Riyadh’s security priorities. It does not erase the political calculation.
Even if the Saudis need Israeli capabilities, that does not mean normalization will advance with it. Bin Salman could receive intelligence, warnings, or operational coordination with American assistance in the future while keeping an Israeli embassy outside Riyadh.
For him, these are two different decisions with different prices.
Israel has become accustomed to thinking about security cooperation as a corridor that ends with normalization. The route may be longer and more complicated: the Saudis may work with Israelis where interests overlap, while publicly maintaining distance as long as domestic legitimacy and the ambition to lead the Arab world require it.
Even so, Israel can accumulate long-term assets in warning systems, intelligence, air defense and freedom of navigation. In the Middle East, security establishments have already found common ground long before leaders agreed to be photographed together.
But Israel’s interest in Yemen is broader than its relationship with Riyadh.
The Houthis have managed over time to harm freedom of navigation to Eilat. Direct commercial activity at the port was severely affected, and even after Israeli strikes in Yemen, major shipping companies have not returned to the route on a significant scale.
The threat to Bab al-Mandab has intensified as the Houthis expanded their control along the western coast.
Mocha, Taiz and Marib are also connected to Israel’s strategic map. The more the Houthis hold the coast and resources, the closer they come to a situation in which they can maintain a long-term threat to the southern gateway of the Red Sea and rely more heavily on their own revenues.
Marib and Mocha are thousands of kilometers from Eilat, but the strategic distance between them has narrowed significantly. Developments there affect the Houthis’ ability to finance forces, hold territory and pressure shipping routes connecting Eilat to the Indian Ocean.
The range of missiles and drones, together with Houthi control of the coast, makes the number of kilometers less reassuring.
Stable Houthi control over the coast, ports and resources could create a problem for Israel in the far south that resembles, in some ways, the challenge it has faced in the north: an armed organization backed by Iran but with its own interests and decision-making ability, holding territory, missiles and drones, and capable of applying pressure on an economic artery without defeating the IDF on the battlefield.
The Saudi story also offers Jerusalem a less comfortable lesson.
The rejection bin Salman received in Washington could increase the value of Israeli capabilities in his eyes, but it is also worth examining what happened between Riyadh and Washington.
The debate in Washington is not theoretical. The prolonged war with Iran depleted American interceptor stocks, and Saudi Arabia itself is now seeking missile-defense systems from its allies.
Opening another campaign against the Houthis would require the US to dedicate more aircraft, munitions, and defensive systems to a theater where it is currently attempting to remain behind the scenes.
And in November, Trump faces midterm elections.
Washington is assisting Riyadh and is currently avoiding taking responsibility for the war in Yemen. It can maintain that position as long as the Saudis contain the Houthis and the economic damage remains manageable.
A more serious disruption to oil routes and energy prices would make that choice more complicated.
Israel’s position in Washington is different from Saudi Arabia’s, as are the depth of its ties and its military capabilities. The differences are significant. Still, no American president decides to use force on behalf of an ally without calculating the American interest, the cost, the duration of the campaign, and the military’s other missions.
This week, Trump met in New York with leaders and representatives from Gulf states and other countries in the region, with Iran and the regional war at the center of the diplomatic agenda.
At the same time, Qatar is pushing for a regional security framework that would include Iran, while Saudi Arabia is advancing an idea for a regional nonaggression agreement with Tehran.
After months of war and disruptions in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, Gulf states are seeking protection from Iran while simultaneously trying to reduce the possibility of another confrontation with it.
Jerusalem and Riyadh are looking at the same map and seeing different things.
Israel views Iran and its proxies as a threat that should be weakened as much as possible. The Saudis must add a simple fact to their calculation: Iran will remain on the other side of the Gulf even the day after.
The détente with Tehran did not provide them with security, but the channel itself remains useful. Therefore, they can fight the proxies when necessary while continuing to speak with Tehran.
One battlefield, different calculations
Riyadh has operated this way for several years. It does not want to place all of its security in the hands of a single party, and it has no interest in living in a permanent confrontation with all of its rivals.
Bin Salman is maintaining the alliance with Washington, speaking with Tehran, and expanding his circle of partners so that he is not dependent on one actor.
In practice, each relationship serves a different need: America provides weapons and security, China is an economic partner and mediator, Turkey and Pakistan add military depth, and the channel with Iran is intended to lower tensions.
Israel may also have a place on that list in areas where it has capabilities that Saudi Arabia needs.
This gives bin Salman more options. The past few weeks have reminded him what those options are worth when he truly needs them.
Bin Salman is still searching for those who will protect Saudi Arabia. Israel could find itself part of the answer he assembles. However, Jerusalem should be at least as interested in understanding why he is forced to assemble that answer in the first place.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.

The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.

The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.

The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
