Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.
Queen Mary and Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization Christina Egelund will present the Teaching Prize 2026 to teachers from seven higher education institutions.
The award recognizes educators for inspiring and engaging students, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization said in a press release.
Each recipient receives 500,000 DKK. Of that amount, 200,000 DKK is a personal award, while 300,000 DKK must be used to develop new teaching activities.
The awards will be presented at the Opera in Copenhagen.
“For this year’s seven prize recipients, good teaching is about awakening the students’ curiosity and creating engagement,” Egelund, from the Moderates, said.
She added that the recipients had also created learning environments where students felt comfortable asking questions and making mistakes.
The seven recipients come from different areas of higher education.
Assistant Professor Amalie Trangbæk teaches political science at Aarhus University. Assistant Lecturer Brian Jørgensen teaches communication design at Design School Kolding, while Associate Professor Bjarne Schmidt teaches mathematics, physics and engineering didactics at the University of Southern Denmark.
The other recipients are Associate Professor Lars Plauborg Pedersen from Syddansk Erhvervsakademi, Associate Professor René Kirk Johansen from the maritime and polytechnic education center Martec, Associate Professor Gry Segoli from Københavns Professionshøjskole and Associate Professor Lene Krogstrup Jakobsen from UC SYD in Esbjerg.
Educational institutions nominate candidates for the prize each year. Relevant groups of rectors then assess the nominations and decide which candidates are put forward to the Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization.
Several Danish newspapers said Wednesday that Denmark and Greenland welcomed the new security and defense agreement, even as they raised questions about its consequences.
Berlingske called the deal a “triumph for wise and persistent diplomacy” in an editorial.
“If the agreement turns out to be worth the paper it is written on, foreign policy history was written in New York on Tuesday,” the newspaper wrote.
Politiken described the agreement signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump as a “diplomatic masterpiece.”
Politiken said the deal protects Greenland’s territorial integrity, but also described it as a high-risk agreement whose details remain open to interpretation.
Kristeligt Dagblad called it a “historic agreement on the security of the Kingdom of Denmark’s Arctic area” and said the Danish government could be satisfied with the result.
Other newspapers focused more strongly on the risks.
Ekstra Bladet described the agreement as a costly victory. It raised concerns that the U.S. could use Greenland for activities unrelated to NATO, including establishing its “Golden Dome” missile defense system there.
“We are paying a high, but unavoidable price,” Ekstra Bladet wrote. “We can well call it a victory, as long as we remember how dearly it was bought.”
Information described the agreement as a victory for the Kingdom of Denmark but also as a “submission to a tyrannical superior power.”
Despite its positive assessment of the agreement, Berlingske also warned that uncertainty remains because Trump is president.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.

“Hybrid attacks against Denmark and Danish companies are unfortunately a new normal that we have to relate to,” he said in a press release.
DI describes the situation as serious and calls for closer cooperation between public authorities and the business sector.
Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.

Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.
Queen Mary and Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization Christina Egelund will present the Teaching Prize 2026 to teachers from seven higher education institutions.
The award recognizes educators for inspiring and engaging students, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization said in a press release.
Each recipient receives 500,000 DKK. Of that amount, 200,000 DKK is a personal award, while 300,000 DKK must be used to develop new teaching activities.
The awards will be presented at the Opera in Copenhagen.
“For this year’s seven prize recipients, good teaching is about awakening the students’ curiosity and creating engagement,” Egelund, from the Moderates, said.
She added that the recipients had also created learning environments where students felt comfortable asking questions and making mistakes.
The seven recipients come from different areas of higher education.
Assistant Professor Amalie Trangbæk teaches political science at Aarhus University. Assistant Lecturer Brian Jørgensen teaches communication design at Design School Kolding, while Associate Professor Bjarne Schmidt teaches mathematics, physics and engineering didactics at the University of Southern Denmark.
The other recipients are Associate Professor Lars Plauborg Pedersen from Syddansk Erhvervsakademi, Associate Professor René Kirk Johansen from the maritime and polytechnic education center Martec, Associate Professor Gry Segoli from Københavns Professionshøjskole and Associate Professor Lene Krogstrup Jakobsen from UC SYD in Esbjerg.

Several Danish newspapers said Wednesday that Denmark and Greenland welcomed the new security and defense agreement, even as they raised questions about its consequences.
Berlingske called the deal a “triumph for wise and persistent diplomacy” in an editorial.
“If the agreement turns out to be worth the paper it is written on, foreign policy history was written in New York on Tuesday,” the newspaper wrote.
Politiken described the agreement signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump as a “diplomatic masterpiece.”
Politiken said the deal protects Greenland’s territorial integrity, but also described it as a high-risk agreement whose details remain open to interpretation.
Kristeligt Dagblad called it a “historic agreement on the security of the Kingdom of Denmark’s Arctic area” and said the Danish government could be satisfied with the result.
Other newspapers focused more strongly on the risks.

“We are paying a high, but unavoidable price,” Ekstra Bladet wrote. “We can well call it a victory, as long as we remember how dearly it was bought.”
Information described the agreement as a victory for the Kingdom of Denmark but also as a “submission to a tyrannical superior power.”
Despite its positive assessment of the agreement, Berlingske also warned that uncertainty remains because Trump is president.

The leaders of Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign a security and defense agreement concerning Greenland on Tuesday.
The ceremony is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. local time, or 4:30 p.m. Danish time, at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office described it as “a joint agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region.”
The agreement will be signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, head of Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government.
Few details about the agreement have been released since it was announced Friday.
Trump said on Truth Social that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen has said the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We are not ceding sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I never will as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcasters DR and TV 2 on Monday.
She said sovereignty could be maintained alongside closer defense cooperation with other countries.
The USA plans to reopen a former military base in Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a military presence on Greenland’s east coast, Reuters reported Monday.
The eastern site is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish military unit operating in Greenland.
Reuters attributed the information to three unnamed sources familiar with a defense agreement involving Greenland, Denmark and the USA. Danish public broadcaster DR also reported that the USA plans two new bases.
The agreement’s text has not been published, and its details may change before it is signed, Reuters reported.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Greenlandic head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement Tuesday at the United Nations headquarters in New York.

Trump has said it gives the USA “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”

‘Nowhere else to go’: Gaza families shelter in buildings that may collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:25:23 UTC
14:25:23 KST

‘Nowhere else to go’: Gaza families shelter in buildings that may collapse
Three years of Israel’s war has left families in Gaza living in damaged buildings, with few safe alternatives available.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – The partially collapsed roof above Masada Abu Jarad’s apartment is now made up of broken concrete with twisted steel bars protruding from its edges.
And underneath the section of the room that is now open to the elements after the building’s partial collapse, Masada’s family have pitched a tent to provide shelter.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US rapper Macklemore announces Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
- list 2 of 3Israel’s policies threaten ‘very existence’ of Palestinians, Abbas tells UN
- list 3 of 3Gaza’s recovery needs reach $71.5bn amid ‘most severe economic crisis’: UN
The 60-year-old knows the structure is dangerous. The Palestinian Red Crescent and the Civil Defence visited the family last week and warned them that they should leave. But in Gaza, where Israel refuses to allow proper reconstruction to take place after almost three years of its genocidal war, there are few places for them to go.
“We have no options,” Masada says. “I want to leave, but who will give me an alternative?”
She has lived in the building in Gaza City’s Palestine Square area for the past year, after returning to northern Gaza from displacement earlier in the war. But this still isn’t home. Masada’s family is originally from Beit Lahiya in the far north of the Strip, but had to leave early in the war after Israel decimated the area. They are still unable to return.
After repeated displacement, the prospect of moving again without a safe destination has become exhausting. And even if they could move, the cost is prohibitive.
“Even if there is a better place, tell me how I can afford to rent it,” Masada said.
Masada’s experience reflects a wider housing crisis across Gaza for the Palestinians who have survived Israel’s war, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians.
A joint assessment by the United Nations, World Bank, and European Union found that 371,888 housing units, 76.6 percent of the housing stock, had been destroyed or damaged as of October 2025. The assessment also found that rebuilding Gaza will need more than $71bn over the next decade.
The dangers of Gaza’s depleted and damaged housing stock became starkly visible on September 16, when a six-storey war-damaged residential building in Gaza City collapsed, killing 21 people, including 12 children, according to the UN and Gaza Civil Defence.
The collapse has become a warning for families living in other damaged structures.
‘I stay awake so they can sleep’
Abdullah Abu Hajar, 40, lives with his wife and five children in the al-Najma building in Gaza City’s southern Remal neighbourhood.
The six-storey building is severely damaged and unstable. About 17 families, roughly 50 to 60 people, are living there, according to Abdullah.
On the outside walls, municipal notices warn residents and passers-by that the building is unsafe and at risk of collapse.
At night, while his wife and children try to sleep, Abdullah stays awake and listens.
Every unfamiliar sound, such as concrete shifting, stones moving or an unexplained creaking somewhere inside the building, puts him on alert.
“I stay awake all night, keeping watch,” he said. “I can’t close my eyes. I keep just listening to sounds around me.”
Abdullah explained that he feels worried for his children, even though they have adapted to the danger. But he has not.
And after the September 16 building collapse, he grew even more fearful. Since then, he said, he has barely slept.
“I’m already on edge,” he said. “But I don’t know where I can go.”
Abdullah and his family were displaced from Beit Hanoon in northern Gaza after it was attacked by Israel, and moved repeatedly during the war, eventually finding the al-Najma building.
His extended family faces the same uncertainty. Abdullah said that one of his relatives has been moving between southern and northern Gaza, looking for a place where he can pitch a tent.
“I told him to come and stay with us,” Abdullah said. “But he is hesitant because of the condition of this building. At the same time, he has nowhere else to go.”
A room among the rubble
For Islam Hassanein, 36, the same fears are entwined with the place she calls home.
A mother of five, Islam has spent nearly a year living with her family in a single room on the third floor of a damaged building.
She found the room after searching for somewhere to stay. It was filled with rubble and debris.
“We cleaned it and stayed in it,” she said.
The building is leaning and visibly damaged. The plumbing doesn’t work, so the family uses a bathroom outside. There is little that resembles a family home.
But leaving has proved no easier than staying. “We keep looking, but we can’t find anywhere,” she says. “They might even force us out of here. What are we supposed to do?”
Islam says she would leave immediately if she were offered a safe place.
“If they find us a good place and provide us with a tent, we will leave from the morning,” she says. “But where is this place? And where is the tent?”
The building itself regularly reminds her of the dangers.
“Every day, you hear the cracking,” she says. “People who live here tell us, ‘It’s cracking.’ Then a column fell, and they took us out of the building temporarily.”
The potentially deadly risks will become harder to manage as winter approaches, with its colder and wetter weather.
Water can enter through exposed roofs and walls, and the already weakened structure will face additional pressure from heavy rain.
“Last winter was terrifying,” Islam said. “We were constantly afraid that the building would collapse. I spent most days in my family’s tent because this building was full of openings and would flood whenever it rained.”
“Now, I am very afraid of this winter, and I don’t know what we are going to do.”
The UN says thousands of people are sheltering in damaged buildings considered unsafe because better housing options are unavailable.
Israeli restrictions on the entry of tents, tarpaulins and other essential shelter materials are making the situation more difficult, leaving Gaza in a state of limbo, unable to move on from the war, particularly as Israel can choose to escalate the conflict at any time.
UNICEF estimates that nearly 84 percent of Gaza’s population, more than 1.76 million people, are living in overcrowded displacement sites or damaged and inadequate shelters, with little protection from cold, heavy rain and flooding.
Islam says the war has forced families to take risks they once would have considered unthinkable.
She worries about her five children, but sees few choices available to her.
“They are all afraid,” she said. “But what can we do? If there is an alternative, I will leave. We leave it to God.”

Israeli scientists help solve genetic mystery linking hearing loss and gray hair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:14:36 UTC
14:14:36 KST

Imagine looking into a microscopic world where the slightest structural flaw can quiet the world entirely.
For an extended Palestinian family, a rare form of congenital hearing loss accompanied by silvery-gray-colored hair in children offered a profound genetic mystery.
An international team of researchers has now cracked the case.
By identifying a critical role for the FMN1 gene, scientists have uncovered how a single microscopic protein maintains the inner ear’s structural integrity, bridging the gap between human genetics and cellular mechanics.
The groundbreaking study by researchers from Bethlehem University, the University of Washington in Seattle, and Tel Aviv University (TAU) has just been published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences under the title “Formin-1 maintains cochlear microtubule architecture required for hearing in humans and mice.”
The study was conducted by Lara Kamal, who earned her bachelor’s degree at Jordan University of Science and Technology, then worked at Bethlehem University, and is now completing her doctorate at TAU.
The project team included Prof. Moien Kanaan (director of the Hereditary Research Lab in the Department of Life Sciences at Bethlehem University); world-renowned Prof. Mary-Claire King, Dr. Amal Aburayyan, and Dr. Suleyman Gulsuner of the University of Washington; and hearing expert Prof. Karen B. Avraham, Dr. Roni Hahn, and Dr. Shahar Taiber of TAU.
Having identified the FMN1 gene as essential for human hearing, they traced how a rare genetic variant disrupts Formin-1, a vital protein encoded by the gene essential for inner ear architecture and hearing.
By combining human genomics with decades-old mouse models, they proved that loss of Formin-1 disrupts the dynamic network of interlinking protein fibers that give the cell its shape and mechanical support, and helps transport materials in the organ of Corti – a sensory receptor organ for hearing located inside the cochlea, the hearing organ of the inner ear.
The discovery began with a Palestinian family in which four children, among three sets of cousins, were born with bilateral, moderate hearing loss accompanied by silver-gray-colored hair. The children are otherwise completely healthy.
The parents were not first cousins (consanguineous), but all are members of the same extended family.
Genomic analysis revealed that the affected children carried two copies of a rare variant in FMN1 that led to the loss of the protein Formin-1.
Genetic defects in other formin proteins have been linked with neurological, kidney, reproductive, and cardiac disorders, but the new discovery is the first in the world in which a human condition has been linked to a genetic defect in FMN1.
From mice to men
To investigate how loss of the protein causes hearing impairment, the team studied a mouse model that had no functional Formin-1. These mice were created in the early 1990s, but their hearing had not been studied before.
The authors found that these mice presented a hearing loss similar to that of the Palestinian family. The mouse could then be studied to discover the underlying cellular changes within the cochlea.
The mice’s abnormalities appeared soon after birth and continued with age. The structural disruption was accompanied by reduced auditory nerve activity and a lower number of auditory nerve fibers.
Formin-1 is also part of a molecular complex involved in transporting melanosomes (the pigment-containing organelles that contribute to hair and skin color), and the researchers hypothesized that the hearing loss and altered pigmentation could therefore arise through different biological effects of the same genetic defect.
“The discovery adds FMN1 to the more than 200 genes known to be essential for normal hearing and expands our understanding of the mechanisms underlying inherited hearing loss,” said Avraham, who is not only the senior author but also dean of TAU’s Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences.
“This discovery provides additional evidence for understanding that hearing depends not only on sensory hair cells and auditory neurons, but also on precise organization of supporting cells to maintain the cochlea’s structure and mechanics,” she continued.
“As gene therapy for deafness becomes a reality, revealing the underlying genetic causes of hearing loss has become critical to treatment. Each new gene adds another part to our understanding of the complicated puzzle of auditory function.
“This work has shown that global partnerships can drive meaningful scientific advances, helping to pave the way for future genetic therapies and interventions.
“While the supporting cells are essential for the entire cascade of hearing to function normally, they do tend to be overlooked, as they are not the main cells leading to hearing function. But without them, the sensory hair cells cannot survive,” she explained.
The team members predicted a developmental window in which treatment would have to occur and perform gene replacement with the intact gene, delivered with an adeno-associated virus that might delay or prevent the hearing loss from occurring.
The pigmentation phenotype could actually provide a clinical clue for physicians to identify people with FMN1-related hearing loss, said Avraham.
“If high-throughput genetic screening is done, this discovery would allow the clinicians to first look for mutations in this gene.”
The team members have collaborated for almost 30 years.
“The work with the human family was conducted in Prof. Kanaan’s and Prof. King’s labs on different continents, while Lara Kamal worked in mine,” said Avraham.
“It has been a remarkable connection, with 24 co-authored scientific publications since then. The world seems to be disintegrating around us, but our scientific cooperation has been working well,” she continued.
“We are learning more and more about the mechanisms involving deafness that can help us put all the pieces together: hair color and deafness.”
Genetics and interconnections
In fact, Kanaan has worked with King and with Shaare Zedek Medical Center geneticist Prof. Ephrat Levy-Lahad for years to study breast cancer genes in Palestinian women.
King became renowned around the world for proving that inherited breast cancer is caused by mutations in a gene she named BRCA1. Her work transformed how scientists understand hereditary breast and ovarian cancers, leading to modern genetic testing and screening.
In 1984, she was acclaimed for her use of mitochondrial DNA sequencing to help identify Argentinian children kidnapped and illegally adopted during the Dirty War between 1976 and 1983.
“Our Israeli-Palestinian-American collaboration has led to fine science and to fine careers of devoted young scientists from all three populations,” King declared.
“We’ve shown that with persistence and confidence, good science can be carried out even in very difficult circumstances. There is a lot to be said for stubbornness on behalf of science,” she continued.
Breast cancer is a major health concern for women around the world, yet many populations lack the same genetic risk assessment as the general population, added Kanaan.
“Until recently, Palestinian women lacked access to genetic testing and cancer risk evaluation. The Middle East Breast Cancer Study the three of us conducted is changing that.”
Asked how certain they were that the FMN1 variant is responsible for the hearing loss, King noted that “we are sure because both the human family and the mouse with loss of function of FMN1 have the same hearing loss.”
“The mouse is from an inbred strain, and this is its only difference from the non-mutant strain, which has normal hearing,” she continued.
“The project involved studying the human family, working with the database created by Moien Kanaan for the Palestinian population, hearing deficits in the mouse, and functional evidence of abnormal supporting cells due to the mutation.
“This is the first time we encountered this particular FMN1 variant, which is not present in any public database or in the Palestinian genetic database created by Kanaan based on his studies of other inherited conditions in the Palestinian population.”
When asked why the lab mice created in the early 1990s had not been examined then for hearing loss, King explained that “these mice do not have problems of balance, so it can be difficult to recognize hearing loss in a mouse if balance is normal.
“And the geneticists who created the FMN1-mutant mouse were focusing on skeletal abnormalities during development, not on hearing. It apparently didn’t occur to them to evaluate their hearing.
“We think there are other people in the world carrying mutations in FMN1 whose hearing loss would very likely have been attributed to something else, because FMN1 has not previously been included in panels of genes surveyed for deafness.”
Kamal explained that she learned of the family at Bethlehem University: “My role was characterizing the family. The most difficult part is the responsibility of giving the family an answer; they already have two children with hearing loss.
“The children have hearing aids and have undergone speech therapy. I worked closely with them all.”
Kamal said that many genetic problems are caused by consanguinity in the Israeli Arab and Palestinian populations, but “fortunately, the rate is going down significantly; with the growth of better and higher education among the women, they are more aware of the problem of marrying close relatives.”

Using babies, Israeli study reveals why AI fails to truly understand animal calls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:14:02 UTC
14:14:02 KST

Humans have always wanted to talk with animals.
Dog owners try to understand their pets. At the same time, parents make great efforts to communicate with their babies before they start to produce words.
King Solomon is said to have done it, and so did Adam and Eve.
Others who accomplished it were a variety of fictional figures – Dr. Dolittle (Hugh Lofting’s physician who learned animal language from his parrot); Tarzan (Edgar Rice Burroughs’s iconic lord of the jungle who communicated with various jungle beasts); and Mowgli (Rudyard Kipling’s The Jungle Book hero who grew up with wolves).
“Talking with other creatures would not only make it possible to empathize with animals, learn about other levels of consciousness, and enrich our understanding of life. It would also have immense practical value,” suggested Prof. Yosef Yovel, who has worked in the zoology department of Tel Aviv University (TAU) for the last 15 years.
“Farmers might benefit from a machine that allows them to ask a cow about its health, though it might turn them into vegetarians,” he continued.
“Such a machine would also come in handy once we land on a planet inhabited by some simple alien life form, while if advanced aliens ever make it to Earth, they will probably already have such a machine.”
Even as artificial intelligence masters human language, a groundbreaking study he and his team conducted reveals a fundamental flaw in how AI decodes the animal kingdom: it hears the volume and pitch, but entirely misses the point.
The researchers have now discovered why AI is getting animal and human toddler communication all wrong.
For years, scientists have turned to AI to unlock the secrets of bird calls, bat chatter, and whale songs, but the new research published in Current Biology under the title “The challenge of decoding animal communication using AI” suggests our high-tech translators might be looking at the problem completely backward.
The TAU experts explained that while AI is a powerful tool, it needs a paradigm shift – moving away from raw audio analysis toward understanding neural and perceptual meaning.
The study was conducted by Mor Taub, Inbal Arnon, Amiyaal Ilany, Mirjam Knörnschild, and Yoav Ram, and it was supervised by Yovel.
The team also included scientists from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, the University of Edinburgh, the Natural History Museum-Leibniz Institute for Evolution and Biodiversity Science, and Humboldt University (both in Berlin).
Two sounds that look completely different on a spectrogram can carry the same message to a receiver, while the same acoustic sound can mean entirely different things depending on the context – proving that communication relies heavily on the receiver’s perception, not just the physical properties of the sound wave.
A spectrogram is a visual representation of the spectrum of frequencies of a signal as it changes over time. When applied to audio, it is essentially a picture of sound often referred to as a sonograph, voiceprint, or spectral display.
A standard 2D spectrogram uses three dimensions of data mapped onto a flat image.
Misleading communication system
The researchers found that acoustically similar sounds do not necessarily carry similar meanings, while sounds that appear different may convey the same information to the receiver.
Therefore, classifying sounds by their acoustic similarity, as most studies do, may create a misleading picture of the communication system and the meaning of the messages it conveys, Yovel added.
They discovered that humans listening to a toddler’s sequences perceive increasing urgency, apparently from subtle acoustic modifications. None of the tested AI models captured the ordering of those vocalizations according to urgency.
“In recent years, there has been growing excitement about the possibility of using AI to decode animal communication, but our study shows that these promises should be treated with caution,” said Yovel, who earned his bachelor’s degree in physics and biology and his master’s degree in neurobiology from TAU, followed by a PhD in biology from Germany’s University of Tübingen.
“Identifying acoustic patterns is not necessarily the same as deciphering meaning: to understand what an animal is ‘saying,’ we need to know how the animal receiving the message perceives it and responds to it,” he added.
“The path toward truly deciphering animal communication will require a combination of AI, behavioral observations, experiments, and research into the nervous system. Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool, but it is no substitute for the perspective of the animal itself.”
To investigate the problem, the team used a unique communication system – the vocalizations of human toddlers who have not yet fully developed speech.
Unlike animal vocalizations, in this case the researchers could try to know how the humans to whom the vocalizations are directed interpret them.
The recordings included vocalizations made in three contexts: distress, calling to a specific person (the mother or the father), and asking for food.
The researchers analyzed the recordings using a classical acoustic method and two state-of-the-art deep neural networks: one trained on animal vocalizations and another trained on adult human speech.
The models were asked to group the vocalizations according to their characteristics.
The results showed that the deep neural networks performed better than the classical acoustic method, but even they failed to classify the toddlers’ vocalizations by their meaning.
In some cases, they grouped together vocalizations carrying different messages; in others, they separated different vocalizations intended to convey the same message.
The models also failed to identify how a sequence of vocalizations expressed increasing urgency, a distinction that the human ear perceives naturally.
According to the researchers, reliably deciphering animal communication will require combining AI tools with behavioral observations, playback experiments, and sometimes measurements of brain activity.
Using context
Every species has its own unique perceptual world, and understanding what animals are “saying” therefore requires more than analyzing sound alone: it also requires examining how they hear the sound and respond to it.
“We cannot connect specific signals with meaning. The basic idea is that AI models will find the largest differences between the signals, but these are not necessarily the important differences for the brain,” Yovel explained.
“We can take an example from the stickleback fish during the breeding season. Males have a red abdomen and are very aggressive. The red color is, for them, the most important signal for detecting another male. They don’t care about the shape of the fish or how it moves.
“Researchers showed long ago that if they take a sphere and color code it in red, the fish will perceive it as another fish. AI models would never detect this unless we specifically ask them to pay attention to color.
“This is exactly the point with baby and other animal vocalizations. AI will look for the most significant acoustic difference, but these are not necessarily equivalent to the important differences for the brain.
“The human brain is using context. AI language models can learn to do this too with human language, but it’s far more difficult with non-human language.”
When asked why they chose pre-linguistic toddlers rather than an animal species whose communication they already studied, Yovel explained that “the reason was that we wanted to know something about the meaning, so we studied.”
“I thought I knew something about the meaning of their vocalizations. With bats, I needed to guess what they received, but my brain understood human toddler vocalizations,” he continued.
“I can’t be sure, but when my toddler calls for me, I am more certain what he wants. The sample size was small, but we only intended to use this as a case to highlight and exemplify the problem. We also used a data set of real human words and showed that the result was completely different.”
Asked if a toddler could produce acoustically similar sounds for completely different purposes depending on the context, he agreed: “This is exactly one of the big challenges in decoding animal communication because animals will do this as well.”
There has been enormous excitement about AI potentially decoding whales, bats, birds, and other animals.
“Nearly all of these studies are finding patterns in animal communication. That’s the first step, but we are very far from understanding meaning or even knowing how to do that exactly.”

US intelligence warns Saudi Arabia has not ruled out nuclear weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
05:11:04 UTC
14:11:04 KST

Classified documents provided to Congress include an assessment by the U.S. intelligence community that Saudi Arabia has not ruled out the option of developing a nuclear weapons program, The Washington Post reported Friday evening.
The report comes amid concerns raised by numerous experts over an agreement reached in July between the U.S. administration and Riyadh that would allow the kingdom to develop a civilian nuclear program under less stringent safeguards than are customary. Unlike similar agreements with other countries, the deal also opens a path for Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium domestically, potentially to the relatively high level of 20%.
The agreement, signed in July after years of negotiations between Washington and Riyadh, provides the legal framework for U.S. companies to operate in Saudi Arabia and develop nuclear facilities, including civilian power plants. Saudi Arabia, whose crown prince and de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman said in 2018 that the kingdom would pursue a nuclear weapon if Iran developed one, refused during negotiations with the United States to relinquish the ability to enrich uranium domestically or sign a stringent safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency, known as the Additional Protocol. The United Arab Emirates, by comparison, accepted such restrictions as part of its 2009 civilian nuclear agreement with the United States, which has since been regarded as the "gold standard" for agreements of this kind.
Instead, the July agreement includes U.S. safeguards that Washington has said will be sufficient to prevent Saudi Arabia from using its civilian program to develop nuclear weapons in the future. But details subsequently reported about the agreement have raised significant concerns among experts and Democratic lawmakers in Congress, who have sharply criticized it.
According to The Wall Street Journal, the agreement would not immediately allow Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium itself. Initially, as the United Arab Emirates does, it would have to import enriched uranium from abroad. During the first two years, however, the two countries would conduct a study examining the "economic feasibility" of enriching uranium on Saudi soil and the safeguards that would be required to prevent such a program from being used to develop a nuclear weapon, or at least the capability to do so. The Washington Post has also reported that the agreement calls for a two-year study into whether enrichment in Saudi Arabia is feasible and necessary.
The Journal reported that if the United States and Saudi Arabia determine that domestic enrichment is necessary, U.S. companies and their foreign suppliers would build a facility where enrichment would initially be limited to 5%. A further study would then examine the possibility of raising enrichment to 20%, a relatively high level. While experts note that uranium enriched to that level also has civilian uses, they say reaching 20% completes much of the technical work required to enrich uranium to weapons-grade levels of about 90%.
Experts have raised concerns about the possibility that some enriched material could be secretly diverted for military purposes. The Trump administration, by contrast, argues that the involvement of U.S. companies in the program would prevent that risk. Administration officials also argue that the agreement is important because it keeps Riyadh from turning to China or Russia for help developing its nuclear program. Under the agreement as described by people familiar with it, any Saudi enrichment would be controlled by U.S. companies using technology that would not be shared with the Saudis.
The Washington Post reported Friday that, in addition to the intelligence assessment warning that Riyadh has not ruled out developing nuclear weapons, the classified documents sent to Congress last month also included the State Department's assessment. People who spoke with the newspaper said the State Department appeared more confident in the safeguards established under the agreement and in assurances provided by the Saudi government.
The Saudi government did not respond directly to the Post's request for comment but referred the newspaper to an earlier statement by Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman, who said the kingdom's nuclear program would be peaceful and developed with the highest levels of responsibility and transparency.
President Donald Trump has said the agreement with Saudi Arabia will not take effect unless the kingdom joins the Abraham Accords and normalizes relations with Israel. The agreement has nevertheless already been submitted to Congress for review. Under U.S. law, Congress has 90 days while in session to review it. Lawmakers seeking to block the agreement would ultimately need sufficient support to overcome a presidential veto.
Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon told the Post that the United States should not rely on Saudi assurances on an issue of such importance.
"It’s bogus as hell," he said, arguing that Saudi demands to retain the ability to enrich uranium domestically indicate an ambition to develop a program that would not be entirely civilian.
"If they’ve given up the intent to develop a nuclear weapon, then they’d give up domestic enrichment and reprocessing power, right? They’d accept massive inspections from the IAEA," Merkley added.
Merkley and other Democratic senators sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday criticizing the agreement. They argued that the Trump administration was departing from precedent by accepting looser restrictions and agreeing to a process they said would almost certainly allow Riyadh to acquire uranium enrichment capabilities and potentially develop a nuclear weapon.

"Despite having the world’s largest navy, the United States was unable to keep the Strait of Hormuz open even for a few hours," he said.
The spokesman added that the United States claimed the strait was open in order to prevent oil prices from rising, while control of the waterway was in the hands of the IRGC’s naval forces.
According to Mohebbi, before the war, dozens to more than 100 vessels passed through the strait each day, but currently, only oil tankers belonging to Iran's trading partners were permitted to pass, and only with Tehran's permission.
Mohebbi also addressed US claims of military and technological superiority, saying Washington had used propaganda to try to project an image of capability.
However, during the recent war, advanced US air, naval, and ground equipment came under retaliatory attacks by Iran's Armed Forces, he said, asserting that the Islamic Republic would not stop punishing the US until its seven conditions were fulfilled, and expressing confidence in Iranian missiles’ capability to destroy multilayered American air-defense systems.
Recently, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei said the country had declared its conditions for renewed talks with the United States, saying that Washington should agree to Tehran’s terms if it wanted to escape the quagmire of its war of aggression against the Islamic Republic.
